translation:
24 BOOK
On Agallocho. Chapter 21.

Agallocho is a wood that comes from India and Arabia, similar to the wood of Thuia, distinctly dotted, fragrant, astringent to the taste, with some bitterness. Its bark resembles leather and is somewhat varied in color. Agallocho is chewed, or the mouth is rinsed with its decoction to freshen the breath. Ground into powder, it is sprinkled over the whole body to prevent sweating. It is used in perfumes in place of incense. The root, drunk at the weight of one dram, dries up moisture, soothes the ardor and weakness of the stomach. Drunk with water it helps with pains in the sides, the liver, the body, and with dysentery.

A   The modern Greeks, the Arabs, and the modern Latins all call it universally Aloe-wood; of which, though it commands a good price, one finds today quite a good supply in Venice, where when burned it gives off a most pleasant fragrance. It is not long since the good quality began to be imported; before, while one could find a piece here and there, it was quite rare, and the apothecaries commonly used in its place (as mentioned above) only the Olibastro of Rhodes, which Ruellius holds to be the Aspalatho. Agallocho (according to the reports of the Portuguese, who with their voyages have tamed the Atlantic Ocean) grows on the island of Taprobana and in other neighboring regions, and they have brought back to Portugal and Spain the finest logs, which, even without being lit, give off (as they say) a most pleasant fragrance when handled; and according to their reports it is also highly prized in the lands where it grows. But of this great excellence and quality I have not yet seen proof, even though in Venice one does find what is considered good. Some have dreamed that the tree of Agallocho has never been seen by men, and that it grows in the earthly Paradise and is carried from there by the rivers that, according to Holy Scripture, flow out of it. But it is well accepted as true (as Serapion briefly notes) that infinite pieces are carried from the great river Ganges in India, brought there by other rivers flowing into it. For these rivers, flowing through the regions where Agallocho grows, sweep up as they swell countless trunks together with many and diverse kinds of timber, as one sees in our Italian rivers when they flood excessively. What is found in Venice gives ready evidence of this, for it is seen all torn, broken, rough, and fragmented from the long journey through the water, which is why it is no marvel that when touched and smelled one does not find that sweet fragrance said to be found in what is brought directly from the forests to Portugal and Spain. Agallocho (as Serapion writes) is of various kinds, hot and dry in the second degree, and it is the opinion of Avicenna that it benefits the defects of the heart, and therefore he placed it among his other cordial remedies. I do not find that Galen makes mention of this in his books on the properties of simples. But in the Succedanea he says that Centaury may serve in place of Agallocho.

On Narcaphtho. Chapter 22.

Narcaphtho comes from India. It is a bark similar to that of the Sycamore. It is burned as incense to produce a good fragrance, and it is mixed with perfume compositions. It is used as a fumigant for obstructions of the womb.

T   Dioscorides writes so briefly of Narcaphtho, and gives so few signs of its nature, that it is difficult for me to give that true account I would most certainly desire, especially since I find that neither Theophrastus nor Pliny left any record of it in their volumes. Yet it is truly to be believed, if Narcaphtho is brought here, that it is the very Tigname of the apothecaries, as can be affirmed by various conjectures. For Tigname means nothing other than Thimiama, and Thimiama in Greek means nothing in our vernacular but perfume, and since Narcaphtho is used mainly for perfuming, its proper name having been dropped, only the name of the purpose for which it is used has been kept, the word Timiama being corrupted into Tigname. Furthermore, Dioscorides says that both alone and mixed with other fragrances when burned it gives off a good scent — which is easily proved true of the Tigname of the apothecaries, since it is so commonly used in fragrant compositions; not only is it used alone for perfuming, but few perfume compositions are made without Tigname. This explains why it is not surprising that the proper name of the tree was dropped and the name of the perfume was adopted instead. Serapion calls Narcaphtho "Lasahàten" and says it has virtues similar to fragrant Calamus.

On Cancamo. Chapter 23.

Cancamo is a liquid from a tree of Arabia, very similar to Myrrh, with a rather strong taste. It is used to make perfume. It is used with Myrrh and Storax to perfume garments. They say that drinking the weight of three obols dissolved in water or honey-vinegar reduces fat in stout persons. It is given to those who suffer from ailments of the spleen, epilepsy, and asthma. Drunk with honey-water it promotes menstruation. It quickly relieves

text:
PRIMO 25

te le cicatrici de gli occhi, & bagnato con uino cura la debilità di quelli. Non è piu efficace A
cosa del Cancamo per i flussi delle giengie, & per il dolor de i denti.

L uero Cancamo, che corrisponda all' historia, che ne scrisse Dioscoride ueramente à i tempi nostri non ci si porta,
I ne d'Arabia, ne d'altri luoghi: Per ilche manifestamente s'ingannano coloro, che si credono, che il Cancamo sia
quella gomma rossa, & trasparente, laquale usano alcuni per la uera Lacca, & dico per la uera Lacca, percio-
che così chiamano gli Arabi il Cancamo scritto dalli Greci: Che adonque questa gomma non sia il uero Cancamo, si dimo-
stra per non si ritrouarne essa alcuno odore tanto masticandola, quanto facendone profumo, come dice Dioscoride ritro-
uarsi nel Cancamo. In oltre errano alcuni Spetiali, liquali mettono spesso nelle Spetie di Dialacca, la Lacca artificiale,
che si fa nelle tentorie della secca del uerzino, della Grana, & del Cremese, laquale per i colori rossi scuri usano li Di-
pintori: Nel che s'ingannano, per seguire la dottrina de gli Arabi, & li loro manifesti errori. Percioche Serapione, il-
quale, chiama il Cancamo Lacca, quantonque nel principio del capitolo segua precisamente nel scriuer suo l'historia di Dio
scoride, confonde poscia allegando certe autorità Arabiche, ogni cosa, dicendo, che Rasis dice, che la Lacca cascaua dal
cielo in su gli Alberi à modo di manna, & Isach, che la si faceua della secca del cremese nelle tentorie. Il che ha dato
manifesta cagione d'errare alli Spetiali, alli quali è ueramente, per esser stati così ingannati dagli Autori, piu da perdo
nare, che ad alcuni altri delli moderni, che errano per loro istessi senza essere ingannati da altri, tra liquali ritrouio io B
nuomente li Reuerendi padri, che hanno commentato l'Antidotario di Mesue, liquali consegliano, che mancando la Lac-
ca, cioè il Cancamo, si debbi porre in suo luogo nella Dialacca magna di Mesue quella gomma, che chiamano sangue di
Drago in lachrime, la quale è del tutto nelle sue operationi contraria al Cancamo, percioche questo è aperitivo, & pro-
uoca i mestrui, & percio messo in questa compositione fatta per aprir le opilationi, & quella è efficacemente costret-
tiua, & però usata per ristagnare il sangue, per consolidare le ferite, & le rotture dell'ossa, & per ritenere, & non
per prouocare i mestrui. Io ueramente nelli succidanei, che si credono esser di Galeno, ne manco altroue non ritrouо,
che cosa si debbi usare in luogo del Cancamo, & però conseglio li diligentissimi Spetiali, che in tal difetto si conseglino
sempre con li Medici, che li sono piu famigliari.

Del Ciphi. Cap.xxiiii.

Il Ciphi una compositione di profumo dedicata alli Dei, laquale abondante-
mente usano i Sacerdoti d'Egitto. Mescolasi negli Antidoti, & dassi à bere alli
stretti di petto. Se ne fanno piu compositioni: delle quali questa n'è una. To- C
glie di Cipero mezzo sestario, & altretante bacche di Ginepro ben mature,
d'uua passa eletta, & ben piena curata dalli fiocini dodici mine, di ragia purgata cinque
mine, di calamo, & gionco odorato, d'aspalatho egualmente di tutti una mina, di mir-
rha dodici, di uino uecchio sestari noue, di mele mine due. Pesta poscia l'uua passa ben pri-
ma netta da i fiocini, & incorporala con la Mirrha, & col uino, & aggiugneui poi tutte l'al-
tre cose peste, & bene stacciate, & lasciale in infusione à macerarsi per uno giorno intero.
Dipoi cuoci il mele, & come lo uedi uenire uiscoso, aggiugneui la ragia liquefatta, & me-
scola diligentemente con l'altre cose ben trite, & serbalo in un uaso di terra cotta.

Itrouansi alcuni uolumi di Dioscoride, & massime delli piu antichi (come recita il dotto Marcello Fiorentino)
R che mancano di questo capitolo del Ciphi, il che fa ageuolmente credere, che piu presto ui sia stato aggiunto da
qualche curioso Medico, che postoui da Dioscoride. Del che ne da non picciolo inditio prima il pensare, che scri-
uendo Dioscoride de semplici non haueria cosi fuor di proposito, interpostoui questa compositione, & poscia perche non
si ritrouа, che Pauolo egineta, ilqual si uede manifestamente nel suo libro ricercare tutti i semplici di Dioscoride n'hab- D
bia fatto mentione alcuna. Impero che se egli hauesse approuato, che questo capitolo fusse stato legitimo, & non adul-
terino, non l'haueria così facilmente taciuto.

Del Croco. Cap.xxv.

L Croco ottimo nell'uso della medicina è il Coriceo, fresco, & ben colorito, &
c'habbia nelle sue fila alquanto di bianco, & quello, ch'è lungo, intero in tut-
te le sue parti, non fragile, pieno, non sminuito di cosa alcuna, & quello, che ba-
gnato tinge le mani, non ha odore di muffa, non è humido, non tignato, & al-
quanto acuto. Ma quello, che non sera così, ò è uecchio, ò è stato bagnato. Il secondo luo-
go di bontà si da al Coriceo d'una prouincia, che confina con Licia. Il terzo al Licio del
monte Olimpo, & il quarto à quello di Egide città di Etholia. Il Cirenaico, & il Centu-
C
description: Pietro Andrea Matthioli's landmark Italian translation of Dioscorides De Materia Medica. The first vernacular edition to make classical Greek botanical medicine accessible to European physicians.
translation:
BOOK ONE 25

it heals the scars of the eyes, and bathed in wine it cures their weakness. Nothing is more effective A
than Cancamo for fluxes of the gums and for toothache.

The true Cancamo, which corresponds to the history written about it by Dioscorides, is not found in our time,
I neither from Arabia nor from any other place. For this reason, those who believe that Cancamo is
that red and transparent gum, which some use as true Lacca — and I speak of true Lacca, because
that is what the Arabs call the Cancamo written of by the Greeks — are clearly deceived. That this gum is not the true Cancamo is shown
by the fact that it has no odor either when chewed or when burned as incense, as Dioscorides says is found in Cancamo. Furthermore, certain Apothecaries err in frequently putting into the preparations of Dialacca the artificial Lacca,
which is made in the dye-houses from brazilwood, grain, and crimson, and which painters use for dark red colors.
In this they err by following the doctrine of the Arabs and their manifest errors. For Serapion,
who calls Cancamo Lacca, although at the beginning of the chapter he closely follows the history of Dioscorides
in his writing, then confuses everything by citing certain Arab authorities, saying that Rasis states that Lacca fell from
the sky onto trees like manna, and Isach that it was made from the dried crimson in the dye-houses. This has given
clear cause for error to the Apothecaries, who, being so deceived by the Authors, are more forgivable B
than certain other modern writers who err of their own accord without being misled by others, among whom I have recently found
certain Reverend Fathers who have commented on the Antidotary of Mesue, and who advise that when Lacca,
that is Cancamo, is lacking, one should put in its place in the great Dialacca of Mesue that gum called Dragon's Blood
in tears — which is in all its properties the opposite of Cancamo, since Cancamo is aperitive and promotes
menstruation, and is therefore placed in this composition made to open obstructions — whereas Dragon's Blood is strongly astringent,
and is used to staunch blood, to consolidate wounds and fractures of bone, and to retain, not
to promote, menstruation. I, for my part, in the succedanea attributed to Galen, nor anywhere else, find no
indication of what should be used in place of Cancamo, and I therefore advise the most diligent Apothecaries that in such a deficiency they take counsel
always with the Physicians most familiar to them.

On Ciphi. Chapter 24.

Ciphi is a perfume composition dedicated to the Gods, abundantly used by
the Priests of Egypt. It is mixed into Antidotes and given to drink to those with chest ailments. Several compositions of it exist, of which this is one. C
Take half a sextary of Cyperus, and an equal amount of well-ripened Juniper berries,
choice raisins, well filled and cleaned of their stems, twelve minae, five minae of purified resin,
one mina each of calamus, sweet rush, and aspalathus equally, twelve of myrrh,
nine sextaries of old wine, two minae of honey. First pound the raisins well,
cleaned of their stems, and incorporate them with the Myrrh and the wine, then add all the
other things pounded and well sifted, and leave them to steep and macerate for a full day.
Then cook the honey, and when you see it becoming viscous, add the melted resin and
mix diligently with the other well-ground ingredients, and preserve it in an earthenware vessel.

Some volumes of Dioscorides are found, especially among the most ancient (as the learned Marcello of Florence records),
R that lack this chapter on Ciphi, which makes it quite credible that it was added by
some curious Physician rather than placed there by Dioscorides himself. Of this, no small indication is given first by the consideration that
Dioscorides, writing on simples, would not so incongruously have inserted this composition, and furthermore because it is not found D
that Paulus of Aegina, who is clearly seen in his book to have researched all the simples of Dioscorides, has
made any mention of it. For if he had approved that this chapter was legitimate and not
an interpolation, he would not so easily have passed over it in silence.

On Saffron. Chapter 25.

The best Saffron for medicinal use is the Corycian, fresh and well-colored, with
some white in its threads, and which is long, whole in all its parts, not fragile, full, not diminished in any way, and that which when
dampened stains the hands, has no smell of mold, is not moist, not discolored, and is
somewhat pungent. But that which is otherwise is either old or has been wetted. The second rank
of quality is given to the Corycian from a province bordering on Lycia. The third to the Lycian of
Mount Olympus, and the fourth to that of Aegae, a city of Aetolia. The Cyrenaican and the Centu-
C

text:
26 LIBRO
A ripino sono di minor uirtu di tutti quelli di Sicilia. Tutto il Croco ha natura domesti-
ca. Nondimeno gl'Italiani per la copia del liquore, & bellezza del colore, l'usano per tin-
ger li cibi, che si fanno ne i mortari: per ilche si uende assai caro. Quello ch'in medici-
na è piu utile, è quello, che scriuemo prima. Sophisticasi il Croco con il Ccocomagma-
te pesto, ouero mescolatoui uin cotto: aggiontoui perche piu pesi, spiuma d'argento, &
piombaggine: ma discuopre la magagna la poluere, che ui si troua dentro, & massime se
ui si sente l'odore della sapa. Vuole Thessalo, che'l Croco si commendi solo per l'odo-
re. Dicono alcuni, che il Croco beuto con acqua al peso di tre dramme ammazza. Ha uir-
tu di maturare, mollificare, & leggiermente costrengere. Prouoca l'orina. Fa buon colo-
re. Beuto con uino passo uale contra alla ebriachezza. A pplicato con latte humano fer-
ma i flussi de gli occhi. Mettesi utilmete nelle beuande, che li sanno per le interiora, & ne
pessoli, & ne gli impiastri, che si fanno, & per la natura delle donne, & per il sedere. Sti-
mola il Croco à lussuria, & mitiga impiastrato l'infiammaggioni, che tendono al fuo-
B co sacro. E utile alle posteme delle orecchie. Bisogna accioche facilmente si pesti, metter-
lo in un uaso di terra caldo, ouero al sole, & uoltarlo con prestezza. Le sue radici beute con
passo prouocano l'orina.

Del Crocomagma. Cap.xxvi.

IL Crocomagma si fa delle cose aromatiche, le quali si spriemono dall'onguen-
to Crocino, formate poscia in pastelli. L'ottimo è quello, che è odorato, & che
spira mediocramente odore di Mirra, graue, nero, non legnoso, liscio, ama-
retto, & quello, che ben bagnato fa colore di Croco, & gustato tinge gran-
demente i denti, & la lingua, & quello, che molti anni si conseruua, come è quello, che
si porta di Soria. Ha uirtu di nettare le caligini de gli occhi. Prouoca l'orina, scalda,
matura, & mollifica. Egli ripresenta quasi le uirtu del Croco, perche contiene in se gran
C parte di quello.

Il Croco ueramente notò à tutto il Mondo, & chiamasi (anchora, che sia uocabolo Arabico,) per tutta Italia-
E' & massime in Toscana Zaffarano: Ma del Coriceo, ne di quello del monte Olimpo à, questi tempi non se ne
porta à noi, & imperò tiene il principato à Venetia quello, che si porta dall'Aquila città d'Abruzzo. Troua-
sene dell'ottimo, & migliore assai dell'Aquilano in ogni sua parte in Alemagna in Austria in sul territorio di Vienna
città principale di quella prouincia: Ma di quello pochissimo ne passa in Italia. Percioche mal uolentieri gli Ongari,
& i Thedeschi per l'uso grande, che fanno delle spetie, se lo lasciano cauare del Paese loro. Nasce anchora in Toscana in
alcuni luoghi, & massime in quel di Siena dell'elettissimo, il qual puo stare con tutti questi al paragone. Fece del CRO-
CO mentione Galeno al settimo delle facoltà de i semplici cosi dicédo. Il Croco ha anchora un poco del costrettiuo, la
quale ha del terreo, & del frigido. Ma eccede in esso la uirtu calida, di modo che tutta la sua essenza arriua al secondo
grado di calidità, & al primo di siccità, & imperò ha egli una certa uirtu di maturare, alche l'aita quel poco, che ha di
costrettiuo. Veramente tutti quei medicamenti, che non son troppo calidi, & hanno un poco del stitico, hanno la pari fa-
coltà dell'essenze, che chiamiamo emplastice, & maturatiue.

D Dell'Helenio. Cap.xxvij.

LO Helenio fa le foglie simili al uerbasco, che produce le foglie piu strette, ma-
piu aspre, & piu lunghe: in alcuni luoghi non fa fusto, la sua radice bianche-
ggia. Et qualche uolta rosseggia, è odorata, grossa, & al gusto alquanto acuta,
dalla quale si spiccano le propagini, et piantansi nel modo, che s'ufa di fare
con i gigli, & con l'Aro. Nasce in luoghi montagnosì, & ombrosi, & secchi. Cauasi la radi-
ce la state, & tagliata in pezzetti si secca. La discottione sua beuta prouoca l'orina, & i me-
strui. Gioua la radice tolta con mele in forma di Lattuario alla tosse, à gli asmatici, rotti,
spasimati, alle uentosità, & à morsi de serpenti. In somma ha ella uirtu di scaldare. Le foglie
cotte nel uino s'applicano utilmente alle sciatiche. E utile l'Helenio allo stomacho condi-
to con uino passo: & imperò gli artefici del cödire seccatolo prima alquanto, & poscia cotto
lo, l'insondono in acqua fresca, & poi lo mettono nel uino passo, & lo conseruano per usare.

A The Apennine varieties are of lesser virtue than all those of Sicily. All Crocus has a domestic nature. Nevertheless, the Italians, for the abundance of liquid and beauty of color, use it to dye foods prepared in mortars: for which reason it sells at a high price. That which is most useful in medicine is the one we described first. Crocus is adulterated with pounded Crocomagma, or with cooked wine mixed in: and to make it weigh more, they add silver foam and lead compounds: but the powder found within it reveals the fraud, and especially if one detects the smell of grape syrup. Thessalus holds that Crocus is commendable only for its scent. Some say that Crocus drunk in water at the weight of three drams kills. It has the virtue of ripening, softening, and mildly astringent action. It promotes urine. It gives good color. Drunk with raisin wine it is good against drunkenness. Applied with human milk it checks flows from the eyes. It is usefully added to drinks that are beneficial for the bowels, and in suppositories, and in poultices made for women's conditions and for the rectum. Crocus stimulates lust, and applied as a poultice soothes inflammations tending toward
B sacred fire. It is useful for abscesses of the ears. To grind it easily one should place it in an earthen vessel when warm, or in the sun, and turn it quickly. Its roots drunk with raisin wine promote urine.

On Crocomagma. Chapter 26.

Crocomagma is made from aromatic substances pressed out of Crocine ointment, then formed into pastilles. The best is that which is fragrant, and which breathes a moderate odor of Myrrh, heavy, dark, not woody, smooth, and somewhat bitter, and that which when well moistened produces a Crocus color, and when tasted strongly stains the teeth and tongue, and that which keeps for many years, like the kind brought from Syria. It has the virtue of clearing cloudiness from the eyes. It promotes urine, warms, ripens, and softens. It represents nearly all the virtues of Crocus, since it contains a large
C part of it.

Crocus is truly known throughout the entire world, and is called (though the word is Arabic) throughout Italy, and especially in Tuscany, Zaffarano: But from Corycus, nor from that of Mount Olympus, none reaches us in these times, and so the principal trade belongs to Venice for that which comes from the city of Aquila in Abruzzo. One finds the best and finest, much superior to the Aquilan, in every part of Germany, in Austria, in the territory of Vienna, the principal city of that province: but very little of it passes into Italy. For the Hungarians and Germans, who make great use of spices, are reluctant to let it be taken out of their country. It also grows in Tuscany in some places, and especially around Siena, of the finest quality, which can stand comparison with all the others. Galen mentioned Crocus in the seventh book on the faculties of simples, saying this: Crocus also has a little of the astringent, which has something of the earthy and the cold. But the warm virtue prevails in it, so that its whole essence attains the second degree of heat and the first of dryness, and therefore it has a certain virtue of ripening, to which that little astringency contributes. Indeed all those medicines which are not too warm and have a little astringency share the same faculty of what we call emplastic and maturative essences.

D On Elecampane. Chapter 27.

Elecampane produces leaves similar to those of mullein, but narrower, rougher, and longer: in some places it produces no stalk; its root is whitish. And sometimes it is reddish, fragrant, thick, and rather sharp to the taste, from which offshoots are taken and planted in the same way as is done with lilies and with Arum. It grows in mountainous, shady, and dry places. The root is dug in summer, and cut into pieces and dried. Its decoction drunk promotes urine and menstruation. The root taken with honey in the form of an electuary is beneficial for coughs, asthmatics, those with ruptures, those with spasms, for flatulence, and for serpent bites. In short, it has the virtue of warming. The leaves cooked in wine are usefully applied to sciatica. Elecampane is beneficial for the stomach seasoned with raisin wine: and therefore the preservers of it, drying it a little first and then cooking it, soak it in fresh water, and then place it in raisin wine, and keep it for use.

Helenio,che noi Toscani chiamamo Lella,& altri Enola,& Enoa,è cosa molto nota in Italia. Chiamasi da Gre
L' ci Helenio. Percioche disse fauolando nelle sue poesie Homero,che ella haueva preso quel nome da Helena, per

peroche non solo le produce maggiori del uerbascho,che ha piu stretta foglia,ma molto piu grandi di quello,che di tut-
ti i uerbaschi produce le foglie piu ampie,& piu lunghe. Il che puo forse accadere per il uariare delle qualità de luoghi,
oue la nasce,ouero,che il testo di Dioscoride è stato corrotto dalli scrittori, come in molti altri luoghi si ritrouà,&
massime nel presente capitolo. Percioche recita il dotto Marcello fiorentino hauer hauto egli un Dioscoride uecchio,
& approuato,nelquale si ritrouaua questo di piu,che non è scritto ne gli altri Dioscorides in questo proprio capitolo, B

& in his semen uerbascho simile,tactu pruritum faciens. Cioè l'Helenio produce da se un fusto grosso,hirsuto,angolo-

ride della proprietà dell' Enola l'amaritudine grande,ch'ella ha in se, perche si puo pensare,che mancando in questo
capitolo tutte quelle parole soprascritte,si si possino ageuolmente desiderare queste altre,che rememoraffero dell'ama-

Scrisse del E N O L A Galeno al.vi. delle facoltà de semplici cosi dicendo. La radice dell'Helenio herba è ueramente mol
to utile. Non scalda subito nel primo gusto,per il che è da dire,che la non sia eccessiuamente calida come il pepe tal bian- C
co,qual nero,ma con una certa superflua humidità. Per il che si mette ella ragioneuolmente ne gli Elettuarij,che si fanno
per cauare i grossi,& uscosi homori dal petto,& dal pulmone. Rubifica applicata le membra oppresse lungamente da
frigidi homori,come sono le sciatiche,& le picciole dislogagioni delle gionture causate da humidità.

Dell'Oglio. Cap.xxvij.

O oglio,che è ottimo nel uso della sanità,è quello,che si caua dalle oliue imma-
ture,ilquale chiamano omphacino,cioè acerbo. & di questo quello è il miglio
re,che è nuouo,odorato,& non mordace al gusto. Questo è utile nel comporre
gli onguenti,& è sano allo stomacho per esser egli costrettiuo. Ristringe le
giengie,& tenutolo in bocca ferma i denti,& prohibisce il sudore. Quello è piu atto,& piu
utile ne medicamenti,che è piu uecchio,& piu grasso. Ogni oglio communemente scalda,
mollifica il uentre,preferua il corpo dal freddo,& sallo piu pronto in le sue attioni. Spegne
la mordacità delle medicine ulceratiue, quando si mescola con esse. Dassi contra li ueleni D
mortiferi beendolo,& uomitandolo spesso. Purga il uentre beuto al peso d'una hemina
con altretanto di succhio di Ptisana,ouero con acqua. Toltone caldo tre sestarij di quel-
lo,che ui sia cotto dentro Ruta,gioua à i dolori di corpo. Caccia i uermini,& fassene criste-
ri per i dolori di fianco. Il uecchio è piu caldo,& piu ualentemente risolue. Ongendosene
chiarifica gli occhi. Mancàdone del uecchio per farlo imitare l'anticho si cuoce in un ua-
so per sino,che diuenta spesso come mele. Impero che così ritiene tutte le forze del uecchio.
Quello che si fa delle oliue saluatiche maggiormente costrigne,& nell'uso de sani tiene il se
condo luogo. Adoperasi ne dolori del capo in uece del Rosado. Prohibisce il sudore,& il

& la scabbia. Diuentano tardi cannuti coloro,che giornalmente se n'ongono il capo.
Fassi l'oglio bianco in questo modo. Tolle di quello,che per se stesso piu biancheggia,
ma non però piu uecchio d'un anno,alla misura di cento hemine,& mettelo in un uaso

FIRST BOOK 27

Ground and drunk, it is good for spitting of blood. Crateua reports that another species of Enola grows in Egypt, which produces branches a cubit in length, spreading along the ground after the manner of Serpollo. Around these branches it produces leaves similar to lentils, but longer and more dense. Its root is pale, about the thickness of a little finger, thick near the stem, thin at the tip, and covered in black bark. It grows in coastal places and on hillsides. One of its roots drunk with wine is useful against the bites of venomous animals.

Helenio, which we Tuscans call Lella, and others call Enola or Enoa, is a plant very well known in Italy. It is called by the Greeks Helenio, because Homer said in his poems, speaking in fable, that it took its name from Helen, having been born from her tears on the island of Helena at the death of Canopus, her governor, when, bitten by a snake, he lost his life. But we see that our plant produces leaves much larger than those described by Dioscorides; for it produces them not only larger than those of Verbascum, which has a narrower leaf, but much larger than any Verbascum that produces the widest and longest leaves of all. This may perhaps happen due to the varying qualities of the places where it grows, or because the text of Dioscorides has been corrupted by scribes, as one finds in many other places, and especially in the present chapter. For the learned Marcello of Florence reports having had in his possession an old and authoritative manuscript of Dioscorides, in which was found this additional passage, not written in the other copies of Dioscorides in this very chapter, namely: "Caulem ex se mittit Helenium, crassum, hirsutum, cubitalem, & aliquando maiorem, angulosumque, flores luteos, & in his semen uerbascho simile, tactu pruritum faciens." That is, the Helenio produces from itself a stem that is thick, hairy, angular, a cubit high, and sometimes taller, with yellow flowers, and in these a seed similar to Verbascum, which causes itching where it touches. This does not surprise me, that in this same chapter Dioscorides should have passed over in silence the great bitterness of Enola, which it has in itself, because one may think that, those words above being absent from this chapter, one might easily expect these others, which would recall the bitterness; for Dioscorides would never have passed over in silence so manifest a quality. Pliny did not omit it when speaking of Enola in chapter 5 of book 19. Enola, as Hippocrates testifies, when eaten greatly cheers the spirits. For which reason some said that it makes one forget all the sorrows of the mind. It preserves beauty in the face and throughout the whole body. It arouses Venus, and when eaten by mice it kills them. Avicenna speaks at length of it, and somewhat confuses it with the Egyptian variety. Of the Enola which, according to the physician Crateua, grows in Egypt, none is brought into Italy. Galen wrote of Enola in book 6 of his work on simples, saying: The root of the herb Helenio is truly very useful. It does not heat immediately on first taste, for which reason it is to be said that it is not excessively hot like pepper, whether white or black, but has a certain superfluous moisture. For which reason it is quite reasonably included in the electuaries that are made to draw out thick and viscous humors from the chest and lungs. Applied to limbs long oppressed by cold humors, such as sciatica and the small dislocations of joints caused by moisture, it brings color back to them.

On Oil. Chapter 27.

The oil that is best for use in health is that which is drawn from unripe olives, which they call omphacino, that is, unripe. And of this kind the best is that which is new, fragrant, and not harsh to the taste. This is useful in making ointments, and is good for the stomach because it is astringent. It tightens the gums, and held in the mouth firms the teeth, and inhibits sweating. That which is more useful in medicines is the older and fattier kind. Every oil commonly warms, softens the bowels, protects the body from cold, and makes it more ready in its actions. It extinguishes the mordacity of ulcerative medicines when mixed with them. It is given against deadly poisons by drinking it and vomiting it up repeatedly. It purges the bowels when drunk in the weight of one hemina mixed with an equal amount of ptisan juice or with water. Taking three sextaries of it heated, in which Rue has been cooked, it benefits pains in the body. It expels worms, and enemas of it are made for pains in the side. The older oil is warmer and resolves more vigorously. Rubbed on, it clarifies the eyes. When old oil is lacking and one wishes to imitate it, it is cooked in a vessel until it becomes as thick as honey, for in this way it retains all the virtues of the old. That which is made from wild olives is more astringent, and in use for healthy people holds the second place. It is used for pains of the head in place of Rosado oil. It prevents sweating and the falling out of hair. It cleanses dandruff, ulcers of the head that fester, mange, and scabies. Those who anoint themselves with it daily grow gray more slowly. White oil is made in this manner: Take that which is naturally most white, but no more than one year old, to the measure of one hundred heminae, and put it in a vessel.

Dell'Eleomele. Cap.xxix. B

In palmira di Soria da un certo tronco d'albero distilla un oglio piu grosso del
mele, al gusto dolce, ilquale chiamano Eleomele. Beutone il peso d'un sesta
rio con una hemina d'acqua purga la cholera,& altri crudi homori, ma colo
ro,che lo beono diuentano quasi stupidi,& senza forze. Il che non è da teme
re suegliandoli,& non lasciandoli dormire. Fassi parimente della grassezza de rami di
questo albero oglio delquale, quello è eccellente,che è uecchio,grasso,denso,& non tor
bido. Ha uirtu di scaldare. Ongesi priuatamente per chiarificare gl'impedimenti de gli oc
chi. Conferisce alla scabia,& à i dolori de nerui.

Eleomele non si porta à noi,anchora che piu merce si ci portino di Soria,ne manco ho mai ritrouato alcuno,
L' che l'habbia uisto in Italia. Hermolao Barbaro huomo ueramente dotto sta in dubio,si l'Eleomele sia,ò non sia la
Manna, fondandosi piu nel significato del uocabolo,che nella proprietà,& nell'essenza della cosa. Impero che tie
ne egli quasi come per certo,anchora che del tutto non l'esprima,che l'Eleomele,& l'Aeromele,ilquale non uuol dire al
tro,che mele del aria,sieno una cosa medesima. Perilche non mi posso se non marauegliare,che non hauesse forza dica C
re di dubio un tanto huomo la scrittura di Plinio suo familiarissimo,& quella di Dioscoride,i quali di commune senten
za affermano,che l'Eleomele è un Oglio,che distilla da un tronco d'un albero in Palmira di Soria,& non che sia ne liquo
re,ne mele,che ui caschi dal cielo,ò dall'aria,& tanto piu,che nel processo del capitolo afferma Dioscoride,che oltre à
quello,che per se stesso distilla dal albero,se ne fa artificialmente della grassezza de suoi rami.

Dell'Oglio Ricino,ouero Cicino. Cap.xxx.

L'O oglio Ricino si fa in questo modo. Toglìesi la quantità de i Ricini ben matu
ri,che si uuole,& distesi poscia à seccare al sole, nel modo,che ui si distendono
l'altre cose in su le grati, tanto ui si lasciano stare,che la corteccia,che gli uefte si
rompe,& gli casca da dosso. Pigliasi poi la carne loro,& messa in un mortaio
diligentemente si pesta,& mettesi poscia in un uaso di metallo stagnato insieme con ac
qua à bollire al fuoco,& come si uede,che gli habbia reso tutto il suo homore,leuato il ua
so dal fuoco,si ricoglie tutto l'oglio,che nuota di sopra con un nicchio di gongola. Ma D
in Egitto,doue piu abondantemente s'usa, si fa altrimenti. Imperoche mandano i Rici
ni ben mondi alla macina,& come sono ben macinati, messigli in certe sporte ne sprie
mano l'oglio per il torcolo. Sono maturi i Ricini,quando facilmente escono fuore del lo
ro guscio. E buono l'oglio Ricino all'ulcere del capo,che humigano,alle opilationi,&
prefocatoni della madrice,alla rogna,alle posteme calde del sedere,& leua uia le disfor
mi cicatrici,& i dolori dell'orecchie. Messo ne gli impiasti li fa piu efficaci,& beuto pur
ga l'acqua,& i uermini del uentre.

Chiamasi l'oglio Ricino,ouero Cicino communemente oglio di Cherua,anchora che poco sia in uso nelle Spetia
C rie. impero che il seme,che chiama Dioscoride Ricino,non è altro,che la Cherua,ouero la Cataputa maggiore
de gli Arabi,laquale chiama Serapione anchora Pentadattilo, come piu ampiamente nel quarto libro se dirà,
quando nel proprio capitolo si parlara di tutta la pianta. Manon preterirò però di dire,che Ricino non uuol dire altro

FIRST 29

It penetrates within, and is to be considered the best and superior to all others, like the Sabine oil. That washed oil is less harsh than all the others we have amply demonstrated above, but how one should wash it most properly is taught in the present treatise, which will deal with the composition of medicines, where the doctrine of Sicyonian oil and every other similar oil will be discussed. For now my intention is to treat of Simple medicines. That which is pressed from wild olives is not of simple temperament, for it constricts and dries. This is sharper than all the others, and less so is the Histrian, and after that the Spanish. The thickest is that of Libya and Cilicia. Thin and yet somewhat fatty is the Sabine, and mediocre among all these, which we have mentioned, is that which grows in the Cyclades islands, in Greece, and in Asia. The thick is judged by its viscosity, and the thin by its transparency and by how quickly it penetrates when applied to the body. One may therefore, by the reasons stated above, recognize the qualities of all oils, which are equivocally called ointments, such as Rose oil, Quince oil, Lily oil, and every other sort made from flowers, fruits, buds, and leaves. Each of these becomes an ointment when prepared with aromatic substances, and thus every other oil varies in its temperament according to the qualities of the things infused into it.

On Eleomele. Chapter XXIX.

In Palmyra of Syria, from a certain tree trunk, there distills an oil thicker than honey, sweet to the taste, which they call Eleomele. Drinking the weight of a sextarius with a hemina of water purges cholera and other crude humors, but those who drink it become nearly stupefied and without strength. This is not to be feared if one keeps them awake and does not let them sleep. Likewise, from the fatty substance of the branches of this tree an oil is made, of which the best is that which is old, thick, dense, and not turbid. It has the virtue of warming. It is applied externally to clarify obstructions of the eyes. It is useful for scabies and for pains of the nerves.

Eleomele does not come to us, even though much merchandise is brought to us from Syria, nor have I ever found anyone who has seen it in Italy. Hermolaus Barbarus, a truly learned man, is in doubt whether Eleomele is or is not Manna, basing himself more on the meaning of the word than on the property and essence of the thing. He holds it as nearly certain, though he does not fully express it, that Eleomele and Aeromele, which means nothing other than honey of the air, are one and the same thing. For which I cannot but marvel that the writings of Pliny, his great friend, and those of Dioscorides did not give so great a man cause to doubt, since they both affirm with common accord that Eleomele is an oil that distills from a tree trunk in Palmyra of Syria, and not a liquid or honey that falls from the sky or from the air; and all the more so because in the course of the chapter Dioscorides affirms that beyond what distills by itself from the tree, it is also made artificially from the fat of its branches.

On Castor Oil, or Cicino. Chapter XXX.

Castor oil is made in the following way. One takes a quantity of ripe castor beans and spreads them out to dry in the sun, in the manner one spreads other things on racks, leaving them until the skin that covers them splits and falls away. One then takes the flesh and pounds it diligently in a mortar, then puts it in a tin metal vessel with water to boil over the fire, and when one sees that it has rendered all its moisture, removing the vessel from the fire, one collects all the oil that floats on top with a mussel shell. But in Egypt, where it is used most abundantly, it is done differently, for they send the cleaned castor beans to the mill, and when they are well ground, putting them in certain baskets, they press the oil out with a press. The castor beans are ripe when they come easily out of their shell. Castor oil is good for ulcers of the head that are weeping, for obstructions and suffocations of the womb, for mange, for hot swellings of the seat, and it removes unsightly scars and pains of the ears. Added to poultices it makes them more efficacious, and drunk it purges water and worms from the belly.

Castor oil, or Cicino, is commonly called oil of Cherua, though it is little used in apothecaries. For the seed that Dioscorides calls Ricino is nothing other than the Cherua, or the greater Cataputa of the Arabs, which Serapion also calls Pentadattilo, as will be said more fully in the fourth book when the whole plant will be discussed in its own chapter. Yet I will not fail to say that Ricino means nothing other than

A ueramente, che quelle zecche grosse, che attaccate adosso à porci, à cani, à capre, & à diuersi altri animali si ritrouano li
uide, & piene di sangue, & perche questo seme in ogni sua parte si rassembra à quel sordido animaletto, è stato chiamato
anch'egli Ricino, tirando il nome dalla molta sembianza, che ha con quello. Di questo oglio scrisse Mesue nel trattato ch'et
sa de gli ogli, chiamandolo oglio di Cherus, et oltre alle uirtù assegnategli da Dioscoride, disse, che molto s'acconuiene alle
uentosità grosse, et che per questo giouà à dolori di stomacho, di fiachi, et similmente colici onto, beuto, et messo ne i cristeri.

Dell'oglio delle Mandole. Cap.xxxi.

O oglio delle Mandole, ilquale alcuni chiamano Metopio, si fa in questo mo
do. Toglie la quarta parte d'un moggio di Mandole amare ben monde, & ben
secche, & con uno pestello di legno leggiermente pestale in un mortaio fin
che uadino in pasta, & gittali sopra due hemine d'acqua calda. Lasciale poi cosi
per mezza hora in infusione, & ritornale à pestare piu fortemente, & poscia spriemele in un
uaso, leuando con una gongola quello, ch'es'appicca alle dita. Aggiogne poi di nuono alle
B mandole spriemute una hemina d'acqua, & come serano bene abbombate, sa una altra
uolta il medesimo. Ogni mezzo moggio di mandole rende una hemina d'oglio. Vale à i
dolori, presocationi, conuersioni, & infiammaggioni della madrice. Gioua à dolori di te
sta, & à i dolori, suoni, et sussili dell'orecchie. Vale à i defetti delle Reni, alle pietre, che ui si ge
nerano, al ritenimento dell'orina, à strettura di fiato, & à i difetti di melza. Tolle meschiato
con mele, radice di giglio, & cera di Cipro, ouero cerotto Rosado le macchie, le ruuidezze,
& le crespe della faccia. Fortifica la uista, & mondifica applicato con uino la sarfarella, &
l'ulcere del capo, che humigano.

E Sendo il dolce il uero ricompenso del amaro, mi pare ueramente di douer dire (tacendoselo Dioscoride) anchora
dell'Oglio delle mandole dolci, imperoche pochi Spetiali si ritrouano, che lo faccino realmente, & secondo il do
uere. Fassi adunque secondo Mesue cosi. Togliefi delle migliori, & più dolci mandole la quantità, che si uuole ben
monde da tutte due le scorze, & pestansi, lasciandosi poscia per cinque hore in luogo ben caldo. Ripestansi dipoi alquanto,
& portansi al torchio, & cauasene l'oglio. Cuocesi anchora la pasta loro in uaso di uetriato, ouero di stagno nel bagno, che
chiamano di Maria per alquanto spatio di tepo, & poscia cosi calda si porta sotto al Torchiello, & cauasene l'oglio più
abondamente. Tritansi anchora le mdole ben monde, & mettonsi nei sacchetti inuolti in più doppi di panni sotto
C l'arena, ouero cenere calda, & come sono ben calde se ne spreme suor l'oglio. Ma i nostri Spetiali senza mondare altri
menti le mandole pigliando ogni rottume delle comune, lequali sempre son mescolate con qualcuna delle amare, dipoi che
l'han peste assai grossamente le mettono in un uaso di rame sopra al fuoco, & le scaldano di tal sorte, che quasi l'arro
stiscono, & se non fusse, che pur le sbruffano con un poco d'acqua del tutto s'abbrustolato abbero, & cosi poscia le portano
sotto al torchiello à cauar l'oglio, ilquale il piu delle molte puzza tanto d'abbrustolato, che offende mirabilmente il naso,
nò accorgendosi, che per sparammiur faticba, per uertiscono tutta la sua uirtu lenitùa, & pettorale. Imperò che pestan
do le mdole senza módare, uiene à prendere l'oglio nell'abbrustolarsi le mandole, la natura del guscio, il quale è stittico,
secco, aspro, & sabroso, il che parimente gliacrescte quello arrostire le mandole nello scaldarle. Al che hauendo bauto
auuertenza il peritissimo Mesue uolse, che à fare l'oglio buono delle mandole dolci, che le mandole fussero ben monde,
& che poscia le si scalddssero con un certo caldo soaue, lento, & piaccuole, come in diuersi modi qui di sopra s'è scritto. Ha questo oglio, quando si fa diligentemente uirtu molto lenitius, & imperò beùone il peso di quatro once lenisce il
corpo alli costipati, l'asprezza della gola, del Polmone, & di tutte le parti esteriori, & humetta tutte le durezze, &
D siccità de membri, & delle gionture, & imperò conferisce molto agli Ethici, ingrassa, & moltiplicasi seme, & applicato
gioua ai dolori della madrice, & della uisciga mestoui con la Siringa. Quello delle mandole amare oltre alle uirtù asse
gnategli da Dioscoride, apre l'opilationi, & caccia le uentosità del corpo.

Dell'oglio Balanino, Cap.xxxij.

Assi l'oglio Balanino nel medesimo modo, che quello delle mandole. Leua
questo del uso le macchie, le lentigini, il uaiuolo, & le cicatrici nere. Solue il uen
tre. Nuoce allo stomacho. Distillasi nell'orecchie per i dolori, per il suono, & pi
sussili di quelle insieme con grasso c'oca utilmente. Fannosì nel medesimo mo
do l'oglio di Sisamo, & quello delle Noci, & hanno la medesima uirtu, che l Balanino.

L' Oglio Balanino, ilquale si fa della Ghianda Onguentaria, si chiama appresso à i Prosumieri, & Spetiali oglio di
Ben, per chiamarsi cosi dagli Arabi il frutto, onde egli si sprieme, come ampiamente diremo nel processo di que
sto al quarto libro, quando quiui nel proprio capitolo si parlara della Ghianda Onguentaria chiamata dalli gre

A In truth, those large ticks which attach themselves to pigs, dogs, goats, and various other animals are found alive and full of blood; and because this seed resembles in every part that vile little creature, it has also been called Ricino, taking its name from the great resemblance it has to that creature. About this oil, Mesue wrote in his treatise on oils, calling it the oil of Cherus; and beyond the virtues attributed to it by Dioscorides, he said that it is very well suited for large flatulences, and that for this reason it is beneficial for pains of the stomach, of the flanks, and similarly for colic when rubbed on, drunk, or administered in enemas.

On the Oil of Almonds. Chapter 31.

The oil of almonds, which some call Metopio, is made in the following way. Take a quarter of a bushel of bitter almonds, well cleaned and well dried, and with a wooden pestle grind them lightly in a mortar until they form a paste, then pour over them two measures of hot water. Leave them to soak for half an hour, then return to grinding them more vigorously, and afterward press them into a vessel, removing with a spatula what sticks to the fingers. Add again to the pressed almonds one measure of water, and when they have swelled up well, repeat the process once more. Every half bushel of almonds yields one measure of oil. It is good for pains, suffocations, displacements, and inflammations of the womb. It is helpful for headaches, and for pains, ringing, and hissing in the ears. It is good for defects of the kidneys, for stones that form there, for retention of urine, for tightness of breath, and for ailments of the spleen. Mixed with honey, root of lily, and wax of Cyprus, or rosado ointment, it removes blemishes, roughness, and wrinkles of the face. It strengthens the sight, and applied with wine it cleanses dandruff and ulcers of the head that weep.

E Since the sweet is the true counterpart of the bitter, it seems to me truly necessary to speak (Dioscorides being silent on it) also of the oil of sweet almonds, for few apothecaries prepare it properly and as they should. According to Mesue it is done thus: take of the best and sweetest almonds the desired quantity, well cleaned of both skins, and grind them, then leave them for five hours in a warm place. Grind them again somewhat, then bring them to the press and extract the oil. The paste can also be cooked in an earthenware or tin vessel in a water bath, called the bath of Mary, for some time, and then while still warm brought to the small press to yield the oil more abundantly. The almonds can also be ground well cleaned and placed in bags wrapped in several layers of cloth and buried under hot sand or warm ash, and when they are well heated the oil is pressed out. But our apothecaries, without properly cleaning the almonds, taking all the scraps of the common ones — which are always mixed with some bitter ones — after having pounded them rather coarsely, put them in a copper vessel over fire and heat them in such a way as to almost roast them, and were it not that they spray them with a little water, they would be entirely burnt; and then they bring them to the small press to extract the oil, which most of the time smells so strongly of burning as to offend the nose wonderfully. Not realizing that, in order to save effort, they destroy all its soothing and pectoral virtue. For in grinding the almonds without cleaning them, the oil takes on from the burning the nature of the husk, which is astringent, dry, harsh, and rough, which is likewise increased by that roasting of the almonds in heating them. The most expert Mesue, having taken note of this, wished that to make good oil of sweet almonds, the almonds should be well cleaned, and then warmed with a certain gentle, slow, and pleasant heat, as has been written here above in various ways. This oil, when prepared diligently, has a very soothing virtue; and thus drinking four ounces of it loosens the body of the constipated, relieves the roughness of the throat, the lungs, and all the external parts, and moistens all hardness and dryness of the limbs and joints; and thus it greatly benefits those with wasting disease, it fattens, and it multiplies the seed; and applied it helps pains of the womb and of the bladder when introduced with a syringe. That of bitter almonds, beyond the virtues attributed to it by Dioscorides, opens obstructions and drives out flatulences of the body.

On Balanine Oil. Chapter 32.

Balanine oil is made in the same way as that of almonds. Applied externally it removes blemishes, freckles, smallpox marks, and black scars. It loosens the bowels. It is harmful to the stomach. It is instilled into the ears for pains, for ringing, and for hissing in them, mixed usefully with goose grease. Sesame oil and walnut oil are made in the same way, and have the same virtue as the Balanine.

L' Balanine oil, which is made from the ointment acorn, is called among perfumers and apothecaries oil of Ben, because the Arabians so name the fruit from which it is pressed; as we shall discuss at length in the course of this work in the fourth book, where in the proper chapter we shall speak of the ointment acorn called by the Greeks

al sole, & le parti sue, che di sopra si seccano, si rincorporano continuamente nel-

mollificatiuo. Fassi similmente l'oglio del Grano Gnidio mondato. Beuto purga il cor-

d'Egitto per condimento delle uiuande lori. Il Melanthion tanto uale, quanto il Rafani- C

Oglio del Iusquiamo (imperoche così si chiama il Hiosciamo nelle Spetiarie) anchora, che appresso à poche per-

Dell'Oglio di Mirtho. Cap. xxxiiij.

Il modo di fare l'oglio di Mirtho è così. Toglionsi le piu tenere foglie del Mir-
tho nero saluatico, ouero del domestico, & pestansi, & cauasene il succhio, con il
quale si meschia il pari peso d'oglio omphacino, & fassi cuocere insieme à fuo-
co di carbone ricogliendolo poi l'oglio, che nuota di sopra. Fassi anchora piu fa-
cilmente in questo modo. Cuoconsi in oglio, & acqua ben peste le foglie piu tenere del Mir-
tho, & ricogliesi poscia l'oglio, che nuota. Alcuni priuatamente lo fanno al Sole mettendo

and Mirabolano. In this same manner, Mesue wrote about the art of making his own oil, saying that it is astringent, cleansing, and aperitive against obstructions. Applied externally, it dissolves scrofula and hard tumors. It is beneficial for cold ailments of the spleen and liver, and is useful against spasms and other diseases of the cold nerves, and against joint pains. This oil has the property that, as it ages, it does not become stale or rancid, and therefore perfumers, when blending mixtures for scenting gloves with musk, amber, civet, and other sweet fragrances, use no other oil but this one. It is no wonder then that the fruit from which this oil is extracted was called by the ancients the "ointment acorn." For its liquid alone is the most suitable and most frequently used in the blending of precious and fragrant ointments. Mesue also wrote that the oil of sesame was made in the same manner as almond oil, first shelling it, then pounding and pressing it with the same technique; and as he affirms, it fattens the body, increases semen, soothes roughness — especially of the throat — clarifies the voice, and softens hard tumors. The oil of sesame is then used in many compound oils available in apothecaries. As for walnut oil, I do not find it used in medicine, but I do know that in Lombardy, because of the scarcity of olive oil, it is burned daily in lamps.

On the Oil of Henbane, of Spurge Flax, of Safflower, of Radish seed, B
of Nigella, and of Mustard. Chapter 33.

The oil of henbane is made as follows. Take the seed fresh, dry, and white, pound it and soak it in water, as we described for almond oil. Then lay it in the sun, and the parts that dry on top are continuously folded back into the mass. This is done until it turns black and begins to smell. It is then pressed and, once strained, stored. It is useful for earaches, and small weights are soaked in it since it is emollient. The oil of spurge flax grain, hulled, is made similarly. Drunk, it purges the body. In the same way, one obtains what is called Cnicino oil, which has the same virtue as oil of spurge flax, though somewhat less effective. The same method applies to the oil made from radish seed, which is beneficial for those who, after long illness, become infested with lice. It removes roughness from the skin of the face, and Egyptians use it as a condiment for their foods. The oil of nigella is as effective as that of radish. C Mustard oil is made as follows: the seed is ground and soaked in hot water; oil is added and it is pressed; applied by rubbing on old aches and pains, it draws to itself the humors that have accumulated in any part of the body.

The oil of henbane (for that is what Hiosciamo is called in apothecaries), though used by only a few persons, is nonetheless an excellent remedy for relieving all pain where other remedies fail, in any part of the body, and especially for hot tumors of the genital members, both male and female. It is very useful in the most acute pains of the ear, when dripped inside with castor or saffron. It prevents gonorrhea when rubbed on the kidneys and testicles; it stops the red and white menstrual flows of women when placed in the uterus with small weights, and rubbed along the spine. It is effective against pains and inflammations of the breasts, and held warm in the mouth it relieves toothache; and more than anything else, mixed with various other simples, it prevents the regrowth of hair. The oil of spurge flax grain, which country folk call "mountain pepper" and have frequently used for purging — since it is genuinely suited to their stomachs — is not used medicinally, being too violent in its operation. But the Cnicino oil, derived from safflower seed, according to Mesue, when drunk is beneficial for overflow of bile, for obstructions, and for both stomach and colic pains. It wonderfully helps those with tightness in the chest, and clears the voice. Drunk, it purges phlegm both by D vomiting and through the bowels. The oils of radish seed and of nigella are not used, nor is that of mustard, though I have made it myself more than once — albeit not without tears, so pungent is the fume it releases when pressed.

On the Oil of Myrtle. Chapter 34.

The oil of myrtle is made as follows. Take the most tender leaves of the wild black myrtle, or of the domestic variety, pound them and extract the juice, mix this with an equal weight of unripe olive oil, and cook them together over a charcoal fire, then collect the oil that floats on top. It can also be made more easily in the following way: cook the most tender myrtle leaves, well pounded, in oil and water, then collect the oil that floats on top. Some make it privately by placing it in the sun,

Dell'oglio del Lentifco,& del Terebintho. Cap.xxxvi. A

NEl modo,che si fa l'oglio Laurino,si fa medesimamête anchora quello del Lentifco,cauandolo dal suo frutto,quando è maturo,& dando corpo all'oglio,come fu detto nel Laurino.Sana questo la rogna de cani,& de gli altri animali quadrupedi.È utilissimo ne pessoli,nelle medicine delle lassitudini,& in quelle della lebbra. Prohibisce il sudore. Ne si fa altrimenti quello del Terebintho,ilquale rinfresça, & costrigne.

Assi l'oglio del Lentifco in piu luoghi in Toscana,& massime nel Contado nostro di Siena.Fassi nell'Helba,& in
F Giglio isole del Thireno,& non guari lontane dalle nostre Maremme,in questo modo.Prendono buona quantità
di frutti di Lentifco stati prima ricolti alquanti giorni,& pongonli poscia à bollire in acqua à lento fuoco,& come cominciano à crepare,ne spriemono fuore l'oglio senza dargli compagnia d'altro oglio; imperoche per se stfso, ne fa assai. Credonsi uniuersalmente i Paesani doue egli si fa,che à usarlo ne i cibi sia valoroso rimedio à far buona uista. Lodollo assai Galeno nel.v.libro delle compositioni de Medicamenti secondo i luoghi, alle Giengiue infiammate,& ancho alla Lingua,ritenendolo in bocca. Quello,che si fa de frutti del Terebintho, liquali chiamano gli Arabi Grani uerdi, B non si porta in Italia,& imperò non s'usa. Di questo parlando il Manardo da Ferrara nella prima Epistola dell'ottauo libro,si marauiglia,che Dioscoride dicesse, c'habbia egli uirtu d'infrigidare.Per dir egli poscia nel cap.del Terebintho, che'l suo frutto ha uirtu di scaldare,& imperò tiene egli,che questo Testo sia corrotto,& mendoso,& proualo per hauere trouato un Dioscoride oue solamente è notato il modo di far l'oglio senza esserui delle uirtu sue memoria alcuna. Ha questo,come afferma Mesue, uirtu di saldare le ferite,& conserisce allo spasimo,al tiro, & alle durezze de nerui, & mettesi molto frequentemente ne gli impiasiri.

Dell'oglio Masticino. Cap.xxxvij.

FAssi l'oglio Masticino del Mastice trito,ilquale conferisce à tutti i difetti della madrice.Scalda temperatamête,mollifica,& costregne. E' utile alle durezze,& flussi dello stomacho,& alla desinteria.Monda la faccia da ogni macchia, & fa bellissimo colore.L'eccellente si fa nell'Isola di Chio.

Olto breuemente se ne passo Dioscoride nel scriuere il modo di far l'oglio di Mastice,dicendo solamente,che si C
M faceua col Mastice trito senza insegnarne il modo di farlo.Gli Spetiali d'hoggi di per la maggior parte,hauendosi dimenticato,che Mesue uuole,che si faccia in bagno di Maria,fanno bollire il Mastice in oglio comune,& uino bianco sopra à i carboni, sino che si consumi tutto il uino. Ma io l'ho fatto alcune uolte molto eccellente per lambico di uetro.

Della Compositione de gli Onguenti. Cap.xxxviij

PErche gli Onguenti sono utili in alcune malattie, ò in mescolarli con li medicamenti,ò in ongersene,ò in odorarli, pensiamo douersi d'essi conseguentemente trattare,& imperò nel prouarli bisogna,che il naso sia giudice se respirino l'odore di quelle cose,di cui si compongono.Questo è ueramente l'ottimo giuditio, come che in alcuni non si possa osseruare,à alcune cose,che ui si mettono,lequali auāzano d'odore tutte le altre,come in quel dell'Amaraco,del Zaffarano,del Fiengreco, & alcuni de gli altri,liquali solamente si prouano,& si conoscono per pratica.
D

Dell'Onguento Rosado. Cap.xxxix.

QVello delle Rose si fa così. T'olle di Squinanto cinque lire,& otto once,d'oglio due lire,& cinque once. Pesta,& infondi in acqua,& cuoci meschiando continuamente,& come l'harai colato,mettilo con mille Rose ben asciute dall'humidità in uenti lire,& cinque once d'oglio,& poscia per un dì con le mani prima onte d'odorato mele spesse uolte meschiàle,leggiermente stringendole, & lascia così per tutta una notte,dipoi spriemilo,& come sara andata al fondo la residenza,trasportalo di quel uaso in un'altro,che sia bene abbombato di mele,& serbalo. Tolte dipoi quelle Rose spriemute in uno altro uaso,gittali di nuouo sopra del medesimo oglio spessito otto lire, & tre once,& spriemile un'altra uolta,& così hauerai il secondo,& si tu uorrai fare il terzo,& il quarto infondegli uolta,per uolta l'oglio,& spriemilo. FIRST BOOK. 33

On the Oil of Mastic-tree and of Terebinth. Chapter 36.

In the same manner as lentisk oil is made, so too is terebinth oil prepared, by extracting it from its fruit when ripe, and giving body to the oil, as was said regarding laurel oil. It cures mange in dogs and other four-footed animals. It is most useful in pessaries, in medicines for fatigue, and in those for leprosy. It inhibits sweating. The oil of Terebinth is made in no other way, though it refreshes and is astringent.

Lentisk oil is made in many places in Tuscany, and especially in our own territory of Siena. It is also made on the island of Elba and
F on Giglio in the Tyrrhenian Sea, not far from our Maremma, in this manner. They take a good quantity of lentisk berries that have been gathered some days before, and then set them to boil in water over a slow fire, and as they begin to crack open, they press out the oil without mixing it with any other oil; for by itself it produces enough. The country people where it is made universally believe that using it in food is a powerful remedy for good eyesight. Galen praised it greatly in his fifth book on the Compositions of Medicines by region, for inflamed gums and also for the tongue, by holding it in the mouth. The oil made from the berries of the Terebinth, which the Arabs call green grains, is not brought to Italy, and so is not used here. Speaking of this, Manardo of Ferrara in the first letter of his eighth book marvels that Dioscorides said it has the virtue of cooling. For Dioscorides then says in the chapter on Terebinth that its fruit has the virtue of warming; and so Manardo holds that this text is corrupt and faulty, and proves it by having found a copy of Dioscorides where only the method of making the oil is noted, without any mention of its virtues. This oil has, as Mesue affirms, the virtue of closing wounds, and is useful for spasms, cramps, and hardness of the nerves, and is very frequently used in plasters.

On Mastic Oil. Chapter 37.

Mastic oil is made from ground mastic, which is beneficial for all ailments of the womb. It warms moderately, softens, and is astringent. It is useful for hardness and fluxes of the stomach, and for dysentery. It cleanses the face of every blemish, and makes it most beautiful. The finest is made on the island of Chios.

Dioscorides passed very briefly over the method of making mastic oil, saying only that it was made with ground mastic without teaching how to do it. Apothecaries nowadays, for the most part having forgotten that Mesue requires it to be made in a bain-marie, boil the mastic in common oil and white wine over coals until all the wine is consumed. But I myself have made it several times very excellently using a glass alembic.

On the Composition of Ointments. Chapter 38.

Since ointments are useful in certain illnesses, whether for mixing with medicines, or for anointing, or for inhaling, we think we ought consequently to treat of them, and in testing them, the nose must be the judge of whether they breathe the scent of the things of which they are composed. This is truly the best judgment, although in some cases it cannot be observed, since some ingredients that are added surpass all others in scent, as in that of Amaracus, of Saffron, of Fenugreek, and several others, which can only be tested and recognized by practice.

On Rose Ointment. Chapter 39.

Rose ointment is made as follows. Take five pounds and eight ounces of squinancywort, two pounds and five ounces of oil. Pound it and steep it in water, and cook it stirring continuously, and when you have strained it, put it with one thousand roses well dried of their moisture into twenty pounds and five ounces of oil, and then for one day, with hands first anointed with fragrant honey, mix them frequently, squeezing them gently, and leave it thus for an entire night; then press it out, and when the residue has settled to the bottom, transfer it from that vessel to another well sealed with honey, and store it. Then take those pressed roses, put them in another vessel, pour upon them again eight pounds and three ounces of the same thickened oil, and press them another time, and thus you will have the second pressing; and if you wish to make a third and fourth, pour the oil over them turn by turn and press it out. But however many times you do it,

A   The vessels should be anointed with honey this many times. Beyond this, if you wish to make the second infusion, put into the oil — which was first pressed — an equal number of fresh roses dried of all moisture, and mixing them with hands greased with honey, squeeze them; doing this up to the third and fourth time, and each time you return to do it, add fresh roses, cutting away first that small whitish part they have at the base of their petals, for this makes it more effective. This is done up to the seventh infusion and no more. It is necessary, however, that the press be anointed with honey, and that the oil be well separated from the juice of the roses, because even the smallest part that remains corrupts the whole ointment. Some others take only the roses, removing that small white part at the lower extremity, to the weight of six ounces, and submerge them in a sextarius of oil, and set them in the Sun, and having left them thus for eight days, repeat the infusion three times, up to a period of forty days, and then store it. There are others who first give body to the oil with fragrant calamus and with aspalathus, and others mix in alkanet to give it color, and salt so that it does not spoil. It has the virtue of cooling and of constricting; it is useful in heat conditions and in plasters. Drunk, it loosens the body and quenches the burning of the stomach. It fills deep ulcers and mitigates those that are malignant and difficult to heal. Applied to ulcers of the head that suppurate, and to the hot pustules thereof. It is usefully applied to headaches at the beginning of the illness. Kept in the mouth, and used as a rinse, it helps with toothache. It is effective applied to hardness of the eyelids. Clysters are made from it for internal ulcers and for itching of the womb.

    Dioscorides calls oils all those which are extracted without adding any other oil, either from tree fruits or from seeds, and
C  he then calls ointments all those others which are composed of oil and other materials, as is clearly understood here in the Rosado
    and in the others that follow, since these ointments of his are nothing other than oils.
And therefore, treating of Oil, Galen in book vi of the Faculties of Simples said this: For the reasons already given, one must recognize the other species of oils, which some equivocally call Ointments, such as the Rosado, that of Quinces, and of Lilies, and every other that is made by macerating within it flowers, fruits, shoots, and leaves. Of these, then, each one that is prepared with aromatic things is subsequently called an ointment. The Rosado oil used today in pharmacies is truly very far from that of Dioscorides, and is rather to be judged better than otherwise, on account of the great artistry and diligence that go into composing it, although few apothecaries, to avoid the labor, make it according to the doctrine of Mesue, who wrote of it several methods with the greatest diligence. It is made with roses that are not yet fully open — that which they call Rosado omphacino — leaving part of it in a bain-marie (as has been said above in other cases) and part in the sun, and there are those who, to make it more effective, first wash the oil thoroughly with rose water, and having done so for a longer period, with three or four infusions of those roses that are still not fully open, and at the last pressing they add the juice of those same roses not yet fully ripe, and set it in the sun for more and more days, and then separate and store it. This quenches inflammations, comforts, consolidates, thickens, and prevents the flow of matter to the afflicted parts. Drunk, it is good for dysentery, and is much used in wounds of the head, because it greatly comforts and marvelously prevents inflammation.

        On the Elatine Ointment.          Chapter 40.

D   One spins and then pounds the rind of the fruits of the Palm, at the time when it is not yet fully in flower, and placing it thus in a vessel, pours omphacine oil over it. It is then left to stand three days, and then putting it into a press one squeezes it, and stores it in a clean vessel, and uses it. To make it, one takes as much rind by weight as omphacine oil. It corresponds in its virtues to the rosado, but does not soften the body.
L'  The Elatine ointment, which was made in ancient times from the husks of Dates, is not in use in our times.

        On the Meline Ointment.          Chapter 41.

    The Meline ointment is composed in this manner. Take one congius of oil, and mix it with ten sextarii of water, and add to it three ounces of pounded palm bark, and one ounce of camel's hay. for the space of ten days, and then leaving them to soak for two days in the oil, they press it out A
and store it. This oil has the virtue of cooling and of constricting. It is useful for ulcers

Oil of quinces, as used in apothecary shops, is made from not fully ripened fruit cut into small pieces in
L' Omphacine oil, and set in the sun with a good quantity of the fruit's own juice, and then in the bath of Mary, repeating

On Oenanthine Ointment. Chapter 42.

The flower of the wild vine is gathered at the time when it breathes most of its scent, and when it
is somewhat faded it is placed in Omphacine oil, stirred and mixed, and left
to rest for two days; it is then pressed and stored. It has astringent virtue, and corresponds
in its virtues to those of roses. Yet it neither softens nor dissolves the body.
The best is that which most breathes the scent of the wild vine.

L' The ointment of the flowers of the wild vine, which the ancients called Oenanthine, requires no further annotation, since
the method to be followed in making it is made perfectly clear here.

On Teline Ointment. Chapter 44.

Take five pounds of fenugreek, one of sweet calamus, and two of cyperus,
and put all of it to soak in nine pounds of oil for seven days, stirring three times
each day, and then press it out and store it. Some others use cardamom in place of the calamus
and xylobalsam in place of the cyperus. Others first thicken the oil with these things, then put
the fenugreek in as an infusion and press it. It has the virtue of softening and of ripening
abscesses. It is especially suited for all hardnesses in the private parts of women. It is applied
below to women who have difficulty in childbirth, after the moisture has first been expelled and
their parts dried. It is beneficial for inflammation of the liver, and is put into clysters used for
the straining of labor pains. It cleanses dandruff and ulcers of the head that are moist, and
mixed with wax is good for burns and for ringworm. It removes blemishes from the face. It is
put into hair-smoothing preparations to make the face radiant. One should choose that which is fresh
and does not have a strong smell of fenugreek, which leaves the hand smooth, and which is at once
sweet and bitter to the taste. For this is the most choice.

The luminaries of the apothecary shops, following Rasis, have another method (though not currently in use) of making fenugreek oil,
H which the Greeks call Teline, in which, beyond sweet calamus and cyperus, eight ounces
of elaterium are added.

On Marjoram Ointment. Chapter 44. D

Take wild thyme, cassia, southernwood, flower of watermint, leaves of myrtle,
and marjoram in equal portions, but in such quantity as one may reasonably judge sufficient.
Pound all together, and pour over them as much Omphacine oil as the virtue of the
ingredients being infused requires. Leave these things thus for four days, then press them out,
and put back into them an equal weight of each of those same ingredients fresh, and leaving them
for as long again, press them out. For in this way the oil is made more potent. One should therefore
choose that marjoram which is greenish-dark, which breathes well of its scent, and which is
moderately sharp to the taste. It has the virtue of warming and of drying. It is sharp, and is
suited for disorders and obstructions of the private parts of women. It provokes the menses,
the afterbirth, and childbirth. It is good for suffocations of the uterus. It eases
pains in the loins and in the groin. But it is more effective when used with honey. For

puto diftinguere qual foffe di loro ftato più eccellente. La feconda caufa, che induffe Diofcoride à chiamare l'uno Sanfuc-
cino, & l'altro Amaracino è perche in Cizico, come fi legge in quefto al proprio cap. nel. iij. libro, il Sanfucco fi chiama
Amaraco, donde quefto unguento fi portaelettiffimo, & per effer così da i Ciziceni ottimi compofitori di quello, chia-
to fecondo il loro coftume Amaracino, non uolfe Diofcoride cambiargli altrimenti il nome, ma lo lafciò in quel proprio,
C che egli da Cizico s'haueua riportato.

Dell'oglio del Bafilico. Cap. xlv.

Faffi l'oglio del Bafilico, come quello del Liguftro, in quefto modo. Prende
uenti lire d'oglio, & undici, & otto once di foglie di Bafilico, & lafciale un gior-
no, & una notte in macera, & poi fpriemelo, & riponlo, & come harai cauato
del colatoio le cofe fpriemute, rinfondele nella medefima quantità d'oglio,
& rifpriemele, che harai cofi il fecondo. Non fi fa il terzo, imperoche'l Bafilico non lo pa-
tifce. Tolle dipoi la medefima quantità di Bafilico frefco, & ritornauelo à infondere, come
dicemmo nel Rofado, & come ui fara ftato in infufione il pari fpatio di tempo rifpriemelo
di nuouo, & riponlo, & fe tu'l uorrai fare tre ò quattro uolte infondeui ogni uolta del Bafi-
lico nuouo. Puoffi fare d'oglio omphacino, ma l'altro modo è migliore. Tàto puo quefto,
quanto quello del Sanfucco. Ma non è tanto efficace.

Dell'unguento dell'Abrotano. Cap. xlvi.

Fare l'onguento d'Abrotano, fi toglie noue lire, & cinque once di quello oglio
odorifero, che fi prepara per fare il Ligufrino, & infondeuifi dentro otto lire di
foglie d'Abrotano per ifpatio d'un giorno, & d'una notte, & poi fi fprieme, &
uolendofi ferbare in lungo fe ne cauano le prime foglie, et ui fe n'infondono del-
le nuoue, & pofcia fi fprieme. Scalda, & giouoa alle opilationi, & durezze della madrice.
Prouoca i meftrui, & le fecondine.

Dell'unguento dell'Anetho. Cap. xlvij.

Olleffi à far l'onguento dell'Anetho otto lire, & noue once d'oglio, & undici, &
otto once di fiori d'Anetho. Lafciafi tutto in macera per un giorno. Spriemefi
pofcia con le mani, & ferbafi. Ma uolendofi fare d'un'altra infufione, ui fi ritor-
nano
