76 BOOK

On the Dog Briar. Chapter 104.

The Dog Briar is a shrub that grows into a tree considerably larger than the Briar, whose leaves are much broader than those of the myrtle. Around its branches it has firm, stout thorns. It produces a white flower, and a somewhat elongated fruit, resembling the pit of an olive, which as it ripens turns red, and has inside a certain down. The fruit, dried and cooked in wine, and the decoction drunk, stops fluxes of the body: but one must first remove that down of its, because it harms the windpipe of the lung.

I It does not seem to me that the Dog Briar is truly that species of wild rose which produces flowers rather similar to those roses called Musk roses, and fruit similar to that of the rose-bush, as some believe; for it would have sufficed to tell Dioscorides that it resembled the rose-bush, without saying that it grew into a tree much larger than the Briar, and that its leaves were similar to those of the myrtle, from which this wild Rosaio differs greatly, and the fruits are truly much larger than olive pits. In this belief I have since been confirmed by Pliny; for he calls the wild rose-bush particularly Cynorhodon, that is Dog Rose; praising its root wonderfully for the bite of rabid dogs in book 8, chapter 41, and likewise in book 25, chapter 2, where he says that the ancients understood by Dog Rose only those sponges that grow on it; and then writing of the Cynosbatos, that is Dog Briar, he made it into two species very different from the wild rose-bush, as one sees in chapter 24 of book 24, saying that one species has leaves like the sole of a man's foot, and the other like those of the caper. I am further moved, beyond this, by the history written of it by Theophrastus in chapter 17 of book 3, saying thus: The Dog Briar produces red fruit similar to the Pomegranate, and in size is midway between the shrubs and the Pomegranate tree. Its leaves are similar to those of the Vitex. Which shows there is no small difference between the Dog Briar and the wild Roses, of which he later wrote a particular history in chapter 6 of the sixth book, having first spoken at length of the domestic ones, saying thus: The small trees of the wild roses have branches and leaves rougher and more coarse than the domestic ones, and the flowers less colorful and less fragrant, and they are not as large as the domestic ones. Which shows that the wild rose-bush, which they call Cynorhodon, is one thing, and the Dog Briar, called by the Greeks Cynosbatos, is another; and therefore Marcello Vergilio of Florence is manifestly wrong in believing them to be one and the same thing, not perceiving how differently one writes from the other, his most familiar Pliny. To which point the venerable Fathers who have commented on the antidotary of Mesue, not having paid attention, say erroneously that the wild Roses are that plant which the Greeks call Cynosbatos. GALEN wrote of it in book 7 on the Faculties of Simples, saying thus: The fruit of this plant is somewhat astringent, but the leaves moderately so, and therefore its particular use is known to everyone. One must truly beware of that which has inside a kind of wool, which harms the windpipe of the lung.

On the Privet. Chapter 105.

The Privet is a tree that produces around its branches leaves similar to those of the olive, but broader, more tender, and greener, and white flowers, mossy and fragrant. Its fruit is black, similar to that of the elderberry. The finest grows in Ascalon and in Canopus. The leaves are astringent, and therefore when chewed they help ulcers of the mouth, and when used as a poultice they help carbuncles and the most violent inflammations. The decoction applied to burns from fire is useful. Ground and infused in the juice of the herb lanaria, they make the hair red. The flower, ground and applied with vinegar to the forehead, eases headache. The Ligustinum ointment mixed with warm things warms and softens the nerves.

We in Tuscany call the Privet Giustrico; others call it Olivetta, others Oluella, and others Chambrosene.
The Arabs call it Alcanna. It grows abundantly along hedgerows beside the public roads throughout Italy, and flowers at the end of Spring and the beginning of Summer. Some believe the Privet to be a certain species of bindweed, which winds itself along hedges around the shrubs, producing its white flowers similar to Bellflowers. In this opinion Servius the grammarian, commentator of Virgil, let himself be carried away, being little truly curious to learn its true history from Pliny or another authentic author. Others have believed the Privet to be the Caprifolium of the Arabs, which is the Ptxiacantha of Dioscorides, and not the Peryclimenum, as Ruellius thinks; but these too have been greatly mistaken. Galen wrote of it in book 7 on the Faculties of Simples, saying thus: Of the Privet the leaves and the tender tips are used, and they are of a mixed nature both in their faculties and in their qualities. For they have something digestive together with a watery substance, somewhat warm, and they have something astringent from a cold and earthy substance. For which reason some make a bath of their decoction for burns from fire, and beyond this use it also against many fiery inflammations, and likewise against carbuncles. For they dry without any irritation or sharpness. They are likewise useful when chewed for ulcers that arise on their own in the mouth.

A Phillirea è uno albero della grandezza del Ligustro, & produce le frondi an A

ferrato nel suo bottone, oltre al piccuolo della fronde prodotta per suo ligamento, pende ligato da uno altro piccuolo.
Resta uerde sino, che sta serrato, come che poscia nell'aprirsi alquanto gialleggi. Fiorisce la Tilia con gli alberi domestichi,
& fa il suo frutto tondo, alquanto lunghetro di quantità d'una faua, dauiso da cinque eminenti neruetti, dentro dalquale è

Del Cisto. Cap. cvij.

translation:
PRIMO
77
On the Phillirea. Chapter 106.

The Phillirea is a tree the size of the Privet, and its leaves are similar to those of the olive, though broader and darker; its fruit resembles that of the Lentisk, being black, sweetish, and growing in clusters. It grows in rough places. Its leaves are astringent and as useful as those of the wild olive where there is need of binding. Chewed, they are good for ulcers of the mouth, or used as a wash with their decoction. Drunk, they provoke urine, and likewise the menses.

All the modern interpreters of Dioscorides — namely Hermolaus, Ruellius, and Marcello Fiorentino — have believed that the Phillirea described by Dioscorides is truly the tree called Tilia, being deceived by the similarity of the name, since in Greek the Tilia is called Phillira, and not Phillirea. None of these so-called learned men, following one another's footsteps, having discerned this, called the Phillirea "Tilia" in their Latin interpretations. This led many to believe that Dioscorides did not know the Phillirea, since in every respect the Phillirea differs from the Tilia. This shows that these interpreters, besides having erred in translation, did not know what the true Tilia is; for had they had knowledge of it, they would easily have recognized their manifest error. Theophrastus wrote of the Phillira — that is, the true Tilia — in the tenth chapter of the fourth book, saying thus: Among the species of the Tilia, the male and female differ from each other in material, form, and in bearing or not bearing fruit. The wood of the male is hard, knotty, and yellow; the contrary is true of the female, which is white. The bark of the male is thicker, smoother, and harder, and therefore less flexible and tractable than that of the female. The male is sterile, while the female produces abundance of both flowers and fruits. The flower, enclosed in its bud, hangs besides the small stalk of the leaf produced for its support, fastened by another small stalk. It remains green while still closed, but upon opening turns somewhat yellow. The Tilia flowers together with the cultivated trees, and bears a round fruit, somewhat elongated, about the size of a bean, divided by five prominent ribs, inside which is a tiny seed resembling that of the Orache. The leaves are similar to those of Ivy, but more rounded near the stalk and pointed from the middle onward. They are slightly curled at the edges, all notched, and sweet and satisfying to the taste, and therefore much sought after by livestock for grazing. The contrary is seen in the fruit, which is never eaten by any animal. The trunk has little pith and is slightly softer than its wood, since the rest of the wood is soft and sweet. All these features Theophrastus gave for the Tilia, and they are found fully realized in our Tilia. But in my judgment they are not found in the Phillirea of Dioscorides, since the latter bears leaves like the olive, and the former like the Ivy. The Phillirea bears fruit like the Lentisk — a small, reddish berry resembling millet — while the Tilia produces a fruit the size of a bean, green and divided into sections by five ribs, with a seed inside similar to that of the Orache. This clearly demonstrates the difference between them. Furthermore, the height of our common Tilia and the breadth occupied by its dense branches confirms this, since the Phillirea of Dioscorides is a small shrub resembling the Privet. And if Pliny says that the Tilia is a rather low tree, while our experience shows the contrary, one must think that he was deceived by the similarity of the word into confusing the text of Theophrastus — from whom he drew the history — with that of Dioscorides. This leads me further to believe, seeing that he assigns to a single species — namely our common one — in chapter eight of book twenty-four, the virtues that Dioscorides attributes to the Phillirea, besides many others proper to it, as Ruellius has since done following him. The Phillirea then is a tree very different from the Tilia, but is not known in Italy in our times. The bark of the true Tilia, chewed and then applied as a plaster, consolidates fresh wounds; its leaves, ground up, resolve swellings of the feet; and the liquid that drips from it when it is cut to the pith causes hair to grow again and prevents the rest from falling out.

On the Cistus. Chapter 107.

The Cistus, which some call Citharus or Cissarus, grows in rocky places, and is a branchy, leafy shrub, not very large. It produces round, rough, and hairy leaves. The male bears flowers resembling those of the pomegranate, and the female bears white flowers. It has astringent virtue, and therefore its flowers, first ground and then drunk twice a day in harsh wine, are good in dysenteric fluxes. Applied as a liniment they stop creeping ulcers, and mixed with wax they help burns from fire and old ulcers.

On the Hypocistis. Chapter 108.

The Hypocistis, which some call Erythranum or Cytinus, grows at the roots of the Cistus and resembles the flower of the pomegranate. Three distinct varieties are found, of three different colors: red, green, and white. Its juice is extracted as from the acacia. Some, having taken the dry Hypocistis and ground it, infuse it...

loroso l'Hipocisto, quanto l'Acacia, ma maggiormente costringe, & disecca. Beuto, &
messo ne cristeri, ristagna i flussi stomachali, & disenterici, gioua à gli sputi del sangue, & à
i flussi delle donne.

Ascono il Cisto, & l'Hipocisto in piu luoghi di Toscana, ma copioso si ritroua ne piu aspri, & sassosi luoghi del-
N l'Apennino, & imperò douerebboro ueramente i buoni Spetiali fare ogni fatica, & usare ogni diligenza, di farsi
portare, ò di Toscana, ò d'altri luoghi l'uno, & l'altro. Imperoche senza il uero Hipocisto non si puo comporre
la Theriaca, ne altri assai medicamenti necessarij all'uso cotidiano della Medicina. Questi, che uolgarmente è in uso, è uer-
amente una mistura contrafatta del succhio spessito al Sole di quella radice, che noi chiamiamo in Toscana Safsfrica, oue-
ro Barba di becco, & Dioscoride chiama Tragopogono, & è nasciuto questo manifesto errore, impero che gli Arabi
chiamano il Cisto barba di becco, & di qui uiene, che coloro, che fanno il comune Hipocisto delle Spetiarie, credendosi,
che la barba di becco sopradetta sia quella, di cui intendono gli Arabi, ne sprìemono il suchio, & poscia lo condensano al
Sole, et cosi ingannano parimête se stessi, et poscia tutti coloro, che l'usano, in cambio del quale sarebbe assai manco male usa
re l'Acacia, quando pure anchora ella ci si portasse sincera. Imperoche cosi ritrouo scritto qui da Dioscoride, et parimente
B da Galeno nelli sucidanei. Puoisi anchora mancando l'Hipocisto uero prendere in suo luogo il succhio de balaussi, come si
uede in questo nel capitolo del Melagrano. Plinio ingannato dalla similitudine del uocabulo, confonde assi il scioccamente
l'historia del Cifso, che uuol dire Hedera, con quella del Cisto, & imperò fu dànato dal duttissimo Leoniceno. Fece del Ci-
sto mentione GALENO al. vij. delle facoltà de Semplici, così dicendo. Il Cisto, ouero Cistaro è uno alborsello, & al gu-
sto, & in ogni sua particolare operazione costrettituo, nientedimeno le frondi, & li germini teneri, pesi, & applicati sono
così disseccatiui, & costrettiui, che possono consolidare assai bene le ferite. I fiori sono piu ualorosi, di modo che beuti con
uino sanano i flussi disenterici, & le debolezze, et flussi stomachali. Sanano impiasrtati ulcere putride. E la uirtu loro
ueramente non poco costrettiua di modo, che si possono mettere nel secondo ordine. Noi è il Cisto così frigido, che non
habbia però un certo tepido calore. Quello, che chiamano Hipocisto è molto piu costrettituo, che nò sono le frondi, & im-
però è ualorissimo rimedio à tutti i flussi, come di sputo di sangue, di mestrui di donne, di stomacho, et di disenteria. Cor-
robors, & conforta tutte le membra del corpo debilitate per troppa humidità, et imperò i mette egli utilmente nelle epi-
thime stomachali, & del fegato, ne per altro si mette nella Theriaca, se non perche fortisfici, & corrobori i corpi.

C Del Ladano. Cap.cix.

Vna altra spetie di Cisto, ilqual chiamano alcuni Ladano, che cresce in albor-
scello, simile al Cisto, ma produce le frondi piu lunghe, e piu nere, lequali han-
no sopra di loro nel tempo della primauera, una certa grassezza. Sono costret-
tiue, & fanno tutti gli effetti del Cisto. Fassi di questo il Ladano. Imperoche
pascendosi delle sue frondi i becchi, & le capre si gli attacca quella tenace grassezza alle
barbe, & al uello delle coscie, & cosi se la riportano, & gliela pettinano poscia i Pastori, & li
quefannola, & colanla come si fa col mele. Fannone poi pastelli, & li ripongono. Sono alcu-
ni altri, che tirando, & sbattendo certe funi sopra à questi alborselli raschiano poi la gras-
sezza, che ui s'appicca, & fannone pastelli, & cosi poscia la serbano Lodasi per il migliore
quel Ladano, ch'è odorato, uerdeggiante, trattabile, grasso, non areoso, non sordido, ragio
so, come è quello, che nasce in Cipri. Il manco stimato, & il manco buono, è quello di Libia,
& d'Arabia. Ha il Ladano uirtu di scaldare, di costrignere, mollisiare, & aprire. Meschia-
D to con uino, mirrha, & oglio di mirto prohibisce il cascare dei capelli. Vnto con uino spe
gne le macchie delle cicatrici, & imbellisce la pelle. Distilasi con acqua melata, ouero con
oglio rosado nelle orecchie, che dogliano. Applicato in profumo tira fuore le secondine, &
messo ne i pessoli mollisfica le durezze della madrice. Mettesi utilmente nelle medicine mi-
tigatiue de i dolori, & parimente della tosse, & ne gli impiasrtri molisficatiui. Beuto con ui-
no uecchio, ristagna il corpo, & prouoca l'orina.

Hiamasi uolgarmente il Ladano, da chi Laudano, & da chi Odano, del quale com, che asai sene ritroui del con-
C trafatto, sofisticato, & di poco ualore, Nondimeno n'ho però sempre ritrouate dell'elettissimo in Venetia ap-
presso à piu profumieri, & spetialmente alla profumeria del Moro in sul ponte li Rialto. Di questo adunque, in
cui ueramente si ritrouano tutte quelle bone parti, che ui si richieggono debbono i buoni, & diligenti Spetiali cercar d'ha
uere nelle botteghe loro, & lasciare il contrafatto à coloro, che postasi la coscienza dopò ulle spalle non si curano uniuer-
salmente in ogni lor cosa, se quel, che comprano sia buono, ò cattiuo, pur che pochi denariui corrino. Plinio confondendo
assai (come nel precedente capitolo dicemmo) per la conformità de nomi l'historia del Cifso, che uuol significar l'hedera,

translation:
78 BOOK

A in water, and then cook it, and do everything that is done in making licio. The Hypocistis is as valuable as Acacia, but it binds and dries more strongly. Drunk, and used in enemas, it stops stomach and dysenteric fluxes, helps with spitting of blood, and with women's fluxes.

The Cistus and Hypocistis grow in many places in Tuscany, but are found most abundantly in the rougher and rockier places of the
N Apennines, and therefore good Apothecaries ought to take every care and use every diligence to have both brought to them, either from Tuscany or from other places. For without the true Hypocistis one cannot compound the Theriac, nor many other medicines necessary for daily use. What is commonly in use is truly a counterfeit mixture, made from the thickened juice dried in the Sun of that root which we in Tuscany call Safsfrica, or Barba di becco, and which Dioscorides calls Tragopogon, and this manifest error has arisen because the Arabs call the Cistus "barba di becco," and from this it comes that those who make the common Hypocistis in the apothecary shops, believing that the above-mentioned barba di becco is what the Arabs mean, press out its juice and then condense it in the Sun, and so they deceive themselves, and then all those who use it, in place of which it would be far less harmful to use Acacia, if only that too were brought to us pure. For so I find written here by Dioscorides, and likewise
B by Galen in his Succedanea. One may also, in the absence of true Hypocistis, take in its place the juice of balausti, as one sees in the chapter on the Pomegranate. Pliny, misled by the similarity of the words, very foolishly confuses the history of the Cifso, which means Hedera (ivy), with that of the Cistus, and was therefore condemned by the most learned Leonicenus. Galen made mention of the Cistus in book seven of the Faculties of Simples, saying thus: The Cistus, or Cistarus, is a small shrub, and in taste and in all its particular operations it is astringent; nonetheless its leaves and tender shoots, when pounded and applied, are so drying and astringent that they can consolidate wounds quite well. The flowers are more potent, so that drunk with wine they cure dysenteric fluxes and weaknesses, and stomach fluxes. Applied as a plaster they heal putrid ulcers. Their virtue is truly not a little astringent, so that they may be placed in the second order. The Cistus is not so cold as to lack a certain gentle warmth. That which is called Hypocistis is much more astringent than the leaves, and is therefore a most valuable remedy for all fluxes, such as spitting of blood, women's menstrual flows, stomach ailments, and dysentery. It strengthens and fortifies all the members of the body weakened by excessive moisture, and therefore he usefully puts it in stomach and liver epithymes, and it is placed in the Theriac for no other reason than to fortify and strengthen the body.

C On Ladanum. Chapter 109.

Another species of Cistus, which some call Ladanum, grows as a small shrub, similar to the Cistus, but produces longer and darker leaves, which in springtime have upon them a certain sticky substance. They are astringent and produce all the same effects as the Cistus. From this the Ladanum is made. For when goats and she-goats feed on its leaves, that tenacious sticky substance clings to their beards and to the fleece of their thighs, and so they carry it back, and the Shepherds then comb it off them, melt it, and strain it as one does with honey. They then make it into pastilles and store them. There are others who, by drawing and beating certain ropes over these small shrubs, scrape off the sticky substance that clings to them, and make it into pastilles, and so store it. The best Ladanum is praised as that which is fragrant, greenish, workable, fatty, not gritty, not foul-smelling, nor fibrous, like that which grows in Cyprus. The least prized and least good is that from Libya and Arabia. Ladanum has the virtue of warming, binding, softening, and opening. Mixed with wine, myrrh, and oil of myrtle, it prevents hair loss. Rubbed on with wine it removes the marks of scars and beautifies the skin. Distilled with honeyed water, or with rose oil, it is used in the ears when they ache. Applied as a fumigation it draws out the afterbirth, and placed in pessaries it softens hardnesses of the womb. It is usefully placed in medicines that mitigate pains, and likewise in coughs, and in emollient plasters. Drunk with old wine, it binds the body and provokes urine.

Ladanum is commonly called, by some Laudano, and by others Odano, of which, although much counterfeit, sophisticated, and of little value is to be found, I have nonetheless always found the finest quality in Venice at several perfumers, and especially at the perfume shop of the Moro on the Rialto bridge. Of this therefore, in which are truly found all the good qualities required of it, good and diligent Apothecaries ought to seek to have it in their shops, and leave the counterfeit to those who, having set their conscience aside, care not at all in any matter whether what they buy is good or bad, so long as they spend few pennies. Pliny, confusing greatly (as we said in the previous chapter) through the similarity of names the history of the Cifso, which means ivy,

L l'incarnate, & le bianche. Hannosì le rosse per le piu eccellenti, & dopo queste l'incarnate, & imperò si tengono
per le manco buone le bianche nostre comuni, non connumerando però con queste quella sorte di bianche molto
C odorisere, lequali in Toscana propriamente si chiamano Damaschine, & in a tri luoghi Moschette; imperoche queste so-
no le piu solutiue di tutte l'altre, & le piu odorifere. Sono le Rose composte di diuerse sustanze, il perche contengono in se
secondo le parti sue piu superficiali, & piu intrinsiche, diuersi temperamenti. Hanno primamente dalle parti terree, &
acquee, lequali mediocremente posseggono, la sustanza, & la stiticità. Dalle aerce alquanto di dolce, & d'aromatico, &
da quelle, che seguendo la natura del fuoco son calde, & sottili, l'amarezza, & il color rosso quelle, che son rosse. Nelle
fresche l'amaritudine uence la stiticità, & imperò perche la prima operatione loro solutiua, laquale non cognobbero gli
antichi Greci, procede dall'amarezza; le fresche soluono il corpo, & non le secche. Il succhio eccellente per comporre
diuersi medicamenti, si fa delle rose, & anche delle incarnate, quantunque non sia cosi utile. L'infusioni, che si fanno per
il Siropo rosado solutiuo, si fanno per il piu delle incarnate; Ma migliori, & piu solutiue sono le Moschette, che noi chia-
miamo Damaschine, quando sene potesse hauer copia; Percioché mangiansosi. xx. ò. xxv. delle loro odoratissime frondi
auanti al cibo soluono commodamente il corpo, & senza molestia alcuna. Il succhio delle Rose è apertiuo, risolutiuo,
astfersiuo, & solutiuo, & imperò solue egli la cholera, & mondifica il sangue da quella. Vale al trabocco di fiele, & alle
oppilationi dello stomacho, & del fegato. Conforta il cuore, conferisce al suo tremore, & caccia fuore gli homori, che ne
sono causa. Vale alle febri choleriche, come sono le Terzane di tutte le spetie. Connumerano i moderni Medici tra le me-
D dicine benedette l'infusione delle Rose, di cui si fa il Siropo solutiuo; Imperoche senza molestia, & senza alcun detri men-
to della natura solue il corpo, & purga la cholera. Le Rose bianche comuni (non dico le Moschette damaschine) non per
altro s'adoperano, che per far acqua; imperoche in queste non e quella uiua uirtù solutiua, come è nelle rosse, & nelle in-
carnate, & però parmi, che contra ogni ragione riprenda in questo il Manardo da Ferrara Mesue; Percioché quantun-
que nelle Moschette, lequali son bianche si troui piu uirtù solutiua, che in tutte l'altre; Nondimeno è da pensare, che Mes
sue non intendesse di queste, come cosa da lui non conosciuta, ma solamente delle comuni bianche usuali, alche puo ageuo-
lmente uerificare il saper noi, che nuoue sono le Moschette in Italia, ne si ritroua, che fussero cognosciute dagli antichi. So-
no ueramente le Rose da essere stimate, & tenute care, non solo per ornamento de i giardini, & per il giocondo spettaco-
lo, che rappresentano alla ufta, la Primauera, ma piu assai per la molta conferenza, che hanno con uarij, & diuersi medi-
camenti importanti alla uita dell'huomo. Le Rose saluatiche sono assai piu stittiche, & costrettiue, che le domestiche, ma
meno odorifere, ne si ritroua in loro uirtù alcuna solutiua, & imperò dicena Theophr asto al.vi.cap.del.vi.libro. Le Ro-
se saluatiche sono piu aspre delle domestiche, ne i rami, & nelle frondi. Hannoil fiore meno odorifero, & manco tinto di
colore, ne cosi egli ampio, come è quello delle domestiche. Ritrouasene oltre alle predette in piu, & uarij giardini d'Italia
di colore giallo, ma d'horribile odore. Cerchi appresso à Plinio al.iiij.cap.del.xxi.libro, chi è curioso di sapere le diuer-
sità delle

translation:
82 BOOK

A thick, until it condenses, and kept thus for eye liniments. The leaves of roses are dried in the shade, turning them often, so that they are not spoiled by mold or excessive heat. The decoction of the dried ones made in wine, well pressed, is useful for pains of the ears, head, gums, eyes, rectum and its intestine, and of the womb, applied with a feather, or administered as an enema. The dried red roses without pressing out the juice, applied as a plaster, treat inflammations of the chest area, moisture of the stomach, and erysipelas. The dried roses ground into powder are sprinkled on abrasions of the thighs, and mixed into antidotes for wounds, and into those compositions called Antheres. Burned, they serve to beautify the eyelashes. The centers of dried roses, powdered and applied to the gums, prevent fluxes that descend to them. Their buds, taken as a drink, stop fluxes of the body and spitting of blood.

On Rose Pastilles. Chapter 112.

B Rose pastilles are compounded in this manner. Take forty drams of fresh roses, dried of all moisture, just as they begin to wilt, ten of Indian nard, and six of myrrh. Grind everything together, and form pastilles weighing three obols each, and when they are well dried in the shade, put them in an unlined earthen vessel, sealing it so that no air enters. There are some who add two drams of costus, and as much of Iris of Illyria, and mix with honey and wine of Chios. They are used by women to wear around the neck in necklaces, to mask the unpleasant odor of sweat. They are likewise used as a powder to be sprinkled on the body after the bath, washing it off afterwards when dry with fresh water.

The roses that belong to Medicine are of several kinds; but those most common in Italy are the red ones,
L the incarnate, and the white. The red are held to be the most excellent, and after these the incarnate, and therefore the white ones common among us are considered the least good, not counting among these that kind of very fragrant white roses which in Tuscany are properly called Damaschine, and in other places Moschette; for these are
C the most laxative of all, and the most fragrant. Roses are composed of diverse substances, which is why they contain, according to their more superficial and more intrinsic parts, diverse temperaments. They have primarily from their earthy and watery parts, which they possess moderately, substance and astringency. From the airy parts somewhat sweetness and aroma, and from those following the nature of fire, warmth and subtlety, bitterness, and the red color in those that are red. In the fresh ones the bitterness overcomes the astringency, and therefore because the first laxative action, which the ancient Greeks did not recognize, proceeds from the bitterness; the fresh ones loosen the body, and not the dried ones. The excellent juice for compounding various medicines is made from the roses, and also from the incarnate ones, although it is not so useful. The infusions made for the laxative rose syrup are made mostly from the incarnate ones; but better and more laxative are the Moschette, which we call Damaschine, when one can obtain a supply; for if one eats twenty or twenty-five of their most fragrant petals before meals, they comfortably loosen the body without any discomfort. The juice of roses is aperitive, resolvent, cleansing, and laxative, and therefore it purges bile and cleanses the blood of it. It is good for overflow of bile, and for obstructions of the stomach and liver. It comforts the heart, helps its trembling, and drives out the humors that cause it. It is good for bilious fevers, such as tertian fevers of all kinds. Modern physicians count among the blessed medicines the infusion of roses, from which the laxative syrup is made; for without discomfort and without any detriment to nature it loosens the body and purges bile. White roses common among us (I do not mean the Damaschine Moschette) are used for nothing other than making water; for in these there is not that lively laxative virtue as in the red ones and the incarnate ones, and therefore it seems to me that Manardo of Ferrara is wrong to criticize Mesue in this matter; for although in the Moschette, which are white, more laxative virtue is found than in all the others, nevertheless one must think that Mesue did not mean these, as something unknown to him, but only the common ordinary white ones, which is easily verified by our knowledge that the Moschette are new in Italy, nor is it found that they were known to the ancients. Roses are truly to be esteemed and held dear, not only for the ornament of gardens, and for the joyful spectacle they present in Spring, but much more for the great usefulness they have with various and diverse medicines important to human life. Wild roses are considerably more astringent and constringent than the domestic ones, but less fragrant, nor is any laxative virtue found in them, as Theophrastus noted at chapter 6 of book 6. Wild roses are more rough than domestic ones in their branches and leaves. Their flower is less fragrant and less richly colored, and not as large as that of the domestic ones. There are found, besides those already mentioned, in various gardens of Italy roses of yellow color, but of horrible odor. Let whoever is curious to know the various

84 LIBRO

A le caligini de gli occhi, et guarisce la scabbia, la smania, et i flussi uecchi delle palpebre. Giuoua all'orecchie, che menano marcia, al gorgozzule, alle gingiue ulcerate, alle fessure delle labbra, & del sedere, & alle scorticature, ungendone i loro luoghi. Mettesi ne i crisieri, & beesi per i flussi stomachali, & disenterici. Dassi con acqua al sputo del sangue, & alla tosse. Giuoua al morso del cane arrabbiato mangiato in pilule alla quantità d'una faua, ouero beuto con acqua. Vngendone i capegli gli imbiondisce. Sana i panarici delle dita, & l'ulcere putride, et corrosiue. Applicato ristregne i flussi delle donne. Beuto con latte, ouero rolto in pilule giuoua à i morsi de gli animali rabbiosi. Dicesi che l'Indiano si fa d'un alborsello, che si chiama Lonchite, ilquale è spinoso con rami dritti, di lunghezza di tre gombiti, & qualche uolta maggiori, piu grossi del Rouo, & escono assai insieme dalla radice. La sua corteccia spezzata rosseggia, & le sue frondi rassembrano quelle dell'Oliuo, lequali (secondo che si dice) cotte nell'aceto, & beute sanano l'infiamgasioni della melza. Vagliono à trabocco di fiele, & prouocano i mestrui, & oltre à questo, si crede, che trite, & beute crude faccino il

B medesimo, & di piu affirmasi, che beuto mezzo ciatho del suo seme purghi la fiema, & che sia anchora rimedio de ueleni.

L Licio, che uolgarmente si tiene hoggi nelle Spetiarie, è ueramente assai nelle sembianze sue disconuenuole da
I quello, che qui ne scriue Dioscoride; Imperò che'l nostro non s'accende non è rosso di dentro, ne risponde al giustarlo alcuna amaritudine. Ilche dimostra essere ueramente contrafatto di piu, et diuersi succhi. Dicono alcuni, che si fa questo, che è in comune uso delle bacche del Ligustro. Altri dicono di quelle della Matrisella; altri di quelle del Saguinello, & altri di tutte queste insiememente peste: Nondimeno faccisi come si uoglia, è però cosa certa che il uero non si ci porta à tempi nostri di Licia, onde s'ha egli preso il nome. Nascono gli alberi, da cui si potrebbe cauare il uero (secondo che riferisce il Brasauola) nelle Alpi di Liguria. Ma la poca cura, che s'ha della piu parte delle cose, che sono in uso per le medicine non lascia conoscere quello, che spontaneamente ne concede la natura. Cominciansi però à portare in Italia i frutti del suo alborsello, liquali sono simili al pepe, & parimente si ci porta qualche pezzo del uero, poscia che ne è stato fatto querela à coloro, che nauigano in Alessandria. Mancandone il Licio si puo in suo luogo usare la Morca dell'oglio cotta in uso di rame, ouer amente i Sommacchi; percioche cosi ritrouo io essere la dottrina di Dioscoride, come si puo chiaramente uedere legendosene à luoghi proprij la loro historia. Scrisse del Licio Galeno al. vij. delle facoltà de Semplici, cosi dicendo.

C La Pixiacantha albero spinoso, di cui si fa quel medicamento liquido chiamato Licio, quale usano per è liuidi, p' l'infiamgagioni della bocca, & del sedere, all'ulcere formicose, putride, & contumaçi, all'orecchie, che menano marcia, alle scorticature, & à i panarici delle dita. E'nelle facultà sue diseccatiua, & composta di sustanze di diuerse spetie chiamate da Greci Eterogenee. Delle quali l'una è di parti sottili composta, calida, & digestiua, & l'altra è frigida, et terrestre, da cui ha ella la uirtu costrettina. Ma questa qualità nel Licio è ueramente poca; percioche piu hae gli dei digestiuo, & del diseccatiuo, nel che ascende al secondo ordine, & ritrouasi nella caldità sua quasi temperato, & imperò usano questo medicamento in uarie, & diuerse cose. Vsanlo dico come afterssiuo, all'ulcere malignie, & putride, & come costrettiuo, à i flussi stomachali, disenterici, & femminili. Nasce questo Licio abondantissimamente in Licia, & Capadocia; Ma quello, che nasce in India è ueramente piu ualoroso.

Dell'Acacia. Cap. cxiiij.

D Asce l'Acacia in Egitto, & è uno alborsello spinoso, si folto di rami, che non si distende in alto. Produce il fiore biaco, & il seme simile à i lupini, chiuso ne i baccelli, del quale si sprieme il succhio, & seccasi all'ombra. Quello, che si fa del maturo è nero, et quello dell'immaturo rosseggia. Lodasi quello, che tende alquanto al rosso, & che è odorato, quanto porta l'Acacia. Cauanlo alcuni ispriemendo insieme le frondi, e'l seme. Nasce anchora di questa spina, una gomma. Ha l'Acacia uirtu di ristrignere, & di rinfrescare. Il suo succhio è conuenuole alle medicine de gli occhi. Giuoua al fuoco sacro, alle bugance, all'ulcere serpiginose, alli pterigij delle dita. Beuto, & messo ne i crisieri ferma i flussi delle donne, rimette, la radrice dislogata, & ristagna i flussi del corpo. Sana applicato l'ulcere della bocca, & riduce gli occhi, che escono del suo luogo, et fa neri i capelli. Lauasi nell'acqua poluerizzato per le medicine de gli occhi, tanto che rimutandogliela spesse uolte resti chiara nel fine, & cosi poscia se ne formano i trocisci. Brusciasi mettendola nella fornace in un uaso di terra crudo, quando si cuocono le tegole. Brusciasi anchora sopra à gli ardenti carboni soffiando continuamente. Fomentansi le giunture smosse con la dicottione di tutta la pianta. Quella della sua gomma è eccellente, che di figura si rassembra à i
uermini

translation:
84 LIBRO

A It clears dimness of the eyes, and cures scabies, itching, and old discharges of the eyelids. It is useful for ears that produce pus, for sore throats, for ulcerated gums, for cracks in the lips and seat, and for abrasions, by anointing those places. It is given in enemas, and drunk for stomach fluxes and dysentery. Given with water, it is used for spitting blood and for coughs. It is useful against the bite of a rabid dog, taken in pills the size of a bean, or drunk with water. Anointing the hair with it turns it blond. It heals whitlows of the fingers, and putrid and corrosive ulcers. Applied, it restrains the fluxes of women. Drunk with milk, or dissolved in pills, it helps against the bites of rabid animals. It is said that the Indian kind comes from a small shrub called Lonchite, which is thorny with straight branches three cubits long, and sometimes more, thicker than bramble, with many growing together from the root. Its crushed bark turns reddish, and its leaves resemble those of the olive, which (as they say) cooked in vinegar and drunk, cure inflammations of the spleen. They are useful against overflow of bile and promote menstruation; and moreover it is believed that, ground and drunk raw, they do the

B same, and furthermore it is affirmed that drinking half a cyathus of its seed purges phlegm, and that it is also a remedy against poisons.

I The Lycion that is commonly kept today in apothecaries is in its appearance very unlike what Dioscorides describes here; for ours does not ignite, is not red inside, nor does it have any bitterness to taste it. This shows it to be truly adulterated with many and various juices. Some say it is made from the berries of the privet, which are in common use. Others say from those of the wild marjoram; others from those of the dogwood, and others from all of these pounded together. Nevertheless, however it is made, it is certain that the true Lycion is not brought to us in our times from Lycia, from where it takes its name. The trees from which the true kind could be obtained (as Brasavola reports) grow in the Alps of Liguria. But the little care taken over most things used in medicine prevents us from recognizing what nature spontaneously provides. The fruits of its shrub are beginning to be brought to Italy, which are similar to pepper, and likewise some pieces of the true kind are brought to us, since complaint has been made to those who sail to Alexandria. In the absence of Lycion, one may use in its place the lees of oil cooked in a copper vessel, or else Sumac; for so I find to be the doctrine of Dioscorides, as may be clearly seen by reading the places proper to their history. Galen wrote of Lycion in book seven of the Faculties of Simples, saying thus:

C The Pyxicantha is a thorny tree from which is made that liquid medicine called Lycion, which is used for bruises, for inflammations of the mouth and seat, for creeping, putrid, and stubborn ulcers, for ears that discharge pus, for abrasions, and for whitlows of the fingers. In its faculties it is drying, and composed of substances of various types which the Greeks call heterogeneous. One of these is composed of subtle parts, is warm and digestive, and the other is cold and earthy, from which it draws its astringent virtue. But this quality in Lycion is truly little; for it has more of the digestive and drying, in which it rises to the second degree, and its warmth is found to be nearly temperate, and therefore this medicine is used for various and different purposes. They use it, I say, as a detergent for malignant and putrid ulcers, and as an astringent for stomach, dysenteric, and feminine fluxes. This Lycion grows most abundantly in Lycia and Cappadocia; but that which grows in India is truly more potent.

Of Acacia. Chapter 114.

D Acacia grows in Egypt, and is a small thorny shrub, so dense with branches that it does not grow tall. It produces white flowers, and seeds similar to lupins, enclosed in pods, from which the juice is pressed out and dried in the shade. That which comes from the ripe plant is black, and that from the unripe is reddish. That which tends somewhat to red and is fragrant is praised as best in Acacia. Some extract it by pressing the leaves and seeds together. A gum also comes from this thorn. Acacia has the virtue of astringency and cooling. Its juice is suitable for medicines of the eyes. It is useful for erysipelas, for carbuncles, for creeping ulcers, for pterygium of the fingers. Drunk and given in enemas, it stops the fluxes of women, reduces a dislocated uterus, and checks fluxes of the body. Applied, it heals ulcers of the mouth, reduces protruding eyes, and blackens the hair. It is washed in water when powdered for medicines of the eyes, changing the water frequently until it remains clear at the end, and then troches are formed from it. It is burned by placing it in the furnace in an unfired earthen vessel when the tiles are being fired. It is also burned over hot coals with continuous blowing. Joints that have been put out are fomented with a decoction of the whole plant. That of its gum is excellent, which in shape resembles
worms

text:
86 LIBRO
Del Vitice. Cap.cxv.

A IL Vitice,ilquale altrimenti si chiama Agnos,& parimente Lygos,è pianta,che cresce in albero.Nasce in luoghi aspri,& inculti appresso alle riue de i fiumi.Ha i rami lunghi,et malageuoli da rompere.Produce le frondi come d'Oliuo,ma piu tenere.Enne di due spetie,una cioè che produce i fiori biàchi,porporizzanti, & l'altra del tutto porporei.E'il suo seme simile al Pepe.Ha uirtu,et facoltà calida,et costrettiua.Il seme beuto giouà al morso de gli animali uelenosi,& conferisce à i difetti della melza,& à gli hidropici.Fa abondare il latte,et prouoca i mestrui beuto con uino al peso d'una dramma,disecca la sperma,offende la testa,& prouoca il sonno. La dicottione del seme,& delle frondi uale sedendosi in essa alle infiammagioni,& altri difetti de i luoghi naturali del le donne.Il seme beuto con pulegìo,applicato,& profumato prouoca i mestrui. Vnto leua il dolore del capo,& distillasi à i lethargici,& phrenetici in sul capo con oglio,& aceto. Le frondi sparte per terra,& parimente fumentate cacciano gli animali uelenosi,& applicate
B guariscono i morsi delle serpi.Impiastrate con burro,& frondi di uiti risoluono le durezze de i testicoli.Il seme applicato cò acqua mitiga le fessure del sedere,& aggiuntoui le frondi, cura le giunture smosse,& le ferite.Credesi,che li usandanti,che portano in mano un bastò ne di Vitice non si scortichino per il caminare,in alcuna parte del corpo.Chiamasi da i Greci questo albero Agnos,cioè casto,impero che le dòne,che osseruauano castità ne sacrificii di Cerere appresso à gli Athenìesi,si faceuano i letti delle frondi del Vitice.Chiamasi Lygos, cioè uimina,per essere i suoi rami molli,& arrendeuoli.

L Vitice,che uolgarmente si chiama Agno casto,è in Italia notißima pianta,& come testifica Plinio al.ix.capo del
I xxiilj.libro,è di due spetie,bianco cioè,& nero,maggiore,& minore.Cresce il nero,ilquale è il maggiore,alla grandezza del Salcio,et il bianco,ilquale è il minore,è piu folto di rami,et piu sarmentoso,et ha le sue frondi bianc che,et lanuginose,il suo fiore è meschiato di bianco,et di porpora,et quello del maggiore è puramente porporeo.Il Vitice è sempre il primo albero,che fiorisce nella Primauera.È,secò do che riferisce Galeno al.vi.libro delle facoltà de Semplici, caldo,et secco nel terzo ordine,et composto di parti molto sottili.al gusto acuto,& costrettiuo,il cui seme è piu ualoroso d'ogni altra cosa per cacciare la uentosità del corpo.Sminuisce il desiderio del coito,& parimente il seme generatiuo, non solamente disseccando,come credono alcuni,ma cacciando la uentosità,senza laquale in quello atto non si puo fare. Le frondi,secondo che riferisce Plinio,mescolate con la farina d'orzo maturano quelle posteme,che sono malageuoli da matura re.Giouà il seme beuto al morso di quelle spetie di ragni,che per occulta proprietà del loro ueleno sanno indurire il
C membro genitale.Il seme,& le frondi trite con Aphronitro,& aceto sanano le uolatiche,& le lentigini,& con mele guariscono l'ulcere,& le posteme della bocca.

Del Salice. Cap.cxvi.

IL Salice è albero uolgare,le cui frondi,seme,corteccia,et liquore hanno uirtu costrettiua.Le frondi trite,et beute con un poco di uino,& di pepe uagliono à i dolori de i fianchi,& tolte sole con acqua non lasciano ingrauìdare le donne.Rista gna il seme beuto lo sputo del sangue.Il che fa parimente la sua corteccia.La cui cenere macerata in aceto guarisce i porri,et i calli,che s'impiastrano con essa.Il succhio delle frondi,et della corteccia cotto con oglio rosado in un guscio di Melagrano,gioua à i dolori delle orecchie.La dicottione d'ammendune gioua per uia di fomento alle podagre,& mon
D difica la farfarella,Cogliensene il liquore intaccandogli la corteccia nel tempo,ch'ei produce il fiore,& ritrouasi poi congelato nelle intaccature,& è utile per tutti gli impedimenti, che offuscano la uista.

Vantunque Dioscoride non habbia trattato del Salcio,se non sotto una spetie;Sono nò dimeno(come s'ha da Theophrasto al.xiij.del.iij.libro,et da Plinio al.xxxvij.del.xvi.)i Salci di piu,et diuerse spetie,come sono quelli,di cui
Q per tutta Lombardia se ne fanno pertiche,et pali per le uigne.Quelli di ben giallo colore,che si fendono per legare le cerchia delle botti.Quelli de i quali se ne fanno ceste alla grossa per usare in uilla,et quelli,che sono di tutti i piu sottili chiamati in Toscana Venchi,di cui fanno i panieri.Tre sono i succhi del Salcio recitati da Plinio,anchora che Dioscoride facesse mentione solamente d'uno,de i quali l'uno rifuda per se stesso dal tronco à modo di Gomma,l'altro dall'intaccare,che si fa nella corteccia,& il terzo cola da i tronconi,quando si gli tagliano i rami nell'Autunno.Non ritrouò,chi dica della sua spuma bianca,laqual dopo il disforire si uede in grossi fiocchi pendere da i suoi ramuscelli,& portarsi poscia dal uento per l'aria à modo di piume.E'il Salcio albero,che non s'inuecchia,& del suo legno,per eser molto tiglio so,tenace,& leggiero,se ne fanno le targhe,& le rotelle.
description: Pietro Andrea Matthioli's landmark Italian translation of Dioscorides De Materia Medica. The first vernacular edition to make classical Greek botanical medicine accessible to European physicians.
translation:
86 BOOK
On the Chaste Tree. Chapter 115.

A The Chaste Tree, which is also called Agnos and likewise Lygos, is a plant that grows into a tree. It grows in rough and uncultivated places along the banks of rivers. It has long branches that are difficult to break. It produces leaves like those of the Olive, but more tender. It is of two kinds: one that produces white flowers tinged with purple, and the other entirely purple. Its seed resembles Pepper. It has warm and astringent properties. The seed drunk gives relief from the bite of venomous animals, and benefits disorders of the spleen and those with dropsy. It increases the flow of milk, and provokes menstruation when drunk with wine at the weight of one dram; it dries up the sperm, troubles the head, and induces sleep. A decoction of the seed and leaves is beneficial when sat in for inflammations and other disorders of women's private parts. The seed drunk with pennyroyal, applied and fumigated, provokes menstruation. Rubbed on, it takes away headache, and dripped on the head with oil and vinegar it helps those suffering from lethargy and frenzy. The leaves scattered on the ground, and likewise used as fumigation, drive away venomous animals, and applied
B they heal the bites of serpents. Made into a poultice with butter and vine leaves they dissolve hardnesses of the testicles. The seed applied with water eases fissures of the seat, and with leaves added, it cures dislocated joints and wounds. It is believed that travelers who carry a staff of Chaste Tree do not chafe any part of their body while walking. The Greeks call this tree Agnos, meaning chaste, because women who maintained chastity in the rites of Ceres among the Athenians made their beds from the leaves of the Chaste Tree. It is called Lygos, meaning withies, because its branches are soft and flexible.

The Chaste Tree, commonly called Agno casto, is a well-known plant in Italy, and as Pliny testifies in book 24, chapter 9,
I it is of two kinds, white and black, the greater and the lesser. The black, which is the greater, grows to the size of a Willow, and the white, which is the lesser, is more densely branched and more twiggy, and has white, woolly leaves; its flower is mixed with white and purple, while that of the greater is purely purple. The Chaste Tree is always the first tree to flower in Spring. According to Galen in book 6 on the Properties of Simples, it is hot and dry in the third degree, and composed of very subtle parts, sharp to the taste and astringent; its seed is more effective than anything else for dispersing flatulence from the body. It diminishes the desire for coitus and likewise the generative seed, not only by drying, as some believe, but by driving out the flatulence without which that act cannot take place. The leaves, according to Pliny, mixed with barley flour, ripen those abscesses that are difficult to bring to a head. The seed drunk helps against the bite of those kinds of spiders which, by some hidden property of their venom, cause hardening of the
C genital member. The seed and leaves ground with Aphronitro and vinegar heal ringworm and freckles, and with honey they heal ulcers and abscesses of the mouth.

On the Willow. Chapter 116.

The Willow is a common tree, whose leaves, seed, bark, and sap all have astringent properties. The leaves ground and drunk with a little wine and pepper help with pains in the sides, and taken alone with water they prevent women from conceiving. The seed drunk stanches the spitting of blood. The bark does the same. Its ash macerated in vinegar cures warts and calluses when applied as a poultice. The juice of the leaves and bark cooked with rose oil in a pomegranate rind helps with earaches. A decoction of both is useful as a fomentation for gout, and
D it cleanses dandruff. The sap is collected by cutting into the bark when the tree produces its flower, and it is later found congealed in the cuts; it is useful for all impediments that cloud the sight.

Although Dioscorides treated the Willow under only one kind, there are nonetheless (as we learn from Theophrastus in book 3, chapter 13, and from Pliny in book 16, chapter 37) willows of many and diverse kinds, such as those throughout Lombardy from which poles and stakes for vineyards are made; those of fine yellow color that are split to make barrel hoops; those from which coarse baskets for farm use are made; and those which are the finest of all, called in Tuscany Venchi, from which baskets are woven. Three kinds of sap from the Willow are described by Pliny, although Dioscorides mentioned only one: the first exudes by itself from the trunk like gum, the second comes from cutting the bark, and the third drips from the trunks when the branches are cut in autumn. No one has described its white foam, which after flowering can be seen hanging in large tufts from its small branches, and is then carried through the air by the wind like feathers. The Willow is a tree that never ages, and from its wood, which is very tough, strong, and light, shields and bucklers are made.

PRIMO 87

On the Wild Olive Tree. Chapter 117. A

The leaves of the wild olive, which some call the Oleaster and others the Olive of Ethiopia, have the virtue of being astringent. Ground up and made into a poultice, they treat the sacred fire, carbuncles, epinyctides, creeping ulcers, corrosive ulcers, and hangnails of the fingers. Made into a liniment with honey, they cause the scab of cauterizations to fall off, cleanse sordid ulcers, and dissolve lumps and inflammations when applied with honey. They rejoin the scalp when it has been torn from the bone, and chewed they are good for ulcers of the mouth, especially in children. The juice does the same, as does a decoction of them. The juice, applied, stanches the flow of blood and the menstrual flow in women. It represses and prevents growths on the eyes, and likewise pustules, and prevents cataracts and ulcerations of those parts, and is therefore very usefully employed in collyria made for corrosions of the eyelids. The method of preparing it is as follows: the leaves are pounded, and when pounded they are sprinkled with wine or rainwater and squeezed. The juice is then dried in the sun and made into lozenges, but it is better and keeps longer when expressed with wine than with water. It is good for ulcerated ears and for those that are moist and running with pus. The leaves, mixed with barley flour, are conveniently applied as a poultice in stomach fluxes. The branches and flowers are burned so that their ash may serve in place of Spodium, placing them in an unglazed earthen vessel covered and well sealed at the mouth, and leaving them inside until the vessel is fired in the furnace. They are then quenched with wine and kneaded again with wine and re-fired. The ash is then washed in the same manner as white lead is washed, and made into lozenges, since this ash is no less effective for diseases of the eyes than Spodium. The burned branches of the domestic olive have the same virtues, but they are not so effective, and therefore, being not so strong, they are more suitable in eye medicines. The foam that exudes from the green wood of the wild olive when it burns cures mange, dandruff, and ringworm. And the olive stones, made into a liniment, cure dandruff, corrosive ulcers, and creeping ulcers. The kernel of the stone causes rotten and scabby nails to fall off when applied to them with grease and flour.

On Salted and Preserved Olives. Chapter 118. C

Preserved olives, pounded and applied, prevent blisters from rising in burns from fire. They cleanse sordid ulcers. Rinsing the mouth with their brine tightens the gums and firms loose teeth. Fresh olives that are reddish in color before they ripen are more useful to the stomach and are binding to the body. But the black and fully ripe ones spoil more easily, harm the stomach, offend the eyes, and cause headache. Dried, and made into a liniment, they arrest spreading ulcers and break up carbuncles.

On the Oil of Wild Olives. Chapter 118.

The oil made from wild olives, held in the mouth and used to rinse it, benefits putrid and inflamed gums. It firms loose teeth, and used warm it helps with catarrhs descending to the gums. But it must be applied with a small piece of wool wound around the tip of a probe, until they turn white. D

On the Liquor, or Gum, of the Olive of Ethiopia. Chapter 120.

The gum of the olive of Ethiopia resembles Scammony, is red, condensed into tiny droplets, and biting. That which resembles Ammoniac and turns blackish, and which does not bite, is truly worthless. A similar gum also distills from our own olives, both domestic and wild. This gum, rubbed on, is good for weaknesses, white spots, and scars of the eyes. It provokes urine and the menstrual flow. Placed in the cavity of teeth, it effectively removes pain from them. It is numbered among poisons, promotes childbirth, cures mange and impetigo, and this olive of Ethiopia is also called the wild olive.

LIBRO
Della Morca dell'Oglio. Cap.cxxt.

A Morca è la feccia dell'Oliue spriemute, laquale cotta in un uaso di rame di Cipri fino, che si spessisca come mele, è costrettiua, & è nelle uirtu sue in ogni effetto simile al Licio. Mauale particolarmente con molta utilità à i dolori de denti applicata con aceto, ò con uino, ouero con uino melato. Mettesi ne medicamenti de gli occhi, & in quelli, che si fanno per costipare i pori della carne. Inuechiandosi di uenta più ualorosa. Mettesi nell'ulcere del sedere utilissime, in quelle de membri uirili, & de luoghi naturali delle donne. Cotta con oglio omphacino alla spessitudine del mele circondandone i denti guasti, gli fa cadere. Vnta con dicottione di lupini, & chameleonta, sana la rogna de gli animali quadrupedi. Impiastrasi calda la fresca non cotta utilmente alle podagre, & altri dolori di giunture. Vntone una pelle, che habbi la lana, & applicata à gli hidropici, risolue l'enfsagione.

B Sendo gli Oliui, l'Oliue, l'Oglio, la Gomma de gli Oliui, & la Morca tutte cose, & frutti d'una medesima pianta, non m'è parso fuore di proposito scriuerne insememnte, & così sodisfare à quanto farà dibisogno à ciascuna parte. Nascono gli Oliui saluatichi nel Contado di Siena, & in uari altri luoghi di Toscana abondantemente, & molto più piccioli de gli altri domestichi, spinosi, & di più breui frondi. L'Oliue loro, delle quali se ne caricano senz'amisura, sono assai minori delle domestiche, ma al gusto assai più saporite. Fannone manifestamente fede i Tordi, i Merli, & gli Storni, imperoche assai più uolentieri mangiano le saluatiche, che le domestiche. Custodiscono i nostri Contadini, che si dilettano d'uccellare questi Oliui saluatichi da gli augelli con grande arte, sino che le domestiche sieno del tutto ricolte, one poscia co'l uischio prendono una infinità de Merli, & di Tordi tutto il mese di Decembre, & di Gennaio. Pochi sono in Toscana, che ricolgbino l'Oliue saluatiche per far Oglio. Impero che l'abondanza delle domestiche, fa che poco s'apprezzino le saluatiche. Ritrouο appresso à gli antichi dieci sorti d'Oliue, cioè le Pausie, l'Algiane, le Liciniane, le Sergie, le Netie, le Calmine, l'Orchie, le Regie, le Circite, & le Murtee. Ben che Virgilio solo di tre sorte scriuesse, come ueramente à tempi nostri, non di più, che di tre sorte se ne ueggono in Toscana, & massime in quel di Siena. Delle quali, quelle della prima forte, come che le sieno prodotte dai più piccioli Oliui, sono non dimeno di bella, & notabile grossezza, simili alle Bolognesi. Mangiansi queste acconcie in salamuoia ne i cibi; imperoche per far Oglio sono del tutto inutili. Le seconde belle e di grossezza, e di colore (anchora che sieno delle prime assai minori) sono le migliori, che si ritrouino per far Oglio: Imperoche le lo fanno aureo, dolce, chiaro, & saporito di tutta eccellenza. Gli Oliui, che le producono si chiamano uolgarmente Oliuastre, & sono alberi di grandissima procerità, con i suoi rami, che ampiamente s'allargano. Le terze poscia sono quelle, che son communi à tutta Italia. L'eccellenti acconcie in salamuoia si portano à Roma, & in altri luoghi d'Italia, oue si ritrouino le più laute mense, d'Ispagna. Fra l'Oliuo, & la Quercia è (secondo, che gli antichi scrissero) mortale inimicitia, di modo, che piantandosi Oliui appresso alle Quercie presto si perdono. Diuentano sterili gli Oliui quando sono pasciuti dalle capre nel primo loro germogliare, al che non si ritroua rimedio. Ma se per altra cagione gli Oliui non portano il frutto è ualoroso, & prouato rimedio scoprirgli le radici tutto il tempo del Verno. La Gomma de i saluatichi, ouero Ethiopici Oliui, come che à molte cose la sia utile, non dimeno à i tempi nostri non è in uso nelle Spetiarie, ne so che la si ricolga. Alcuni s'hanno pensato (come dicemo di sopra nel capitolo dell'Acacia) che la sia la Gomma Arabica, che s'usa nelle Spetiarie, & altri, che la sia la Gomma Elemi. Ma dimostra ueramente, che la Gomma dell'Oliuo Ethiopico non sia la Gomma Elemi, ne l'Arabica il non si ritrouare, che alcuna di queste sia al gusto mordace, & ulceratiua, & per uedersi che quella, che chiamiamo uolgarmente nelle Spetiarie Gomma Elemi, più presto è una Ragia, ouero liquore prodotto da qualche à noi incognito albero forse simile al Pino, all'Abeto, ouero al Pezzo, che spetie di Gomma di sorte alcuna. Imperoche al fuoco, così come fanno l'altre Ragie, subito si fonde, et si liquefia tutta come cera. Ilche non fa alcuna sorte di Gomma. Ma come che non s'habbi à i tempi nostri alcuna chiarezza da qual pianta habbi la Gomma Elemi la sua origine; Non dimeno per quanto hanno esperimentato i Medici de nostri tempi, & massimamente Chirurgici, è ella la più eccellente di tutte l'altre sorti di Ragie nel medicare le serite del capo. Della morca utilissime dell'Oglio altro non resta à dire, se non che come scriue Catone, è utile à mesolarla con la Calcina per intonicare i magazzini, & le botteghe dei panni, & de i drappi di seta. Imperoche la prohibisce i ragni, le tignuole, & altri uermicelli, & nociui animali, & oltre à ciò l'humidità, che rifuda dalle mura.

Della Quercia, delle Ghiande, del Faggio, & dell'Ilice. Cap.cxxij.

D Gni Quercia ha uirtu costrettiua, & massime quella corteccia sottile, ch'è fra la grossa corteccia, & il legno, & così medesimamente quella pellicina sotto al guscio delle Ghiande. Dassi la dicottione loro ne i flussi disenterici, & stomachali, & allo sputo del sangue, & mettonsi trite ne i pessoli de i luoghi segreti delle don

68

BOOK
On Olive Lees (Morca). Chapter 121.

Morca is the sediment of pressed olives, which when cooked in a vessel of fine Cypriot copper until it thickens like honey, is astringent, and in all its virtues is in every respect similar to Lycion. It is especially useful, with great benefit, applied to toothaches with vinegar, or with wine, or with honeyed wine. It is used in preparations for the eyes, and in those medicines made to close the pores of the skin. As it ages it becomes more potent. It is most useful applied to ulcers of the anus, and to those of the male genitals, and to the natural parts of women. Cooked with omphacine oil to the thickness of honey, and applied around decayed teeth, it causes them to fall out. Rubbed on with a decoction of lupins and chameleon-thistle, it cures mange in four-footed animals. Applied warm, the fresh uncooked kind is usefully employed against gout and other joint pains. Rubbed onto a woolen fleece and applied to those with dropsy, it resolves the swelling.

Since olive trees, olives, olive oil, olive gum, and olive lees are all one and the same plant and its fruits, it did not seem to me out of place to write about them all together, and thus satisfy the needs of each subject. Wild olive trees grow in the countryside around Siena, and in various other places in Tuscany very abundantly, and are much smaller than the cultivated ones, thorny, and with shorter leaves. Their olives, of which enormous quantities are gathered, are much smaller than the cultivated ones, but in taste far more flavorful. The thrushes, blackbirds, and starlings bear clear witness to this, since they eagerly prefer the wild ones to the cultivated. Our countrymen who delight in fowling carefully watch these wild olives for birds with great skill, until all the cultivated olives have been fully harvested; and thereafter with birdlime they catch an infinite number of blackbirds and thrushes throughout the entire month of December and January. There are few in Tuscany who gather the wild olives to make oil, because the abundance of the cultivated kind means the wild ones are little valued. I find recorded among the ancients ten varieties of olive: namely the Pausiae, Algianae, Licinianae, Sergiae, Netiae, Calminae, Orchiae, Regiae, Circitae, and Murteae. Although Virgil wrote of only three varieties, so too in our own time no more than three kinds are seen in Tuscany, especially around Siena. Of these, those of the first kind, though they come from the smallest trees, are nevertheless beautiful and of notable size, similar to those of Bologna. They are eaten pickled in brine in foods; for making oil they are entirely useless. The second kind, beautiful in size and color (though considerably smaller than the first), are the best for making oil, producing it golden, sweet, clear, and of the most excellent flavor. The olive trees that bear them are commonly called "olivastre," and are trees of the greatest height, with their branches spreading widely. The third kind are those common throughout all Italy. The finest ones preserved in brine are sent to Rome and to other places in Italy and Spain, where the most lavish tables are to be found. Between the olive and the oak there is (according to the ancient writers) a mortal enmity, so that when olive trees are planted near oaks they soon perish. Olive trees become sterile when browsed by goats during their first sprouting, for which no remedy has been found. But if for any other reason olive trees fail to bear fruit, a proven and effective remedy is to uncover their roots throughout the entire winter season. The gum of the wild, or Ethiopian, olive, although it is useful for many things, is nonetheless in our times not in use in apothecaries, nor do I know that it is gathered. Some have supposed (as we said above in the chapter on Acacia) that it is the Gum Arabic used in apothecaries, and others that it is Elemi gum. But it is truly shown that the gum of the Ethiopian olive is neither Elemi nor Arabic gum, since none of the latter two are found to be sharp and ulcerative to the taste; and because what we commonly call Elemi gum in apothecaries is rather a resin, or liquid produced from some tree unknown to us, perhaps similar to the pine, fir, or spruce, rather than any sort of gum. For at fire, just as other resins do, it immediately melts and becomes entirely liquid like wax, which no kind of true gum does. Although we do not have in our own time any certainty as to which plant Elemi gum comes from, nevertheless, from what the physicians of our time have experienced, and especially surgeons, it is the most excellent of all kinds of resins for healing wounds of the head. Of the great usefulness of olive lees there remains nothing more to say, except that as Cato writes, it is useful to mix it with lime for coating warehouses and shops for cloth and silk fabrics; because it keeps away spiders, moths, and other small worms and harmful creatures, and moreover the moisture that seeps from walls.

On the Oak, Acorns, Beech, and Holm Oak. Chapter 122.

Every oak has astringent virtue, and especially that thin bark which lies between the outer bark and the wood, and likewise the thin skin beneath the shell of acorns. Their decoction is given in dysenteric and stomach fluxes, and in spitting of blood, and they are ground and inserted as pessaries into the private parts of women

On Chestnuts. Chapter 123.

The Sardinian acorns, which some call Chestnns, or Lopime, or Acorns of Jove, are astringent, and have the same effects as acorns, and especially that thin skin they have between the flesh and the outer bark. The pulp, when eaten, is useful for those who have drunk the poison called Ephemeron.

Chestnuts are a fruit very well known throughout all Italy, as are likewise the trees that produce them. Although in ancient times there were various species, and various names given to them to please those from the places whence they were brought; nevertheless in Tuscany there are only the domestic and the wild varieties. The domestic ones shell easily, and the most prized of these are those called Marroni, being much larger and much finer than the others. In the mountains where little grain is grown, they are dried on racks over smoke, then shelled and made into flour, which admirably serves in place of bread. The trees are useful for building houses, for making beams, joists, planks, staves, and barrel hoops. But as firewood they are entirely useless. Chestnut trees love the mountains far more than the plains, because by their nature they enjoy the cold, and for this reason they are seen to thrive much more to the north and in shaded places than elsewhere. Chestnuts, especially the dried ones, powerfully stop fluxes of the stomach and of the body, and are good for spitting of blood. Ground with honey and salt they are usefully applied to the bite of a mad dog. They dissolve hardnesses of the breasts when plastered on with vinegar and barley flour. They provoke lust because they are very flatulent. Eaten abundantly at meals they cause headache, generate wind, constipate the body, and are hard to digest. But those roasted under the ashes are much less harmful when eaten afterwards with pepper and salt, or with sugar.

On Galls. Chapter 134.

The gall is the fruit of the Oak, of which there are two kinds: one called Omphacite, small but rough, knotted like the joints of fingers, firm and not pierced; and the other smooth, light, and pierced. The Omphacite is praised as the better, because it is the more efficacious. Both have a strongly astringent virtue. Ground to powder they dissolve superfluities of the flesh, stop fluxes of the gums and uvula, and heal ulcers of the mouth. Their kernel placed in the cavities of teeth relieves toothache. Burned on coals until thoroughly ignited, then quenched with wine, or vinegar, or sour brine, they stop bleeding. Sitting in their decoction is an efficacious remedy for repositioning a prolapsed womb and stopping its fluxes. Steeped in vinegar or water they turn the hair black. Applied ground with wine, or water, in the form of a liniment, or drunk, they benefit dysenteric and stomach fluxes. These should be mixed with foods, or cooked whole in water, together with some other suitable thing for similar ailments. In sum, the Galls are to be used for binding and drying wherever needed.

Galls are very well known and common, and are produced, as Pliny says, by all plants that produce acorns. They grow when the Sun leaves the sign of Gemini; and when touched by too much heat, they dry out and become hollow. The oak trees produce them in addition to acorns, in larger and smaller forms called Omphaciti. The larger ones possess this particular virtue, that each year with their fruiting they foretell the goodness or badness of the coming year; for if, when those gathered in March that are dry and not pierced are broken open, flies are found inside, it signifies abundance; spiders, famine; and worms, mortality. Let no one marvel that these animals are born from galls, for I myself have seen it many very many times, and few, or almost none, can be found that are not pierced and from which the animal born inside has not already emerged, but that are found pregnant with one of these three animals; and therefore one may say that the Oak produces both fruit and animal. Knowing this, our ancient fathers not without reason said that the Oak was sacred to Jove. Galen wrote of Galls in book seven of the Faculties of Simple Medicines, saying thus: The Gall called Omphacite is a notably acrid medicine, and for the most part earthy and cold, by which it dries and represses fluxes, and moreover binds and brings together all relaxed and languid members, and powerfully resists all fluxes. For which reason one may say it is dry in the third degree and cold in the second. But the other, which is large, pale, and light, is also desiccative, but so much less than the other as it partakes less of that acrid quality, and therefore cooked by itself and applied as a plaster it is a not inconsiderable medicine for inflammations and relaxations of the anus. It is cooked where there is need to bind only a little in water, and where much, in wine. And it grows so much the stronger as the wine is more austere. Moreover, galls that are burned acquire the virtue of stopping blood, from which they take on warmth and sharpness, and therefore are more subtle and more desiccative than the raw ones. Del Rhu. Cap. cxxv.

IL Rhu, che si mette sopra alle uiuande chiamato da alcuni Erithro, è un seme d'u-
no alborfcello buono per conciare le cuoia, così chiamato: percioche coloro, che
conciano le cuoia, l'usano per ispessire le pelli. Cresce questo alborcello fra i sassi
d'altezza di due gombiti. Sono le sue frondi lunghette, rossigne, & per intorno
dentate. Produce il frutto racemoso, denso, di grandezza di quello del Terebintho, ma al-
quanto stiacciato, di cui è molto utile la corteccia. Hanno le sue frondi uirtu costrettiua, et fan
no tutti gli effetti dell'Acacia. La loro dicottione fa i capelli neri, & mettesi per la disenteria
ne crisieri, ne bagni per sederui dentro, & nelle beuande. Distillasi nell'orecchie, che humi-
gano. Le frondi applicate con mele, ouero con aceto curano le canchrene, & i pterigi delle
dita. La dicottione delle frondi secche spriemuta, & poscia ricotta alla spessitudine del mele
uale quanto il licio. Il seme fa i medesimi effetti. Mettesi conueneuolmete nei cibi di coloro,
che patiscono i flussi disenterici, ouero stomachali. Applicato nei linimenti con acqua prohi
bisce l'infiammagioni, et le posteme, nelle rotture dell'ossa, nelle liuidezze delle percosse, &
nelle scorticature. Leua l'asprezza della lingua fregatoui con mele. Stagna i flussi bianchi
delle done, et guarisce l'hemorrnoide applicatoui con carbone di quercia trito. L'acqua doue
sia stato primo questo seme in infusione, cotta, et condensata è piu efficace, che l'istesso seme.
Produce questo alborcello una goma, la quale messa nella cocauta di deti ne leua il dolore.

Hiamasi il Rhu de i Greci, ilquale, secondo che dice Plinio al.xi. del.xxiiii. non ha nome alcuno in latino, comune-
C mente nelle Spettarie Somacho uocabolo tirato da gli Arabi, come sono assaissimi de gli altri già detti di sopra.
Imperoche Serapione con tutti gli altri Arabici chiamano il Rhu Sumach. Vsarono il Rhu gli antichi in cambio
di sale per condimento de i lor cibi, et imperò Dioscoride nel principio del cap. lo chiama Rhu, che si mette in su le uiuade.
Il cui costume s'osserua per quanto ho inteso fin hoggi in Soria, & in Egitto, doue nasce il Rhu piu eccellente. Nasce ne in
Italia in piu luoghi in su l'Appenino con tutte queste note, che gli assegna Dioscoride. Conciasi con le sue frondi le cuoia di
quelli eccellenti Cordouani, che chiamano Somachi dal nome di queste frondi, con che s'ispessiscono, et s'increspano. Pensossi
Pietro Crinito Fiorentino, come si legge al. vij. cap. del suo libro dell'honesta disciplina, che il Rhu, ilquale medesimamente in
Cornelio Celso è scritto Rhos Siriacus, fusse la Manna, che si ciporta di Soria. Pensandosi, che Rhos significasse rugiadà.
Imperoche la Manna non è altro, che rugiada. Per il cui errore fu agramente corretto dal Manardo da Ferrara,
come ampiamente nelle sue Epistole alla quinta del primo libro dritta all'istesso Crinito si lege, et si uede. il Ruellio non
sapendo, che cosa si fusse la Fluida di Theophrasto, di cui scrisse al.xviii. cap. dell'historia delle piante si penso, che sotto
quel nome hauesse Theophrasto scritto del Somacho, non accorgendosi, che la Fluida di Theophrasto non è altro, che quel
la pianta, delle cui radici si fa il uischio, laquale esso Ruellio chiama Lantana, come uolgarmente si chiama in piu luoghi
d'Italia. Scrisse del Rhu Galeno al. vij. delle facoltà de Semplici così dicendo. Il Rhu pianta ramosolosa, ha uirtu costiret-
tiua, & diseccatiua, & imperò l'usano i Coriari à ristrignere, & diseccare le pelli, dal quale effetto si chiama pianta da
cuoia. Sono oltre à questo in uso à i Medici primamente i suoi frutti, & il suo succhio molto ueramente austero, & impe-
rò è questo medicamento di quelli, che disseccano nel terzo ordine, & infrigidiscono nel secondo.
