translation:
114 BOOK

A [This section is about the hedgehog.] It is an animal that rarely comes out of its den except at night. It is active during the grape harvest in the vineyards, where it approaches the lowest clusters near the ground, and knocks the grapes off with its paws, then rolls upon them, and so carries them back, impaled on its spines, to its den. It does the same with all other wild fruits when it finds them fallen abundantly under the trees. It is an animal of cold constitution, full of many cold superfluities, upon which its spines are nourished. It alone among all four-footed animals has its testicles attached to its kidneys, like birds, and for that reason it is extremely swift in coitus. When afraid, it curls itself entirely into a ball, and thus makes a fool of dogs that attack it; but if one throws water on it, it immediately stretches out and walks away. Its flesh is more suited for medicine than for food, being both earthy and hard to digest. Rasis attributed to it far more virtues in his treatise on the sixty animals. But since these seem to me more apocryphal than close to the truth, I leave it to whoever is eager for such things to seek them out there, where they may be found.

On the Hippocampus. Chapter III.

B The Hippocampus is a small sea creature. Its ashes, mixed with liquid pitch, or grease, or with Amaracine ointment, and applied, cause hair that has fallen out through mange to grow back.

How the Hippocampus came to have its name I find no particular account of, either among the ancients or among

C the modern writers, although all of them count it among the species of sea locusts. One may readily believe that it took its name from the caterpillars that feed on herbs in the fields and gardens, which the Greeks call Campe, perhaps because it resembles them in appearance. And although Dioscorides says the Hippocampus is a small sea creature, the force of the word itself shows quite the opposite. For the term Hippo, joined to other words, generally signifies something large, as we see in Hipposelinum, Hippolapathum, and Hippomarathrum. But this should not be grounds for condemning Dioscorides and the others who used the name before him. For although compared to large sea fish it is a small creature, it is nonetheless large compared to the type of caterpillar it resembles and from which it took its name. I have seen this creature many times in the fish markets among the fish offal; its body and shape are similar to a medium-sized shrimp, but it does not have forked gills, and it has a rather long neck with a somewhat elongated head, and many legs, and is thus altogether similar to those hairy caterpillars, reddish-black in color, that are found underground in gardens and fields, of similar shape, feeding on the roots of herbs and grain. In Trento these are called Cagne, and in the Val d'Anania, because of their hairiness, Orsolane; and Columella very aptly called them hirsute. These animals are very plentiful in the Trentino region, and they come out of the ground when it rains, and so those who find them troublesome in their gardens often water the ground to bring them out in order to kill them.

On Purpura and Buccinae (sea snails). Chapter IV.

The ash of burnt Purpura desiccates, cleans the teeth, consumes superfluous flesh, purifies and consolidates ulcers. The ash of Buccinae does the same, but burns more powerfully. Whoever burns a Buccina filled with salt in an unglazed earthen vessel will produce a most useful powder for rubbing the teeth. It is usefully sprinkled over burns from fire, and is left in place until it hardens; for as the ulcer is dried, it then falls away by itself. Moreover, a lime is made from Buccinae, as we shall describe when we speak of lime. Those parts in the middle of the Buccinae and Purpura,
D around which their shells wind, are called Ciones. These too are burnt in the same way, and are more efficacious because they have more astringent virtue. The flesh of Buccinae is pleasant and agreeable to the taste, and suitable for the stomach, but does not soften the body.

The Purpura are marine animals covered with a hard shell, and according to Pliny in his ninth book, they contain
S that liquid of great value which is properly called Tyrian purple, used to dye the splendid garments of kings and emperors. These small animals carry this liquid in their throat, in a rather pale vein; it is not found in dead ones, because it dissolves along with their vital spirit, and so fishermen always try to catch them alive. They hide for thirty days during the dog days of summer, and in spring they come together, and rubbing against one another they produce a thick saliva like wax. The Purpura has a tongue as long as a man's finger, and of such hardness that with it they bore through oysters, clams, and every other kind of shellfish on which they feed; knowing this well, fishermen who catch them, finding certain shells with sharp-edged husks scattered along the sea sand,

text:
SECONDO 115

gli tessono tra corde, tra uenchi, & tra giunchi, a modo di nasse, le qua i appicano poscia a lunghe funi, & le gittano in mare. La onde interuiene, che essendo questi cotali nicchi stitibondi, & mezzi merti, come sentono l'acqua subito s'apro no, & i quali correndo le Porpore, per pascersene vi mettono dentro quella lor dua lingua, ma questi come si sentono pun gere, subito riserrando si gliela stringono tra amendune le pareti dei gusci, & funnolesi prigioni, & cosi poscia son ti rati fuore dai Pescatori. viuono le Porpore fuor dell'acqua cinquanta di, alimentandosi solamente della saliua loro, ma muoiono subito che si mettono nell'acqua dolce. Crescono in uno anno quello, che ga bisogna, come fanno l'altre sorti del le Ostriche, & delle Gongole. Le BVCCINE sono anchor esse spetie di Porpore, & chiamansi Buccine per esser simili al corno da sonare, & per hauer elle il becciuolo molto atto à porsi alla bocca. Maggiori di queste sono le Porpore, & hanno il becco lungo à modo di canale onde mettono fuore la lingua loro, tutto composto di sfinoscerchi, al che non si ritro ua nelle Buccine. Hanno amen lune tanti cerchi nel dosso, quanti son viuiute anni. Le Buccine non s'appiccano se non alle pietre, & imperò solamente si ritrouano tra li scogli. Furono celebrate le Porpore, & le Buccine insieme con tutte l'al tre spetie de i Conchili per lunga historia da Atheneo, oue posono ricorrere coloro, che piu oltre desiderano di sapere. Ma per esser le PERLE, le quali hoggi, & per le pompe, & per le uirtu loro sono apprezzate da tutto il mondo, pro dotte da un Marino animale anchor esso connumerato fra cotali spetie di conchili, non essendone stato scritto, ne da Diosco ride, ne da Galeno, & hauendomele la materia, che si tratta, ridotte hora à memoria non ho uoluto, che le lodi, & il bel no me loro rimanghino adietro. Nascono adunque gli animali, che le producono: secodo che recita Plinio al.xxxv.capo del ix.libro nell'Oceano Indico, & in quello, che circonda l'Isola Trapobana, Toide, & Perimola promontorio d'India. Ma Pottimi, & piu stimate Perle sono quelle, che si ritrouano nel mare Rosso d'Arabia. Non sono gli animali, che le producono, come dimostrano ueramente le MADRIPERLE, che si ci portano, molto dissimili dalle Ostriche, et hanno questa pro prietà, che quando il tempo dell'anno le stimola à generare s'aprono la notte, empendosi, & nodrigandosi di generatiua rugiada, della quale ingrauiandosi partoriscono poscia le Perle essendo chiare, & torbide, secondo la qualità della rugia da, che ricolgono. Se quando s'ingrossano è tempo nuuolo, producono poscia le Perle pallide, & torbide. Grosse le fanno quando abondantemente si satiiano, & picciole diuentano per il contrario quando non pigliano rugiada à bastanza, nel che l'impediscono i baleni, percioche balenando quando s'ingrossano, si spaurisono, & si riserrano auanti, che sieno piene di rugiada à sufficiença. Serransi parimente per il romore de i tuoni. La onde poscia generano Perle uane, senza sustanza al cuna, piene di uento. Nell'acqua le Perle son tenere: ma subito, che sene traggono s'induriscono. Dicono alcuni, che le Ma driperle uanno à schiera, & che hanno il loro Re di corpo assai maggiore delle altre, come hanno le Api, che fanno il me le, & imperò non poco s'affaticano i Pescatori in prendere il Re loro, percioche tolto che gli hanno il gouerno, conducono piu ageuolmente l'altre nelle reti. Se s'accorgono quando sono aperte della mano del Pescatore, che le uogli pigliare, la serrano talmente, che gli tagliano crudelmente le dita, facendo elle stesse le uencette loro. Le prese si mettono in alcuni uasi di terra con molto sale. Percioche consumandosi cosi la carne, rimangono poscia le Perle nette nel fondo del uaso. Le piu stimate sono le grosse, lucide, tonde, & graui, cose che rade uolte si ritrouano in una perla sola. Iuba scriue, che le Ma driperle d'Arabia sono simile ad un pettine, spinose come il Riccio marino, dietro ille quali si ritrouano le Perle simili à grani di tempesta. Plinio scriue, che non si ritrouano piu, che quattro, ouer cinque Perle per animale. Ma Amerigo Ve sputo nella sua seconda nauigatione, che ei fece per l'Oceano Athlatico sotto al cerbio dell'Equinottio in Mezzo giorno, afferma hauer egli hauuta tal Madriperla, che uene furo ritrouate dentro centotrinta. & altri, che dopo lui hanno naui gato all'Indie nuoue, dicono di molte piu, & ne recitano historie assai diuerse da quello, che ne scrisse Plinio. Pescansi ancho ra nell'Oceano occidentale uerso settentrione appresso à Scotia, & Inghilterra, ma picciole, & di non troppo lodato co lore, & di queste su fatta quella corazza, che Giulio Cesare dedicò al tempio di Diana. Sono le Perle nell'uso della Medici na, secondo che riferisce Serapione Arabo, & parimente Auicenna, utili molto alli tremori, & debolezze del cuore, & nelli collirii per chiarire la uista, & per diseccare l'acqua, & l'humidità, che scenie ne gli occhi.

Delli Mituli. Cap.v.

Mituli eccellenti son quelli di Ponto, liquali abbrusciati possono, & uagliono tanto, quanto le Buccine. Ma in particolarità laua i come si laua il piombo sono utili con mele nelle Medicine de gli occhi. Sminuiscono la grossezza delle palpe bre, & mondificano l'albugini, & tutte l'altre cose, che offuscano la uista. Met tesi la carne loro utilmente in su morsi de i cani.

Delle Telline. Cap.vi.

Le Telline fresche lubricano il corpo, & massime la dicottion loro. Le sala te abbrosciate, & trite in poluere, & irrorate con liquore cedrino, prohibisco no il rinascer de i peli delle ciglia.

SECOND [Book] 115

They weave them between cords, withes, and reeds, in the manner of fish-traps, and then hang them on long ropes and throw them into the sea. Thus it happens that these shellfish, being somewhat restless and half-dead, as soon as they feel the water open up, and the Murexes, running in to feed on them, put in their two tongues — but these, as soon as they feel the sting, close again and grip them between both walls of their shells, and hold them prisoner, and so they are afterward pulled out by the fishermen. The Murexes live out of water for fifty days, feeding only on their own saliva, but die immediately when placed in fresh water. They grow in one year to their full size, as do the other kinds of Oysters and Gongoles. The BUCCINES are also a species of Murex, and are called Buccines because they resemble a horn to blow, and because they have a mouthpiece very apt for putting to the mouth. Larger than these are the Murexes, which have a long beak like a channel through which they extend their tongue, entirely composed of fine rings, which is not found in the Buccines. Both have as many rings on their backs as they have lived years. The Buccines do not attach themselves except to rocks, and therefore are found only among the cliffs. The Murexes and Buccines, together with all the other kinds of Shellfish, were celebrated at length by Athenaeus, to whom those who wish to know more may turn. But since PEARLS, which today, both for luxury and for their virtues, are prized throughout the whole world, are produced by a marine animal also numbered among these kinds of shellfish, and since nothing has been written about them by Dioscorides or Galen, and since the subject I am treating has now brought them to my attention, I have not wished to let their praise and their fair name pass unmentioned. The animals that produce them are born, as Pliny relates in the thirty-fifth chapter of the ninth book, in the Indian Ocean, and in that which surrounds the island of Taprobana, Toide, and Perimola, a promontory of India. But the finest and most esteemed Pearls are those found in the Red Sea of Arabia. The animals that produce them are, as the MOTHER-OF-PEARL shells that are brought to us truly demonstrate, very unlike Oysters, and they have this property: that when the season of the year urges them to generate, they open at night, filling themselves and nourishing themselves with the generative dew, and becoming heavy with this, they afterward bring forth Pearls that are clear or cloudy, according to the quality of the dew they have gathered. If when they are swelling it is cloudy weather, they produce pale and murky Pearls. They make them large when they feed abundantly, and they become small when they do not take in enough dew, which is prevented by lightning flashes, because when lightning strikes as they are swelling, they are frightened and close up before they are full of dew. They also close at the sound of thunder. And thus they afterward generate hollow Pearls, without any substance, full of wind. In water, Pearls are soft; but as soon as they are taken out, they harden. Some say that the Mother-of-Pearl shells go in schools, and that they have a King whose body is much larger than the others, just as the Bees that make honey have a queen, and therefore the Fishermen take no little trouble to catch their King, because once they have taken him, they lead the others more easily into the nets. If they become aware, when open, of the hand of the Fisherman who wishes to take them, they close so tightly as to cut off his fingers cruelly, taking their own revenge. Those that are caught are put in certain earthen vessels with much salt. For as the flesh thus wastes away, the Pearls remain clean at the bottom of the vessel. The most esteemed are the large, lucid, round, and heavy ones, things that are rarely found in a single pearl. Juba writes that the Mother-of-Pearl shells of Arabia are like a comb, spiny like the Sea-urchin, behind which the Pearls are found resembling hailstones. Pliny writes that no more than four or five Pearls are found per animal. But Amerigo Vespucci, in his second voyage, which he made through the Atlantic Ocean beneath the sign of the Equinox toward the South, affirms that he obtained a Mother-of-Pearl shell in which one hundred and thirty were found inside. And others who after him have sailed to the New Indies speak of many more, and recount histories very different from what Pliny wrote. They are also fished in the western Ocean toward the north near Scotland and England, but small and of not very praiseworthy color, and from these was made that breastplate which Julius Caesar dedicated to the temple of Diana. Pearls, in the practice of Medicine, according to Serapion the Arab, and likewise Avicenna, are very useful for tremors and weaknesses of the heart, and in collyria for clarifying sight, and for drying up the water and humidity that descends into the eyes.

On Mussels. Chapter V.

The finest Mussels are those of Pontus, which when burned are worth as much as the Buccines. But particularly, used as a wash in the same way as lead is washed, they are useful with honey in medicines for the eyes. They reduce the swelling of the eyelids, and cleanse the albugines and all other things that obscure the sight. Their flesh is usefully applied to dog bites.

On Clams. Chapter VI.

Fresh Clams lubricate the body, especially their broth. Those salted, burned, ground to powder, and sprinkled with cedar-oil prevent the regrowth of the hairs of the eyelashes.

116 LIBRO

A Ono alcuni, che tengono, che i Mituli, & le Telline sieno una cosa medesima, della cui opinione ritrouò esere spe
S tialmente Pauolo Giouto homo ueramente dottissimo, ilquale in quel suo trattato delli Pesci Romani s'accostò
(quantunque Medico) piu alla opinione d'Atheneo, che alla scrittura di Dioscoride, per laquale manifestamente
si uede eser differenti i Mituli dalle Telline: Imperò che oltre all'hauerne trattato in due diuersi capitoli, scrisse differen
temente anchora delle uirtu loro, come colui, che ben sapeua eser uer differenza. Ilche fece parimente Galeno al. xi. delle fa
coltà de Semplici, doue trattò delli Mituli al capitolo della Vipera, & delle Telline al suo proprio capitolo, dando à cia
scuno proprie, & diuerse facoltadi. Ne altrimenti fece Pauolo Egineta, come fedele imitatore d'amenduni. Per ilche è sen
za dubbio da dire, che differenti sieno i Mituli, et le Telline. Queste sono notissime in Italia, & massime à Roma, oue se ne
uendono in gran quantità, per eser molto aggradeuoli al gusto quando son bene purgate dalla rena. Ma quali sieno i Mi
tuli in Italia non ritrouò chi à tempi nostri ne dichiari. Il perche si può ageuolmente credere, che non naschino in questi no
stri Mari, & se pur ui nascono, non sieno conosciuti per i Mituli, che separatamente dalle Telline scriuono i Greci.

Delle Chame. Cap. vij.

B La dicottione delle Chame, & parimente delle altre Gongole fatta con poca ac
qua solue il corpo. Beesi questa con uino.

E Chame, quantunque tra l'altre spetie di Conchili fossero per lunga historia scritte da Atheneo, nondimeno tan
L te sono le spetie di questi animali, che malaguolmente si possono distinguere l'un dall'altro. Ma hanno però que
ste oltre all'altre Gongole, questa proprietà, che sempre quasi si ritrouano aperte, & imperò penso, che uere Cha
me si possino ragioneuolmente chiamar quelle, che si ritrouano in su la rena del Mare con liscio nicchio, aperte, di cui gia
n'ho ueduto io assai gran copia in su la riua dell'Hadriatico. Ma per non hauere elle altra particolar facoltà, che s'habbi
no l'altre spetie di Gongole, & di Cappe breuemente me ne paso.

Della Vnghia odorata. Cap. viij.

C La Vnghia odorata è un nicchietto d'una piccolina Gongola, simile à quelli delle
porpore, & ritrouasi nelli paludi d'India, che producono il Nardo, & però rispi
ra di soaue odore, perche si nutrisce ella quiui solamente di Nardo. Ritrouasi
poi, che i paludi per i gran caldi si seccano. L'eccellente Vnghia odorata si porta
dal mar Rosso, bianchiccia di colore, & grassa. Quella di Babillonia è nera, & minore. So
no amendune odorate, & fassene profumo, il cui odore è simile alquanto al Castoreo. E'
l'una, & l'altra coueneuole nelle fumentation, che si fanno per le prefocationi della Madri
ce, & parimente in quelle, che rilicuano dal parosismo del mal caduco. Beute mollificano il
uentre. La cenere delle abbruciate tanto uale, quanto quella delle porpore, & delle buccine.

Vnghie odorate si chiamano nelle Spetiarie Blattæ bisantis, però così le chiamano gli Arabici. Ma in uero quelle,
L' che sono in uso à tempi nostri, sono piu presto da eser chiamate fetide, che odorate, percioche abbruscandole rispi
rano ueramente di fastidioso odore. Io n'ho ben uedute delle eccellenti, ma poche, & imperò auuertischino i diligenti Spe
tiali nel comprarle, che non sieno ingannati.

Delle Chiocciole. Cap. ix.

D E Chiocciole terrestri sono utili allo stomacho, ne facilmente si corrompono.
L'eccellentissime son quelle, che nascono in Sardegna, Libia, Astipalea, Sici
lia, & Chio. Ottime sono anchora quelle delle alpi di Liguria chiamate Poma
tie, cioè coperchiate. Le Marine sono stomachali, & facilmente si digeriscono.
Quelle de i fiumi hanno abomineuole odore. Quelle, che si ritrouano attacate alle siepi, &
alle macchie, lequali alcuni chiamano Sesili, conturbano il corpo, & lo stomacho, & prouo
cano il uomito. I gusci di tutte queste bruściate hanno uirtu di ulcerare, & di scaldare. Mon
dano la scabbia, se uitiligini, & identi. Bruściate insieme con la carne, & triti in cenere, & un
ti con mele giouano alle debolezze della uista, & mondificano le cicatrici, & le bianchezze
de gli occhi, et similmete le macchie della faccia. Le Chiocciole peste crude con i suoi gusci di
seccano l'enfiagioni dell'hidropisia, impiastrateui i suoi gusci di seccano se prima non di
secca tutto l'homore. Allegeriścono l'infiámagioni delle podagre, & cauano impiastrate
le spine, ò altre cose, che rimàgono fitte nel corpo. Trite, & applicate prouocano il mestruo.
La carne loro trita con incenso, & mirrha salda le serite, et massime quelle ne nerui. Incorpo

translation:
116 BOOK

A There are some who hold that Mussels and Clams are one and the same thing, and among those who held this opinion was notably Paolo Giovio, a truly most learned man, who in his treatise on Roman Fish sided more with the opinion of Athenaeus than with the writings of Dioscorides, through which it is clearly evident that Mussels differ from Clams. For beyond having treated them in two separate chapters, he also wrote differently about their virtues, as one who well knew there was a difference. Galen likewise did so in Book XI of the Faculties of Simple Medicines, where he treated Mussels in the chapter on Viper, and Clams in their own chapter, assigning to each their own distinct faculties. Paul of Aegina did no differently, as a faithful imitator of both. Therefore it must without doubt be said that Mussels and Clams are different. The latter are very well known in Italy, and especially in Rome, where they are sold in great quantity, being most pleasing to the taste when well purged of sand. But what Mussels are like in Italy, no one in our times has come forward to clarify. For which reason one may easily believe that they do not grow in our seas, and if they do grow there, they are not recognized as those Mussels which the Greeks write about separately from Clams.

Of Chame. Chapter VII.

B The decoction of Chame, and likewise of the other Gongoles made with a little water, loosens the body. This is drunk with wine.

The Chame, although among the other species of shellfish they were written about at length by Athenaeus, nonetheless there are so many species of these animals that one can hardly distinguish one from another. Yet these have, beyond the other Gongoles, this property: that they are almost always found open, and therefore I think that true Chame may reasonably be called those which are found on the sea sand with a smooth shell, open, of which I have myself seen a great many along the shore of the Adriatic. But since they have no other particular faculty beyond those of the other Gongoles and Cappe, I shall pass over them briefly.

Of the Fragrant Nail. Chapter VIII.

C The Fragrant Nail is a small shell of a tiny Gongole, similar to those of the porphyry shellfish, and is found in the marshes of India that produce Nard, and therefore breathes a sweet odor, because it feeds there solely on Nard. It is found that these marshes dry up in the great heat. The finest Fragrant Nail comes from the Red Sea, whitish in color and thick. That of Babylon is black and smaller. Both are fragrant, and a perfume is made from them, whose scent somewhat resembles Castoreum. Both are suitable in fumigations performed for suffocations of the womb, and likewise in those that relieve the fits of the falling sickness. Drunk, they soften the belly. The ash of the burned ones is as valuable as that of the porphyry shells and whelks.

Fragrant Nails are called in the pharmacies Blattae Bisantis, and so the Arabs call them. But in truth those which are in use in our times are more rightly to be called fetid than fragrant, because when burned they truly give off a foul odor. I have indeed seen excellent ones, but few, and therefore diligent apothecaries should take care when buying them not to be deceived.

Of Snails. Chapter IX.

D Land snails are useful to the stomach and do not easily spoil. The most excellent are those born in Sardinia, Libya, Astypalaea, Sicily, and Chios. Also very good are those from the Alps of Liguria called Pomatie, that is, covered ones. The sea ones are stomach-strengthening and easily digested. Those from rivers have an abominable odor. Those found clinging to hedges and bushes, which some call Sessile, disturb the body and the stomach, and provoke vomiting. The shells of all of these, burned, have the power to ulcerate and to warm. They cleanse the scab, vitiligo, and freckles. Burned together with the flesh and ground to ash, and applied with honey, they benefit weakness of sight, and cleanse scars and whiteness of the eyes, and likewise spots on the face. Snails pounded raw with their shells dry up the swellings of dropsy; applied as a plaster with their shells they dry up the humor, provided the humor has first been dried out. They relieve the inflammations of gout, and applied as a plaster they draw out thorns and other things lodged in the body. Ground and applied they bring on the menses. Their flesh ground with frankincense and myrrh closes wounds, especially those of the nerves. Incorporated

lo, nel quale entra grandissima quantità di Scorpioni ungendone solamente il cuore, & i polsi di tutto il corpo, libera da A
ogni sorte di ueleno tolto per bocca, che non sia corrosiuo, & similmente da tutti i ueleni, che lasciano con i morsi loro gli
Aspidi, & ogni animale uelenoso, come buon testimonio ne fanno coloro, che essendo stati prima unti dai Sacerdoti d'oglio
santo, son stati poscia liberati co'l mio, del quale nella peste ho ritrouato miracolosi effetti, & masime nel preseruarsi, &
similmente nelle petecchie, & nei uermini de i fanciulli, nel che è efficacissimo rimedio.

Dello Scorpione Marino. Cap. xij.

L Fiele del Marino Scorpione è utile alle suffustioni albugini, & debilità de gli
occhi.

Annosi creduto alcuni, che lo Scorpione Marino, & quel pesce, che chiamano Scorpena, stieno una cosa medesima.
H Ma che sia la Scorpena il marino Scorpione, per quanto si legge in Atheneo, & in Aristotile, non si può uera-
mente concedere; imperoche amenduni differentiarono l'uno dall'altro. Vero è, che la Scorpena, laquale uolgar-
mente alcuni chiamano Scarpeta, & altri Scarpena ha una spina in la schiena molto uelenosa, con laquale cerca di trafig-
gere sempre i pescatori, & gia ne sono stati da questa trafitti di coloro, che sene son morti. Il cui effetto, per eser simile al- B
le punture de gli scorpioni ha fatto credere a' molti, che sia la Scorpena, & lo Scorpione una cosa medesima. Non essendo
adunque la Scorpena, lo Scorpione, & non ritrouandone io altre note appresso agli scrittori, non so ueramente deter-
minare, quale egli si sia, quantunque ageuolmente potesse essere egli quello, che si chiama Ragno simile al Cephalos; Per
cioche questo è così nel trafigere di certe spine, che ha addosso uelenoso, come si sia la Scorpena.

Del Dragone Marino. Cap. xiiij.

Il Drago Marino rimedio alle punture della sua istessa spina aperto, et tagliato,
& poscia applicatoui sopra.

L Drago Marino, si quello è di cui secoro memoria ne libri loro Plinio, & Alberto; nò si piglia dai pescatori in
I questi nostri mari; Percioche, secondo che riferiscono costoro, è il Drago Marino una gran bestia formata a modo di
Serpente, ma non ha altre ali, che quelle, che gli seruono per notare, nel che per la grandezza delle sue forze è
uelocissimo, & percio in poco tempo cerca egli grandissimi spatij di mare. E' secondo Alberto bestia uelenosa, & ammax-
za i pesci subito, che gli ferisce con i denti, et così ogni altra sorte d'animali. Dicesi, che se per sorte uien preso da i pesca- C
tori, come si uede tirato alla rena subito ui caua una fossa per nascondersi. Ma in uero chi considera le parole di Diosco-
ride, non par che il suo Drago Marino, anchora che non lo descriua, debbi esser questo, che scrissero Plinio, & Alberto,
Ilche si conosce per due conietture. La prima si è, che questo di Dioscoride punge con una spina uelenosa, alla cui puntura
uale il proprio animale tagliato, & messoui sopra. Et questa altra gran bestia offende solamente co'l morso. L'altra con-
tettura si è, che pare, che facil cosa sia, considerando il breue dire di Dioscoride, hauere questo Drago per rimedio del
suo ueleno. Ilche appare difficilissimo in quell'altra gran bestia; il perche à me pare, che non si possa se non dire, che il
Drago marino scritto da Dioscoride fusse molto diuerso dal sopradetto.

Della Scolopendra Marina. Cap. xiiii.

A Scolopendra Marina cotta nell'oglio, & fattone untione fa cascare i peli, &
tocca con mano causa prurito.

La Scolopendra Marina uno animaletto, secondo che riferisce Plinio à. xliij. cap. del. ix. libro, simile à quello di
E' terra, che noi chiamiamo Centogambe, & dicesi se tali authori son però degni di fede, che quando ella inghiotisce D
l'hamo preparatogli da i Pescatori subito uomita tutte l'interiora, dalle quali spicandole le ritorna poscia à rin-
ghiotire senza patirne nocumento alcuno, & però ho più uolte considerato; che bella cosa sarebbe uederne l'anatomia.

Della Torpedine pesce. Cap. xv.

A Torpedine marina mitiga i uecchi, & lunghi dolori di testa applicataui suso,
& mitiga parimente ogni altro estremo cruciato del corpo. Messa in sul sedere
ritorna dentro il budello, quando esce fuore.

Omnumerasi la Torpedine nelle spetie de i pesci piatti, & cartilaginosi, come sono le raie, le pastinache, & altri
C simili. Rosseggia questa nel dorso, sopr'al quale ha distinte cinque macchie, che ueréggiano, simili à gli occhi, &
sotto al corpo biancheggia. E' questo pesce di tale, & tanta forza, & potestà, che essendo preso nelle retti auanti
che i pescatori lo tocchino con mano, gli stupidisce, & gli addormenta le mani, & le braccia, & similmete preso con l'hamo

translation:
SECOND. 119

in which enters a very great quantity of Scorpions, anointing with it only the heart and the pulse points of the whole body, it frees from A
every kind of poison taken by mouth, provided it is not corrosive, and likewise from all poisons that the Asps leave with their bites, and every
venomous animal; as good testimony is given by those who, having first been anointed by the Priests with holy oil,
were afterward freed by mine, with which in time of plague I have found miraculous effects, especially in preserving oneself,
and likewise against petechiae and worms in children, for which it is a most efficacious remedy.

Of the Marine Scorpion. Chapter XII.

The bile of the Marine Scorpion is useful for cloudings of the white of the eye and weakness of the eyes.

Some have believed that the Marine Scorpion and that fish called the Scorpena are one and the same thing.
H But that the Scorpena is the marine Scorpion, as far as one reads in Athenaeus and in Aristotle, cannot truly
be granted; for both differentiated the one from the other. It is true that the Scorpena, which in common
speech some call Scarpeta and others Scarpena, has a very venomous spine on its back, with which it always seeks to pierce B
fishermen, and already some have been pierced by it and have died. Whose effect, being similar to
the stings of scorpions, has led many to believe that the Scorpena and the Scorpion are one and the same. Since the
Scorpena is not, then, the Scorpion, and finding no other information about it among the writers, I cannot truly determine
what it might be, although it could easily be that which is called the Spider-fish similar to the Cephalos; for
this fish is so similar in piercing with certain venomous spines on its back, as is the Scorpena.

Of the Sea Dragon. Chapter XIV.

The Sea Dragon as a remedy against the punctures of its own spine, opened and cut,
and then applied upon it.

The Sea Dragon, if it is that of which Pliny and Alberto have preserved memory in their books, is not caught by fishermen in
I our seas; for, according to what they relate, the Sea Dragon is a great beast formed in the manner of a
Serpent, but has no other wings than those which serve it for swimming, in which by reason of the greatness of its strength it is
very swift, and therefore in little time it traverses very great stretches of sea. According to Alberto it is a venomous beast and kills C
fish immediately when it wounds them with its teeth, and likewise every other kind of animal. It is said that if by chance it is caught by
fishermen, as soon as it is dragged to the sand it immediately digs itself a pit to hide in. But truly, whoever considers the words of Diosco-
rides, it does not appear that his Sea Dragon, even though he does not describe it, ought to be this one that Pliny and Alberto wrote of,
which is known from two conjectures. The first is that the one described by Dioscorides stings with a venomous spine, against whose sting
the animal itself cut up and placed upon it is the remedy. And this other great beast injures only with its bite. The other con-
jecture is that it seems an easy thing, considering the brief words of Dioscorides, that this Dragon should have a remedy for
its own venom. Which appears most difficult in that other great beast; wherefore it seems to me that one can only say that the
Sea Dragon written about by Dioscorides was very different from the one mentioned above.

Of the Sea Scolopendra. Chapter XIIII.

The Sea Scolopendra cooked in oil, and its ointment made thereof, causes the hair to fall out,
and touched by hand causes itching.

The Sea Scolopendra is a small animal, according to what Pliny reports at chapter 43 of book 9, similar to that of
E' the land which we call Centipede, and it is said — if such authors are worthy of credence — that when it swallows D
the hook prepared for it by the Fishermen, it immediately vomits all its insides, and then, detaching them, swallows them back
without suffering any harm from it, and therefore I have many times considered what a fine thing it would be to see its anatomy.

Of the Torpedo fish. Chapter XV.

The marine Torpedo relieves old and long-lasting headaches when applied to the head,
and likewise eases every other extreme pain of the body. Placed on the seat,
it returns inside the bowel when it comes out.

The Torpedo is numbered among the species of flat and cartilaginous fish, such as rays, stingrays, and other
C similar ones. It is reddish on the back, upon which are five distinct spots that appear greenish, similar to eyes,
and on the underside of the body it is whitish. This fish has such great force and power that when caught in nets before

A & imperò diceua Galeno al, iij. delle facoltà de i cibi. Il fegato della Trigla mirabilmente si loda da i principi de golosi, quantunque mai à me sia egli parso tanto soaue, che meriti d'esser tenuto così in prezzo, & così honorato, ne ancho perche dia al corpo troppo eccellente nutrimento, & similmente dico del suo capo, ilquale dopo al fegato lodano costoro. Ma non sapendo io perche causa ciascuno andasse cercando di questi pesci i piu grossi, per esser i piu piccioli piu saporiti, & piu aggradeuo li allo stomaco; domandandone un giorno un goloso, che n'hauea comprati de i grossi per una gran quantità di denari; mi rispose, che si cercauano i grossi per hauer eglino maggior fegato, et maggior testa. Et nel medesimo luogo nel principio, del capitolo diceua. Le Trigle hanno la carne piu soda, et piu fragile di tutti gli altri pesci, et imperò non e uiscosa, ne grassa, ma di sapore aggradeuo le, & molto familiare alla natura dell'huomo. Figliano le Trigle (come dice Plinio) tre uolte l'anno, & sono tanto ingorde, che si pascono ne i corpi morti de gli huomini. Quelle piu si lodano, che hanno due barbe pendenti dal mento, et le Romane sono assai migliori, che quelle del Regno, et di Vinetia. Disse Atheneo, che il uino doue sia annegata una Trigla, beuto impedisce il coito ne gli huomini, & nelle donne l'impregna. fi. A Vinetia si chiamano le Trigle Spari.

B Dell'Hippopotamo. Cap. xxij.

Testicoli dell'Hippoporamo seccati, & triti si beono al morso delle Serpi.

E' L'Hippopotamo (secondo che riferisce Plinio à xxv. et xxvi. cap. del, viij. libro) una bestia del Nilo assai maggiore del Crocodilo, ilquale ha due unghie ne piedi, come hanno i buoi. Ha la schiena, le crına, & l'anitrire di cauallo, il grugno leuato, la coda torta, & i denti, come di porco cignale, come che non sieno così nocui. Ma Aristotile al, vj. del, iij. libro della natura de gli animali non disse, che i denti quantunque gli eschino fuore di bocca, sieno di porco cignale, ma che la coda ha l'Hippopotamo di cignale, & tutto il corpo non maggiore dell'Asino. La sua pelle non si puo passare con arme alcuna appuntata, se prima non si bagna, & imperò sene fanno gli scudi, gli elmetti, & le rotelle. E' questo animale di tanta astutia, che entrando nei campi delle biade alla pastura, u'entra all'indrieto per parere, che sia uenuto fuore, per non esserui preso. A Roma fu portato uiuo insieme con sei Crocodili da Marco Scauro Edile, facendone spettacolo ne i suoi giuochi. Ha l'Hippopotamo questa natura in se, che quando si sente carico, & troppo ripieno, entra ne i canneti, doue ritrouato alcun tronco di canna già stata tagliata ui frega solo la uena, sino che si caua il sangue, lasciandone uenir fuor tanto, quanto pare à lui, che gli basti, & poscia serra la piaga con belletta, ò con fango. La cenere del suo cuoio impastata con acqua sana le posteme, che si chiamano pani. Allegerisce il suo grasso il freddo, che uiene auanti alle febri, & similmente il suo sterco fiumetato à denti della mascella sua finisira, fregati alle gengiue, sino che escia il sangue, sanano il dolore de denti. La pelle della sinistra parte della fronte legata appresso all'anguinaia, prohibisce il coito.

Del Castoreo. Cap. xxiij.

Il Castoreo ambiguo animale: percioche conuersa insiememente in terra, & nell'acqua: ma piu assai in acqua, doue si ciba di pesci, & di granchi. Hanno i suoi testicoli uirtu contra i ueleni de serpenti. Fanno starnutare, & usansi in diuerse cose uniuersalmente. Beuti con puleggio al peso di due dramme, prouocano i mestrui, & cacciano le secondine, & le creature del corpo. Beonsi con aceto alle uentosità, à dolori di corpo, al singozzo, à mortiferi ueleni, & all'Ixia. Suegliano messi nei crisieri i lethargici, gli addormentati, et gli sopiti per qual si uogli causa. Dissoluti con aceto, & oglio rosado, & odorati, ouero fattone fumeto fanno il medesimo. Beuti, et applicati in forma di

D linimento giouano à gli spasimati, à i tremori delle membra, & à tutti i difetti de i nerui. Hanno uniuersalmente uirtu di scaldare. Quelli sono gli eletti, che nascono da un medesimo principio (pero che gli è impossibile ritrouare due uiscighe serrate in una sola tonica) che hano dentro uno liquore ceragginoso, di graue, et fastidioso odore, forte, mordace al gusto, & fragile. & circondati intorno da piu naturali toniche. Contrafannogli alcuni Trusatori mescolando l'Armoniaco gomma co'l sangue di questo animale, et con gli stessi testicoli, acconciando poscia tutto nelle uiscighe à seccarsi. E ueramente falso quello, che si dice, che se guitato questo animale da i cacciatori si stacchi i testicoli nel fuggire con i denti: Imperoche non se li puo pigliare per esser rattratti, come sono quelli del porco. E' necessario nel torli fuora diuidendo la pelle, conseruar e quel liquore simile al mele colla uisciga, doue sta dentro, & darlo poi quando è seccato à bere.

C Ome si uede per tutta l'Alamagna bassa, ouunque trascorra il fiume del Reno; & per l'Austria, & Vngheria, quunque passi il Danubio, sono i Castorci (come dice Dioscoride) ueramente animali all'acqua, et alla terra communı, uedendosi

124 BOOK

A And so Galen said in the third book on the properties of foods: the liver of the Mullet is wonderfully praised by those who love fine eating, although to me it has never seemed so exquisite as to deserve such esteem and honor, nor because it gives the body particularly excellent nourishment — and likewise I say of its head, which these people praise next after the liver. Not knowing why everyone sought out the largest of these fish, since the smaller ones are more flavorful and more pleasing to the stomach, I once asked a glutton who had bought large ones at great expense; he answered me that large ones were sought because they have a bigger liver and a bigger head. And in the same place at the beginning of the chapter he said: Mullets have flesh firmer and more delicate than all other fish, and therefore it is neither viscous nor fatty, but of an agreeable flavor, very familiar to human nature. Mullets spawn (as Pliny says) three times a year, and are so gluttonous that they feed on human corpses. Those most praised are those with two beards hanging from the chin, and the Roman ones are far superior to those from the Kingdom and from Venice. Athenaeus said that wine in which a Mullet has been drowned, when drunk, prevents coition in men, and makes women pregnant. In Venice Mullets are called Spari.

B On the Hippopotamus. Chapter 22.

The dried and ground testicles of the Hippopotamus are drunk against the bite of Serpents.

The Hippopotamus (according to Pliny in the 25th and 26th chapters of his eighth book) is a beast of the Nile considerably larger than the Crocodile, having two hooves on its feet like oxen. It has the back, the mane, and the neigh of a horse, a raised snout, a curved tail, and teeth like a wild boar, though not so harmful. But Aristotle, in the sixth chapter of the third book on the nature of animals, did not say that the teeth, although they protrude from the mouth, are those of a wild boar, but rather that the tail of the Hippopotamus is like that of a boar, and the whole body is no larger than a donkey. Its hide cannot be pierced by any pointed weapon unless it is first soaked, and so shields, helmets, and bucklers are made from it. This animal is so cunning that when it enters fields of grain to graze, it enters backwards so as to appear to have come out, so as not to be caught there. One was brought to Rome alive along with six Crocodiles by Marcus Scaurus the Aedile, who staged a spectacle with them in his games. The Hippopotamus has this nature: when it feels burdened and too full, it goes into the reed beds, where it finds a stump of reed already cut, and rubs only the vein against it until it draws blood, letting out as much as it deems sufficient for itself, and then closes the wound with clay or mud. The ash of its hide mixed with water heals swellings called "pani." Its fat lightens the cold that comes before fevers, and similarly its dung, rubbed on the teeth of the left jaw at the gums until blood comes out, cures toothache. The hide of the left part of the forehead, tied near the groin, prevents coition.

On Castoreum. Chapter 23.

The Beaver is an ambiguous animal, living equally on land and in water, but much more in water, where it feeds on fish and crabs. Its testicles have virtue against serpent venoms. They cause sneezing and are used universally in many ways. Taken with pennyroyal at the weight of two drams, they promote menstruation, expel the afterbirth, and expel creatures from the body. Taken with vinegar they help against flatulence, bodily pain, hiccups, deadly poisons, and Ixia. Administered in clysters they awaken the lethargic, the drowsy, and those stupefied for whatever cause. Dissolved in vinegar and rosewater and smelled, or used as a fumigation, they do the same. Taken as drink and applied in the form of a

D liniment they help the cramped, those with trembling limbs, and all defects of the nerves. They universally have the virtue of warming. Those considered best come from the same source (for it is impossible to find two sacs enclosed in a single membrane), having inside a waxy liquid of heavy and unpleasant smell, strong, biting in taste, and fragile; surrounded by several natural membranes. Some counterfeiters adulterate them by mixing Ammoniac gum with the blood of this animal and the testicles themselves, then packing everything back into the sacs to dry. It is truly false what is said, that when the animal is chased by hunters, it tears off its own testicles in flight with its teeth: for it cannot reach them since they are retracted, as are those of the pig. When removing them, it is necessary to split the hide and preserve that honey-like liquid together with the sac in which it is contained, and to give it to drink after it has dried.

C As may be seen throughout lower Germany wherever the Rhine flows, and through Austria and Hungary wherever the Danube passes, Beavers (as Dioscorides says) are truly animals common to both water and land, being seen

text:
126 LIBRO

A Delle Rane. Cap.xxv.

E Rane cotte lesse con oglio, & con sale, & mangiate sono la Theriaca de i ue ni di tutte le serpi, & il medesimo fa la loro dicottione beuta. Vagliono anchora contra l'antiche posteme de Tendoni. La cenere delle brusciate ristagna sparsa i flussi del sangue, & fassene utilmente linimento con pece per far rinascere i capel li, che cascano. Il sangue delle Ranocchie uerdi non lascia rinascere i peli, che si cauano dalle palpebre, distillato ne i luoghi, onde furono stirpati. Lauata la bocca con la dicottione delle Rane fatta d'acqua, & d'aceto, gioua à i dolori de denti.

E Ranocchie sono in Italia, & massime in Lombardia abondantissime, & uolgari; Ma non sono però tutte d'una
L spetie, d'un colore, ne d'una natura. Imperoche ne son di quelle, che nascono di putredine, nel bagnare, che fanno le piogge della state la poluere del terreno, et queste hanno breue uita, ne s'usano in cosa alcuna. Ne sono oltre que ste dell'altre, che nascono secondo l'ordine legittimo della natura ne i Mari, ne i fiumi, ne i paludi, & ne i laghi. Ritrouansene anchora di terrestre, le quali noi in Thoscana chiamiamo Botte, & altri le chiamano Rospi, & di quelle, che particolarmente per restare ne i canneti si chiamano Calamite; Ma amendune uelenose, & mortali. Ne i fiumi, ne i paludi, & ne i laghi conuersano quelle, che si mangiano di uerde, & di bigio colore, come che quiui anchora se ne ritrouino di quelle, che non molto sicuramente mangiar si possino. Partoriscon le Ranocchie (secondo che al x. disse Plinio, & noi del continuo sensatamente ueggiamo) neri, & minuti pezzi di uoli di carne, che nò sono altro, che occhi, & coda, ne i quali crescendo si formano poscia le gambe, diuidendosi la coda in quelle di dietro. Viuono (disse Plinio) solamente sei mesi, & poscia senza eser uiste si conuertono in fango, & rinascono all'acque di Primauera quelle istesse, che primamente erano nate; essendone occulta la ragione, perche così operi la natura in loro. Alche si contrapone l'esperienza, che se ne uede il Verno ne i paludi delle Maremme, che non si ghiacciano, oue d'ogni tempo si ueggono, & si ritrouano. E però è da dire, che se l'opinione di Plinio è pur uera, si uerifica solamente in quelle dette di sopra, che nascono di putrefattione di terra, & d'acqua.

Del Siluro pesce. Cap.xxvi.

C Angiato il Siluro fresco ne i cibi nutrisce, & mollifica il corpo; Ma salato da pochissimo nutrimento. Purga il gorgozzule, & chiarifica la uoce. La carne pur del salato impiasrtrata caua fuore le spine, le saette, & ogni altra cosa rimasa fitta ne membri del corpo. Còferisesi fedendosi nella sua salamuoia à i disenterici, imperoche la tira in pelle i flussi. Guarisce i dolori delle sciatiche adoperata ne i cristeri.

On posso se non consormarmi colla bene disputata opinione di Paulo Giouio, nel credere anchor io, che quel pesce già chiamato da gli antichi Siluro, sia quell'istesso, che si chiama hoggi Storione, come per il contrario non mi
N posso in modo alcuno accostare alle molto distorte opinioni d'alcuni altri, de i quali chi uuole, che sia lo Storione il Lupo, chi l'Attilo, & chi l'Hucca; imperoche, come si uede per le belle, & forti ragioni addotte dal Giouio è stato manifestamente prouato, che'l Siluro de gli antichi non fu altro, che lo Storione de i Moderni, il quale lasciando l'antico suo nome da Asturia luogo di Spagna, doue si ritroua questo pesce piu eccellente di tutta Europa, fu poscia chiamato uolgarmente Storione. Di questi se ne prendono in piu luoghi in Italia, & quando son piccoli si chiamano Porcellette, & quantunque piu al meglio si piglino gli Storioni ne i fiumi, come è il Teuere, il Po, & altri, che mettono in Mare; sono nondimeno pesci marini. Ma dilettandosi forte dell'acqua dolce, entrano liberamente per le foci ne i fiumi.

D Dello Smaride pescicolo: Cap.xxvij.

A cenere della testa del Smaride salato, consuma la carne superflua delle labbra dell'ulcere, serma l'ulcere, che pascono, & caccia uia i thimi, & i porri. La cui carne gioua, così come la salamuoia, à i morsi de i cani, & alle punture delli Scorpioni.

Delle Mene. Cap.xxviij.

A testa delle Mene brusciata in cenere, cura impiastrata le callose fessure del sedere, & la loro salamuoia tenuta in bocca, & lauandosene, cura l'ulcere putride di quella.

Q V antunque molto mi sia affaticato di uoler chiarirmi, che pesce sia lo Smaride, nondimeno ne appresso à Plinio, ne appresso Aristotile, ne manco appresso a' tutti gli antichi ho possuto io rintracciarne cosa alcuna. Ec

translation:
126 BOOK

A On Frogs. Chapter 25.

Frogs boiled and cooked with oil and salt, and eaten, serve as a Theriaca against the bites of all serpents, and their broth drunk does the same. They are also useful against old swellings of the tendons. The ash of burned frogs, sprinkled, stops the flow of blood, and is usefully made into a liniment with pitch to restore hair that is falling out. The blood of green frogs prevents regrowth of hairs that have been removed from the eyelids, when dripped on the places from which they were pulled. Rinsing the mouth with a decoction of frogs made with water and vinegar is beneficial for toothache.

Frogs are found in Italy, and especially in Lombardy, in the greatest abundance, and are common; yet they are not all of one species, one color, or one nature. For there are some that are born from putrefaction, in the dampening that summer rains bring to the dust of the ground, and these have a short life and are not used for anything. Beyond these there are others born by legitimate order of nature in the seas, in rivers, in marshes, and in lakes. There are also land ones, which we in Tuscany call Botte, and others call Rospi (toads), and those which particularly, because they stay in the reeds, are called Calamite; but both of these last are venomous and deadly. In rivers, marshes, and lakes live those that are eaten, of green and gray color, though there too some are found that cannot be eaten with full safety. Frogs give birth (as Pliny said in Book 10, and as we continually observe with good sense) to small dark bits of flesh, which are nothing but eyes and tail, from which the legs then grow, the tail dividing into the hind legs. They live (said Pliny) only six months, and then without being seen they turn to mud, and in Spring those same ones that were first born are reborn from the waters; the reason why nature acts thus in them being hidden. Against this, experience shows that they are seen in Winter in the marshes of the Maremma, which do not freeze, where they are found at all times. And so it must be said that if Pliny's opinion is at all true, it applies only to those mentioned above, which are born from the putrefaction of earth and water.

On the Silurus fish. Chapter 26.

C Eaten fresh, the Silurus nourishes and softens the body; but salted, it gives very little nourishment. It purges the throat and clears the voice. The flesh of the salted fish, applied as a plaster, draws out thorns, arrows, and anything else lodged in the members of the body. Used as a sitting bath in its brine it helps those with dysentery, since it draws out fluxes through the skin. Applied in clysters it cures the pains of sciatica.

I cannot but agree with the well-argued opinion of Paolo Giovio, believing myself too that the fish formerly called Silurus by the ancients is the same as what is today called Sturgeon; just as on the other hand I cannot
N in any way align myself with the very distorted opinions of certain others, of whom some would have the Sturgeon be the Lupo, some the Attilo, and some the Hucca; for, as is shown by the fine and strong arguments put forward by Giovio, it has been plainly proven that the Silurus of the ancients was none other than the Sturgeon of the Moderns, which, abandoning its ancient name from Asturia, a place in Spain where this fish is found most excellent in all of Europe, was thereafter commonly called Storione. These are caught in many places in Italy, and when small they are called Porcellette; and although Sturgeons are best caught in rivers, such as the Tiber, the Po, and others that flow into the Sea, they are nonetheless sea fish. But greatly delighting in fresh water, they freely enter the rivers through their mouths.

D On the small fish Smaride. Chapter 27.

The ash of the head of the salted Smaride consumes the excess flesh from the lips of ulcers, arrests spreading ulcers, and drives away thymi and warts. Its flesh is useful, as is its brine, against dog bites and the stings of Scorpions.

On the Mene fish. Chapter 28.

The head of the Mene fish, burned to ash, applied as a plaster cures the calloused cracks of the seat; and their brine, held in the mouth and used to wash with, cures the putrid ulcers thereof.

Q Although I have taken great pains to determine what fish the Smaride is, I have not been able to find any information about it in Pliny, nor in Aristotle, nor indeed in any of the ancients. Ec

SECONDO 127

cetto che pure ho ritrouato, che è un picciolo pesce simile alle Mene, che noi hoggi uolgarmente chiamiamo Menole. Et però non credo, che fallasse, chi dicesse, che le Smaride fussero quei pesci minuti, molto simili alle Mene, i quali à Venetia si chiamano uolgarmente Giroli.

Del Gobio. Cap.xxij.

A dicottione del Gobio fresco messo, & cuscito in uno stomacho di porco, & fatto bollire in. xij. sestari d'acqua, fino che non rimanghino se non due, et poscia colata, & tenuta al sereno, beuta solue il corpo senza alcuna molestia; & applicata in forma di linimento uale al morso de i cani, & delle serpi.

Gobij sono abbondantissimi pesci nelle pescarie di Venetia, imperoche in quelle lagune li circonuicine assai al-
1 lignano. Et però diceua bene Aristotile, che i Gobij stanno assai uolentieri nelle lagune de i Mari, & doue sia poca acqua appresso à i lidi. Chiamansi i Gobij uolgarmente à Venetia Go. Hanno la testa molto grossa, & sono al gusto aggrадeuoli, & delicati, per eser la carne loro tenera, & grassa. La onde al.iij. delle facoltà de i cibi diceua Galeno. I Gobij son pesci, che stanno ne i lidi del Mare, nel numero di quelli, che restano sempre piccoli. Sono al gusto soauissimi, B facili da digerire, & di buono nutrimento, & massime quelli, che si pescano ne i lidi arenosi, & sassosi, & fra gli scogli. Ma è da sapere, che i Gobij non solamente si ritrouano in Mare, ma anchora ne i fiumi, & ne i laghi, come son quelli, che producono il lago di Como, & il lago Maggiore, stimati molto per l'aggradeuale sapore, che lascia nel palato il gusto de i sfegati loro. Ne i fiumi uniuersalmente sono piu piccoli, quantunque qualche uolta di due, & tre once l'uno se ne ritrouino. In su'l Trentino pochi sono i fiumi, che non ne portino assai, come l'Adese, il Lauigio, il Noce, & la Sarca ne fan no giornalmente buona testimonianza. Chiamansi questi, Capitoni, & Marsoni, soauissimi, & gratissimi al gusto, et massime quando hanno l'uuoua, & facilissimi da digerire. In Thoscana se ne ritroua pur qualchuno, et chiamansi Ghiozzi.

Del Tonno. Cap.xxx.

C Hiamano Omotaricho la carne del Tonno salata, laquale mangiata, & beutoli sopra assai uino, di modo, che si prouochi co'l molto bere il uomito, uale al morso di quelle sorti di Vipere, lequali chiamano Presteri; & similmente uale à fare uomitare i cibi, che conturbano lo stomacho. Applicata uale al morso de i cani.

Tonni, de i quali si fa la Tonnina, grossi, & polputi pesci, simili à i porci, sono notissimi ouunque sieno porti di
1 Mare, in su'l Tirrheno molto piu, ch'in su l'Hadriatico; Imperò che questi pesci al tempo del Maggio uengono dal mare Oceano, & entrano per lo stretto di Gibilterra fra le Colonne d'Hercole, partiti in grandissime schiere, in questo nostro Mare d'Italia, che si chiama Tirrheno, & Mediterraneo, onde poscia scorrendo pur qualche schiera, entrano anchora nell'Hadriatico, come che in assai minor qualità. Questi (per quanto recitano alcuni scrittori) son cacciati da un pesce molto grande, ilquale si chiama uolgarmente pesce Spada, per haurer egli in sul muso uno durissimo, et acutissimo osso, simile ad una spada, col quale (come dice Plinio al.xxxij. libro, & referiscono anchora i Marinari, che nauigano per l'Oceano) sfonda, & passa questo pesce le Navi. I Tonni adunque per eser semplicissimi, & timidissimi pesci, si lasciano cacciare da questo pesce Spada, come un branco di pecore dal Lupo, & cosi uscendo dell'Oceano se ne uengono ne i nostri Mari d'Italia. Ma non senza gran sbalso de gli spettatori, si prendono il Maggio, e'l Giugno nell'Isola di Gade, concorrendo à questa pescagione tutto il popolo con grandissimo romore, & di uoci, & di tamburi, & di tirare d'archibusi. Uche molto gioua al pescare di questi pesci; Imperoche per la timidità, & sciocchezza loro, spauriti dal gridare, & dallo strepito grande, si riducono in certi uadi appresso à terra, oue poscia ageuolmente ne prendono con D grandissime reti una schiera alla uolta, de i quali partiti in pezzi, & salati ne i bariglioni, se ne fa la Tonina. Hanno i Toni diuersi nomi, secondo che sono piu gioueni, & piu uecchi. imperoche quando sono piccolini, & nasciuti di poco si chiamano Cordille, & fatti alquanto piu grandi Limarie, & piu poscia crescendo Palamie, lequali si chiamano poi Tonni, come son cresciuti maggiori d'un piede. Plinio uuole, & similmente Atheneo, che uiuino i Tonni assai, & creschino in ismesurati pesci. Assillano i Tonni ne i duri calori punti da un certo uermicello, come assillano i buoi punti dal moscone, & dai tafani. Il perche spesse uolte cacciati dal dolore, uscendo dell'acqua saltano, come se uolasero, in su i Nauigli, nel qual tempo si dannano ne i cibi, come molto noiui. Le pancie loro, come che molto aggradino al gusto; offendono nondimeno poscia tanto piu lo stomacho. Fanno il contrario le parti loro piu magre, lequali se non così bene contentano il Palato, sono però assai manco moleste allo stomacho. Benche, secondo che referisce Galeno al.iij. delle facoltà de cibi, tutti questi pesci cosi grossi hanno la carne dura, malageuole da digerire, di poco nutrimento, & di molte superfluitå, & imperò piu si mangiano salati questi pesci, che freschi, per eser il sale buona causa di rompere la durezza, & la uscosità loro.

SECOND 127

which I have found, that there is a small fish similar to the Mene, which we today commonly call Menole. And yet I do not believe that whoever said that the Smarides were those small fish, very similar to the Mene, which in Venice are commonly called Giroli, was mistaken.

On the Goby. Chapter 22.

A decoction of fresh Goby, placed and sewn inside a pig's stomach, boiled in twelve sestari of water until only two remain, then strained and kept in the open air, when drunk loosens the body without any discomfort; and applied as a liniment it is useful against the bites of dogs and serpents.

Gobies are extremely abundant fish in the fish markets of Venice, since they are found in great numbers in the surrounding lagoons. Aristotle rightly said that Gobies like to stay in the lagoons of the seas and wherever there is shallow water near the shores. They are commonly called Go in Venice. They have very large heads, and are pleasant and delicate to the taste, because their flesh is tender and fat. As Galen said in the third book on the properties of foods: Gobies are fish that stay on the seashore, among those that always remain small. They are most sweet to the taste, easy to digest, and of good nourishment, especially those caught on sandy and rocky shores and among the reefs. It should be noted that Gobies are found not only in the sea, but also in rivers and lakes, such as those found in Lake Como and Lake Maggiore, highly esteemed for the pleasant flavor their livers leave on the palate. In rivers they are generally smaller, though some of two or three ounces each may be found. In the Trentino there are few rivers that do not yield them in abundance, as the Adige, the Noce, the Sarca, and others bear good daily witness. These are called Capitoni and Marsoni, most sweet and pleasing to the taste, and most easy to digest, especially when they carry their eggs. In Tuscany some are also found, and are called Ghiozzi.

On the Tuna. Chapter 30.

They call Omotaricho the salted flesh of the Tuna, which when eaten and washed down with much wine so as to provoke vomiting by drinking heavily, is useful against the bite of those kinds of vipers called Presteri; and it is likewise useful to cause vomiting of foods that disturb the stomach. Applied externally it is useful against the bites of dogs.

Tunas, from which Tonnina is made, large and fleshy fish similar to pigs, are well known in every seaport, especially in the Tyrrhenian Sea rather than the Adriatic; for at the time of May these fish come from the Ocean and enter through the Strait of Gibraltar between the Pillars of Hercules, moving in enormous schools into this our Sea of Italy, called the Tyrrhenian and the Mediterranean, where then some schools also enter the Adriatic, though in considerably fewer numbers. These fish (according to some writers) are hunted by a very large fish, commonly called the Swordfish, because it has on its snout a very hard and sharp bone, like a sword, with which (as Pliny says in book thirty-two, and mariners who sail the Ocean also report) it pierces and runs through ships. Tunas, being very simple and timid fish, allow themselves to be chased by this Swordfish, like a flock of sheep by a wolf, and thus leaving the Ocean they come into our Italian seas. Not without great excitement among the spectators, they are caught in May and June at the Island of Gades, where the whole population gathers for this fishery with great noise, with voices, drums, and the firing of arquebuses. This is very useful for fishing these fish; because owing to their timidity and foolishness, frightened by the shouting and the great noise, they gather in certain shallows near the shore, where they can then easily be caught in great nets, a whole school at a time, and once divided into pieces and salted in barrels, the Tonnina is made from them. Tunas have different names according to whether they are younger or older: when they are very small and newly born they are called Cordille, and when somewhat larger Limarie, and growing further Palamie, and those that have grown more than a foot are then called Tonni. Pliny holds, and likewise Athenaeus, that Tunas live a long time and grow to enormous fish. Tunas are tormented in the great heat, stung by a certain small worm, just as oxen are tormented by gadflies and horseflies. For this reason, driven by pain, they frequently leap out of the water as if flying, onto ships, at which time they are harmful as food, being quite injurious. Their bellies, although they please the palate greatly, afterward harm the stomach all the more. The leaner parts do the opposite: if they do not please the palate quite as well, they are far less troublesome to the stomach. Though according to Galen in the third book on the properties of foods, all these large fish have hard flesh, difficult to digest, of little nourishment, and producing much waste matter; and therefore these fish are better eaten salted than fresh, since salt is a good means of breaking down their toughness and viscosity.

Del Brodo de i Pesci. Cap.xxxij.

L Brodo dei Pesci freschi beuto cosi solo, & similmente con uino solue il corpo.
Fassi per tale effetto particolarmente con i Phicidi, con gli Scorpioni, con le lusi

B I L Garo (secondo che riferisce Plinio à. vij. capitoli del. xxxi. libro) si cosi chiamato appresso à gli antichi, perciò
che si faceua dell'interiora d'un pese, macerate, & risolute con sale, che si chiamaua Garo. Ilche poscia si faceua
similmente con quelle de gli Sgombri, & usauasi questo condimento nelle cucine con grande solennità, per condi
mento di diuersi cibi. Ma di questo non intese Dioscoride: pigliando per il Garo generalmente tutte le salamuoie de i pesci,
& delle carni. Del Brodo de i pesci non accade dir altro, per esser cosa assai dichiarata dall'istesso Authore.

Delle Cimici delle lettiere. Cap.xxxiij.

Annosi utilmete ad inghiottire sette Cimici dilettiera serrate ne gusci delle faue,

gustie di quella.

C I Nfra tutti i Notturni nimici, che ne rompono spesso la dolce quiete del sonno, non hauiamo ueramente i piu cru

di se una tal puzza, che molto piu offende i sentimenti, & gli spiriti, che non fanno i loro cocenti morsi tutte le

milmente puzzolenti, ma di questi non ne ritrouò alcuno uso nella Medicina.

Delle Millepede. Cap.xxxiiij.

E Millepede, che stanno uolentieri sotto à gli orci dell'acqua, sono animali, che
hanno molti piedi, et che subito, che si toccano, s'abbotonano. Beuti nel uino ua
gliono à coloro, che non possono orinare, et al trabocco di fiele. Vngonsi utilme
te con mele alla schirantia, & bolliti triti in un guscio di Melagrano con oglio
D rosado, medicano i dolori delle orecchie distillatoui dentro.

V Olgarissimi animaletti sono le Millepede, lequali noi chiamiamo Porcelletti, & però basti quello che qui chiara
mente ne scriue Dioscoride.

Delle Blatte de i Mulini. Cap.xxxv.

E Interiora delle Blatte, che stanno ne i mulini, & appresso alle macine, peste, et
cotte nell'oglio leuano i dolori delle orecchie distillandouisi dentro.

S Ono (come si legge in Plinio all'ultimo capitolo del. xxix. libro) le Blatte di piu spetie. Ma quelle, che hauiamo
noi in Thoscana, & che uolgarmente chiamiamo Piattole, che si ritrouano la notte nelle cantine appresso à i prinu
li, & similmente ne i mulini, & ne i bagni, sono ueramente sporchissimi, & abomineuoli animali. Rassomigliansi
quasi à i grilli, che cantano di notte, ma sono piu stacciate, & hanno le gambe piu sottili, quasi come quelle de i Ragni, &
però uelocissime al fuggire. Hanno mirabilmente in odio la luce, di modo, che andadosi la notte con lume all'improuisona

128 BOOK

A On Garum. Chapter 31.

Brine made from fish, as well as from the flesh of other animals, halts ulcers that spread when fomented with it. It heals dog bites. Enemas are made from it for dysentery, and also for sciatica. In the case of ulcers, it is used to dry them out and cook them, and in the case of non-ulcerated parts, to bring them to ulceration.

On Fish Broth. Chapter 32.

Fish broth drunk plain, and likewise with wine, loosens the body. It is made for this purpose especially from Phycis fish, from Scorpion fish, from Luside, from Perch, and from other rock fish that are tender, fresh, and of good odor, which are cooked simply in water, with oil and dill.

B I Garum (according to Pliny, in the seventh chapter of his thirty-first book) was so called among the ancients because it was made from the entrails of fish, macerated and dissolved in salt, which was called Garum. This was afterward made similarly from mackerel, and this seasoning was used in kitchens with great ceremony, as a condiment for various foods. But Dioscorides did not mean this: he takes Garum to mean generally all brines of fish and meats. Nothing more need be said about fish broth, as the Author himself has explained it sufficiently.

On Bedbugs. Chapter 33.

It is useful to swallow seven bedbugs enclosed in bean pods before a quartan fever begins. Swallowed plain without beans, they are useful against the bites of Asps. Their smell, when used as a fumigant, revives women who have fainted from the womb; and drunk with wine or vinegar, they make leeches that have attached themselves to the throat detach. Crushed bedbugs, placed in the urinary passage, relieve the discomforts of urination.

C I Among all the nocturnal enemies that so often break our sweet rest in sleep, there are truly none more cruel than bedbugs: for besides biting us, breaking our sleep, and sucking our blood, they leave behind such a stench that it offends the senses and spirits far more than all the burning bites they inflict on every limb of the body. And although they are such most troublesome and filthy animals, nature did not wish to deprive them entirely of some useful faculty. Some modern physicians use them to provoke urination, not by applying them dead and crushed as Dioscorides says, but alive. This seems more fitting to me: because the stirring they make in the urinary canal stimulates the expulsive faculty to urinate. Wild ones are found on green plants, similarly foul-smelling, but these have been found to have no use in medicine.

On Millipedes. Chapter 34.

Millipedes, which like to stay under water jars, are animals with many legs that curl up as soon as they are touched. Drunk in wine they are good for those who cannot urinate, and for overflow of bile. They are usefully applied with honey for quinsy, and boiled and crushed in a pomegranate shell with rose oil, they relieve ear pains when dripped inside.

D Millipedes are very common little animals, which we call Porcelletti, and thus what Dioscorides writes about them here is sufficient.

On Mill Cockroaches. Chapter 35.

The entrails of cockroaches that live in mills and near millstones, pounded and cooked in oil, relieve ear pains when dripped inside.

S There are (as one reads in Pliny, in the last chapter of the twenty-ninth book) several species of cockroaches. But those we have in Tuscany, which we commonly call Piattole, found at night in cellars near the first growth vines, and likewise in mills and baths, are truly most filthy and abominable animals. They resemble crickets that sing at night, but are more flattened and have thinner legs, almost like those of spiders, and are therefore very swift in fleeing. They have a remarkable aversion to light, so that if one goes at night unexpectedly with a lamp...

translation:
SECOND [Book] 129

As for the places where they are found in quantity, they flee and hide with the utmost swiftness. Dioscorides must have been thinking of those used in mills when he wrote about them, and not those we call Barbeggie and other Carp, which are frequently found in beehives and in salted meats. For these too are called Blatte. Their many properties, as assigned by Pliny in the passage already mentioned, I will pass over here, thinking that Medicine can cure those ailments with remedies more wholesome and agreeable than these nauseating, horrible, foul-smelling and detestable creatures.

Of the Sea Lung. Chapter 46.

The Sea Lung, freshly ground and applied as a poultice, is good for gout and for bubo swellings.

Sea Lungs resemble the lungs of animals, and are (as Pliny wrote in Book IX) more like species of plants than of fish, such as sea-nettles, sponges, holothurians, and starfish. They are sometimes seen floating above the waves and signify an approaching sea-storm. When rubbed on sticks and staffs they give off light at night, like burning torches.

Of the Lungs of Certain Animals. Chapter 37.

The lung of the Pig, the Lamb, and the Bear, applied externally, prevents the inflammations in those ailments that shoes commonly cause to the feet. But that of the Fox, drunk dry, helps those with chest constrictions, and its fat, melted and distilled into the ears, removes their pain.

There are many other organs of these animals whose Lungs Dioscorides mentions, which have medicinal virtues, and which will be discussed in their proper places as this second book proceeds. But since these animals are known to all, there is no need to say more here, except that I cannot refrain from noting that bear cubs are not born as shapeless lumps of flesh that the mothers then lick into form, as many have written and is commonly believed. For in the valley of Anama in the jurisdiction of Trento, from a she-bear taken pregnant and very near her time during the hunt, I myself witnessed the hunters draw out bear cubs fully formed in all their members, just like other four-footed animals when they are near birth.

Of the Livers of Certain Animals. Chapter 38.

The liver of the Ass, eaten roasted, is good for epilepsy, but it must be eaten on an empty stomach. The liquid that drips from that of the Goat when it is roasted, placed in the eyes of those who cannot see at night (called night-blind), is beneficial; and it also helps them if they inhale the smoke from it with open eyes while it is roasting. Eaten roasted in food, it is good for all the aforesaid conditions. They say that when those who suffer from epilepsy eat the liver of the Billy-goat, it immediately brings on a seizure. That of Wild Boars, dried and made into powder and drunk with wine, is good for the bites of serpents and birds. It is believed that the liver of a rabid Dog, eaten roasted by those bitten by it, protects them from fear of water. Others also use as a remedy taking the hide of that same Dog that bit them and tying it in a small leather pouch on the arm of the patient. The liver of the Cormorant, salted and aged, drives out the afterbirth when drunk with honeyed water in the measure of two spoonfuls.

Besides the liver of the Ass, the Goat, the Billy-goat, the Wild Boar, and the Cormorant, in our own day certain physicians counted among the most capable use that of the Wolf, giving it dried in powder as something almost divine, for liver fluxes and dropsies — though Galen, in Book XI on the Properties of Simple Medicines, affirmed it to be of little use, saying: I have many times added wolf liver to that medicament for the liver made with Eupatorium, and have not found that so composed it works better than that which is made without it. He likewise said that giving the liver of a rabid Dog along with other things tested by experience was an error, or else that of the interpreter of Paul. Galen made mention of the stomach of the Cormorant, mocking those who hold that eating it — whether boiled or roasted — strengthens the stomach for digestion, and he likewise made fun of those physicians who in the same application use the inner membranes of the gizzards of

Hens; for he says he has had experience of both without any success or benefit. To which certain modern Physicians pay little heed, for as soon as they wish to prescribe something to strengthen the stomach, they always have on their lips that recipe: Stomachi Gallinarum.

On the Penis of the Stag. Chapter 39.
The penis of the Stag, ground up and drunk with wine, is good against the bites of Vipers.

Avicenna says that the penis of the Stag, besides being appropriate for the bite of Vipers as Dioscorides says, is also good for urinary retention and for colic pains, washing it well and then drinking the washing water. It is used ground up in electuaries that provoke coition, according to the opinion of some.

On the Hooves of the Ass and of Goats. Chapter 40.
The ash of the Hooves of the Ass, drunk in the quantity of two spoonfuls, benefits somewhat, as they say, the falling sickness, and kneaded with oil and applied it heals swellings and scrofula. The ash of those of the Goat rubbed on with vinegar causes hair that has fallen out from ringworm to grow back.
Beyond the hooves of the Ass and of the Goat, in use among followers of Rasis in his treatise on the sixty animals are those of the fore-feet of Cows, burned to ash and drunk, to bring in the milk of wet-nurses, and those of the Mule, to prevent women from becoming pregnant; these he claims will also drive away Mice from houses by burning them as a fumigation, so long as they are burned upon the coals throughout the house.

On the Calluses, or Chestnuts, of the legs of Horses. Chapter 41.
Calluses, or Chestnuts, found on the legs of Horses in the parts below the knees, and sometimes above the hooves, ground up as they say and drunk in vinegar, benefit the falling sickness.
Pliny mentions these Calluses, found on the legs of Horses and very well known to everyone, in the eleventh chapter of the twenty-eighth book, praising them for the pain of teeth when ground and put into the ears with oil. But Galen, and likewise Paul of Aegina, beyond what Dioscorides wrote about them, said that some people used them for any sort of animal bite.

On Old Shoes. Chapter 42.
The ash of old shoes, used in the manner of a liniment, is good for burns, for chafings between the thighs, and for abrasions that shoes cause on the feet.

The ash of Old Shoes (as Galen wrote in the eleventh book on the faculties of Simple medicines) benefits abrasions of the feet that have no other inflammation around them, because since it is hot and dry it would otherwise do more harm.
But beyond this the smoke of Old Shoes placed upon coals, held under the nose, is a wonderful thing for reviving women suffering from suffocation of the womb, as I can truly affirm from having cured some of those who, being held for dead, had been abandoned by everyone. This smoke is likewise wonderful for driving away Serpents that frequent houses and the bodies of men, into which while they sleep in the open country with their mouths open they silently enter, as Marco Gatinaria, a physician of our time, writes happened to a certain man of his time at Pavia, for whom though many remedies were tried, nothing helped him except the smoke of Old Shoes. For when the animal, which was a most venomous Viper, sensed it, it immediately came out through the anus without any trouble, to the great astonishment of all present.

On Roosters and Hens. Chapter 43.
Hens opened and applied while still warm are good for the bites of Serpents, but one must replace them frequently by putting on new ones. Their brain is likewise given to drink against the bites of venomous animals, and it is applied to stanch the blood that flows from the membranes of the brain. That little membrane inside the gizzard of the Rooster, resembling a thin plate of horn, which is thrown away when it is cooked, dried and made into powder is usefully given to drink in wine to those who have a weak stomach. Nelle montagne, & altri luoghi frigidi pochissime se ne ritrouano, & per contrario assai se ne ueggono nelle pianure,
& ne i luoghi, oue per i gran caldi crepano i terreni. Passano le Locufte uolando lunghissimi mari, & qualche uolta ne so-

tempi nostri ci han fatto testimonio l'anno del. 1542. l'innumerabili schiere, che uenendo dalle Paludi Meotide, copersero
non solamente tutta Vngheria, & grandissima parte d'Alamagna; ma anchora tutta l'Italia, doue fecero infinitissimi dan-
ni nelle biade minute, et nell'herbe de i prati; magiandosi legumi, il panico, il meglio, et la faggina sino alle radici. I Par-
thi le mangiano ne i cibi, & imperò non è marauiglia, se nelle sacre lettere(come si legge al. xi. cap. del Leuitico)se lodò B
Moise ne i cibi al suo populo hebreo, ne ancho, che San Giouanni Battista le mangiasse insieme co'l mele saluatico nel di-

Dello Ossifrago uccello. Cap.xlvij.

Dicefi che l'uentriglio di quello uccello, che chiamano i latini Ossifrago, beuto à
poco à poco fa orinare le pietre insieme con l'orina.

R Itrouo dell'Ossifrago diuerse opinioni; imperoche appresso ad Aristotile è l'Ossifrago uno uccello simile all'Aqui-
