translation:
SECOND. 133

Fresh locusts are usefully drunk with wine against scorpion bites. People eat them as food until they are satisfied — those who inhabit Lepti, a region of Africa.

Locusts are called in Tuscany, and in other parts of Italy, by various names: namely grilli, saltelli, caualette, saiuppi, and still other names, according to the customs and variety of the regions. They are very well-known animals, though quite harmful to herbs and to grain. According to what Aristotle wrote in chapter twenty-eight of the sixth book on the nature of animals, the males are considerably larger than the females. The females lay their eggs by thrusting their tails into the ground, from which are born certain powdery little worms covered with a thin skin; when this skin breaks open, locusts are generated from them. In mountainous and cold places very few are found, while on the contrary many are seen on plains and in places where the ground cracks from intense heat. Locusts travel flying across very long stretches of sea, and sometimes have crossed from Africa into Italy — as Pliny said — in such quantities that their swarms darkened the Sun as clouds do, causing no small astonishment among men and fear that, settling in their lands, they would lay them waste; for they ruin much and make barren the places where they alight, eating up the grain and herbs down to the very roots. Of this, in our own times, in the year 1542, the innumerable swarms testified, which coming from the Maeotic Marshes covered not only all of Hungary and the greatest part of Germany, but also all of Italy, where they caused immense damage to small grains and to the herbs of the meadows, eating up legumes, millet, panic grass, and beech-mast down to the roots. The Parthians eat them as food, and so it is no wonder that in Holy Scripture (as one reads in chapter eleven of Leviticus) Moses praised them as food for his Hebrew people, nor that Saint John the Baptist ate them together with wild honey in the desert — although there are some commentators who wish to interpret "locusts" as certain roots, and others as certain treetops. Not agreeing with them, I hold it for true that, being Hebrew and a great observer of the Mosaic law, he truly ate these locusts as animals. In some places, such as the region of Cyrenaica, on the island of Lemnos, and in Syria, people go out in great numbers two or three times a year into the countryside to destroy their nests, and then to kill them once they have hatched, as if they were going to fight against great armies. It is said that in India there are some that are three feet long and very fierce biters.

On the Ossifrage bird. Chapter 47.

It is said that the gizzard of that bird which the Latins call the Ossifrage, drunk little by little, causes kidney stones to be urinated out together with the urine.

I find various opinions about the Ossifrage; for according to Aristotle the Ossifrage is a bird similar to the Eagle. When the Eagle drives her chicks from the nest before they are fully grown and finished being reared, in order to see them compete among themselves for the food she brings them, the Ossifrage takes them in and finishes rearing them. The Ossifrage has weak eyesight, having a kind of film over the pupil of its eye. But Pliny, in chapter three of the ninth book, counting it among the species of Eagles, says it is the offspring of the Osprey and the sea Eagle, and does not believe it to be a species in its own right, but that it is born of an Eagle mated with various males. Alberto then holds that the Ossifrage is an aquatic bird larger than the Swan, with a long beak made on the lower part like a sack, in which it stores no small quantity of fish, which it swallows little by little. These are often seen in the lagoon of Orbetello in our Sienese Maremma, and are commonly called Agrotti. But I do not believe that those described by Aristotle and Pliny are seen or come to Italy.

On the Lark. Chapter 48.

The Lark is a little bird that has a small crest on the top of its head, like Peacocks have. Roasted and eaten as food, it heals colic pains.

Larks are well-known little birds, and according to what Aristotle said in chapter twenty-five of the ninth book, they come in two kinds: those with a crest and those without. They live in the fields, eating now little worms, now seeds of various plants. The males sing very well, and they are always among the first little birds to announce summer with their song. Larks fear Sparrowhawks and Merlins so greatly that, chased by them many times, they flee into the very bosoms of people. When male larks are kept for singing in cages, they often become blind in one eye, as experience shows.

On the Swallow. Chapter 49.

If young swallows of the first brood are taken before the moon is full, two stones are found in their gizzards, one of a single color and another varied. These, enclosed in the leather of a calf or a deer and attached to the neck or to the arm, are so beneficial against the falling sickness that often with them some people...

138 LIBRO
A Della Salamandra. Cap. lv.

A Salamandra animale pigro, & vario di colore, si connumera nella spetie delle lucertole. E' una sciocchezza il credere, che non si brusci nel fuoco. Le facoltà sue sono di mangiare, scaldare, & ulcerare la carne. Mettesi nelle medicine ulcerative, & in quelle della lebbra, come si mettono le cantarelle, & riponsi nel modo, che si ripongon quelle. Disfatta la Salamandra nell'oglio fa cascare i peli: & serbasi nel mele, trattegli prima l'interiora, & tagliatagli poscia la testa, & i piedi, per l'uso medesimo.

Eggonsi le Salamandre alla foresta per ogni strada nella valle Anania, & per ogni altro luogo del Trentino, ne i tempi delle molte piogge la Primavera massime, & l'Autunno. Ma nella State per il caldo, & nel Verno per il gran freddo, yarissime volte escono di sotto terra. Sono animali di corpo, & di quantità simili à Ramarri, ma hanno più grossa testa, maggior corpo, più alte gambe, & più breue coda. Quelli sono uelocissimi, & queste tardissime nell'andare. Sono tutte nel colore pezzate, di nero, & di giallo, amenduni iuiussimi colori, & così lucidi, come se con arte fussero bruniti. Sono stom.achose, & abomineuoli alla uista. Di queste scriuendo Plinio à. lxvij. capitoli del. x. libro, La Salamandra (diceua) non si uede se non ne i tempi delle pioggie, & nella sua natura è tanto frigida, che toccando il fuoco lo spegne. Anche fa bene mettendola, come ho prouato io, in sui carboni, come fa la carne crudi di qual si voglia animale. Ma gittata nel corpo del fuoco, oue sia gran uigore di fiamma, è una melansagine il credere, ch'ella non brusci, & che la uiua di fuoco, come iuue il Cameleone dell'aria. Non è differenza secondo Plinio nelle Salamandre; Imperoche le non sono ne maschi, ne femmine, & non generano animale alcuno, ma nascono elle di putrefattione. Il morso loro è uelenoso, come quello delle serpi, & toccando elle frutti, ò herbe con bocca, ui lasciano una certa saliua suo, laquale è ueleno ueramente mortifera, da cui sono stati alcuni inauertentemente auelenati, mangiando cotali frutti, ò herbe insaluate da loro.

Dei Ragni. Cap. lvi.

C Vel Ragno, che chiamano Lupo, fregato ad una pezzuola di lino, ò ad una faldeletta di fila, & applicato alle tempie, ouero alla fronte cura la terzana. La sua tela ristagna il sangue impiastrata in sul luogo: & prohibisce l'infiammagioni nelle ferite, che sono fra carne, & pelle. Enne d'un'altra spetie, che fa le tele bianche, sottili, & spesse, ilquale legato in cuoio (secondo che si dice) & attaccato al braccio, medica la quartana. Vale l'oglio rosado, oue questo sia cotto, à i dolori dell'orecchie distillandouelo.

Ono i Ragni (secondo che scriue Aristotile à. xxxix. capitoli del. ix. libro) di due spetie, mordaci cioè, & molto nociui, & non mordaci, ne nociui ad alcuno. I mordaci sono di due sorti, uno simile à quello, che non morde, che si chiama Lupo, chiamato Pulce, & questo è piccolo, vario di colore, mordace, & libidinoso; l'altro è poscia maggiore, nero, con piedi dinanzi similmente neri, tardo al caminare, & assai debile, & imperò non salta come fal'altro. Nella spetie di quelli, che non nuocono è quello, che si chiama Lupo, ilquale è anch'esso di due spetie, grande cioè, & piccolo. Questo non tese tela, come che il maggiore la tessa piccola, è aspra appresso à terra, & per le siepi. Di questa medesima spetie sono anchora quelli, che fanno le tele grandi, chiamati Sapienti, de i quali si ritrouano similmente de grandi, & de piccioli, & questi son quelli, che tessono nelle nostre case, & di queste due spetie intese Dioscoride. Chiama Plinio quelli, che col mordere lasciano ueleno, Phalangi; Ma dice, che questi non se ne ritrouano in Italia, & secondo che recita egli à. iiij. capitoli del. xxix. libro, sono questi d'assai più spetie, che non scrisse Aristotile, & similmente chiamati particolarmente per diuersi nomi. Causano questi nel mordere diuersi accidenti, secondo che sono diuersi di forma, & di natura; imperoche alcuni fanno punture dolorose, simili à quelle delle uespe; altri come quelle de gli scorpioni; altri contaminano le ginocchia; altri imagriscono i corpi; altri fanno enfiar la bocca; altri fanno perder la usta, & altri uomitare, & orinare cose simili alle tele de i Ragni, nel modo che alcuni morsi da i cani rabbiosi orinano con gran passione cagnoletti di carne, di grandezza d'una uespe. Ma se bene (come disse Plinio) in Italia non sono queste spetie di Phalangi, ui se ne ritrouano un'altra spetie di pessimi, i quali da Taranto città del regno di Napoli, doue ne nasce gran copia, si chiamano Tarantole, lequali fanno ueramente diuersi, et strani accidenti ne gli huomini, ch'elle mordono; Imperoche di questi, alcuni cantano, alcuni ridono, alcuni piangono, alcuni gridano, alcuni uomitano, alcuni dormono, alcuni uegghiano, alcuni saltano, alcuni tremano, alcuni sudano, & alcuni patiscono diuersi altri accidenti, & fanno pazzie, come se fussero spiritati. I quali effetti non si può dire, se non che procedino da diuerse nature di questi animali, come che uogliono alcuni, che le Tarantole faccino questi diuersi effetti secondo i di che le mordono, & ancho secondo l'hora. Di queste ne sono in molti luoghi delle nostre maremme di Siena, & nel patrimonio; Ma uniuersalmente ne sono assai in Puglia, & stannosi ne i campi del grano ascose in terra, doue spesse uolte trafiggono i metitori, che per nò sa

translation:
138 BOOK
A On the Salamander. Chapter 55.

The Salamander is a sluggish animal of varied color, and is counted among the lizard family. It is foolishness to believe that it does not burn in fire. Its properties are to eat away, heat, and ulcerate the flesh. It is used in ulcerating medicines and in treatments for leprosy, applied as one applies cantharides, and preserved in the same way. The Salamander dissolved in oil causes hair to fall out; and it is preserved in honey, after first removing its internal organs and then cutting off its head and feet, for the same use.

Salamanders are seen in the forest along every road in the valley of Anania, and in every other part of the Trentino, especially during times of heavy rain in Spring and in Autumn. But in Summer, due to the heat, and in Winter due to the great cold, they very rarely come out from underground. They are animals of body and size similar to green lizards, but with a thicker head, larger body, higher legs, and shorter tail. The latter are very swift, while salamanders are extremely slow in movement. They are all spotted in color, black and yellow, both very vivid colors, and so bright as if they had been burnished by art. They are repulsive and abominable to look at. Writing about them, Pliny at chapter 67 of book 10, said that the Salamander is only seen in rainy weather, and that its nature is so cold that it extinguishes fire by touching it. It also does well, as I have proven, placed on coals, as does the raw flesh of any animal. But thrown into a fire where there is great force of flame, it is a melancholy delusion to believe it does not burn, and that it lives on fire as the Chameleon lives on air. According to Pliny, there is no difference among Salamanders; for they are neither male nor female, and they generate no offspring, but are born of putrefaction. Their bite is venomous like that of serpents, and when they touch fruits or herbs with their mouths, they leave a certain secretion that is truly deadly poison, by which some people have been unwittingly poisoned by eating such fruits or herbs contaminated by them.

On Spiders. Chapter 56.

C The spider called the Wolf Spider, rubbed onto a linen cloth or a thread bandage and applied to the temples or forehead, cures the tertian fever. Its web, spread as a plaster over a wound, stops bleeding and prevents inflammation in wounds that are between flesh and skin. There is another kind that makes white, fine, and thick webs, which, bound in leather (as they say) and attached to the arm, cures the quartan fever. Oil of roses in which this spider has been cooked is good for pains in the ears when dropped in.

Spiders are (according to Aristotle at chapter 39 of book 9) of two kinds, that is, venomous and very harmful, and non-venomous, harmless to anyone. The venomous ones are of two sorts: one similar to the non-biting one called the Wolf Spider, named the Flea Spider, which is small, varied in color, biting, and lascivious; the other is larger, black, with similarly black front legs, slow in movement and very weak, and therefore does not jump as the other does. Among those that do not harm is the Wolf Spider, which is also of two kinds, large and small. This one does not spin a web, whereas the larger one spins a small, rough web close to the ground and along hedges. Of this same kind are also those that make large webs, called the Wise Spiders, among which there are also large and small ones, and these are the ones that weave in our houses, and it is these two kinds that Dioscorides wrote about. Pliny calls those that leave venom with their bite Phalangi; but he says these are not found in Italy, and according to his account in chapter 4 of book 29, these are of far more kinds than Aristotle wrote, and similarly each is called by its own particular name. These cause various accidents when they bite, according to their diverse form and nature; for some cause painful stings similar to those of wasps; others like those of scorpions; others contaminate the knees; others emaciate the body; others cause the mouth to swell; others cause loss of appetite, and others vomiting, and urinating substances similar to spider webs, in the way that some people bitten by rabid dogs urinate with great pain small lumps of flesh the size of a wasp. But even though (as Pliny said) these species of Phalangi are not found in Italy, another species of the most terrible kind is found there, which from Taranto, a city in the kingdom of Naples where they are born in great numbers, are called Tarantulas, which truly cause diverse and strange accidents in the people they bite; for some of those bitten sing, some laugh, some weep, some shout, some vomit, some sleep, some stay awake, some jump, some tremble, some sweat, and some suffer various other accidents, and act madly as if they were possessed. These effects cannot be explained except as proceeding from the diverse natures of these animals, although some hold that Tarantulas produce these different effects according to the day on which they bite, and also according to the hour. These are found in many places in our marshlands of Siena and in the Patrimony; but they are most abundant universally in Puglia, where they hide in the grain fields underground, where they often sting the harvesters who, not knowing

SECONDO 139

pere Pufanza, non hanno gli stiualetti in gamba. De i quali gia mi ricordo hauere ueduto io alcuni patire assai de predetti accidenti. Ma è gran cosa che'l ueleno uniuersalmente di questi animali si mitigi, & si uinca con la musica de suoni; Percioche ho ueduto io tre, ò quattro di costoro assaliti da diuersi di questi accidenti, esser menati doue si sonauano diuersi istrumenti da ballare, & subito calargli l'afsiliitioni, & ballare anchor eglino gagliar dissimamente, di modo che alcuno non harrebbe pensato, che fufsero stati quelli, che erano morduti dalle Tarantole. Ma cessando il suono ritornanano poscia nei loro primi moti, & rientrauano ne i medesimi accidenti pian piano. Et però si costuma di far sempre sonare di, & notte, sino che si fanano: impero he il lungo suono uince al fine la malitia del ueleno di questi animali, come che in quel mezzo, che si suona, se gli dia della Theriaca, del Muridato, & dell'altre cose, che uniuersalmente sogliono à i morsi delle serpi, & de gli Aspidi.

Delle Lucertole. Cap. lviij.

A testa della Lucertola pesta, & applicatauì sopra, caua fuore le spine, i bronco-ni, & ogni altra cosa fitta nelle membra del corpo. Tira fuore i porri, i calli, & quelle sorti di formiche, che pendono. Il fegato messo nelle concauità dei denti, ne leua uia il dolore. Messa tutta la Lucertola aperta in su le punture de gli Scor pioni, u'allegerisce il dolore.

Della Sepa. Cap. lviij.

A Sepa, la quale chiamano alcuni Chalcidica lucertola, beuta nel uino è rimedio à suoi istessi morsi.

E Lucertole notissimi animali partorisono ancho ese l'uuoua, come fanno le serpi, et sono inimicissime delle chioc ciole. In Arabia son lunghe un gombito, secondo che à xxxix. capitoli del xiii. libro scrisse Plinio, & in India nel monte Nisa se ne ritrouano di lunghe xxiiii. piedi, di colore quali rose, quali gialle, et quali cerulee. Ne sono ancho-ra come pur disse egli nel vi. nell'Isola capraria, la quale è una delle fortunate, di molto grandi, & in grandissima copia. Le Chalcidice non sono in Italia, ma per quanto si dice, nascono in Libia, & in Cipri, doue stanno per la piu parte fra sassi. Della forma di queste ritrouò uarie opinioni; Percioche alcuni uogliono, che le sieno simili alle Lucertole nostre uolgari, & altri, che le sieno quella spetie di serpenti, che si chiamano Cerafte, ouero molto simili à quelli. Nicandro in questo tiene con Dioscoride, che le sieno simili alle nostre Lucertole, & però diceua nelle sue Theriache. Guardarati dalla Sepa, cioè dalla Chalcidica Lucertola, animale ueramente simile alla Lucertola. Ma Aetio al libro xiii. diceua. Il serpente, che si dimanda Sepa, è lungo due gombitti, & essendo grosso dinanzi sia po'cia assottigliando sino alla coda, ua tardamente, ha il capo largo, la bocca appuntata, et tutto picchierato, & scaccato di bianco, et mordendo ammazza in tre, ouero in quattro giorni. Paulania poscia, parlando d'uno Epito Red'Arcadia, dice, che essendo egli à caccia su morduto da una Sepa, serpente simile a una picciola uipera, di colore di cenere uariamente penticchiato, con capo largo, collo sottile, corpo grosso, & coda corta: il cui andare è sempre in storto, come quello del granchio. Il che è proprio delle Cerafte. E però è necessario dire, ò che alcuni di costoro si sieno ingannati, ouero che la Sepa sia di due diiuerse sorti, & che alcuni dell'una, & alcuni dell'altra habbiano scritto. Ma non lasciarò però di dire, che in terra di Roma si ritrouà una certa spetie di Lucertole tutte stellate nella schena, chiamate per stare sotto terra, Terrantole; le quali, per esser molto uelenose, ho piu uolte pensato, che sieno le Chalcidice di Dioscoride.

Dello Stinco. Cap. lix.

Nasce lo Stinco in Egitto, in India, nel mare Rosso, & in Lidia di Mauritania. E' lo Stinco il terrestre Crocodilo di sua propria spetie. Conser uato con sale, & nasturtio, dicono, che la carne delle sue reni beuta al peso d'una dramma con uino accende molto i disiderii di uenere. Ma che beuta con dicottione di lenticchie, et mele, ouero con seme di lattuga, & acqua, opera il contrario. Oltre à questo si mette lo Stinco ne gli antidoti.

Vantunque chiami Dioscoride lo Stinco Crocodilo terrestre; sono nondimeno quelli, che si portano à Venetia Marini del mar Rosso, & quelli d'Egitto del Nilo, & come che sieno nella fattezza loro simili ai Crocodili; non dime no questi, che si portano à noi non sono maggiori delle piu grosse Lucertole, & hanno le loro squame bianche, che tendono al giallo, con una linea bertina dal capo alla coda. Il che non hanno i Crocodili, ma sono di sua natura tutti neri in su la schena. Scriuendo delli Stinchi Pausania disse, che se ne ritrouauano in Libia di quelli lunghi due gombiti. In su quel di Vicenza a una forte di piccolini, & neri, in certi luoghi, liquali adoperano spesso gli Spetiali in cambio di Marini, quando non ne possono hauere d'altri. Ma inuero penso, che poco uaglino per gli effetti, che fanno i Marini. Scrisse de gli Stin-

translation:
SECOND 139

Because of their "Pufanza," they do not have little boots on their legs. Of these I recall having seen some suffer greatly from the aforementioned accidents. But it is a remarkable thing that the venom of these animals is universally mitigated and overcome by musical sounds; for I have seen three or four of those attacked by various of these accidents be carried to where various instruments for dancing were being played, and immediately their afflictions would subside, and they too would dance most vigorously, so that no one would have thought them to be those who had been bitten by Tarantulas. But when the music stopped, they would return to their former state and fall back into the same accidents little by little. And so it is customary to have music played day and night continuously until they recover: for the prolonged sound ultimately overcomes the malice of the venom of these animals, even as in the meantime, while the music plays, they are given Theriac, Mithridate, and other things universally used against the bites of serpents and asps.

On Lizards. Chapter 58.

The head of the lizard, pounded and applied to the skin, draws out thorns, splinters, and everything else lodged in the members of the body. It draws out warts, calluses, and those kinds of hanging growths. The liver placed in the cavities of the teeth removes the pain. The whole lizard, opened and laid upon the stings of scorpions, eases the pain.

On the Sepa. Chapter 58.

The Sepa, which some call the Chalcidic lizard, drunk in wine, is a remedy against its own bite.

Lizards, very well-known animals, also lay eggs as serpents do, and are the greatest enemies of snails. In Arabia they are one cubit long, as Pliny wrote in the thirty-ninth chapter of his thirteenth book, and in India on Mount Nisa some are found to be twenty-four feet long, of colors ranging from rose to yellow and sky-blue. They are also found, as he wrote in the sixth book, on the Island of Capraria, which is one of the Fortunate Islands, in very large numbers and of great size. The Chalcidic lizards are not found in Italy, but according to report they are born in Libya and in Cyprus, where they live mostly among rocks. Regarding their form, he found various opinions; for some maintain they resemble our common lizards, and others that they are a species of serpent called Cerastes, or very similar to them. Nicander in this agrees with Dioscorides, that they resemble our lizards, and therefore wrote in his Theriaca: Beware of the Sepa, that is the Chalcidic lizard, an animal truly resembling the lizard. But Aetius in book thirteen wrote: the serpent called the Sepa is two cubits long, and being thick in front gradually tapers toward the tail, moves slowly, has a broad head and a pointed mouth, and is entirely spotted and checkered with white, and when it bites it kills in three or four days. Pausanias later, speaking of a certain prince of Arcadia, says that while he was hunting he was bitten by a Sepa, a serpent resembling a small viper, ash-colored and variously spotted, with a broad head, thin neck, thick body, and short tail: which always moves sideways like a crab. This is characteristic of the Cerastes. And so it is necessary to say either that some of these writers were mistaken, or that the Sepa is of two different kinds, and that some wrote of one and some of the other. But I will not fail to mention that in the region of Rome there is found a certain species of lizard all spotted on the back, called Terrantole because they live underground; which, being very venomous, I have more than once thought to be the Chalcidic lizards of Dioscorides.

On the Skink. Chapter 59.

The Skink is found in Egypt, in India, in the Red Sea, and in Lydia of Mauritania. The Skink is the terrestrial Crocodile of its own proper kind. Preserved in salt and nasturtium, they say that the flesh of its kidneys, drunk to the weight of a dram in wine, greatly inflames the desires of Venus. But drunk with a decoction of lentils and honey, or with lettuce seed and water, it has the opposite effect. Beyond this, the Skink is added to antidotes.

Although Dioscorides calls the Skink a terrestrial Crocodile, nevertheless those that are brought to Venice are marine ones from the Red Sea, and those of Egypt from the Nile, and although they resemble Crocodiles in shape, those brought to us are no larger than the largest lizards, and have white scales tending toward yellow, with a brownish stripe from head to tail. This the Crocodiles do not have, being by nature entirely black on their backs. Writing of Skinks, Pausanias said that some were found in Libya two cubits long. In the area of Vicenza there are a kind of small, black ones, which apothecaries often use in place of the marine ones when they cannot obtain others. But in truth I think they are of little value for the effects that the marine ones produce. He wrote of the Skin-

text:
140 LIBRO

A chi Plinio à gli.viij.capitoli del.xxviij.libro dicendo,che quelli d'India sono assai maggiori di quelli,che si ci portano d'Arabia, & oltre al lodare egli per le cose ueneree le reni loro,lodò similmente per i medesimi effetti il muso,& i piedi,& tutto il corpo beuto per le ferite delle saette ueleno. Ma hauendomi gli Stinchi reuocati à memoria i Crocodili,che chiamano acquatici,fiere particolari del Nilo,dico,che sono grandissime,& maluagissime fiere,& molto nimiche de gli huomini. Crescono (secondo che riferisce Aristotile ne i libri della natura de gli animali)alla lunghezza di quindici gombiti; come che Plinio dicesse di diciotto. Partorisono le loro uuoa in terra fuor dell'acqua;ma non però maggiori (se ben son grandissime bestie)di quelle dell'oche,delle quali poscia al suo tempo escono i piccioli, secondo la proportione dell'uuoa,nella grandezza loro. Ma è ueramente gran cosa,che un così picciolo animale di nascimeto,diueti poscia così gran bestia. Imperoche quando nascono,sono minori de i Ramari. Il Crocodilo non ha lingua,et egli solo di tutti gli animali muoue le mascelle di sopra,& quelle di sotto tien ferme. Ha occhi di porco,denti crudelissimi,che gli auanzano fuor di bocca,unghie acutissime nelle grisfe,& pelle tanto dura,che resiste ad ogni percossa. Di giorno sta la maggior parte in terra,et la notte quasi sempre nell'acqua. Scriue Plinio à.viij.capitoli del.xxviij.libro,che ne sono di due spetie,maggiore,& minore. La maggiore è quella di questi già scritti,& della minore sono quelli,che scrisse egli,che stanno sempre in terra fra l'herbe,& fra fiori odoriferi. Vagliono,secondo che egli dice,i denti della mascella destra de i maggiori ligati al braccio deston le le cose ueneree. Delle budella de i minori,le quali sono odorifirissime,se ne fa un certo medicamento chiamato Crocodileo,molto utile à i uitij de gli occhi. Mescolato con acqua suanisce tutti i difetti della faccia,come sono,lentigini,pani,uitiligini,& simili infettioni;facendo bellissima pelle. Dicono,che il lor fiele uale oltre à tutte le medicine,à leuare i fiocchi de gli occhi,& altri homori,che ui sieno ingrossati,che intorbidano la uista. La cenere del cuoio d'amenduni impiastrata con aceto sopra à i membri,che si debbono,ò tagliare,ò segare,ne leua di tal forte i sentimenti,che gli amalati nell'operare con ferro non sentono dolore alcuno. Il sangue dell'uno,& dell'altro,untone gli occhi,rischiara la uista. Il cuore dei Crocodili (secondo che si dice) inuolto in lana d'una pecora,che sia tutta nera senza macola alcuna d'altro colore,portato addosso sana la febre quartana. Cura le sciatiche il corpo del Crocodilo leuatone prima il capo,& i piedi,& poi mangiato cotto lesso nell'acqua.

Dei Vermi della terra. Cap.lx.

C I Vermi della terra tagliati minuti,& applicati,sanano le ferite de i nerui. Guariscono la febre terzana;& distillansi utilmente ne i difetti delle orecchie cotti con grasso d'oca. Gioua l'oglio della loro dicottione à i dolori de denti,distillandolo nell'orecchia della parte contraria del dolore. Triti,& beuti con uino passo prouocano l'orina.

Htamansi i Vermi della terra in Thoscana Lobrichi,& sono da i moderni Medici assai adoperati cotti nell'oglio,
c per mitigar i dolori de i luoghi neruosi,& delle giunture. Ma fallano speso alcuni Spetiali nel fare l'oglio loro: Imperoche li mettono à bollire nelle ramine sopra al fuoco de i carboni,& così in un tratto brusciano l'oglio,et arrostiscono i lombrichi. Il uero modo di farlo è à bagno di maria,in un uaso di uetro ben serrato,perche così se ne caua l'homore,& la uirtu,senza brusciare,ne arrostire l'oglio,& i lombrichi anchora. In questo,quando si fa con buona diligenza,ho ritrouato io mirabile giouamento ne i dolori delle gotte calde,ungendo prima con l'oglio il dolore,& poscia impiastrandoui sopra i uermi già cotti,pesti,& incorporati con ugual peso di cerotto di litargirio,che si chiama comunmente triapharmaco. Alche medesimamente à.ix.capitoli del.xxx.libro lodò Plinio la cenere loro impiastrata con mele,& applicata per tre giorni continui,& similmente mesiui fuso cotti con oglio uecchio. Oltre à cio,toltii Lombrichi,& ben lauati con uino,& poscia mesi e fsi così foliti un una boccia ben serrata di uetro à bollire à bagno di Maria per un di naturale,si conuertiscono in un certo liquore uiscoso,il quale per se solo consolida le ferite de i nerui,& delle budella. Ma molto più eccellentemente fa l'opera,accompagnato col Balsamo artifitiale,scritto di sopra nel primo libro al capitolo del uero Balsamo,ò in cambio di questo con oglio di gomma di Larice,ouero d'oglio d'uezzzo; Imperoche così in breue tempo consolida marauigliosamente tutte le ferite fresche di qual si uoglian luogo della persona;eccetto che quelle della testa. Dannosi utilmente i Lombrichi brusciati,& poluerizzati sottilmente à bere con acqua di Marobbio,ò d'Assenzo,ò à loro,che gli è traboccato il fiele,ouero composti in qualche confetto con altre cose appropriate.

Del Topo Ragno. Cap.lxt.

D IL Topo ragno uale à suoi istessi morsi tagliato in pezzi, & messo sopra alla piaga.

Il Topo ragno(secondo che recita Aetio)di colore simile alla Donnola,ma di grandezza simile à i Topi uolgari,
B & ha la bocca appuntata come la Talpa,nella quale tanto di sopra,quanto di sotto ha due ordini di denti,l'uno dentro dall'altro,sottili,& appuntati;& ha la coda assai più corta di quella de i Topi. Fecene similmente mentione

translation:
140 BOOK

A — Pliny, in the eighth chapter of the twenty-eighth book, says that those from India are much larger than the ones brought to us from Arabia, and beyond praising their kidneys for aphrodisiac uses, he likewise praised the snout and feet, and their entire body when drunk as a remedy against arrow-wound poison. But the Skinks having called crocodiles to my mind — those aquatic creatures particular to the Nile — I say that they are very large and very wicked beasts, and greatly hostile to men. They grow (according to Aristotle in his books on the nature of animals) to a length of fifteen cubits, though Pliny says eighteen. They lay their eggs on land, away from the water; yet the eggs are no bigger (great beasts though they are) than a goose's eggs, from which in due time the young emerge, small in proportion to the egg relative to their eventual size. It is indeed a remarkable thing that so small a creature at birth becomes so great a beast in time. When they hatch, they are smaller than lizards. The crocodile has no tongue, and alone among all animals it moves only its upper jaw, keeping the lower fixed. It has the eyes of a pig, teeth most cruel, which jut out from its mouth, very sharp claws on its forefeet, and skin so hard it resists every blow. By day it spends most of its time on land, and by night almost always in the water. Pliny writes, in the eighth chapter of the twenty-eighth book, that there are two kinds, the larger and the smaller. The larger is the kind already described here; the smaller are those he describes as always living on land among herbs and fragrant flowers. According to him, the teeth of the right jaw of the larger kind, tied to the right arm, are useful in aphrodisiac matters. The intestines of the smaller kind, which are very fragrant, are used to make a certain medicine called Crocodileo, very useful for ailments of the eyes. Mixed with water it clears away all blemishes of the face, such as freckles, pimples, discolorations, and similar conditions, making the skin very beautiful. They say that its bile surpasses all medicines for removing cataracts from the eyes and other humors that have thickened there, clouding the sight. The ash of the hide of both kinds, plastered with vinegar on limbs that must be cut or sawed, so deadens feeling that patients feel no pain at all during surgery with iron. The blood of one and the other, smeared on the eyes, brightens the sight. The heart of the crocodile (it is said) wrapped in the wool of a completely black sheep without any spot of another color, and carried on the person, cures quartan fever. The body of the crocodile, with the head and feet removed first and then boiled and eaten, cures sciatica.

Of Earth Worms. Chapter 60.

C — Earth worms, cut into small pieces and applied, heal wounds of the sinews. They cure tertian fever; and distilled usefully in ailments of the ears when cooked in goose fat. The oil of their decoction, dripped into the ear on the side opposite the pain, relieves toothache. Ground up and drunk with raisin wine, they provoke urination.

In Tuscany, earth worms are called Lobrichi, and are much used by modern physicians, cooked in oil, to ease pains in the nerves and joints. However, many apothecaries err in preparing their oil, for they put them to boil in copper pans over a charcoal fire, and in this way they quickly burn the oil and roast the worms. The true method is to make it in a water bath, in a well-sealed glass vessel, because in this way the humor and virtue are extracted without burning or roasting either the oil or the worms. With this method, when done with proper care, I have found it to be wonderfully effective against the pains of hot gout, first anointing the painful area with the oil, and then plastering over it the worms already cooked, pounded, and incorporated with an equal weight of litharge plaster, commonly called triapharmacon. For the same purpose, Pliny praises in the ninth chapter of the thirtieth book their ash plastered with honey and applied for three consecutive days, and likewise their juice when cooked with old oil. Furthermore, taking earthworms and washing them well with wine, then placing them in a well-sealed glass vessel in a water bath for a full day, they turn into a certain viscous liquid which by itself alone consolidates wounds of the sinews and intestines. But it works much more excellently when combined with artificial Balsam, described above in the first book in the chapter on true Balsam, or in its place with oil of larch resin or oil of dwarf pine; for in this way it marvelously consolidates in a short time all fresh wounds in whatever part of the body, except those of the head. Burned earthworms, powdered fine, are usefully given to drink with horehound water or wormwood water; or for those whose bile has overflowed, or composed in some confection with other appropriate things.

Of the Shrew Mouse. Chapter 61.

D — The shrew mouse, cut into pieces and placed over the wound, is a remedy for its own bite.

The shrew mouse (as Aetio relates) is similar in color to the weasel, but in size similar to common mice, and has a pointed snout like the mole, in which it has two rows of teeth both above and below, one set within the other, fine and pointed; and its tail is much shorter than that of common mice. description: Pietro Andrea Matthioli's landmark Italian translation of Dioscorides De Materia Medica. The first vernacular edition to make classical Greek botanical medicine accessible to European physicians.
translation:
SECOND 141

Nicander in his Theriaca says that if the Topo agno (shrew-mouse) passes over the track left by cart-wheels it immediately dies, and therefore the earth found clinging to cart-wheels is very useful against its bites. Of these animals, although they are found throughout all Italy, I myself have seen quite a number in the Anania valley within the jurisdiction of Trento. But there I never heard that their bites are venomous, as many ancient writers report. This perhaps occurs because of the nature of the place, as happens with Scorpions, which likewise do not harm you there, even though they do sting people, as has been discussed at length above in their own chapter.

On Mice. Chapter 62.

It is a most certain thing that mice, when they are kept in houses, cut up finely and applied as a plaster, cure the stings of scorpions; and that when roasted and given to children in their food, they dry up the excess saliva that flows in their mouths.

Mice are of various kinds, for they are found large, small, and medium; domestic, wild, and mountain. But speaking first of those that live in houses, and of those that frequent the fields, according to what Aristotle recounts in the last chapter of the sixth book on the nature of animals, these produce more offspring than any other kind of four-footed animal. He says a female of theirs gave proof of this: for having been shut up pregnant in a store of millet, upon opening the place thereafter, one hundred and twenty young mice were found together with the mother. For this reason, in some places they multiply so enormously in the fields without warning, that men who thought they would harvest the grain the next day have found it all eaten in a single night by mice. And indeed, were it not that in the countryside the rains drown great numbers of them in their burrows, and that pigs kill many of them, and foxes, wild cats, and serpents destroy many more, these animals would multiply so greatly as to drive people out of their houses, as they once forced certain peoples of Phrygia to abandon their cities. So great is nature's drive to reproduce in these animals that, as Aristotle also said, in a certain place in Persia, upon a pregnant female being opened by chance, young were found inside the bodies of the other female fetuses, before they had even been born. Some affirmed, as he also said, as a certain fact, that females become pregnant simply by tasting salt. The mice of Egypt are spiny, like our hedgehogs. A species of mice are also the Dormice, and therefore (as Pliny reports in the first chapter of the 36th book) Roman law forbade dormice to be eaten at dinner. But in our times they have been put to use as food, since men felt it would be a wrong to the palate and throat to let such fat animals go to waste, without considering that on account of their fattiness they ruin the appetite, generate gross and cold humors, and are hard to digest. Their flesh is useful medicinally when they are well fattened, for those who suffer from ravenous hunger, which physicians call bulimia. Mountain mice are finally large in body, like rabbits and sometimes larger, but lower in the leg. They have a head like a hare, but with such short ears that they can scarcely be seen to poke out from the head. They have fur almost like a badger, a short tail, and short legs, with grey forepaws armed with very sharp claws. These animals grow more in bulk than in length, and become marvelously fat. In the Trentino, in whose mountains, and especially on the Tonale, many of them are seen, they are called Marmotane, which word, corrected, means nothing other than Mus montanus (mountain mouse). These animals like to stand upright, as bears do, and often use their front paws in place of hands for eating. They have four very sharp front teeth, with which they bite cruelly anyone who displeases them. Kept in houses, even though their origin is in the peaks of the highest wild mountains, they nevertheless become quite tame, but they are very harmful, for they gnaw clothing and everything else left in the wrong place. In winter they willingly retreat into haystacks and straw, where they sleep for whole months, as dormice do. When frightened they cry out with thin, hissing shrieks, so that their voice sounds more like a whistle than anything else. Their meat is better eaten salted than fresh, because the salt, besides preparing their excessive moisture, removes much of the wild smell they give off. But whether salted or fresh, their meat is very hard to digest, weighs on the stomach, and stirs up excessive heat throughout the body; their fat, however, is praised for softening the nerves and joints of contracted limbs.

On Milk. Chapter 63.

Every milk generally produces good humors, provides good nourishment, and softens the body, even though it causes wind in the stomach and bowels. That of spring is more watery than that of summer, and that generated from green grass softens the body more. The white and uniformly thick kind is praised, as is that which, when dropped onto the fingernail, stays gathered on it and does not spread. Goat's milk is less laxative than the others, because goats for the most part feed on binding pasture, such as

A le quercie, i lentischi, gli oliui, & i terebinthi. La onde è utile il latte loro allo stomacho. Quello di Pecora è grosso, dolce, & molto grasso, e però non cosi conueneuole allo stoma-cho. Il Vaccino, l'Asinino, & il Cauallino, sono migliori per il corpo. Ogni latte generato di pascolo, oue sia Scammonea, Elleboro, Mercorella, & Volubile (come è stato scritto esser quello de monti Giustini) mette sottosopra lo stomacho, e'l corpo: & imperò le Capre, che pascono quiui le frondi dell'Elleboro bianco, che di nuouo spuntano di terra, uomitano el-le prima, & rendone poscia il latte, che beuto fa uomitare, & riuolta lo stomacho. Ogni lat-te, che sia cotto ristagna il corpo, & massime quello, doue sieno spente dentro pietre marine affocate. Gioua comunemente il latte à tutte l'ulcere delle interiora, & massime à quelle del gorgozzule, del polmone, delle budella, delle reni, & della uisciga. Dassi il latte fresco con mele crudo, acqua, & un poco di sale nel prurito della pelle, alle brozze ulcerate, & altri cat-tiui homori. Quello, che è cotto una uolta, è manco uentoso. Il cotto con le pietre affocate, sino che cali la metà, medica ne i flussi l'ulcere delle budella. Ha ogni latte il suo Siero, il-

B quale separato è piu efficace per soluere il corpo. Dassi nelle malattie, che uogliamo purga-re senza cose acute, et mordaci, come sono homori malinconici, mal caduco, lebbra, scabbia, & brozze, che nascono per tutto il corpo. Fassi d'ogni latte quello, che chiamano i Greci Schiston: facendolo bollire in una pignatta nuoua, & mescolandolo con un ramo di fico tol-to cosi uerde dall'albero, et aggiungendoui, come ha bollito tre, ò quattro bollori, per ogni hemina di latte, un ciatho d'aceto melato: percioche cosi si separa il siero dal latte. Ma biso-gna, accioche mentre che si cuoce, non trabocchi fuor del uaso, di continuo con una spogna piena d'acqua fredda bagnare l'orlo della bocca della pignatta, & sommergergli un seta-rio d'argento pieno d'acqua fredda. Dassi poscia à bere di questo Siero sino à cinque mine, interponendo da mina à mina nel berlo passeggiando alquanto di tempo. E buono oltre à quello, che è stato detto, ogni latte fresco à tutti i ueleni corrosiui, & incensiui, come sono cantarelle, bruchi de pini, salamandre, buprestide, iusquiamo, aconito, dorienio, & ephe-mero. Al che priuatamente uale il latte Vaccino. E utile il latte gargarizzato all'ulcere del

C la bocca, & del gorgozzule: & particolarmente per conseruare i denti, et le gengíue uale l'Asi-nino. Il latte di Pecora, di Vacca, & di Capra cotto con picciole pietre marine ferma l'ulce-re de flussi, & similmente i premiti delle pondora, fattone cristeri d'esso solo con ptisana d'or-zo, & spressione di spelta: Imperoche cosi mirabilmente rammorbidisce, & mitiga i dolori delle budella. Infondesi similmente nell'ulcere de i luoghi secreti delle donne. Dolcissi-mo è il latte humano, & molto nutritiuo. Gioua questo sutto dalle poppe à rodimenti dello stomacho, & à thisici. Beesi utilmente da chi hauesse beuto la lepre marina. Mettesi con manna d'incenso ne gli occhi, che per percosse uengono sanguinosi, & ungesi utilmen-te nelle podagre, con opio, & con cera. E ueramente ogni latte nociuo à diffettosi di melza, à fegatosi, alle uertigini, al mal caduco, à malattie de nerui, alle febri, & à dolori di testa: ec-etto se non si desse di quello già detto per purgare. Dicono alcuni che il latte del primo par-to d'una Cagna unto fa cadere i peli, & beuto uale contra à mortiferi ueleni, & fa partorite le creature, che son morte ne i corpi delle madri.

D Del Cascio. Cap.lxiiii.

IL Cascio fresco senza sale mangiato in cibo nutrisce, è utile allo stomacho, & di-stribuiscesi facilmente per le membra di tutto il corpo. Fa carne, & mollifica leg-giermente il corpo. Trouasi differenza di bontà nel Cascio, secondo il latte, del qual egli si fa. Il Cascio cotto lesso, & poscia spriemuto, & arrostito ristagna i flus-si del corpo. Fattone linimento gioua all'infiammagioni, et liuidezze de gli occhi. Il fresco salato di poco nutrisce manco, sminuisce la carne, è contrario allo stomacho, et disturba l'in-teriora. Il uecchio ristagna il corpo. Il siero, che esce dal Cascio nutrisce benissimo i cani. Quello, che chiamano Hippace, è cascio Cauallino, & come che sia d'odore fastidioso: non-dimeno nutrisce efficacemente: corrispondendo nelle sue proportioni al uaccino. Sono al-cuni, che dissero, che l'Hippace era il Caglio del cauallo.

A the oaks, the mastic trees, the olives, and the terebinths. Whence their milk is useful for the stomach. That of the Sheep is thick, sweet, and very fatty, and therefore not so suitable for the stomach. Cow's milk, Ass's milk, and Horse's milk are better for the body. Any milk produced from pastures where there is Scammony, Hellebore, Mercury plant, and Bindweed (as has been written of those of the mountains of Giustini) upsets the stomach and the body: and therefore the Goats that feed there on the leaves of white Hellebore, which newly spring from the ground, first vomit themselves, and then yield milk which, when drunk, causes vomiting and upsets the stomach. Any milk that is cooked restrains the body, and especially that in which heated marine stones have been extinguished. Milk commonly benefits all ulcers of the interior organs, and especially those of the throat, lungs, bowels, kidneys, and bladder. Fresh milk is given with raw honey, water, and a little salt for itching of the skin, for ulcerated pustules, and other bad humors. That which is cooked once is less windy. Cooked with heated stones until it reduces by half, it heals the ulcers of the bowels in cases of flux. Every milk has its Whey, which when

B separated is more effective for loosening the body. It is given in illnesses that we wish to purge without harsh or biting things, such as melancholic humors, epilepsy, leprosy, scabies, and pustules that appear all over the body. From any milk is made what the Greeks call Schiston: by boiling it in a new pot and mixing it with a branch taken green from the fig tree, and adding, once it has boiled three or four times, for every hemina of milk, one cyathus of honey-vinegar: for in this way the whey is separated from the milk. But it is necessary, so that while it cooks it does not overflow out of the vessel, to continuously wet the rim of the pot's mouth with a sponge full of cold water, and to submerge in it a silver setarius full of cold water. This Whey is then given to drink up to five mines, walking a little between each mina while drinking it. Beyond what has already been said, every fresh milk is good against all corrosive and burning poisons, such as blister beetles, pine caterpillars, salamanders, buprestis beetles, henbane, aconite, dorycnium, and ephemeron. For this purpose cow's milk is particularly valuable. Milk used as a gargle is useful for ulcers of

C the mouth and throat: and for preserving the teeth and gums, Ass's milk is especially valuable. The milk of Sheep, Cow, and Goat cooked with small marine stones stops the ulcers of fluxes, and likewise the straining of the bowels, used as a clyster by itself with barley water and spelt extract: for in this way it wonderfully softens and eases the pains of the bowels. It is also instilled into the ulcers of the secret parts of women. Human milk is the sweetest and most nutritious. This drawn directly from the breast benefits gnawing pains of the stomach, and those with consumption. It is usefully drunk by those who have drunk sea-hare poison. Mixed with frankincense gum it is applied to eyes that have become bloodshot from blows, and it is usefully rubbed on gout with opium and wax. Truly every milk is harmful to those with ailments of the spleen, liver disease, vertigo, epilepsy, diseases of the nerves, fevers, and headaches: except if that already mentioned for purging were given. Some say that the milk from the first birth of a Bitch, rubbed on, causes hair to fall out, and drunk is effective against deadly poisons, and causes delivery of creatures that have died in their mothers' bodies.

D Of Cheese. Chapter 64.

Fresh Cheese eaten without salt as food is nourishing, is useful for the stomach, and is easily distributed through all the members of the body. It builds flesh and gently softens the body. There is a difference in quality among cheeses, according to the milk from which it is made. Cheese cooked by boiling, then pressed and roasted, restrains the fluxes of the body. Made into a liniment it is useful for inflammations and bruises of the eyes. Fresh salted cheese nourishes less, diminishes flesh, is contrary to the stomach, and disturbs the interior organs. Old cheese restrains the body. The whey that comes from Cheese nourishes dogs very well. That which is called Hippace is Horse cheese, and although it is unpleasant in smell, it nonetheless nourishes effectively, corresponding in its proportions to cow's milk cheese. There are some who said that Hippace was the rennet of the horse.

it readily absorbs the liquors in which it is steeped, and through its greasy residue, which they call Esipo, it gently softens. Wool soaked in the same manner in vinegar and rose oil is good for pains of the head, the stomach, and all other parts of the body. Wool is also burned for another purpose: because its ash causes an eschar on ulcers, consumes superfluous flesh, and consolidates it. To accomplish this, the wool is first purged and then, having been carded, it is burned in a raw earthen vessel, as other things are burned. In the same way, that material similar to tow found in sea-purple shells is also burned. Some, without purging it of its grease by any other means, card it just as it is, dirty, and sprinkle it with honey before burning it. Others first place several iron rods some distance apart from one another in an earthen vessel with a wide mouth, and on top of them pile many thick sticks of pitch-pine wood; they then lay the wool, sprinkled with enough oil that it does not drip, on top of the pitch-pine wood, and so with pitch-pine and wool they make layers upon layers in the vessel, and finally lighting the pitch-pine they burn it, and they gather the ash, from which, if they find any part of pitch that has dripped from the pitch-pine, they collect it separately and keep it. This ash is then washed for medicines of the eyes in an earthen vessel by pouring water on it and rubbing it vigorously with the hands; then the residue is allowed to settle to the bottom of the vessel, and the first water is gently poured off, and fresh water is added, and the ash rubbed again with the hands, and this is done so many times until, tasting the ash on the tip of the tongue, it only slightly constricts and does not bite. To extract the greasy residue from the wool, which the Greeks call ESIPO, it is done thus. The raw soft wools are taken, not treated otherwise with the root of the herb called Lanaria, and washed with warm water, squeezing out the residue as thoroughly as possible; and then this wash-water, placed in a wide-mouthed vessel, is raised up with another vessel letting it fall from a height, or else it is beaten with a stick vigorously enough to produce a tall foam, and then sea water is sprinkled on it, and the foam being beaten down, the grease that floats on top is collected and set aside in another vessel. This is done again to produce new foam and to sprinkle it again with sea water, and the grease is collected by the same method, and this is repeated as many times as necessary until, the grease being all extracted, the water no longer foams. The Esipo is then worked with the hands, squeezing out any impurity found within it, and finally all the water being drained off, fresh water is added and the Esipo is well washed and mixed with the hands until, tasting it on the tongue, it feels slightly astringent and does not bite, and appears to the eye bright and white; and being thus prepared it is stored in earthen vessels: but all this must be done in the hottest sun. There are some who, draining off the grease of Esipo, rub it in cold water with their hands in the same manner that women wash wax, because it becomes whiter this way. There are also those who take the squeezed residue from the wool and cook it in a laundry basin over a slow fire with water, and then collecting the grease that floats on top they wash it, as said, in water, and then strain it into a vessel of warm water covered with a piece of linen, and set it in the sun until it thickens sufficiently and becomes white. But there are others who change the water every two days and renew it. That which is taken from wool not purged with the herb Lanaria is praised, since it is not rough to the touch, breathes of the smell of raw wool, and when rubbed in a small basin with fresh water becomes white and has no hardness in it, unlike that which is adulterated with fat and wax. Esipo has the virtue of warming, filling, and softening ulcers, and especially those of the fundament and of the natural parts of women, together with melilot and butter. Made into suppositories with wool, it provokes menstruation and causes the delivery of dead children in their mothers' bodies. Mixed with goose-fat it is useful for ailments of the ears and of the genital members. It benefits the corners of the eyes that are being corroded, mange, and calluses of the eyelids, and chapping of the armpits. Esipo is burned in a new earthen pot until all the grease is consumed and it becomes ash. The soot of Esipo is also collected in the manner shown elsewhere, which is usefully employed in medicines for the eyes.

L Raw wool is known to everyone for what it is, and likewise Esipo, called (the Arabic interpreters having corrected the word) today in apothecaries "moist hyssop," and therefore, having for a long time...

146 LIBRO
A storia trattato, & di quella, & di questo Dioscoride, ne ritrouando, che piu ne sia stato detto da altri non mi distendero in questo piu auanti.

Del Caglio d'alcuni Animali. Cap.lxvij.

L Caglio della lepre beuto nel uino al peso di tre oboli, è utile à morsi dei ueleno si animali, à flussi stomachali, & disenterici anchora, & similmente à flussi delle donne, al sangue congelato nello stomacho, & à quello, che si rigitta dal petto. Aita il Caglio della lepre à fare ingrauidare messo nella natura delle donne insieme con boturo, subito che si sono purgate di mestrui. Beuto ammazza la creatura nel corpo della madre: & se si bee dopo al parto fa diuentare le donne sterili. Giuoua priuatamente à flussi stomachali, & disenterici il Caglio del cauallo, ilquale chiamano Hippace. Sono d'una medesima natura i Cagli de i capretti, de gli agnelli, de capriuoli, de daini, de capricorni, delle camozze, de cerui, de uitelli et de bufali, liquali uagliono tutti beuti con uino contra all'aconito, & con aceto contra al latte appreso nello stomacho. Ma priuatamente quello del capriuolo fa le donne sterili, lasciàdoglielo per tre giorni nella natura. Quello del uitello marino ha le medesime facoltà del castoreo, & credesi, che mirabilmente giuoui al mal caduco, & alle strangolagioni della madrice. Cognoscesi se ueramente sia di uitello marino, in questo modo. Prendi il Caglio di qual si uoglia altro animale, & massimamente d'agnello, & infusolo d'acqua, & lasciatolo cosi stare alquanto, toglie poscia quella acqua, & mettila nel caglio del uitello marino: percioche essendo del uero subito si liquefara: ma essendo il contrario, si restara nel suo esser di prima. Cauasi il Caglio dai uitelli marini, quando non possono anchora notare. In somma ogni Caglio fa liquefare le cose apprese, & fa apprendere le liquide.

I Cagli de gli animali sono uolgarissimi, & conosciuti, & secondo che riferisce Galeno al.x. delle facoltà de Semplici, ogni Caglio è acuto, & mordace, digestiuo, & diseccatiuo, & come che Dioscoride, & de gli altri anchora lodassero il Leporino al sangue, che si rigitta per bocca; nondimeno non approuando lo Galeno, cosine scrisse egli. Dissero alcuni, che'l Caglio della lepre ristagna il sangue, che si rigitta dal petto. Ma nuero io non ho mai cognosciuto alcuni, che l'habbia usato, ne manco l'ho uoluto usar io, per eser egli rimedio acuto, & mordace al male, che ricerca il rimedio costrettiuo.

Del Grasso. Cap.lxviij.

IL Grasso d'oca, & di gallina fresco, serbato senza sale, è ueramente commodo à difetti de luoghi naturali delle donne: al che nuoce il salato, & quello, che per uecchiezza è diuentato rancio. Prendesi di qual si uoglia di questi del fresco la quantità che piace, & leuategli ben d'intorno le sue pellicole, si mette in un uaso di terra nuouo, che sia di doppia capacità del grasso, & cosi poscia ben coperto si mette sotto à caldissimo sole, doue liquefacendosi si cola in un altro uaso impecciato, fino che tutto si consumi, poi si ripone in luogo freddo, & s'usa. Alcuni altri in cambio di metterlo al sole, collocano il uaso nell'acqua, che bolla, ouero sopra à lentissimo fuoco de carboni. Curasi anchora il Grasso in altro modo. Imperoche nettatolo prima dalle sue sottili pellicine, si trita, & mettesi à liquefare in un uaso di terra, spargendogli sopra un poco di sale trito, & poscia colatolo per una tela di lino, si ripone. Questo si mette utilmente nelle medicine, che si preparano p le lassitudini. Quel di porco, & quel d'orso si curano in questo modo. Togliefi da questi animali il piu fresco, e'l piu grasso, come è proprio quello de irognoni: & cosi spogliatolo dalle sue pellicine, si mette in assai acqua piouana fredda, nella quale si ua ben disfacendo con le mani: & poscia spremendolo li gli rinuoua l'acqua spesse uolte. Togliefi poi questo cosi molte uolte lauato, & mettesi in una pignatta di terra d'altre tanta capacità, con tanta acqua dentro, che la superi il grasso, & lo ricopra, & cosi si mette sopra à sento fuoco de carboni, continuamente mescolandolo con una bacchetta, & come è ben liquefatto si cola con una tela nell'acqua, & lasciasi apprendere, & cosi separatolo poscia dall'acqua si mette in un'altra pignatta di terra ben lauata, & messagli sopra di nuouo pur dell'acqua, si ritorna à far

A history treated, and of that, and of this Dioscorides, finding that nothing more has been said of it by others, I will not extend myself further on this point.

On the Rennet of Certain Animals. Chapter 67.

The rennet of the hare, drunk in wine at the weight of three obols, is useful against the bites of venomous animals, against stomach fluxes and dysentery, and likewise against fluxes of women, against blood congealed in the stomach, and against that which is vomited from the chest. The rennet of the hare, placed within the womb of women together with butter, immediately after they have been purged of their menses, helps them to conceive. Drunk, it kills the creature in the mother's womb; and if drunk after childbirth, it renders women sterile. The rennet of the horse, which they call Hippace, is privately useful against stomach fluxes and dysentery. Of the same nature are the rennets of kids, lambs, roebucks, fallow deer, ibexes, chamois, stags, calves, and buffaloes, all of which are effective when drunk with wine against aconite poisoning, and with vinegar against milk that has curdled in the stomach. But the rennet of the roebuck in particular renders women sterile, if left within the womb for three days. That of the sea-calf has the same properties as castoreum, and is believed to be wonderfully beneficial against epilepsy and strangulation of the womb. One can tell whether it is truly from a sea-calf in the following manner: take the rennet of any other animal, especially of a lamb, soak it in water, and let it stand a while; then take that water and put it into the rennet of the sea-calf: for if it is genuine, it will immediately dissolve; but if it is counterfeit, it will remain in its former state. The rennet of sea-calves is taken before they are yet able to swim. In sum, every rennet dissolves things that have curdled, and causes liquids to curdle.

The rennets of animals are very commonly known, and according to Galen in book ten on the Faculties of Simple Medicines, every rennet is sharp, biting, digestive, and desiccative; and although Dioscorides and others praised the rennet of the hare for blood that is vomited from the mouth, Galen did not approve of it, as he wrote himself. Some said that the rennet of the hare stanches blood that is vomited from the chest. But truly I have never known anyone who used it, nor have I myself wished to use it, since it is a sharp and biting remedy for an ailment that calls for a constricting remedy.

On Fat. Chapter 68.

The fat of goose and hen, fresh and preserved without salt, is truly beneficial for ailments of the natural parts of women; salted fat is harmful for this, as is fat that has turned rancid with age. Take as much as you wish of the fresh fat of any of these, and having carefully removed all the membranes from around it, put it in a new earthenware vessel of double the capacity of the fat; cover it well, and then place it under the hottest sun, where as it melts it is strained into another pitched vessel, until it is all consumed, and then stored in a cool place for use. Some others, instead of placing it in the sun, set the vessel in boiling water, or over a very gentle coal fire. Fat is also treated in another way: having first cleaned it of its thin membranes, it is minced and set to melt in an earthenware vessel, with a little ground salt sprinkled over it, and after straining it through a linen cloth, it is stored. This is usefully employed in medicines prepared for fatigue. The fat of pig and of bear is treated in the following manner. Take from these animals the freshest and fattest, which is especially that of the kidneys; and thus stripped of its membranes, it is placed in a good quantity of cold rainwater, in which it is thoroughly worked with the hands; and then by pressing it, the water is renewed several times. This fat, thus washed many times, is then placed in an earthenware pot of equal capacity, with enough water inside to come above the fat and cover it; and it is placed over a slow coal fire, stirring it continuously with a stick; and when it is well melted, it is strained through a cloth into water, and left to set; and thus separated from the water it is placed in another well-washed earthenware pot, and again covered with fresh water, and the process is repeated to make

far lentamente liquefare. Togliesi fatto questo dal fuoco, & lasciatolo posare, fino che se ne uada la sua feccia al fondo, si mette poi in un mortaio di pietra, fatto ben prima netto con una spugna abbombata d'acqua: & quiui lasciatolo apprendere, & leuatone poi via ogni fondaccio, che ui si ritroua, si ritorna senza piu metterui acqua di nuouo à liquefare, & liquefatto si rigitta medesimamente nel mortaio. Onde cauato ben netto, si ripone in uaso di terra ben coperto, & serbasi in un freschissimo luogo. Il modo oltra questo di curare, & di preparare quel di ceruo, di becco, & di pecora, è cosi. Qual si uoglia di questi, lauasi, & spogliasi dalle sue pellicine, come è stato gia detto in quel di porco, & mettesi in un mortaio di pietra, accioche alquanto si mollisichi, & messoui dapoi à poco à poco sopra dell'acqua, si frega con mano, sino che non ui si discerna segno di sangue, ne alcuna grassezza, che ui nuoti di sopra: ma sia il grasso tutto bianco, & splendente. Mettesi fatto questo in una pignatta, & girratagli addosso tant'acqua, che lo soprasaccia, si porta à liquefare à lēto fuoco, & mescolasi, & come sia ben liquefatto, si cola nel'acqua. Onde cauandosi appreso si rimette nella medesima pignatta fatta ben netta di nuouo à riliquefare, con quel ordine, ches'è insegnato nelli sopradetti. La terza uolta si liquefa senza acqua, & colasi in un mortaio di pietra bagnato d'acqua: onde cauato poscia, quando è appreso, si ripone nel modo, ch'è stato detto di quel del porco. Quello de buoi, toltolo spetialmente dalle reni, si cura pur dalle sue pellicine, & lauali bene con acqua d'alto mare, & poscia si mette in un mortaio, & pestasi con diligenza, insondendogli però sempre sopra di quell'acqua marina, & essendo finalmente bene ramorbidito, si pone in una pignatta, & si gli gitta disopra tant'acqua pur marina, che lo soprauanzi mezzo buon piede, & cosi si cuoce tanto questo grasso, che perda finalmente ogni suo proprio, & naturale odore. Fatto questo si gli mescola appresso per ogni mina attica di grasso, quattro dramme di cera tirrhena, & colansi insieme raschiandone poi ogni fondaccio, che ui si ritroua, & cosi preparato si ripone in un uaso di terra. Ma poi è necessario tenerlo coperto tanti di al sole, che diuenti bianco, & che perda ogni fastidioso odore. Quello di toro si cura cosi. Prendesi di questo similmente fresco da rognoni, & lauasi con acqua di fiume, & spogliatolo poscia dalle sue cartilaginose inuoglie, si mette in un uaso di terra nuouo con un poco di sale, & liquefassi, & poscia si cola nell'acqua chiara, & come si comincia ad apprendere si malassa, & si rompe ualidissimamente con le mani mutandogli, & rimutandogli l'acqua, sino che sia benissimo lauato. Ritornasi fatto questo nel uaso di prima, & cuocesi di nuouo con la pari misura di uino odorifero, & come ha bollito due bollori, si leua dal fuoco, & lasciasi cosi freddare nel suo uaso per tutta la notte. La mattina poi se gli resta qualche poco di cattiuo odore, si mette in un'altra pignatta nuoua con altretanto del medesimo uino, facendo tutto quello, ches'è gia detto, sino che perda egli ogni corrotto odore. Liquefassi anchora il grasso senza sale, p alcuni difetti, & malattie, alle quali è nociuo il sale: ma questo cosi preparato non diuenta molto bianco. Curasi in questo medesimo modo quel di Panthera, & di Leone anchora. Fannosi odoriferi i grassi di uitello, di toro, & di ceruo, & di questo la mirolla anchora, in questo modo. Leuansigli prima d'attorno le pellicine, & lauansi poscia, come piu uoltes'è detto, & fansi bollire in uino odorifero, & aromatico, nel quale non sia dentro alcuna acqua marina. Leuansi poscia, come son cotti dal fuoco, & lasciasi cosi stare tutta la notte. Fassi la seguente mattina di nuouo liquefare in altretanto del medesimo uino, & colasi poscia diligentemente. Fatto questo si mette in noue hemine di questo grasso cosi preparato sette dramme di gionco odorato d'Arabia. Ma uolendosi fare molto piu odorato, ui si mette del fiore di questo gionco quaranta dramme, & di palma, di casia, di calamo odorato di ciascuno ugual portione: d'aspalatho, & di xilobalsamo di ciascuno una dramma: di cinamomo, cardamomo, & nardo di ciascuno un'oncia, & tutte queste cose si pestano diligentemente, & cosi messo ogni cosa in uno uaso coperchiato, si gli gitta sopra del medesimo uino, & si mette à bollire à fuoco di carboni tre bollori, & leuatolo poscia uia dal fuoco si lascia cosi riposare tutta la notte. La mattina gittasi uia il uino, & si gliene rimette di nuouo di quel medesimo, & lasciasi far tre bollori, & riposare nel medesimo modo. Cauafene la mattina dipoi il grasso, & gittasi uia il uino, & lauato di nuouo il uaso, & netto il grasso dal sedime, & dalla feccia, si riliquefa di

Melt it slowly. Once this is done, remove it from the fire, and let it settle until the sediment sinks to the bottom; then place it in a stone mortar that has first been well cleaned with a water-soaked sponge. Let it set there, and remove all the dregs that are found in it; then, without adding any more water, return it to melt again, and once melted, pour it back into the mortar. When it has been cleanly removed, store it in a well-covered earthenware vessel and keep it in a very cool place. The method, beyond this, for treating and preparing that of deer, goat, and sheep is as follows. Whichever of these one chooses, wash it and strip it of its membranes, as has already been described for that of pig, and place it in a stone mortar so that it softens somewhat; then, adding water little by little on top of it, rub it by hand until no trace of blood or any grease floating on top can be discerned, but the fat is entirely white and gleaming. Once this is done, place it in a pot and pour over it enough water to cover it, then bring it slowly to melt over a low fire; stir it, and when it is well melted, strain it into the water. When it has been removed and set, return it to the same pot, freshly cleaned, to melt again, following the same procedure described above. The third time, melt it without water and strain it into a stone mortar dampened with water; once removed and set, store it in the manner described for that of pig. The fat of oxen, taken especially from the kidneys, is treated by removing its membranes; wash it well with seawater, then place it in a mortar and pound it carefully, always pouring that same seawater over it; and when it has finally been well softened, place it in a pot and pour over it enough seawater to cover it by half a good foot, and cook this fat until it finally loses all its own natural odor. Once this is done, mix in for every Attic mina of fat four drams of Tyrrhenian wax, strain them together, scraping off all the dregs found therein, and store the preparation in an earthenware vessel. It is then necessary to expose it to the sun for several days until it turns white and loses every unpleasant odor. That of the bull is treated as follows. Take it likewise fresh from the kidneys, wash it with river water, and having stripped it of its cartilaginous membranes, place it in a new earthenware vessel with a little salt, melt it, then strain it into clear water; and as it begins to set, knead and break it up vigorously, changing and re-changing the water until it is very thoroughly washed. Return it then to the original vessel and cook it again with an equal measure of fragrant wine; when it has boiled twice, remove it from the fire and let it cool in its vessel throughout the night. If in the morning it still retains some bad odor, place it in another new pot with an equal amount of the same wine, doing everything as already described, until it loses all its corrupt odor. Fat is also melted without salt, for certain defects and ailments in which salt is harmful; but prepared this way it does not become very white. The fat of the panther and of the lion is treated in this same way. The fats of calf, bull, and deer, and also their marrow, are made fragrant in the following manner. First strip them of their membranes, wash them as described many times before, and boil them in fragrant and aromatic wine in which there is no seawater at all. Remove them once cooked from the fire and let them stand the whole night. The following morning, melt them again in an equal amount of the same wine and then strain carefully. Once this is done, add to nine heminae of this prepared fat seven drams of fragrant rush from Arabia. But if one wishes to make it much more fragrant, add forty drams of the flower of this rush, and of palm, cassia, and fragrant calamus, equal portions of each; of aspalathos and of xylobalsam, one dram each; of cinnamon, cardamom, and nard, one ounce each. Pound all these things carefully, and having placed everything in a covered vessel, pour the same wine over it and bring it to a boil over a charcoal fire three times; then remove it from the fire and let it rest the whole night. In the morning, pour out the wine and add fresh wine of the same kind, letting it boil three times and rest in the same manner. The following morning, remove the fat, pour off the wine, wash the vessel again, clean the fat from the sediment and dregs, and melt it again

A Once made fresh and strained, it is kept and used. Fats that have been previously treated in this same way can also be made fragrant; but for fats to absorb scents well, they must first be thickened in the following manner. Take whichever of these fats you like, and boil them in wine together with small branches of myrtle, thyme, sedge, and aspalathus well powdered (though some use only one of these things) and having boiled everything to three boils, remove the vessel gently from the heat, and having strained the fat through a linen cloth, then add the scents as described above. Fats may also be thickened in another way. First pound the fat you wish to use — which should be fresh, pure, and well cleaned of blood — and having prepared it as described several times above, place it in a new earthenware pot with enough old white fragrant wine to cover the fat by eight fingers' breadth. Then boil it over a gentle fire until it has completely lost its natural smell and smells more of wine than of fat; remove the vessel from the heat, and when it is cold, take two pounds of this and place it in another vessel with four measures of the same wine and four pounds of seeds of that lotus from which flatbreads are made,
B and boil it thus over a low heat, stirring continuously, and when it has lost all its fatty smell, strain it and let it rest until it sets. Then take one pound of pounded aspalathus and four pounds of marjoram flowers, and let everything soak in old wine for a whole night, and in the morning combine these macerated things together with the fat in a vessel holding three congii, and having added half a congius of wine, boil everything over the heat until the fat absorbs the virtue and fragrance of the thickening agents, and having thus removed it from the heat, strain it, melt it again, and store it. But if you wish to make it even more fragrant, mix in eight drachms of very rich myrrh, previously macerated in very old wine. The fat of hens and geese is made fragrant in this way. Take four measures of whichever fat you prefer, making sure it is well prepared, and place it in an earthenware vessel, adding aspalathus, wood of balsam, palm bark, and aromatic calamus, twelve drachms of each made into powder, and having added over it a cyathus of Lesbian wine, boil everything over charcoal to three boils, and having then removed the vessel from the heat,
C and let everything cool for a day and a night, then the following day melt everything again and strain the fat through a linen cloth into a clean vessel; and when it has set, store it in a new earthenware pot, well covered, in a very cool place. All these procedures should be done in winter, since fats do not freeze or set in summer. For this reason some, so that they set better, add a little Tyrrhenian wax. In this same way the fat of pork, bear, and all similar animals is made fragrant. Fat is also made fragrant with marjoram in this way. Take one pound of fat, preferably well-prepared ox fat, and mix into it one pound and a half of well-ripened, well-pounded marjoram, and divide it into pieces, first sprinkling it liberally with wine. Then place these pieces in a vessel and leave them well covered for a whole night, and in the morning transfer them to another vessel, pour water over them, and cook gently until the fat loses its smell; then strain it and let it rest for a whole night. In the morning remove the whole mass and clean it well
D of its sediment, add again an equal amount of well-pounded marjoram, and having reformed the pieces as described above, and finally having melted the fat, strained it and cleaned it of its sediment, store it in a cool place. But to preserve any fat of goose, hen, or veal uncorrupted without further treatment, this is done as follows: the fresh fat is removed and washed carefully, then dried in a sieve in the shade, and when the water has drained off well and it is thoroughly dry, it is placed in a white linen cloth and squeezed vigorously with the hands, then threaded on a string and hung in the shade, and after some days it is stored wrapped in fresh paper in a cool place. Fats preserved in honey do not spoil.
