plicato caldo in forma di linimento spegne le lentigini, & l'altre macole della faccia. Beeli
utilmente il canino pur al tossico, et à morsi de cani rabbiosi. Dicesi, ch'il sangue della t'sfug
B gine terrestre beuto gioua al mal caduco, & quello della marina beuto con uino, caglio di
lepre, et cimino uale à morsi de gli animali uelenosi, & à ueleni delle botte, che si fussero beu
ti. Risolue quel del toro, & mollifica le posteme dure applicatoui có posêta. Quello delle ca
ualle, che sono state montate dalli stalloni, si mette nelle medicine corrosiue. Credesi, che
quel del cameleonte, & similmente delle ranocchie uerdi, unto alle palpebre, ne faccia cascar
uia i peli. Et credesi, che quel de mestrui delle donne applicato in forma di linimento, ouero
passandouisi sopra, faccia diuentare le donne sterili. Questo ungendosi leua i dolori delle
podagre, & il fuoco sacro.

G Aleno nel principio del .x. libro parlado de i Sangui di diuersi animali, quantùque del tutto nó nieghi, che nó si pes
sa cauare da loro qualche utilità secondo le uirtù, che gli assegna Dioscoride, & altri, che ne scriuero, non dimeno
dimostra egli eser per la maggior parte la bugia quello, che si scriue delle operationi, & facoltà de i sangui. Per
tioche, secondo che dice egli, è ueramente falso il credere, che'l sangue della Ciuetta buoni liberi gli asmattici, & che quello
del nottolo, ouero pipistrello unto alle poppelle delle fanciulle uergini, nó le lasci crescere, & che pur unto prohibisca al na
scere di peli, come medesimamente non è la uerità, che quello d'agnello gioui al mal caduco, & quello delle ranocchie uer
di, le quali chiamano Bresàti, prohibisca, che nó rinaschino i peli cauati dalle ciglie. Le quali ultime parole dimostrano, che
sia in questo capitolo del sangue di Dioscoride corrotto il testo, & male scritto, imperoche si legge quiui, che'l sangue di
queste ranocchie unto alle ciglia ne fa cadere i peli, uolendo per ò dire, secondo che qui si uede in Galeno, che prohibibet,
che non ui rinaschino unto quando non sono stati cauati. Vna altra corrotta si può facilmente dire, che sia in questo mede
simo capitolo per dir Galeno del sangue de gli stalloni quello, che si legge in Dioscoride del sangue delle Caualle,
che sieno state montate dalli Stalloni. Oltre à ciò dice Galeno, quantunque molti adoperino nelle teste rotte, & tra
panate il sangue della Tortora, & della Colomba, donde non ha pari l'oglio rosado ben fatto, & altri lodino il san
gue de i Galli, & delle Galline à i flussi del sangue de i pánicoli del ceruello, quello del Crocodelo terrestre à fortifi care la
uista, & quello de gli stalloni per corrodere, et per causare l'eschara, per non parere io curioso ne pazzo, non ho uoluto
lasciar mai i molti rimedij prouati da me per il passato, à tutti questi difetti, per confirdarmi più ne sangui di questi anima
li, che in quelli, per sapere io, che coloro, che li prouaranno in queste cose, dannando chi n'ha scritto, si trouarano di gran
lunga ingannati. Il sangue del toro beuto caldo si scriue da gli autori infra ueleni, imperoche soffocca chi lo bee, come nel
vi. dice Dioscoride, & Aetio nel. xiii.

D Del Sterco de gli Animali. Cap.lxxij.

Lo sterco di buoi, che stanno alla pastura in mandria, mitiga applicato fresco l'in
fiammagioni delle ferite: nel quale uso s'inuolta nelle frondi, & scaldasi in su la ce
nere calda, & poscia così ben caldo s'impiastra in sul male. Mitiga questo i dolo
ri delle sciatiche applicatoui suso nel medesimo modo. Fattone linimento con
aceto dísfa la durezze, le scrofole, & i pani. Quel del bue maschio fumentato ritorna partico
larmente la madrice, che esce fuore del suo luogo. Il fumo del brusciato discaccia le farsalle.
Lo sterco delle capre, & massime di quelle, che pasturano ne i monti, uale beuto con uino
à trabocco di fiele, & beuto con cose odorifere prouoca i mestrui, & il parto. Ma per il con
trario ristagna i mestrui trito secco con incenso, & applicato con lana alla natura delle don
ne. Ristagna similméte meschiato con aceto ogni altro flusso di sangue. Onto có aceto puro,
& melato fa rinascere i capelli, & si peli cascati. Medica alle podagre impastato con grascia,
& messoui suso. Vale applicato cotto nel uino, ouero nello aceto, al morso delle serpi, all'ulce

[marginalia:]
lo sterco di capre
onto có aceto puro
et messiato fa rinascere
i capelli et peli pajati.

152 BOOK

A its tunics are dilated. Powdered to the quantity of a lentil and drawn up through the nose with beet juice, it helps with epilepsy. Beyond this, the bile of the gilt-head fish, the pike, the partridge, and the rooster wonderfully stimulates women in intercourse.

On Blood, Chapter 71.

The blood of the goose, the duck, and the kid is usefully employed in antidotes.
That of the wild dove, the turtledove, the common dove, and the wood grouse are suitable as a liniment for fresh wounds and bruises of the eyes, for blood that collects within them, and for those who lose their sight when night comes on. The blood of the dove particularly stops flows of blood proceeding from the membranes of the brain. That of the woodcock, the goat, the hare, and the deer, eaten fried in a pan, stops dysentery and other flows of the body; and drunk with wine it helps against the poisons called "toliichi." Hare's blood applied warm as a liniment removes freckles and other blemishes of the face. Dog's blood is also usefully drunk against poison and against the bites of mad dogs. It is said that the blood of the land tortoise drunk helps epilepsy, and that of the sea tortoise drunk with wine, hare's rennet, and cumin helps against the bites of venomous creatures and against the poisons of toads that might be drunk. That of the bull dissolves and softens hard abscesses when applied with a poultice. That of mares that have been mounted by stallions is used in corrosive medicines. It is believed that the blood of the chameleon, and likewise that of green frogs, anointed on the eyelids, causes the hairs to fall away. And it is believed that menstrual blood applied as a liniment or rubbed over a woman makes her barren. Anointed on, this relieves the pains of gout and erysipelas (sacred fire).

G Galen, in the beginning of the tenth book, speaking of the blood of various animals, though he does not entirely deny that some usefulness may be drawn from them according to the virtues assigned them by Dioscorides and others who wrote on the matter, nevertheless he demonstrates that for the most part what is written about the operations and faculties of blood is falsehood. For, according to what he says, it is truly false to believe that the blood of the owl frees asthmatics, and that of the bat, anointed on the nipples of young virgins, prevents them from growing, and likewise that anointing prevents hair from growing — just as it is not true that the blood of a lamb helps epilepsy, and that of the green frogs called Bresàti prevents the hairs plucked from the eyelashes from growing back. These last words demonstrate that the text of Dioscorides in this chapter on blood is corrupt and badly written, for here one reads that the blood of these frogs anointed on the eyelashes causes the hairs to fall, meaning rather, as one sees in Galen, that it prevents them from growing back after they have been plucked. Another corruption can easily be seen in the same chapter, where Galen says of the blood of stallions what one reads in Dioscorides about the blood of mares that have been mounted by stallions. Beyond this, Galen says that although many use the blood of the turtledove and the dove for broken and trepanned heads — for which nothing surpasses well-made rose oil — and others praise the blood of roosters and hens for flows of blood from the brain membranes, that of the land crocodile to strengthen the sight, and that of stallions for corroding and causing a scab, yet not wishing to appear curious or mad, I have never wished to abandon the many remedies I have tried in the past for all these conditions, to trust more in the blood of these animals than in those others, knowing that those who try them in these cases, condemning those who wrote of them, will find themselves very greatly deceived. The blood of the bull drunk hot is listed by authors among poisons, because it chokes whoever drinks it, as Dioscorides says in chapter six and Aetius in chapter thirteen.

D On the Dung of Animals, Chapter 72.

The dung of oxen that graze together in herds, applied fresh, soothes the inflammations of wounds: for this use it is wrapped in leaves, warmed on hot ashes, and then plastered onto the ailment. Applied in the same way, it soothes the pains of sciatica. Made into a liniment with vinegar, it dissolves hardnesses, scrofula, and bread-like swellings. That of the male ox, used as a fumigation, particularly restores the womb that has prolapsed from its place. The smoke of burned dung drives away moths. The dung of goats, especially those that graze in the mountains, drunk with wine, helps overflow of bile; and drunk with aromatic substances, it provokes menstruation and childbirth. On the contrary, dried and ground with incense and applied with wool to the female parts, it stops menstruation. Mixed with vinegar, it likewise stops any other flow of blood. Anointed with pure vinegar and honey, it causes hair and fallen hairs to grow back. It heals gout mixed with grease and applied. Applied cooked in wine or vinegar, it helps against snake bite and ulcers.

[marginalia:]
The dung of goats
anointed with pure vinegar
and mixed with honey causes
hair and fallen hairs to grow back.

text:
158 LIBRO

Della Cera. Cap. lxxv.

A elettissima Cera è quella, che mediocremente rosseggia, non troppo grassa, pura, & odorisera, con alquanto d'odore di mele. Lodasi per la migliore la Pontica, & quella di Creti. Tiene il secondo luogo di bontà quella, che biancheggia, et che di sua natura è grassa. Fassi la Cera bianca in questo modo. Eleggesi quella, ch'è piu pura, & piu bianca, & rastiasi sottilmente, & mettesi in un uaso di terra nuouo, & mesaui sopra tanta acqua marina, che basti, et sparsoui un poco di nitro, si mette à cuocere, & come ha leuato due, ouero tre bollori, si leua dal suoco, & lasciasi freddare. Et cosi tolto fuore il pastello della Cera, & raschiatolo se ui si ritrouano innomditie, si ritorna à cuocere pur con acqua marina, & hauendo gia bollito (come è stato mostrato) si leua similmente il uaso dal suoco, & preso poscia un fondo d'un uaso di terra nuouo bene abbombato nell'acqua fresca, s'attussa leggiermente nella Cera, di modo che superfistialmente tocchi solamente la Cera disopra, accioche ui s'attacchi ben sottile, & presto ui s'apprenda, et si congie-
B li: & cosi alzato su poscia il fondo, se ne leua uia la girella, che u'è suso condensata, & mettendoui di nuouo detro il fondo abbombato d'acqua fresca, si reitera tante uolte, che sene caua fuore tutta la Cera. Insilansi poscia queste ruotelle di Cera lasciando tanto spatio di filo tra l'una, & l'altra, che non si tocchino: & si sospendono il giorno al sole bagnandole d'acqua, & la notte alla luna, fin che la Cera diuenti bianca. Ma se alcuno la uolesse fare molto piu bianca, faccia tutte queste cose: ma cuochila piu uolte. Sono alcuni, che in cambio d'acqua marina la cuocono in fortissima salamuoia tre, ò quattro uolte, come è stato insegnato, cauandola poi in girelle con una tonda, & sottile scudella, che habbia disopra il suo manico, & mettendo poi le girelle in su l'herba folta distintamente al sole, fino che si faccia bianca. Ma commandano, che si debba fare questo nella primauera: percioche in quel tempo il sole non scalda troppo aspramente, & la rugiada prohibisce, che non si coli la Cera. Ha ogni Cera uirtu di scaldare, mollifica, & mediocremente incarna, & riempie. Dassi nelle beuande alla disenteria: & prese per bocca dieci pisole di Cera grosse, come granella di miglio, prohibiscono, che non s'apprenda alle basie il latte nelle poppe.

L A Cera (secondo che riferisce Galeno al. viij. delle facoltà de Semplici) tiene quasi il mezzo tanto delle cose calde, & frigide, quanto dell'humide, & delle seche, con alquanto d'una certa grossa essenza insieme, & alquanto del uiscoso. Et però puo ella, non solamente diseccare, ma accidentalmente humettare i corpi, prohibendo la traspiratione, che si fa per i pori. Ma è la Cera piu presto materia d'accompagnare con altri medicamenti tanto caldi, quanto freddi, che da usare cosi sola per se stessa, per essere ueramente ella poco digestiua; ma non però è cosi tolta dentro p bocca, come di suore: Percioche l'ha pure un certo poco di uirtu calida digestiua, restatagli dalla molta, che n'haueua il mele.

Della Propoli. Cap. lxxvi.

D Ebbesi eleggere quella Propoli, che è rossa nel colore, odorata, simile alla stirace, trattabile nella sua siccità, & che non manco si tira in lungo, che si faccia il mastice. Scalda, & tira la Propoli ualidamente: & percio caua fuore i bronconi, & ogni altra cosa fitta nel corpo. Gioua receuendone il sumo alla tosse antica: & applicata in su l'impetigini le sana. Trouasi la Propoli appresso à i pertugi de cupili, onde entrano le Api, simile alla cera, & d'aspetto, & di natura.

Q Vantunque, secondo che scriue Dioscoride, & similmente. M. Varrone, si ritroua la Propoli ne i cupili appresso à i pertugi, ouero spiracoli, onde entrano dentro, & escono fuore le api: Plinio nondimeno al. vij. cap. del. xi. libro uuole, che sia la Propoli quel primo fondamento, à cui attaccano le api i sialoni, & la cera, sotto laquale dice egli, che sono due altri fondamenti, l'uno de i quali chiamamo Pisocero, & l'altro Metyn. Di questa facendo mentione Galeno al. viij. delle facoltà de i semplici diceua. La Propoli non è cosi altersiua, come ualentemente è attrattiva. È nella sua essenza sottile, & però scalda nel fine del secondo grado, ouero nel primo del terzo. Ma essendo la Propoli, la cera, e'l mele, delle qual cose per i tre precedenti cap. trattò Dioscoride, tutta materia fatta con mirabile artifistio dalle api; non è male il sapere, secondo che in piu luoghi recita Plinio nel. xi. et. xxi. libro, che le Api sono di due spetie, saluatiche cioè, & domestiche. Le saluatiche sono horride, pelose, & molto stizzo se, ma ualentissime nell'operare, in far assai mele, & assai cera. Le domestiche sono di due sorti, delle quali quelle si lodano, che son corte, uarie di colore, & ben raccolte in se stisse, come

158 BOOK

On Wax. Chapter 75.

The finest wax is that which is moderately reddish, not too greasy, pure, and fragrant, with something of the smell of honey. Pontic wax and that of Crete are praised as the best. Second in quality is that which is whitish and by its nature greasy. White wax is made in the following way. Choose the purest and whitest wax, scrape it finely, and place it in a new earthenware vessel; pour over it enough sea water to cover it, scatter a little nitre over it, and set it to boil. When it has given two or three boils, remove it from the fire and let it cool. Then take out the cake of wax and scrape it; if any impurities appear, return it to boil again in sea water, and having already boiled (as has been shown), remove the vessel again from the fire, then taking the base of a new earthenware vessel well rounded, dip it lightly into the cold fresh water, pressing it gently into the wax so that it touches only the surface of the wax above, so that a thin layer sticks to it and quickly sets and congeals.
B Then raising the base up, remove the ring of wax that has condensed upon it, and filling it again with fresh water, repeat this many times until all the wax has been removed. Then thread these little discs of wax on a string, leaving enough space between one and the next so they do not touch, and suspend them during the day in the sun wetting them with water, and at night in the moonlight, until the wax becomes white. But if anyone wishes to make it much whiter, let him do all these things but boil it more times. There are some who, instead of sea water, boil it in very strong brine three or four times, as has been taught, drawing it out into rings with a round and shallow dish that has a handle on top, then placing the rings on thick grass in the open sun, until it becomes white. They recommend doing this in spring, because at that time the sun does not heat too harshly, and the dew prevents the wax from melting. All wax has the property of warming, softening, and moderately filling and closing wounds. It is given in drinks for dysentery; and ten pills of wax taken by mouth, as large as millet grains, prevent milk from curdling in the breasts.

L Wax (according to Galen in book eight of his work on the Properties of Simple Medicines) holds roughly equal quantities of hot and cold qualities, and of moist and dry, together with a certain amount of a thick essence, and some viscosity. It can therefore not only dry, but accidentally moisten the body, by blocking the perspiration that occurs through the pores. But wax is more properly a vehicle for combining with other medicines, both hot and cold, than something to be used alone by itself, since it is in truth of little digestive power; yet it is not so completely without effect taken internally as it is externally, since it retains a certain amount of the warm digestive virtue that it had from the honey.

On Propolis. Chapter 76.

D One should choose that propolis which is red in color, fragrant, similar to storax, workable in its dryness, and which can be drawn out lengthwise so as to resemble mastic. Propolis heats and draws powerfully, and therefore extracts splinters and anything else embedded in the body. Its smoke inhaled is beneficial for chronic coughs, and applied to scabby skin it heals it. Propolis is found near the entrances of beehives, where the bees go in and out, resembling wax both in appearance and in nature.

Q Although, as Dioscorides writes, and likewise M. Varro, propolis is found in hives near the holes or vents through which the bees enter and exit, Pliny nevertheless in book seven, chapter eleven, maintains that propolis is the first foundation to which bees attach their combs and the wax, beneath which he says there are two other foundations, one of which we call pisocero and the other metyn. Galen, making mention of this in book eight of his work on the Properties of Simple Medicines, said: propolis is not so alterative as it is powerfully attractive. In its essence it is subtle, and therefore heats at the end of the second degree, or at the beginning of the third. Now since propolis, wax, and honey, the three things treated by Dioscorides in the three preceding chapters, are all materials made with wonderful artistry by bees, it is not without value to know, as Pliny recounts in several places in books eleven and twenty-one, that bees are of two kinds, namely wild and domestic. The wild ones are rough, hairy, and very irritable, but most efficient in their work, making much honey and much wax. The domestic ones are of two varieties, of which those praised are the short ones, varied in color, and compact in themselves, like

dilettano d'andare ben profumati d'odori, quando si ritrouano in ulla, oue sieno le api. Muoionsi le api secondo che di-
cono alcuni quando trafiggono: percioche nel lasciare la spina, ui lasciano gran parte delle interiora. Dimostrano esser

attese alle Api con mirabil cura. Hanno diuisi fra loro gli esercitij, come gli uediamo diuisi fra gli huomini nelle fabriche
delle castella, & de i palazzi: perche quelle, che uanno fuore sono sòlamente diputate à portare il Mele, & la Cera. Ma
di quelle, che restano à casa à lauorare, alcune compongono i fialoni, alcune gli ripoliscono, alcune porgono la materia,
alcune l'apparecchiano, & alcune con grande ordine scaricano quelle, che uengono di fuore. Perdendosi in tutto il se-
me delle Api, si possono tornare à far nascere d'un giouencho del due anni, nel modo che distinctamente insegno Vergi-

Del Grano. Cap.lxxvij.

LO eccellentissimo Grano per la coseruation della sanità ne i sani, è il nuouo, &
quello che è cresciuto, & essi maturato à bastanza, & che rosseggia nel colore. Lo
dasi dopo questo quello, che ha tre mesi, chiamato da alcuni Sitanio. Mangiato
il Grano crudo genera nel corpo i uermi lunghi, & ritondi. Gioua masticato al C
morso de cani applicatoui sopra. Il pane, che si fa del fiore della farina del grano nutrisce as-
sai più di quello, che si fa della farina non burattata, ilquale chiamano i Greci Sincomisto.
Quello, che si fa di farina di Grano di tre mesi è più leggiero, & digeriscesi più ageuolmen-
te. Questa medesima farina impastata con succhio di lusquiamo s'applica utilmente in for-
ma di linimento alle uentosità delle budella, & à flussi, che discendono à i nerui: & impasta-
ta con aceto melato spegne le lentigini. La sembola cotta con fortissimo aceto, & ap-
plicata calda guarisce la scabbia, & mitiga nel principio ogni sorte d'infiammagioni. Cotta
nella dicottione della ruta risolue l'enfiagioni delle poppe, che uengono dopo al parto: so-
uiene à morsi delle uipere, età dolori di corpo. Il leuito, che si fa di farina di Grano, per esser
egli calido, & attrattivo, giuoua à difetti delle piante de i piedi, & massime à i calli: peroche
li diminuisce. Matura, & rompe insieme con sale le picciole posteme, & i foroncoli. La fari-
na del Grano di tre mesi impastata con uino, ouero con aceto si mette utilmente in forma di
linimento in su i morsi, ouero in su le punture di tutti gli animali ueleno si. Cotta questa à D
modo di colla gioua lambendola à gli sputi del sangue: & cotta con menta, & con boturo
conferisce alla tosse, & all'asprezza delle fauci. Il fiore della farina del Grano cotto nell'ac-
qua melata, ouero nell'oglio con acqua pura, risolue impiastrato tutte l'infiammagioni:
& il simile fa il pan crudo, & cotto nell'acqua melata, per esser egli mollificatiuo, & al-
quanto rinfrescatiuo, & massime mescolandosi con esso herbe, ò succhi, che ui conferischi-
no. Il pan duro, & secco ristagna il corpo mangiato per se solo, & con altre cose conuenien-
ti. Sana il pan fresco infuso nella salamuoia l'impetigini uecchie. La colla, che per incollare
le carte de i libri, si fa del fiore della farina, presa tepida in beuanda alla misura d'un cuc-
chiaro, ristagna gli sputi del sangue.

On the contrary, those that are long like wasps are little esteemed. Bees hate foul odors and flee from them as if they were deadly things; but pleasant scents carry far and often greatly annoy those who enjoy going about heavily perfumed when bees are present. Bees die, as some say, when they sting, because in leaving their sting they leave behind a great part of their entrails. Sick bees show it by not working and sitting in the sun outside their hives, waiting for others to bring them food. Those that die inside the hives are promptly carried out by the others with wonderful orderliness. Bees have a King who governs them, and every swarm has its own; nor do they swarm out of the hives unless the King departs first. When he leaves, the whole crowd follows and settles wherever he settles first. When their King dies inside the hive they do not carry him out as they do the others, but all remain in a state of melancholy, do not go out, do not pasture, do not work; gathering all together with a certain mournful humming around him, they pile themselves one on top of another over him — for which reason he must be removed from beneath them, otherwise they all die of hunger. Bees delight in the sound of metals and in having planted near their quarters thyme, melissa, roses, violets, lilies, cytisus, beans, peas, coriander, poppies, sage, rosemary, and melilot. Keeping them near cornel trees kills many of them, because the flower of that tree causes them a flux that destroys them, though in men that same flower stops bodily fluxes. Likewise they do not like to be where there are olive trees, since their flowers greatly annoy them; whereas keeping them near other trees is beneficial, both for their flowers where they may pasture and likewise for the convenience of settling when they swarm out in spring. Bees truly have great order and great governance in their operations, as Aristomachus of Soli diligently observed over thirty-eight years, always tending to bees with wonderful care. Their tasks are divided among themselves, just as we see tasks divided among men in the building of castles and palaces: those that go out are solely appointed to bring back honey and wax. Of those that stay at home to work, some build the cells, some polish them, some supply the material, some prepare it, and some in great order unload those that come in from outside. When all the seed of the bees is lost, one can make them breed again from a two-year-old bullock, in the manner that Virgil teaches in detail in his Georgics.

On Wheat. Chapter 77.

The most excellent Wheat for preserving the health of healthy persons is the new grain, that which has grown and ripened sufficiently and is reddish in color. Next best after this is that of three months, called by some Sitanion. Eating raw wheat generates long and round worms in the body. Chewed and applied to dog bites it is beneficial. The bread made from the finest sifted flour of wheat nourishes much more than that made from unbolted flour, which the Greeks call Syncomisto. That made from three-month wheat flour is lighter and more easily digested. This same flour kneaded with the juice of henbane is usefully applied as a liniment against flatulence of the bowels and against fluxes descending into the nerves; and kneaded with honeyed vinegar it removes freckles. The bran boiled in very strong vinegar and applied hot cures scabies and at the outset mitigates all kinds of inflammations. Boiled in a decoction of rue it resolves swellings of the breasts that come on after childbirth; it helps with viper bites and bodily pains. Leavened bread made from wheat flour, being warm and drawing, is useful for defects of the soles of the feet and especially for calluses, because it reduces them. Mixed with salt it matures and breaks small pustules and boils. Wheat flour of three months kneaded with wine or with vinegar is usefully applied as a liniment to the bites or stings of all venomous animals. Cooked in the manner of a paste and licked, it helps with spitting of blood; and cooked with mint and with butter it helps the cough and the roughness of the throat. The finest wheat flour cooked in honeyed water or in oil with plain water, spread on as a plaster, resolves all inflammations; and raw bread does the same when cooked in honeyed water, since it is softening and somewhat cooling, and especially when mixed with herbs or juices that aid the same purpose. Dry, hard bread eaten alone and with other suitable things restrains the bowels. Fresh bread soaked in brine cures old skin eruptions. The paste used to glue the pages of books, made from the finest flour and taken warm as a drink in the measure of a spoonful, stops the spitting of blood.

Wheat, so called by us Tuscans, is called in Lombardy "formento," from which for our daily sustenance we make — I say good — bread, for wheat bread is the most praised, the most nutritious, and the most pleasing to the taste of any other bread. A to in graso terreno, netto da ogni meseuglio, malagevole da rompere, pieno, grave, lucido, liscio, di colore quasi d'oro, & di età di tre mesi, quando sene fa la farina: percioche, come dice Galeno al primo delle facoltà de gli Alimenti, interviene qualche volta, che'l grano a veder lo di fuore di bel colore, dimostri esser ben pieno, & nondimeno ingannando l'occhio è fiappo, & leggiero. al perche facendo egli nel macinarsi assai sembola, fa poscia il pane semboloso, ilquale non solamente non nutrisce, ma riempie lo stomacho di molte superfluità. La farina, che più si loda, è quella, che si fa del buon grano, non macinata troppo trita, ma che habbia la sembola grossa, & quella, che non è macinata di fresco, ne di lungo tempo: imperoche la troppo trita fa il pane semboloso, la macinata di fresco è piena d'un certo caldo nonnaturale datogli nel macin aria dalla pietra della macina, & la vecchia stata macinata lungo tempo il più delle volte fa di muffa, ò di Pol vere, ò d'altro fastidioso odore. A' volere adunque fare uno eccelentissimo pane, cerchisi oltre all'hauere la buona farina, buona acqua per impastarlo, che sia chiara, di buone fonti, & che non sappi ne di fango, ne d'altro malo odore: mettendovi tanta portione di lievito, che non habbi poscia il pane à diventare acetoso. Fatta, & formata la pasta, non troppo tenera, ne troppo dura, si malassia prima, & si rimena benissimo: formandone poscia i pani di mediocre grandezza, i quali come sono lieviati à bastanza, si cuocono in un forno caldo à supplimento, ben spazzato dalla cenere, et che sia proportionato alla quantità del pane: perche, così come in un forno grande il poco pane, ò si secca troppo, ò si bruscia, così l'assai in un picciolo s'ammassa, & cuocesi male. Et come che noi in Thoscana nel nostro pane non mettiamo dentro sale, come si mette in altri luoghi d'Italia: nondimeno, secondo l'opinione de i Medici, il sale molto vi conferisce. Conuertirassi il Grano seminato ne i campi ageuolmente in gioglio, quando il tempo dell'anno ua molto piovoso, & molto freddo, del che sene dira poi al suo istesso capitolo. Passi del Grano stretto fra due lamine di ferro mediocremete affocate, un oglio, il quale comentando alcuni alle fistole, alla ruvidezza della pelle, & alle crepature causate dal freddo. Il Grano applicato di fuore, secondo che disse al .viij. delle facoltà de Semplici Galeno, scalda nel primo grado, quantunque non sia egli disseccatiuo, ne infrigidatiuo, ha alquanto del uscioso, & dell'oppilatino. Il Grano mangiato cotto (come hauer provato in se stesso affermò Galeno al primo delle facoltà de gli Alimenti) è malagevole da digerire, grave allo stomacho, ventoso, & vaporabile molto alla testa.

Dell'Orzo. Cap. lxxviij.

C L buono Orzo è quello, che è bianco, & ben mondo. Nutrisce l'Orzo manco del grano: nondimeno la ptisana, per il uscioso homore, che rende nel cuocersi, nutrisce molto più, che non fa la polenta, che si fa d'Orzo. Accommodasi la Ptisana, che si fa d'orzo, à tutte l'acutezze de gli homori, all'asprezze delle fauci, & similmente all'ulcere: alche giuoua medesimamente quella, che si fa del grano, laquale nutrisce maggiormente il corpo, & prouoca l'orina. Data la Ptisana d'orzo cotta con seme di finocchio in bevanda, prouoca il latte: & come che la prouochi l'orina, & sia aftersiva: genera nondimeno ventosità, et nuoce allo stomacho: matura le poste me. La farina d'Orzo cotta con acqua melata, & fichi secchi, risolue tutte le posteme, & mescolata con pece, ragia, & sterco di colombo, matura le durezze. Leua i dolori del costato mettaui fuso insieme con mililoto, & gusci de papaueri. Applicasi utilmente in forma di linimento alle ventosità delle budella con seme di lino, di fiengreco, & ruta. Impastata con cera, pece liquida, orina de fanciulli, & oglio matura le scrofole. Mescolata con frutti di mirto, & uino, overo con pere saluatiche, ò con more di rovi, ò con gusci di melagrano mal maturo, ristagna i flussi del corpo. Composta con aceto, & mele cotogne allegerisce l'infiammagioni delle podagre. Cotta nell'aceto fortissimo, et fattone impiastro nel modo, che si fa di questa medesima farina d'oglio, & d'acqua, & applicata calda guarisce la sabbia. Il liquore, che si sprieme della infusa nell'acqua cotto dipoi con pece, & con oglio è maturatiuo. Il cauato dall'infusa prima nell'aceto, & poscia cotto con pece, gioua à i catarri, che scendono alle giunture. La polenta, che si fa di farina d'Orzo, ristagna il corpo, & mitiga l'infiammagioni.

On meno è in Italia volgare l'Orzo, che si sta il grano, del quale secondo che recita Theophr. asto at. iiij. cap. del viij. libro, sene ritrouano più spetie, come si uede nelle granella, & nelle spighe loro. imperoche le granella sono in alcune spighe rotonde, picciole, & raccolte in se stesse, & in alcune altre lunghe, & maggiori. La differenza delle spighe è, che alcune hanno solamente due ordini di granella, altre tre, altre quattro, et altre per il più fino a cinque, & sei. Oltre à cio sono alcune spighe lunghe, & radei alcune corte, & folte di granello: alcune alte, & lontane dalla frondi, & alcune basse, & circondate da quelle: tanto s'è dilettata la natura di variar nell'orzo. Vedesi similmente differenza nel colore delle granella, ritrouandosene di bianche, & di rose, lequali si crede, che saccino più farina, che le bianche. Seminasene una spetie in Francia, laquale chiamano Orzo mondo per uscir egli mondo delle spighe, quando si trebbia, come fa il grano. Conuertirassi l'Orzo, che sente troppo humidità, ò di terreno, ò di pioggie, quando è seminato ne i campi.

A grown in rich soil, free from every weed, difficult to break, full, heavy, bright, smooth, of color nearly golden, and of three months age, when flour is made from it: for as Galen says in the first book on the Properties of Foods, it sometimes happens that wheat which looks fine from the outside appears to be well-filled, yet deceiving the eye it is soft and light inside. For in milling it produces much bran, and thus makes bran-filled bread, which not only does not nourish but fills the stomach with many superfluities. The flour most praised is that which is made from good wheat, not ground too fine, so that it retains coarse bran, and that which has not been ground too recently nor too long ago: for flour ground too fine makes bran-filled bread, flour ground too recently contains a certain unnatural heat imparted to it in the mill by the millstone, and flour that has been ground a long time mostly smells of mold, or dust, or some other disagreeable odor. To make an excellent bread, one should seek, beyond having good flour, good water for kneading — water that is clear, from good springs, tasting of neither mud nor any bad odor — adding just enough leaven so the bread will not turn sour. Once the dough is made and shaped, not too soft nor too hard, it is first kneaded and then worked thoroughly: then loaves of moderate size are formed, and when they have risen sufficiently, they are baked in a hot oven well swept of ash, and proportioned in size to the quantity of bread: for just as in a large oven a small amount of bread either dries out too much or burns, so in a small oven a large amount clumps together and bakes poorly. And although we in Tuscany do not put salt in our bread as they do in other parts of Italy, nonetheless according to the opinion of physicians, salt greatly benefits it. Wheat sown in fields readily turns to darnel when the season is very rainy and very cold, of which more will be said in its own chapter. The oil pressed from wheat passed between two moderately heated iron plates is commended by some for fistulas, for roughness of the skin, and for chapping caused by cold. Wheat applied externally, as Galen said in the eighth book on Simple Medicines, warms in the first degree, though it is neither desiccating nor cooling; it has some tendency toward looseness and obstruction. Wheat eaten cooked (as Galen himself affirmed from personal experience in the first book on the Properties of Foods) is difficult to digest, heavy on the stomach, windy, and very prone to causing vapors in the head.

On Barley. Chapter 78.

C Good barley is that which is white and well cleaned. Barley nourishes less than wheat: yet ptisan, because of the slippery humor it produces in cooking, nourishes much more than barley porridge. Ptisan made from barley is suited to all acute humors, to roughness of the throat, and likewise to ulcers: in this it is similar to that made from wheat, which nourishes the body more and promotes urination. Barley ptisan cooked with fennel seed, given as a drink, promotes milk: and though it promotes urination, and is cleansing, it nonetheless generates windiness and is harmful to the stomach; it ripens abscesses. Barley flour cooked with honey-water and dried figs resolves all abscesses, and mixed with pitch, resin, and pigeon dung, ripens hard swellings. It relieves pains in the side when applied mixed with melilot and poppy husks. Applied usefully as a liniment for intestinal flatulence with linseed, fenugreek, and rue. Kneaded with wax, liquid pitch, children's urine, and oil, it ripens scrofulous swellings. Mixed with myrtle berries and wine, or with wild pears, or blackberries, or husks of unripe pomegranate, it checks flows of the body. Prepared with vinegar and quince honey, it relieves inflammations of the joints. Cooked in very strong vinegar and made into a plaster in the same way as this same flour with oil and water, and applied warm, it cures gravel. The liquid pressed from barley steeped in water and then cooked with pitch and oil is maturing. That extracted from barley first steeped in vinegar and then cooked with pitch is good for catarrhs descending to the joints. The porridge made from barley flour checks the body and soothes inflammations.

Barley is no less common in Italy than wheat, and as Theophrastus recounts in the fourth chapter of his eighth book, several varieties are found, as can be seen in their grains and their ears. For the grains are in some varieties round, small, and gathered close together, and in others long and larger. The difference in the ears is that some have only two rows of grain, others three, others four, and others up to five and six. Moreover some ears are long and sparse, others short and dense with grain: some are tall and far from the leaves, others low and surrounded by them: so greatly has nature delighted in varying barley. There is likewise a difference in the color of the grains, some being found white and some pink, and the pink ones are believed to produce more flour than the white. One variety is grown in France, which they call hulless barley because it comes out of the husk clean when threshed, as wheat does. Barley that receives too much moisture, whether from the soil or from rain, when sown in the fields, will turn.

fields, just as easily as darnel, as barley also does. Writing about Barley in book seven of his work on the properties of simples, Galen said: Barley is cold and dry in the first degree, and in addition has somewhat of a cleansing quality. Its flour dries somewhat more than that of peeled fava beans; but in all other respects, for external applications to parts of the body, barley flour and peeled fava bean flour are entirely alike. But eaten as food, barley is better than fava beans, because in cooking it loses its flatulent quality — which fava beans do not, however long you cook them. Furthermore, in the first book on the properties of foods, Galen also said: Prepare barley however you wish, it never becomes heating, though it becomes drying when first roasted and then made into polenta, and moistening when made into ptisan — especially following the proper method. Because the modern physicians, not having found this method according to the order of Galen and the other ancients, take in its place very well cooked barley, pounded thoroughly in a stone mortar and then passed through a sieve, adding to it, some pine nuts, some sugar, some almond milk, and some poppy seeds — even though Manardo of Ferrara does not praise, for our times, either the modern ptisan or that of the ancients, because it is, as he says, food not customary to us Italians, and also because our barley is not of the same quality as that of the ancients. His opinion is entirely and truly foreign to all modern physicians of the Hippocratic and Galenic schools. The bread made from barley, in addition to being heavy on the stomach and generating cold, thick humors, provides little nourishment and generates much flatulence, even though some say it is good for gout.

On Zitho and Curmi. Chapter 79.

Zitho, which is drunk, is made from barley. When drunk it provokes urination, but is harmful to the kidneys and nerves, and especially to the membranes of the brain. It generates flatulence and bad humors in the body, and causes people to become leprous. The ivory that is soaked in Zitho becomes workable for making all kinds of things. Made from barley in the same way is a drink called Curmi, which is used in place of wine, but it causes headaches, generates bad humors, and is harmful to the nerves. These drinks are also made from grain in the regions of Brittany and Iberia facing the west.

As can be gathered from Dioscorides, Zitho is clearly a drink made from barley and grain, similar to what is called Cerevisia, as Pliny shows in the last chapter of book twenty-two, saying thus: From grains is made a drink which in Egypt is called Zitho, in Spain Celia and Cera, and in France Cerevisia. Not very different from this is Curmi: for it too is made from barley, being grain steeped in water, and is drunk in place of wine. So one can easily say that the Zitho and Curmi of the ancients were not far removed from the Cerevisia, or Beer, which is used in our own times in the northern regions throughout all of Germany, Bohemia, Poland, Flanders, France, and other regions of Europe. Nor do I think one can say there is any other difference between Zitho and Curmi — although both are drinks made from barley and grain — except that they are made by different methods, or by allowing the barley and grain to cook and ferment more in one than the other, as is done in Germany and Bohemia with their beers. For although they are made from barley and grain, they nevertheless produce in various ways sweet, bitter, rough, cloudy, and clear varieties. In Bavaria, a province of Germany, they steep barley and grain with a decoction of hop flowers to make their beer — hops which they cultivate in their fields on trellises and on trees, just as we cultivate our vines. For, as they report, these flowers give a wine-like flavor to the beer and make it more pleasing to the palate. Beer makes one drunk if too much is consumed, just like wine, and its ill effects last longer than those of wine.

On Zea, or Spelt. Chapter 80.

Zea is of two kinds. One is a simple single-grain variety, and the other, which is called Dicoccos, meaning double grain, because it has two small grains joined together in two husks. This nourishes more than barley, and is pleasant in food. Nevertheless its bread nourishes considerably less than bread made from wheat.

The Zea described by Dioscorides is not what throughout all of Italy is called Spelta — indeed among us it has practically disappeared. But that Zea is the same as Spelta may be conjectured from what Dioscorides writes about it, making it of two kinds, namely simple grain and double — for both of these are found in Tuscany. Pliny furthermore, in chapter eight of book seventeen, says that Zea grew most abundantly in Campania, and was specifically called Seme there, which shows — since Zea was so plentiful in Italy — that it could easily have persisted there down to our own times. This being true, Zea can be nothing other than Spelta, which we in Tuscany privately call biada, following the practice of the ancients who called it Seme: for just as seme is a name common to all seeds, so biada is common to all grains.
