A Ruellio strives with very fine words to make us believe that the Water Pepper described by Dioscorides is the same herb that the apothecaries have always used (though falsely) as the true Eupatorium. In this matter, though Ruellio has been a most learned and thoroughly consulted man not only in the science of simples but also in fine letters, it seems to me that he is greatly deceiving himself: for the Water Pepper of Dioscorides produces leaves like those of mint, though somewhat larger, more tender, and whiter, strong in taste and acute in flavor like Pepper (not bitter, as Ruellio corrupts the text of Dioscorides to make it suit his purpose); whereas what the apothecaries call Eupatorium produces hemp-like leaves, hard, hairy, bitter in taste, and neither strong nor sharp like Pepper. Furthermore, the Water Pepper has no odor at all, while this plant called Eupatorium has a truly remarkable fragrance, for which reason it has been considered (though unknown to the ancients) a plant of no small worth. Moreover, the Water Pepper produces a stem full of nodes, with some hollows at the joints where the leaves and little branches originate, and the seed in clusters along the branches near the leaves, also of sharp flavor; whereas this so-called Eupatorium produces no joint on its stem more prominent than any other herb, and bears no seed in clusters of sharp taste. It does however produce flowers at the tips of its branches, of a flesh color, not very unlike those of Tragorigano, which as they ripen become downy, and afterward produce a bitter seed, as is the herb itself and the whole plant — notwithstanding that Ruellio calls it sharp — which Ruellio, imagining this Eupatorium to grow on the banks of ditches near water, supposed it to be the Water Pepper,

B paying no attention to its other characteristics. Thus, as can be evident to anyone from the reasons given, it truly seems to me that in this matter Ruellio did not exercise the mature judgment that his fine qualities required: for he ought at least to have considered whether, in tasting this Eupatorium, he had sensed bitterness in it — for if so, the ancients would not have used it (as Dioscorides says) mixed with salt as a seasoning for food, bitter things being so offensive to human nature. But in truth (however little it may please Ruellio) the Water Pepper is found in Italy, and one can say nothing else than that it is that species of Persicaria most sharp in taste, in whose leaves that black spot is not seen which is visible in the other. For its leaves are long, larger than those of mint, more tender, and whiter. The stem is entirely knotted and hard. The hollows are near the branches. The seed grows upon them in clusters of sharp flavor, and this plant is found for the most part growing in watery places, as Dioscorides said.

Of Ptarmica. Chapter 151.

C Ptarmica, which the Latins call Sternutamentaria, is a plant that has many round and slender stems, similar to those of Abrotanum: around which are many long and olive-like leaves, at the top of which is a small round head, similar to that of chamomile, sharp in taste, which when smelled causes sneezing, from which it has taken its name. The leaves plastered together with the flowers remove bruises. The flowers cause sneezing most effectively. It grows in the mountains and in rocky places.
N Ptarmica grows abundantly in Tuscany. It also grows in the mountains of the valley of Anaunia in the jurisdiction of Trento, with stems quite slender, like those of Abrotanum, laden with dense leaves, whitish and smaller than those of the olive tree, and for this reason many call it Olivella. At the top it produces a round head, in which, and throughout the whole plant, there is so sharp an odor that it causes sneezing powerfully. Of this plant, brooms are made in Tuscany, and it has no other use among us.

Of the Radicetta, or herb Lanaria. Chapter 152.

D The herb Lanaria, which the Greeks call Struthion, well known and common, is used by those who wash wool to clean it. Its root is sharp and promotes urination. Taken with honey in the quantity of a spoonful, it helps coughs, liver ailments, and asthma. It also loosens the bowels; taken with opoponax and capers roots, it breaks bladder stones and expels them through the urine; it reduces hardness of the spleen. Applied to the natural parts of women it promotes menstruation, and manifestly destroys the unborn in the womb. Applied as a plaster with polenta and vinegar it heals scabies. Boiled with barley flour in wine it dissolves small tumors. It is mixed into plasters and collyria made for clearing the sight; smelled, it causes sneezing. It purges by mouth when ground with honey and infused into the nose.
B In the time of Dioscorides, the herb Lanaria was in such common use among all people for washing wool that he took no care to write down the distinguishing features of its form. This means that since its use has since declined and it is no longer so commonly known in our time, one can hardly judge well what it looks like and what its qualities are in Italy today. The Arabs call this root Condisi and use it greatly to cause sneezing; but it is not found in the apothecaries' shops, though it appears frequently in recipes. And so whether it grows in our time in Italy, I dare not assert,

Del Ciclamino. Cap. cliij.

L Ciclamino ha le frondi d'hedera, porporee, uarie, con alcune macole di so-
pra, & di sotto biancheggianti. Fa il gambo lungo quattro dita, nudo, & sen-
za frondi: sopra ilquale sono i fiori rossi in forma di rose. La radice è nera,
stiacciata, simile ad una rapa, laquale beuta in acqua dolce, purga per le par-
ti di sotto la flemma, & l'acqua: beuta, & applicata prouoca i mestrui. Diceli, che si scon-
ciano le donne grosse, che gli passan sopra: attaccata addosso fa presto partorire. Beesi nel
uino contra à tutti i ueleni, & particolarmente al lepre marino. Impiastrata gioua à i
morsi de serpenti: messa nel uino imbriacca. Beesi con passo, ouero in uino melato inac-
quato, à trabocco di fiele, al peso di tre dramme: ma bisogna poscia mettere gli amala-
ti in luogo caldo con assai couerte addosso à sudare: Imperoche il sudore uien fuor gial-
lo del colore del fiele. Il succhio della radice si tira su pe'l naso, per purgare la testa. Ap-
plicasi con lana al sedere in forma di sopposta, per fare andar del corpo. Vnto questo all'om
bilico, & al pettenecchio fin giù appresso alle coscíe, mollifica il corpo, & fa sconciare le
donne: unto con mele à gli occhi uale alle suffusioni, & debolezze di quelli: mettesi nelle
medicine, che fanno sconciare: unto con aceto al sedere, quando esce fuore il budello, lo
riduce. Cauasi il succhio dalle radici peste, & cuocesi, fino che s'ingrossa, come mele. La ra-
dice purga, & netta la pelle: ripercuote, & prohibisce il nascere delle pustole, & delle bolle:
guarisce per se sola, ouer meschiata con mele, le serite: impiastrata fa disfare la melza: gio-
ua alla faccia cotta dal sole, et fa rinascere i capelli cascati per pelagione. La sua dicottioe è
buona da far bagni à i membri smossi, alle podagre, all'ulcere della testa, & alle bugancie.
L'oglio uecchio, doue sia fritta dentro la radice, unto salda l'ulcere. Scauasi la radice, & em-
piesi d'oglio, & mettesi poscia à cuocere in su la cenere calda, & aggiugneuesi qualche uol-
ta della cera Tirrhena, accioche si facci unguento tenace, & uiscoso, utile principalmente al
le bugancie. Serbasi la radice tagliata in sette, come la scilla. Dicono alcuni, che s'adopera à
gl'incanti amorosi, pesta, & formata in pastelli. Nasce il Ciclamino in luoghi opachi, &
ombrosi, & massimamente sotto à gli alberi.

D'Vn altro Ciclamino. Cap. cliij.

Vui un altro Ciclamino, ilquale chiamano alcuni Cissanthemo, ouero Cisso-
phillo, che ha le frondi d'hedera, quantunque minori. Produce i fusti nodosi, &
grassi, i quali s'auolgono attorno à gli alberi circonuicini. Il cui fiore è bianco,
& odorato: i frutti son acinosi, come uua, simili, quantunque sien più teneri, à i corim
bi dell'hedera, il cui sapore è acuto, & la sostanza uiscosa: è la sua radice inutile: nasce in luo
ghi asperi. Il seme beuto in due ciathi di uino bianco al peso d'una dramma quaranta di con
tinui, risolue la melza per orina, et per il corpo. Beesi all'asma, et altre stretture di petto, ch'im
pediscono il respirare: purga beuto le donne di parto.

Hiamasi uolgarmente il Ciclamino Pan porcino. E' pianta notissima, & uolgare, quella dico, che è in uso hoggi
nelle Spetiaríe: imperoche l'altra spetie scritta qui da Dioscoride à i tempi nostri non è in uso, ne si conosce in Ita-
lia, quantunque uoglia il Ruellio, che sia il Ciclamino della seconda spetie quella pianta, che uolgarmente da i sem-

To confirm, for having not yet found anyone who can show it to you. Pliny mentioned this plant in chapter three of his nineteenth book, in the following manner. That herb called Radicetta has a juice truly very well suited for cleaning wool, and it is a great marvel that it makes it white and soft. It grows when sown everywhere, but the finest, which grows on its own, is found in Asia and Syria in harsh and salty places. That which comes from beyond the Euphrates river is the most praised of all. This plant produces a stalk like the Ferula, but slender, the young shoots of which the neighboring inhabitants eat as food. It dyes everything it is cooked with: it has leaves similar to the olive. The Greeks call it Struthion. It produces flowers in summer that are very pleasing to the eye, though of no scent. The leaves are thorny, and the stalk is woolly; it produces no seed, but grows a large root, which is cut for the use already mentioned. This is the Radicetta, or Lanaria herb, which according to Galen in the seventh book on the faculties of simples, is strong in taste, and hot in the fourth degree. It is astringent and causes sneezing, as do all other things that are hot in their temperaments and sharp in taste.

Of Cyclamen. Chapter 153.

Cyclamen has ivy-like leaves, purple, varied, with some spots above that are whitish below. It puts forth a stem four fingers long, bare and without leaves: upon which are red flowers in the form of roses. The root is black, flat, similar to a turnip, which when drunk in fresh water, purges phlegm and water from the lower parts; drunk and applied, it provokes menstruation. It is said that large women who step over it miscarry: attached to the body it causes quick delivery. It is drunk in wine against all poisons, and particularly against sea-hare poison. Applied as a plaster it helps against serpent bites; placed in wine it intoxicates. It is drunk with raisin wine, or with diluted honeyed wine, overflowing with bile, at a weight of three drams; but afterward the sick must be placed in a warm room with many coverings to sweat: because the sweat comes out yellow, the color of bile. The juice of the root is drawn up through the nose, to purge the head. Applied with wool at the seat in the form of a suppository, it moves the bowels. Rubbed on the navel and the pubic region down toward the thighs, it softens the body and causes miscarriage in women: rubbed with honey on the eyes it is good for cataracts and weaknesses of them; it is placed in medicines that cause miscarriage; rubbed with vinegar at the seat, when the bowel protrudes, it reduces it. The juice is extracted from pounded roots and boiled until it thickens like honey. The root purges and cleans the skin; it repels and prevents the appearance of pustules and blisters; it heals wounds by itself, or mixed with honey; applied as a plaster it dissolves the spleen; it benefits the face burned by the sun and causes hair that has fallen from mange to grow back. Its decoction is good for baths for displaced limbs, for gout, for ulcers of the head, and for chilblains. Old oil in which the root has been fried, rubbed on, heals ulcers. The root is hollowed out and filled with oil, and then placed to cook on warm ashes, and sometimes some Tyrrhenian wax is added, so that it becomes a thick and viscous ointment, useful principally for chilblains. The root is kept sliced into seven pieces, like squill. Some say it is used in love charms, ground and formed into pastilles. Cyclamen grows in shaded and shadowy places, and especially under trees.

Of Another Cyclamen. Chapter 154.

There is another Cyclamen, which some call Cissanthemo, or Cissophillo, which has ivy-like leaves, though smaller. It produces knotty and thick stems, which wind around nearby trees. Its flower is white and fragrant; its fruits are berry-like, like grapes, similar, though more tender, to the clusters of ivy, whose taste is sharp, and the substance viscous; its root is useless; it grows in harsh places. The seed drunk in two cups of white wine at the weight of one dram for forty consecutive days dissolves the spleen through urine and through the body. It is drunk for asthma and other constrictions of the chest that impede breathing; drunk, it purges women in childbirth.

Cyclamen is commonly called Sowbread. It is a well-known and common plant, that is, the one which is used today in apothecaries' shops; because the other species described here by Dioscorides is not in use in our times, nor is it known in Italy, although Ruellius would have it that the plant commonly called by seed-sellers [the page continues]

A plicisti, & da gli Spetiali si chiama Sigillum sanctæ Mariæ. Ma per il Sigillum sanctæ Mariæ non intende egli la Prassi-
nella, ouero i Ginocchietti, ne mâco il Secatul di Serapione, ne quella spette di Persicaria, che ha sopra le frondi quella ma
cola nera, come tengono uniuersalmente gli Spetiali: ma intende d'una altra pianta, laquale secondo i lineamenti, & lafor-
ma, che eg'i gli attribuisce, mi pare, che ueramente non sia altro, che la Vite nera, scritta da Dioscoride nel fine del iij. li
bro, laquale chiamiamo noi in Thoscana Tamaro, & questa dice egli chiamarsi da gli Arabi Bothomarien, onde dice hauer
tirato gli Spetiali, & il Volgo il uocabolo del Sigillum sanctæ Mariæ. Nelche mi inse stamente s'inganna: percioche Sera
pione, & tutti gli altri Arabici, per il Bothomarien, non intendono altro, che'l Pan porcino della prima spette. Ritro-
uasi, secondo che scriue Mesue, del Pan porcino due spette, maggiore cioè, & minore. Il maggiore fa la radice, come una
rapa, è'l minore come le nocciuole, & come ceci. Il maggiore ueramente è noto à ciascuno, ma il minore scritto da Mesue
non ho ue luto io in Italia altroue, che nella ualle Anania della guaridizione di Trento, doue sene ritroua infinitissime pian
te. Le cu radici non son piugrandi d'una nocciuola. Oltre à ciò disse pur Mesue, che tolto il Pan porcino per bocca, ouero
messo ne i cristeri solue li flemma uiscosa, & conferisce à i dolori colici, flemmatici, & similmente à quelli, che si fanno,
quando s'inluristono, & si ritiengon poscia le feci nelle budella. Tiratone il succhio su per il naso, conferisce à i dolori an
tichi del capo, alle frigide emigranee, à i paralitici, & à tutte l'infirmità frigide del ceruello. Fece del Ciclamino men
B tione Galeno al. vij. delle faculta' de semplici, così dicendo. Hail Ciclamino uarie, & diuerse forze: imperoche è effersi-
uo, incisiuo, aperituo, & attrattivo. Et tanto è forte nelle facultà sue, che ungendosi, ouero impiast randosi insu'l uen-
tre, solue il corpo, & ammazza le creature nella madrice.

Della Dragontea maggiore. Cap.clv.

NAsce la Dragontea maggiore in luoghi ombrosi appresso alle siepi. Produce il
gambo dritto, alto due gombiti, & grosso come un bastone, diuerso di colori, &
liscio, di modo che del tutto rappresenta un serpe: sono le sue macole per la piu
parte porporee. Produce le frondi l'una inuolta nell'altra, simili alla rombice. Il
seme nasce nella sommità del fusto, racemoso, prima di colore di cenere, quantunque nel
maturarsi diuenti di colore di zaffarano, & rosso. E' la sua radice grande, ritonda, bianca, ri
coperta da sottil uelame. Cogliesi l'herba nel maturarsi il seme, & sprsemesene poscia il suc-
chio, & seccasi all'ombra. La radice si caua, quando si mietono le biade, & tagliasi in fette, le
C quali infilate si seccano all'ombra. Questa beuta con uino inacquato scalda: lessa ouero ar-
rostita con mele, & fattone lettouario, gioua à gli asmatici, à i rotti, à gli spasimati, à i catarri,
che discendon dal capo, & alla tosse: beuta con uino muoue i uenerei appetiti: pesta, & fat-
tone unguento con mele ferma, & purga l'ulcere maligne. & corrosiue, massimamente ag-
giuntoui la uitalba. Fansi di questa, & di mele lauande da schizzare nelle fistole, & nella
madrice, per tirar fuori le creature: unta medesimamente con mele spegne le uitiligini, &
stirpa i polipi del naso, & i cancheri. E' utile il succhio nelle medicine de gli occhi: Impe-
roche gioua alle caligini, fiocchi, & nuuolette di quelli. L'odore dell'herba fresca fa scon-
ciare le donne. Ilche fanno similmète trenta granella del suo seme, beute in aceto annac
quato. Hanno usato alcuni il succhio d'ammenduni ne i dolori delle orecchie, distillan-
douelo con oglio: le frondi nelle ferite fresche, & nelle bugance, mettendouelle suso cot-
te nel uino, come cose costrettiue. Oltre à ciò si dice, che coloro, che si fregaranno le ma-
ni con le frondi di questa pianta, ouero che portaranno in mano la sua radice, non po-
D tranno esser morsi dalle uipere.

Della Dragontea minore. Cap.clvi.

LA Dragontea minore produce le frondi d'hedera, ma grandi, tutte penticchiate
di bianco. Il fusto produce ella dritto, alto due gombiti, di diuersi colori, tutto pe
ticchiato di porporee macole, di modo che rappresenta in tutto un serpe grosso,
come un bastone. Il frutto è racemoso nella sommità del fusto, prima uerde, &
poscia nel maturarsi di colore di zaffa rano, al gusto seruente, & mordace. La radice è al-
quanto ritonda, bulbosa, simile all'aro, uestita di sottile inuoglio. Nasce in luoghi ombrosi
appresso alle siepi. Il succhio del seme distillato nelle orecchie, mitiga i dolori di quelle: mes
so nel naso con lana, ne stirpa fuore i polipi, & ferma i cancheri applicatoui suso. Beuto il
seme al numero di trenta granella con aceto annacquato, fa sconciare le donne grauide. Di

A The apothecaries call it Sigillum sanctæ Mariæ. But by Sigillum sanctæ Mariæ he does not mean the Pratsinella, nor the Ginocchietti, nor Serapion's Secatol, nor that species of Persicaria which has a dark spot on its leaves, as the apothecaries universally hold: rather he means another plant, which from its features and form, as he describes them, seems to me to be none other than the Black Vine, written of by Dioscorides at the end of the third book, which we in Tuscany call Tamaro; and this, he says, is called Bothomarien by the Arabs, from which term he says the apothecaries and common people derived the name Sigillum sanctæ Mariæ. In this he is entirely mistaken: for Serapion and all the other Arabic writers by Bothomarien mean nothing other than the Cyclamen of the first kind. According to what Mesue writes, there are two kinds of Cyclamen, namely the greater and the lesser. The greater has a root like a turnip, the lesser like hazelnuts and chickpeas. The greater is indeed known to everyone, but the lesser, described by Mesue, I have never found in Italy anywhere except in the Val d'Anania in the district of Trento, where it grows in infinite abundance. Its roots are no larger than a hazelnut. Moreover Mesue himself said that Cyclamen taken by mouth, or administered in enemas, dissolves viscous phlegm and is useful for colic pains, phlegmatic pains, and likewise for those that occur when one strains and the stool is then retained in the bowels. Drawing its juice up through the nose is useful for chronic headaches, cold migraines, paralytics, and all cold ailments of the brain. Galen mentions Cyclamen in book seven on the properties of simples, saying: Cyclamen has various and diverse powers, for it is erosive, incisive, aperitive, and attractive. And it is so powerful in its faculties that when rubbed or plastered on the belly, it loosens the body and kills the creatures in the womb.

Of the Greater Dragonwort. Chapter 155.

The greater Dragonwort grows in shady places near hedges. It produces a straight stem, two cubits tall and as thick as a staff, of varied colors and smooth, so that it altogether resembles a serpent: its spots are for the most part purple. It produces leaves one folded within the other, similar to dock. The seed grows at the top of the stem in clusters, at first ash-colored, though upon ripening it becomes saffron-colored and red. Its root is large, round, white, covered with a thin skin. The herb is gathered when the seed ripens, and the juice is then pressed out and dried in the shade. The root is dug when the grain is harvested, and cut into slices, which are strung and dried in the shade. Drunk with watered wine it warms; boiled or roasted with honey and made into an electuary, it is good for asthmatics, for those with ruptures, for spasms, for catarrhs descending from the head, and for coughs; drunk with wine it stimulates venereal appetites; pounded and made into an ointment with honey it firms and purges malignant and corrosive ulcers, especially when clematis is added. Washes made from this plant and honey are used for injecting into fistulas and into the womb to draw out the afterbirth; rubbed with honey it likewise extinguishes skin blemishes, removes nasal polyps, and treats cancerous sores. The juice is useful in eye medicines, for it benefits dimness, cataracts, and clouding of the eyes. The odor of the fresh herb causes women to miscarry, as do thirty grains of its seed drunk in watered vinegar. Some have used the juice of both kinds for earaches, instilling it with oil; the leaves on fresh wounds and bruises, applied warm in wine, act as astringents. It is also said that those who rub their hands with the leaves of this plant, or carry its root in their hand, will not be bitten by vipers.

Of the Lesser Dragonwort. Chapter 156.

The lesser Dragonwort produces ivy-like leaves, but large, all speckled with white. It produces a straight stem, two cubits tall, of various colors, entirely spotted with purple spots, so that it altogether resembles a large serpent, like a staff. The fruit grows in clusters at the top of the stem, first green, then upon ripening saffron-colored, and is biting and sharp to the taste. The root is somewhat round, bulbous, similar to that of Arum, clothed in a thin skin. It grows in shady places near hedges. The juice of the seed instilled into the ears alleviates their pain; placed in the nose on wool it removes polyps therefrom, and applied to cancerous sores it arrests them. Thirty grains of the seed drunk with watered vinegar cause pregnant women to miscarry. Di-

per il mezzo non ha costola alcuna, & però la chiamano alcuni Herba senza costola. Esce da questa fronde un breue, et
sottil fusto, la punta delquale termina in una picciola linguetta, che nel colore gialleggia, & perche si rassembra alla lin-
gua d'un serpe la chiamano alcuni Serpentina. E' quest'herba (secondo che recitano alcuni) per consolidare le ferite fre-
sche mirabile, & massime l'oglio, che si fa con essa al sole, come si fa quello delle rose. Et imperò molto la lodano alle rot-
ture intestinali, & massime de i fanciulli.

Dell'Aro.                    Cap.clvij.

O Aro, ilquale è chiamato da Soriani Iupha, produce le frondi di dragōtea, ma
piu lunghe, & manco penticchiate. Fa il fusto rossigno, lungo una spanna, come
un pestello, dalquale nasce il seme di colore di zaffarano. Produce la radice bian
ca, come quella della dragontea, laquale per effere men forte, si mangia cotta nei
cibi. Condisconsi le foglie nel sale per l'uso de i cibi, & mangiansi parimente secche, cotte per
B  se sole. Hanno la radice, il seme, & le frondi le uirtu medesime della dragontea. Priuata-
mente gioua la radice dell'Aro impiàstrata con sterco di bue alle podagre. Serbasinel me-
desimo modo, che quella della dragontea, & per effer ella men forte, è piu usata à man-
giarsi ne i cibi.

N    Asce l'Aro copiosamente per tutta Thoscana ne i campi, nelle uigne, ne i fossi, & appresso alle siepi, & massime
nelle nostre maremme di Siena, doue si chiama uolgarmente Gigaro, uocabolo corrotto da Iaro. Fanno delle radici
di questa le donne acque, & lisci per polirsi, & farsi bianca la faccia, di non poco ualore. Et imperò quella misiu-
ra, che si fa di quelle, chiamata Gersa, fa mirabilmente lucida, & bianca la carne. Di questo fece mentione Galeno al
vi. delle facoltà dei semplici, cosi dicendo. L'essenza dell'Aro è terrestre, ma calda. E' oltre à ciò aftersiua, ma non cosi for
te, come la dragontea. Scalda l'Aro, & disecca nel primo ordine.

Dell'Arisaro.                    Cap.clviij.

C    L'Arisaro una picciola herba. La cui radice è grāde, come una oliua, molto piu
acuta, che quella dell'Aro. Et però ferma impiàstrata l'ulcere, che māgiano. Fan
nosi d'essa efficacissimi collirij contra le fistole. Impiàstrata la radice a i membri
genitali di tutti gli animali quadrupedi gli corrompe.

L'    Arisaro, secondo che à.xvi. capitoli del.xxxiiij. scrisse Plinio, nasce in Egitto simile all'Aro, ma molto minore de
frondi, & de radici. Questo ueramente à i tempi nostri non si ritroua chi ce lo mostri in Italia, ne alcuno de i mo
derni, ne de gli antichi scriue, che la ui nasca. Et percio non se ne puo dare altra notizia, non portandosi ci elle
d'Egitto, oue copiosamente si ritroua.

Dell'Asphodelo, ouero Hastula regia.          Cap.clix.

D    O Asphodelo è pianta quasi nota à ciascuno. Produce le frondi simili al Porro
maggiore, et il fusto tutto liscio, nella cui sommità è il fiore, ilqual chiamano an
therico. Ha le radici lūghe, & ritonde, simili alle ghiāde, al gusto acute, che di sua
natura scaldano. Queste prese in beuanda prouocano l'orina, & i mestrui. Beu-
te con uino al peso d'una dramma, medicano à i dolori del costato, à i rotti, à gli spasimati, &
alla tosse. Fanno uomitare mangiate ne i cibi alla quatità d'una tessera. Dannosi utilmente
al peso di tre dramme contra 'l morso de serpenti: ma bisogna impiàstrare anchora 'l morso
con i fiori, con le frondi, & con le radici cotte nel uino. Impiàstrasi con queste medesime l'ul
cere sordide, & quelle, che mangiano. Cotte con seccia di uino s'applicano alle infiāmagio-
ni delle poppe, & de testicoli: à piccioli tumori, & alle posteme, che nascono nelle parti car-
nose: & con polenta alle nouelle infiammagioni. Cuocesi il succhio delle radici cō uino uec-
chio dolce, mirrha, & zaffarano, & fassene cosi efficacissimo medicamento per gli occhi. Di
stillasi il succhio per se stesso tepido, ouero insieme con incēso, mele, mirrha, & uino nell'orec
chie, che menano marcia. Distillato nell'orecchia della parte contraria mitiga il dolore dei
dēti. La cenere delle radici unta fa rinascere i capelli casati. L'oglio cotto nelle radici scauate
cōserisce alle bugance ulcerate, & alle cotture del fuoco: distillato nell'orecchie gioua alla sor
dità. La radice spegne le uitiligini prima fregate al sole cō una pezza di lino, et poscia impia

A    From May until mid-June: because it is very tender, it perishes in a short time. It produces a single frond which has no rib down the middle, and therefore some call it "Herb without a rib." From this frond grows a short and slender stem, whose tip ends in a small tongue-shaped blade that is yellowish in color, and because it resembles the tongue of a serpent, some call it Serpentina. This herb is (according to some) wonderful for healing fresh wounds, and especially the oil made from it in the sun, as one makes oil from roses. And therefore it is greatly praised for intestinal ruptures, especially in children.

On Aro.                    Chapter 157.

Aro, which the Syrians call Iupha, produces fronds like those of the dragonwort, but longer and less divided. It produces a reddish stem, a hand's span long, like a pestle, from which grows the seed, the color of saffron. It produces a white root, like that of the dragonwort, which, being less strong, is eaten cooked in foods. Its leaves are preserved in salt for use in food, and are likewise eaten dried or cooked by themselves. The root, seed, and fronds have the same virtues as the dragonwort. Privately, the root of Aro, plastered on with ox dung, is good for gout. It is preserved in the same manner as the dragonwort, and because it is less strong, it is more commonly used as a food.

N    Aro grows abundantly throughout all of Tuscany in fields, vineyards, ditches, and beside hedgerows, and especially in our marshlands of Siena, where it is commonly called Gigaro, a word corrupted from Iaro. Women make from its roots waters and rinses to polish and whiten the face, of no small value. And therefore the preparation made from them, called Gersa, makes the skin wonderfully bright and white. Galen mentioned this in book six of the Faculties of Simples, saying thus: The essence of Aro is earthly but warm. It is moreover cleansing, though not as strongly as the dragonwort. Aro warms and dries in the first degree.

On Arisaro.                    Chapter 158.

C    Arisaro is a small herb. Its root is large, like an olive, and much more pungent than that of Aro. Plastered on, it therefore stops ulcers that eat into the flesh. From it are made very effective collyria against fistulas. Plastered on the genitals of all four-legged animals, it corrupts them.

L'    Arisaro, according to what Pliny wrote in chapter sixteen of book thirty-four, grows in Egypt similar to Aro but with much smaller fronds and roots. At the present time no one in Italy can be found to show it to us, and neither any modern nor any ancient writer records that it grows there. And therefore no further information about it can be given, as it is not brought here from Egypt, where it is found in abundance.

On Asphodelo, or Hastula regia.          Chapter 159.

D    Asphodelo is a plant almost known to everyone. It produces fronds similar to the greater leek, and a completely smooth stem, at the top of which is the flower, which they call antherico. It has long, round roots, similar to acorns, sharp in taste, and by nature warming. Taken as a drink they stimulate urine and menstruation. Drunk in wine at the weight of one dram, they remedy pains in the side, ruptures, spasms, and coughs. Eaten with food in the quantity of a playing piece, they cause vomiting. They are usefully given at the weight of three drams against snake bites; but one must also plaster the bite with the flowers, fronds, and roots cooked in wine. With these same things, foul ulcers and those that eat into the flesh are plastered. Cooked with wine lees, they are applied to inflammations of the breasts and testicles; to small tumors and to abscesses that arise in fleshy parts; and with polenta to new inflammations. The juice of the roots is cooked with old sweet wine, myrrh, and saffron, and made into a most effective medicine for the eyes. The juice is distilled warm by itself, or together with frankincense, honey, myrrh, and wine, into ears that discharge pus. Distilled into the opposite ear, it eases toothache. The ash of the roots, rubbed on, causes hair that has fallen out to regrow. The oil cooked in hollowed roots benefits ulcerated chilblains and burns; distilled into the ears it helps deafness. The root removes skin blemishes, after first rubbing them in the sun with a piece of linen, and then plastering

text:
SECONDO 201

strataui fuso. Il seme, & i fiori beuti nel uino resistono marauigliosamente à i ueleni della A
scolopendra, & de gli scorpioni. Purgano questi medesimi il corpo.

Hiamasi l'Hastula regia, laqual chiamano i Latini Albuco, uolgarmente Amphodillo. E' pianta uolgare à tutte
C le Spettarie. E' ueramente bello il uedere nel cauarla su di terra la grande moltitudine delle radici, che gli pendono
attorno: percioche tal pianta n'ho cauatojo in sui monti, che gli ho ritrouato piu di cento radici attaccate d'in
torno. Scriue Theophrastio, che genera l' Amphodillo nel scapo, doue è dentro il seme, alcuni uermi, liquali fanno poscia
l'ali, come quelli, che fanno la seta, & uolansene uia quando per la maturità della pianta si gli rompe l'inuoglio. Mangia
uansi anticamente (se Hesiodo ne riferisce il uero) le radici dell' Amphodillo ne i cibi cotte con sale, & oglio, & similmen
te composte con fichi secchi. Lodolle Nicandro poeta molto nelle sue theriache contra à i morsi delle serpi, & punture de
gli scorpioni. Fece dell'Amphodillo mètione Galeno al .yi. delle facultà de semplici, par lan foue in questo modo. E' la radice
dell'Amphodillo utile come è quella dell'aro, dell'arisaro, et della dragôtea, p esser anchor ella astrinsiua. La cenere delle
radici è piu calda, piu secca, piu sottile, & piu potente nel digerire. Ilperche fa rinascere ualentemente i peli, che cascano.

Del Bulbo che si mangia. Cap.clx.

L Bulbo, che si mangia è uolgare, & noto à ciascuno. Mangiato ne i cibi è utile B
allo stomacho. Il rosso, che si porta d'Africa muoue il corpo. L'amaro, che si
rassembra alla scilla fa digerire, & molto piu è conueneuole allo stomacho. Tut
ti i Bulbi sono acuti, scaldano, sono uenerei, fanno aspra la lingua, & il gorgo
zzule, nutrìscono assai, generano carne, son uentosi. Impiastràsi à i membri rotti, & dislogati,
& in su i dolori delle giunture: cauano i bronconi, & le spine. Applicati soli, ouero insieme
con mele giouano alle cancrene, & alle podagre. Giouano anchora impiastrati con mele, &
con pepe pesto à gl'hidropici, & à i morsi de cani: prohibiscono il sudore, & leuano i dolo
ri dello stomacho. Mondificano la farfarella, & l'ulcere del capo, che menano, quando ui si
impiastrano insieme con nitro brusciato. Spengono insieme con tuorli d'uuoua i liuidi, &
le margini del uaiuolo, & con mele, ouero con aceto le lentigini. Medicano alle percosse del
l'orecchie, & dell'unghie delle dita applicatiui suso insieme con polèta. Arrostiti sotto alla ce
nere calda, & applicati insieme con la cenere delle mene, guariscono i fichi. Brusciati, & me
scolati con alcionio spengono le macole della pelle della faccia, & le negrezze delle cicatri
ci, & massime fac̃done untione al sole. Cotti nell'acero, & mangiati sono coueneuoli à i rot C
ti. Ma è da guardarsi dal troppo mangiarneimperoche nuocono à i nerui.

Del Bulbo che fa uomitare. Cap.clxi.

L Bulbo, ilqual chiamano uomitorio, ha le frondi piu lente, & piu uencide, &
molto piu lunghe, che quello, che si mangia. La radice è simile à quella, ricoperta
di nera spoglia. Questa mangiata, ouer beutone la sua dicottione, gioua à i disfet
ti della uisciga, & fa uomitare.
Q Vantunque tanto il Bulbo, che si mangia, quanto quello, che fa uomitare fussero notissimi à Dioscoride, sono non di
meno hoggi à i moderni Medici del tutto incogniti. Et però mene taccio anchor io l'historia loro.

Della Scilla. Cap.clxij.

La Scilla seruente, & acuta. Vsasi piu arrostita, che altrimèti, & imperò si circon D
da, & si ricuopre di pasta, ouero di creta, & mettesi nel forno, ouero sotto à carbo
ni fino che sia ben cotta la pasta, che si gli mette attorno. Togliesi poscia uia, & se
la si ritroua, che la non sia ben cotta, & fatta tenera, & siappa, si ricuopre di nuo
uo di pasta, ouero di luto, & ricuocesi: peroche quella, che nò è cosi arrostita, non si puo dare
senza graue pericolo de i membri interiori. Arrostiscesi anchora messa nel forno in un uaso
di terra ben coperto. Prendefi della Scilla gittando uia gli scogli di fuore, le parti, che so
no piu di dentro, & cuoconsi tagliate in pezzetti mutandogli, & rimutandogli l'acqua,
fino che piu non gli si ritrouine fortezza, ne amaritudine. Infilansi poscia di modo che non
si tocchino l'una con l'altra, & seccansi all'ombra per fare l'oglio, il uino, & l'aceto scillitico.
Vagliono gli scogli della Scilla delle parti piu interiori fritti nell'oglio, & pesti con ragia
contra alle crepature dei piedi. Impiastrasi la Scilla cotta nell'aceto in sui morsi delle uspe
R iij
description: Pietro Andrea Matthioli's landmark Italian translation of Dioscorides De Materia Medica. The first vernacular edition to make classical Greek botanical medicine accessible to European physicians.
translation:
SECOND 201

When strained through wine, the seeds and flowers resist wonderfully the poisons of the A
scolopendra and of scorpions. These same things also purge the body.

It is called Hastula regia, which the Latins call Albuco, commonly Amphodillo. It is a plant common in all
C the apothecaries. It is truly beautiful to see, when digging it out of the earth, the great multitude of roots hanging
around it: for I have dug up this plant on the mountains and found more than a hundred roots attached all around
it. Theophrastus writes that the Amphodillo generates in its stalk, where the seed is inside, certain worms which then
grow wings, like silkworms, and fly away when the covering of the plant splits open at maturity. The roots of
Amphodillo were eaten in ancient times (if Hesiod reports truly) cooked with salt and oil and similarly prepared
with dried figs. Nicander the poet praised it highly in his theriac remedies against the bites of serpents and the stings of
scorpions. Galen mentioned Amphodillo in book six of the Properties of Simples, saying in that place as follows: The root
of Amphodillo is useful, like that of aro, of arisaro, and of dracontea, because it too is astringent. The ash of the
roots is hotter, drier, finer, and more powerful in digesting. Hence it powerfully restores hair that has fallen out.

On the Bulb that is eaten. Chapter 160.

The Bulb that is eaten is common and well known to everyone. Eaten in food it is useful B
for the stomach. The red one, which is brought from Africa, moves the bowels. The bitter one, which
resembles the squill, aids digestion and is much more agreeable to the stomach. All
bulbs are sharp, they warm, they are aphrodisiac, they roughen the tongue and the throat,
they nourish well, they generate flesh, and they are flatulent. They are applied as a poultice to broken and dislocated
limbs, and to pains of the joints: they draw out splinters and thorns. Applied alone or together
with honey they help cangrenes and gout. Applied as a poultice with honey and
ground pepper they also help those with dropsy and those bitten by dogs: they suppress sweating and relieve pains
of the stomach. They cleanse dandruff and running ulcers of the head when applied there
together with burnt nitre. Together with egg yolks they extinguish bruises and
the margins of smallpox, and with honey or vinegar, freckles. They treat blows to
the ears and to the nails of the fingers when applied thereon together with polenta. Roasted under hot
ash and applied together with the ash of mene, they heal figs. Burnt and mixed C
with alcionio they remove spots from the skin of the face and the darkness of scars,
especially when anointed with the mixture in the sun. Cooked in vinegar and eaten they are good for broken-
boned people. But one must beware of eating too many of them, because they harm the nerves.

On the Bulb that causes vomiting. Chapter 161.

The Bulb which they call the emetic has leaves that are softer and more supple and
much longer than the one that is eaten. The root is similar to that one, covered
with a black skin. This one, eaten or its decoction drunk, is good for ailments
of the bladder and causes vomiting.
Q Although both the edible Bulb and the emetic Bulb were very well known to Dioscorides, they are none
the less today entirely unknown to modern physicians. And therefore I too pass over their history in silence.

On the Squill. Chapter 162.

The Squill is heating and sharp. It is used most often roasted, and is therefore wrapped D
and covered in dough, or in clay, and placed in the oven or over coals
until the dough placed around it is well cooked. It is then removed, and if one finds
that it is not well cooked and made tender and soft, it is covered again with new
dough or clay and cooked again: because that which is not thus roasted cannot be given
without great danger to the internal organs. It is also roasted placed in the oven in an earthen
vessel well covered. From the Squill one takes, discarding the outer layers, the parts that are
more toward the inside, and these are cooked cut into small pieces, changing and re-changing the water,
until no more strength or bitterness is found in them. They are then strung up in such a way that
they do not touch one another, and dried in the shade, to make oil, wine, and scillitico vinegar.
The inner layers of the Squill fried in oil and ground with resin are good
against cracks of the feet. The Squill cooked in vinegar is applied as a poultice on the stings of wasps
R iij

text:
202 LIBRO

A re. Dafsi una parte dell'arrostita, con otto parti di sale pur arrostito al peso d'un cucchiaio, ouero di due da digiuno per far andare del corpo. Mettesi nelle beuande, & nelle medicine odorate, & in quelle, che si fanno per prouocar l'orina, per l'hidropísie, per i uomiti dello stomache, & debolezze di quello. Gioua fattone lettouario con mele al peso di tre oboli, à trabocco di fiele, à dolori di corpo, alla tosse uecchia, à strettura di petto, & à uomiti. Cuocesi co mele, & mangiasi ne i cibi per tutte queste cose, & particolarmente per corroborare la digestione: solue per il corpo le materie uiscose, & tenaci. Lessa, & mangiata nel medesimo modo fa i medesimi effetti: ma non è da dare à coloro, che hanno ulcerato alcun membro interiore. Vngonsi utilmente con l'arrostita le bugancie, i porri, & i calli. Il seme della Scilla trito, & impastato con mele, & con fichi secchi, & mangiato mollifica il corpo. Appiccata la Scilla sopra à gli usci delle case prohibisce gl'incantamenti.

Del Pancratio, cioè Scilla minore. Cap.clxiij.

B IL Pancratio, il quale chiamano alcuni Scilla minore, produce la radice simile al bulbo maggiore, di colore rosso, porporino. Il cui sapore è feruente, & amaro. Le frondi sue son simili à quelle del giglio, ma piu lunghe. Ha questa la uirtu me desima della Scilla, & preparasi, & dassi al medesimo modo, & al medesimo peso per le infirmità, oue fa ella dibisogno, quantunque sia men forte della Scilla. Impastali il succhio cauato dalla radice con farina d'orobo, & fansene trocisci, i quali commodissimamente si danno à gl'hidropici, & à coloro, che patiscono nella melza.

A Scilla maggiore si chiama uolgarmente nelle Spettarie Squilla. E' nota à tutti gli Spetiali, & ueramente molto buona, & utile per le medicine: imperoche senza la Scilla non si puo far la buona, & la uera Theriaca. La minore, la quale chiama Dioscoride Pancratio non è à i tempi nostri in uso, ne manco si ritrova in Italia alcuno che la dimostri. Delche non accade, che molto si curino gli Spetiali: percioche in uece di questa piu ualentemente supplisce la maggiore, della quale se ne mostrano nelle Spetiarie due spetie, bianca cioè, & nera. Et però uogliono alcuni, che sia la bianca il maschio, & la nera la femmina (secondo che recita il Ruellio) quantunque secondo la ragione delle cose naturali doueffe effer il contrario. Vsano à i tempi nostri alcuni Medici per l'infirmita frigide del ceruello, & de i nerui, di mettere la Squilla cruda, tagliata per oin minuti pezzi oli con mele in un uaso di uetro tutti la State al sole, usando poscia quel mele diligentemente colato per rimedio eccellentissimo al mal caduco. E' la Scilla (secondo il dir di Galeno al. viij. delle faculta de semplici) ualentemente incisíua, ma non però così ualentemente calida; Imperoche la non pasa nel caldo, che ella possiede, il secondo grado.

Del Capparo. Cap.clxtiij.

IL Capparo è una piàta spinosa, strata per terra in ritonda figura. Sono le sue spine ritorte à modo d'hamo, come quelle de i roui. Produce le frondi tonde, simili à quelle de i pomi cotogni. Il suo frutto è simile alle oliue, il quale aprendosi produce un fiore bianco, dopo al quale ui rimane un certo che, come una ghianda lunga, il che dimostra nell'aprirsi le granella, simili à quelle del melagrano, picciole, & rosse. Ha molte grandi, & legnose radici. Nasce in sottil terra, in luoghi aspri, nell'Isole, & nelle ruine de gli edifitij. Condiscesi il suo frutto, & il fustio nel sale per uso de i cibi. Conturba il corpo, è inimico allo stomacho, fa sete: benche cotto è più conueniètte allo stomacho, che màgiato crudo. Beuto il seme quaranta giorni continui al peso di due dramme sminuisce la melza, & fa orinare i trombi del sangue. Gioua beuto medesimamente à i dolori delle sciatiche, à paralitici, à rotti, & à gli spasimati: prouoca i mestrui, & purga la flemma della testa per bocca. Gioua la dicottione del seme lauandosene la bocca à i dolori de denti. La corteccia della radice secca uale à tutte le cose predette: mondifica tutte l'ulcere uecchie, & sordide, & quelle, che son fatte callose. Impastata con farina d'orzo, & fattone impiàstro, gioua à coloro, che patiscono nella melza. Morduta gioua à i dolori de denti. Trita, & unta con aceto spegne le uitiligini bianche. Le frondi, & le radici peste risoluono le durezze, & le scrofole. Il succhio, che si sprieme dalle radici distillato nell'orecchie, u'ammazza d'tro i uermi. Il Capparo, che nasce nella marmarica Libia è grandemente uentoso, & quello che nasce in Puglia fa uomitare. Quello, che si porta dal mar rosso, & di Libia è acutissimo: la onde ulcera la bocca, & rode le gengiue per sino all'ossa. Ilperche si danna nell'uso de i cibi.

translation:
202 BOOK

A Take one part of the roasted [squill], with eight parts of salt likewise roasted, to the weight of a spoonful, or two spoonfuls on an empty stomach, to purge the body. It is used in drinks, in aromatic medicines, and in those prepared to stimulate urination, for dropsy, for vomiting from stomach weakness and disorders. Made into an electuary with honey at the weight of three obols, it helps with overflow of bile, bodily pains, chronic cough, tightness of the chest, and vomiting. Cooked with honey and eaten in food, it is good for all these things, and particularly to strengthen digestion: it dissolves viscous and tenacious matter from the body. Boiled and eaten it produces the same effects; but it should not be given to those who have ulcerations of any internal organ. Roasted squill is beneficially applied to chilblains, leeks-sores, and calluses. The seed of the squill, ground and mixed with honey and dried figs and eaten, softens the body. Hung above the doors of houses, the squill wards off enchantments.

On Pancratium, that is, the lesser Squill. Chapter 163.

B Pancratium, which some call the lesser Squill, produces a root resembling the larger bulb, reddish-purple in color. Its flavor is hot and bitter. Its leaves are similar to those of the lily, but longer. It has the same virtue as the Squill, and is prepared and administered in the same way and for the same ailments, though it is less potent than the Squill. The juice extracted from the root is mixed with orobus flour and made into lozenges, which are very conveniently given to those with dropsy and to those who suffer in the spleen.

The greater Squill is commonly called Squilla in the apothecaries' shops. It is well known to all apothecaries, and truly excellent and useful in medicines: for without the Squill, one cannot make the genuine Theriaca. The lesser one, which Dioscorides calls Pancratium, is not in use in our time, nor can anyone be found in Italy today who can identify it. This need not overly concern apothecaries, since the greater one, which is shown in apothecaries' shops in two varieties — white and black — serves its purpose more powerfully. Some hold that the white is the male and the black the female (as Ruellius records), though according to natural reasoning it ought to be the opposite. Nowadays some physicians, for cold afflictions of the brain and nerves, place the Squill raw, cut into small pieces, with honey in a glass vessel and leave it in the sun all summer, then use that honey, carefully strained, as an excellent remedy for epilepsy. The Squill (according to Galen, book 8 of Simple Medicines) is powerfully incisive, but not quite so powerfully heating; for its heat does not exceed the second degree.

On the Caper. Chapter 164.

The caper is a thorny plant, spreading along the ground in a rounded shape. Its thorns are curved like fishhooks, like those of brambles. It produces round leaves, similar to those of quince. Its fruit resembles olives; when it opens it produces a white flower, after which there remains something like a small oblong acorn, which when opening reveals small seeds resembling those of the pomegranate, small and red. It has large, woody roots. It grows in thin soil, in rough places, on islands, and among the ruins of buildings. Its fruit and stem are preserved in salt for use in food. It troubles the body, is unfriendly to the stomach, and causes thirst; though when cooked it is more agreeable to the stomach than when eaten raw. The seed drunk for forty consecutive days at the weight of two drams reduces the spleen and causes blood clots to be passed in urine. Drunk likewise it helps with pains of the sciatic nerve, with paralytics, with ruptures, and with spasms; it provokes menstruation and purges phlegm from the head through the mouth. A decoction of the seed, used as a mouth rinse, helps with toothache. The bark of the root dried is good for all the above: it cleanses all old and foul ulcers, including those that have become callous. Made into a poultice with barley flour, it helps those who suffer in the spleen. Chewed, it helps with toothache. Ground and rubbed on with vinegar, it extinguishes white vitiligo patches. The leaves and roots, pounded, dissolve hardnesses and scrofula. The juice pressed from the roots, distilled into the ears, kills worms within them. The caper that grows in Marmaric Libya is extremely flatulent, and that which grows in Puglia causes vomiting. That which comes from the Red Sea and from Libya is most pungent, and thus ulcerates the mouth and gnaws the gums down to the bone — which is why it is condemned for use in food.

text:
204 LIBRO

A saluatico.Il terzo è piccolino:produce il fior giallo,& è di graue odore. Il quarto è simile à
questo,ma fa il fior bianco simile al latte.Le frondi,i fiori,et i fusti di tutti questi,quando son
uerdi,& teneri ulcerano,& brusciano con dolore,come fa il fuoco:& imperò impiastrati
fanno cadere l'unghie corrotte,guariscono la scabbia,spégono le margini,cauano le formi
che,che si rassembrano à i thimi,& sanano la pelagione.La dicottion loro applicata tepida,
giova alle bugancie. La radice secca,& trita messa nel naso fa starnutare:messa sotto à i
denti ne leua il dolore,ma gli fa rompere.

Hiamasi(quantunque male)il Ranonculo,ouer Batrachio scrittone qui da Dioscoride,quasi per tutta italia,come
C ben dicemo disopra al capitolo del Coronopo,Pie coruino,ouero Pie di gallo. E herba uer amète nota à ciascuno,
& ritrouansene in italia piu spetie.Tra lequali uen'è una(quantunque se la taccia però egli)non punto dissimile da
quella prima,che produce la radice simile à una grossa castagna,bianca,& ulceratiua,laquale ho spesso usataio il uerno p
far uscagare,qñ non ho potuto hauer l'herba.Oltre à cio quello,che in Sardegna si chiama Apio rustico,chiamano alcu
ni Apium risum;imperoche si crede,che ridendo muoiono coloro,che se lo mangiano,come che dichino alcuni altri,à i
B quali è piu da esser creduto,che mangiato questo Apio di Sardegna fa ritirare tutti i nerui,& però in tal modo fa slarga
re,et distendere la bocca,che morendo,se ne chi lo magia,si rascbra nell'aspetto à uno,che rida:et imperò diceva Salustio.
Nasce in Sardegna una certa herba,laquale si chiama Sardonia simile all'Apio saluatico,laquale ammezzàdo gli huomi
ni talmente gli storce la bocca,et le parti circonstanti,che pare uer amète,che ridino nel morire.ilche medesimamente diss
Dioscoride par ladone nel.vi.libro,dove trattò de i ueleni,in questo modo. Quell'herba,che si chiama Sardonia è uer amète
spetie di Ranonculo.Beuta questa,ouer magiata ne cibi fa alienare la mente,et facèdo ritirare le labbra della bocca giù un
certo spasimo,che par proprio,che ridino coloro,che se l'hanno mangiate. A questo giova dopo che s'è fatto il vomito,il
bere copiosamente acqua melata,et latte,et ungere poscia tutto il corpo cò unguenti,che possino bene scaldare. Oltre à uo
giova mirabilmente lo stare in un bagno d'acqua calda meschiato con oglio,fregando poscia ualidissimamente,et ungendo i
patienti,in somma la cura di questo è la istessa cura dello spasimo. Dell'altre spetie nò accade narrarne altre,la historia p esser
elle notissime à ciascuno. Ma uolendosi sapere in quàto errore sieno coloro,che tégono il Ranonculo p il pie coruino,ouera
pie di cornacchia,leggisi il comèto nostro fatto disopra al cap.del Coronopo,et ritrouarassene quiui quàto fa dibisogno.

Dell'Anemone. Cap.clxvij.

C O Anemone è di due spetie,l'uno delle quali nasce in luoghi saluatichi,l'altro in
luoghi coltiuati,il quale è di uarie spetie:Imperoche uno,p'duce il fior rosso, l'al
tro bianco,come il latte,& l'altro porpooreo.Le srondi di questi son simili al co
riandro,ma intagliate piu minutamère appresso à terra. I fusti sono lanuginosi,
& sottili,sopra à i quali sono i fiori simili à quelli del papauero,in mezzo à i quali sono le te
ste nere,ouer cerulee.Hanno la radice grande,come una oliua,& qualche uolta maggiore,
& in alcuni è diuisa da certi nodi.Quello,che nasce al saluatico,è in tutte le sue parti mag
giore di quello,che nasce al domestico.Ha le frondi piu larghe,& piu dure,il capo piu lun
go.Il fiore è rosso,& le radici son molte,& capillari.Enne di quello,che ha le frondi nere,il
quale è maggiormente acuto.Sono ammenduni acuti,& per questa cagione il succhio tira
to su per il naso purga la testa. La radice masticata tira la flemma:cotta in uino passo,& im
piastrara medica l'infiàmagioni,le debolezze,et le cicatrici de gli occhi,et modifica l'ulcere
D fordide.I fusti,et le frondi cotte cò pisana,et màgiate ne cibi,fanno abondare il latte:appli
cate cò lana à i luoghi naturali delle donne,prouocano i mestrui:impiastrate guariscono la
scabbia.Sono alcuni,che ingannandosi,si pensano,che l'Argemone si chiami Eupatorio:
perche per la similtitudine del colore,che hanno ammenduni questi ne fiori,non sanno se
parare l'Argemone,& quella spetie di papauero,laqual chiamano Rheda,delquale dire
mo nelle spetie de papaueri,dal saluatico Anemone:Imperoche i fiori dell'Argemone,&
del papauero chiamato Rheda,hanno il colore men tinto,& ammenduni fioriscono piu
tardi.Oltre à cio l'Argemone ha il succhio giallo,molto al gusto acuto,& il papauero
detto Rheda,quantunque l'habbia anchor egli acuto,il ha nondimeno bianco,come latte.
Appresso l'argemone,& il rheda hanno le teste simili al papauero saluatico,ma nell'Ane
mone è piu grosso nella cima,& nel rheda piu sottile. L'Anemone per il contrario non sa
succhio alcuno,ne ha il uasetto simile à quel del papauero,ma ha una certa cima simile allo
sparago.Nascono quelli per il piu ne i campi.
description: Pietro Andrea Matthioli's landmark Italian translation of Dioscorides De Materia Medica. The first vernacular edition to make classical Greek botanical medicine accessible to European physicians.
translation:
204 BOOK

A The third is very small and produces a yellow flower, and has a strong odor. The fourth is similar to this one, but produces a white flower like milk. The leaves, flowers, and stems of all these, when green and tender, cause ulcers and burn with pain like fire; and therefore, when applied as a poultice, they cause rotten nails to fall off, heal scabies, relieve swellings, remove warts that resemble thyme-plants, and cure pellagra. Their decoction, applied warm, benefits swollen glands. The dried and ground root, placed in the nose, causes sneezing; placed under the teeth, it removes pain but causes them to break.

What is called (however incorrectly) Ranunculus, or Batrachium, as described here by Dioscorides, is known throughout almost all of Italy, as we noted above in the chapter on Coronopus, crow's-foot, or cock's-foot. It is indeed a plant well known to everyone, and in Italy there are many species. Among these there is one (which he does not mention) not at all unlike the first, which produces a root resembling a large chestnut, white and ulcerative, which I have often used in winter to cause sweating when I could not obtain the plant. Beyond this, what is called Wild Celery in Sardinia is called by some Apium risum (laughing parsley), because it is believed that those who eat it die laughing; though some others, who are more credible, say that this Sardinian Celery, when eaten, causes all the nerves to contract, and in this way stretches and distends the mouth so that those who die from eating it appear to be laughing; and thus Sallust said: In Sardinia grows a certain herb called Sardonia, resembling Wild Celery, which, when it kills men, twists their mouths and the surrounding parts so that it truly appears that they are laughing as they die. Dioscorides likewise reported this in Book VI, where he treated of poisons, in the following manner: The herb called Sardonia is truly a species of Ranunculus. Drunk or eaten in food, it causes madness, and by contracting the lips of the mouth in a certain spasm, it makes those who have eaten it appear to be laughing. For this condition it is helpful, after vomiting has been induced, to drink copious amounts of honey-water and milk, and then to anoint the whole body with ointments that can warm it well. It is also wonderfully beneficial to stay in a bath of warm water mixed with oil, and then to rub vigorously and anoint the patients; in short, the cure for this is the same as the cure for spasms. Of the other species there is no need to speak further, as their history is well known to everyone. But if one wishes to know how much in error are those who take the Ranunculus for the crow's-foot, let them read our commentary above on the chapter on Coronopus, where they will find as much as is needed.

On the Anemone. Chapter 167.

C The Anemone is of two species: one grows in wild places, the other in cultivated places, and the latter is of various kinds: for one produces a red flower, another white like milk, and another purple. The leaves of these resemble those of coriander, but more finely cut, growing close to the ground. The stems are woolly and slender, and above them are flowers resembling those of the poppy, in the middle of which are dark or blue-green centers. They have a large root, like an olive, and sometimes larger, and in some plants it is divided by certain nodes. The one that grows wild is in all its parts larger than the cultivated one. Its leaves are broader and harder, its head longer. The flower is red, and the roots are many and hair-like. There is also one that has dark leaves, which is more potent. Both are sharp, and for this reason the juice drawn up through the nose purges the head. The root, when chewed, draws out phlegm; cooked in raisin wine and applied as a poultice, it heals inflammations, weaknesses, and scars of the eyes, and treats foul ulcers. The stems and leaves cooked with pearl barley and eaten in food increase milk production; applied with wool to the natural parts of women, they promote menstruation; applied as a poultice they heal scabies. There are some who, deceiving themselves, think that the Argemone is called Eupatorium, because, due to the similarity of color that both share in their flowers, they cannot distinguish the Argemone, and that species of poppy called Rheda (of which we shall speak in the species of poppies), from the wild Anemone. For the flowers of the Argemone and of the poppy called Rheda have less vivid color, and both bloom later. Furthermore, the Argemone has yellow juice, very sharp to the taste, and the poppy called Rheda, although its juice is also sharp, has it white like milk. Moreover, the Argemone and the Rheda have heads similar to the wild poppy, but in the Anemone the head is larger at the top, and in the Rheda it is more slender. The Anemone, on the contrary, has no juice at all, nor does it have a seed-vessel resembling that of the poppy, but has a certain head resembling asparagus. These plants grow for the most part in fields.

Dell'Argemone. Cap.clxviii.

L'Argemone è del tutto simile al papauero saluatico. Ha le srondi intagliate, co
me l'anemone: il siore rosso, & la testa in la parte piu alta dal gambo, piu lunga

sua ritonda, & il suo succhio di colore di zaffarano, & di sapore acuto. Leua i

Itrouansi alcuni testi di Dioscoride, che hanno dell'Argemone due diuersi capitoli, & alcuni altri, che solo hanno
R il qui di sopra approuato da noi. il perche è opinione di piu dotti huomini, che ui sia il secóto stato aggiunto, et per

Dell'Anagallide. Cap.clxix.

A Anagallide è di due spetie, ma differenti però solamente nel fiore: Imperoche
l'una, laquale è la femmina il produce celeste, & l'altra, laquale è il maschio, lo fa
rosso. Sono ammendune piccioleppiante, che giacciono per terra. Le cui srondi
son picciole, & alquanto ritonde, di figura simile all'Helsine: procedono da un
gambo quadrangolare, & fanno il seme ritondo. Hano ammendune uirtù di mitigare: spen
gono l'infiammagioni, cauano i bronconi, & le spine fuor de membri, & sermano l'ulcere,
che mangiano. Il succhio loro gargarizzato purga la testa, & tirato su per la narice della
parte contraria leua il dolore de denti. Messo ne gli occhi con mele attico ne leua uia i fiocchi,
& gioua alle debolezze della uista. Beuto con uino gioua contra al morso delle uipere, &
contra à i difetti del fegato, & delle reni. Dicono alcuni, che quella, che fa il fiore celeste, ritor
na dentro il budello, che escie dal sedere, & l'altra impiastrata lo fa uenir fuore.
Anagallide tanto maschio, quanto femmina, laquale comunemente si chiama Morsi us gallinae, è notissima à ciascuno,
L' quantunque di gran lunga s'ingannino coloro, che si pensano, che sia l'Anagallide quella, che chiamiamo noi in

translation:
SECOND BOOK. 205

There are those who truly believe that the wild poppy described by Dioscorides and the Anemone are one and the same thing, or if not the same thing, at least plants of the same species. This does not seem to me to be the true intention of Dioscorides: for if he had meant that the Anemone and the wild poppy were plants of the same species, he would not have divided the species from the species, nor would he have written about them in two different chapters so far apart from one another, nor, as one sees at the end of the chapter, would he have differentiated the Anemone from the wild poppy, saying that the Anemone does not release any liquid when broken, as the poppy does, which emits milk, and that the head which the Anemone has in the middle of its flower does not resemble at all that of the poppy, but rather the tip of an asparagus. Although Brasavola maintains that the Anemone of Dioscorides is that wild poppy which produces the reddest flowers, he fails to notice that when broken these immediately drip their stems with milk, and furthermore that this plant has a long root, not round like an olive, and its head, like all other poppies, is not at all similar to the tips of asparagus. The true Anemone of both species I have seen many times in the valley of Anania in the jurisdiction of Trento, entirely consistent with the description of Dioscorides, as is indeed the one which M. Mapheo dei Maphei has in his most pleasant Garden in Venice. Ruellius affirms that the Anemone grows abundantly in France, and that it is the plant which the Herbalists call Herba venti. This does not correspond to what I found in Simon of Genoa, who expressly states that the greater Herba venti is the Vetriuola, or Parietaria, and the lesser is the lesser Consolida.

Of the Argemone. Chapter 168.

The Argemone is entirely similar to the wild poppy. Its leaves are cut, like the anemone's; the flower is red, and the head at the highest part of the stem is longer than that of the poppy called Rheda, and wider at the top. Its root is round, and its juice is saffron-colored and sharp in taste. It removes specks and little clouds from the eyes. The leaves applied as a poultice relieve inflammations.

Some texts of Dioscorides are found which give two different chapters on the Argemone, and others which contain only the one we have approved above. For this reason it is the opinion of more learned men that the second was added later, since it is not found in some manuscripts of Dioscorides, and neither Galen nor Paul made any mention of it in their works. So that everyone may be satisfied, having separated that chapter from the text, I give it here with commentary. The other Argemone also has leaves similar to the wild poppy. Applied fresh as a poultice it heals cuts; it extinguishes inflammations of the eyes. It is usefully drunk with water for dysentery, consolidates wounds, and is useful for inflammations. Applied as a poultice it helps spasms, and drunk as an immediate remedy it counteracts the bites of venomous animals. Pliny, in book 8 chapter 25, says there are three species of it, and that the one most recommended is that whose root smells of incense. The Argemone grows throughout the countryside of Tuscany, and likewise in the valley of Anania, with all the same characteristics assigned to it by Dioscorides. It has therefore been no small error on the part of past Physicians and Apothecaries to have always used in place of the Argemone the Eupatorium, which they also call Agrimonia. Of this we will speak at greater length (God willing) below in the fourth book at its proper chapter. Galen wrote very briefly of the Argemone in the sixth book on the properties of Simple medicines, saying nothing more than that the Argemone is astringent and digestive.

Of the Anagallis. Chapter 169.

The Anagallis is of two species, differing however only in the flower: for the one, which is the female, produces a sky-blue flower, and the other, which is the male, makes it red. Both are small plants that lie along the ground. Their leaves are small and somewhat round, in shape similar to Helsine; they grow from a square stem, and produce a round seed. Both have the virtue of mitigating: they suppress inflammations, draw out splinters and thorns from the limbs, and stop ulcers that eat away flesh. Their juice, used as a gargle, purges the head, and drawn up through the nostril on the opposite side relieves toothache. Applied to the eyes with Attic honey it removes specks, and benefits weak eyesight. Drunk with wine it helps against the bite of vipers, and against disorders of the liver and kidneys. Some say that the one which produces the sky-blue flower returns into the bowel when it comes out from the seat, and the other, applied as a poultice, makes it come out.

The Anagallis, both male and female, commonly called Morsus gallinae, is well known to everyone, although those are greatly mistaken who think that the Anagallis is the plant we call in Tuscany Centone, and in Lombardy Pauarina, which produces a white flower: for the true Anagallo produces a flower either sky-blue or red, and a square stem, not round as the Centone does. Galen wrote of the Anagallo in the sixth book on the properties of Simple medicines, saying thus: the one and the other Anagallo, that is both the one that produces the sky-blue flower and the one that makes it red, is astringent, and beyond this possesses some degree of heat and an attractive virtue, in such a way that it can draw to itself things that dry up and remain in the members of the whole body.

206 LIBRO

Dell' Hedera. Cap.clxx.

Al'Hedera nelle sue spetie molte differenze, lequali spetie generalissime per il piu sono solamente tre, una bianca, una nera, & una, laquale priuatamente chiamano Helix. La bianca produce il fior bianco. La nera, laquale chiamano Dionisia, nero, ò simile al zaffarano, & la chiamata Helix non produce frutto alcuno, ma alcune sottili uiticelle, & le frondi breue, rosse, & fatte à cantoni. Sono tutte l'Hedere acute, & costrettiue: nuocono à i nerui. I fiori di tutte alla quantità di quanto sene possa torre con tre dita, beuti due uolte il di con uino, guariscono la disenteria, & ungonsi tutti con ceroto utilmente in su le cotture del suoco. Le frondi quando son tenere, cotte nell'aceto, oue ro impastate crude nel pane, medicano la melza. Il succhio delle frödi, & de i corimbi messo nel naso con unguento irino, mele, ouer nitro, giouà à gli antichi dolori della testa: alche si sparge in sul capo anchora con aceto, & oglio rosado. Distillasi con oglio nell'orecchie, che menano, & ir quelle, che dogliono. I corimbi della nera beuti, oueramente il succhio delle
B frondi, fanno il corpo languido, & conturbano la mente: tolti però in maggior quantità. Distillasi nell'orecchia della parte contraria l'oglio rosado, nel quale in un guscio di melagrano habbiro bollito cinque acini d'hedera tolti dal corimbo, per il dolore de denti. Fanno i corimbi impiastrati i capelli neri. Le frondi di tutte le spetie cotte nel uino, medicano à tutte l'ulcere, quantunque maligne, & alle cotture del suoco: spengono cotte nel medesimo modo le macole della faccia. I corimbi triti, & applicati à i luoghi naturali delle donne, prouocano i mestrui, & beuti al peso d'una dramma dopo le purgationi de mestrui, le fanno diuentare sterili i picciuoli delle frondi infusi nel mele, & applicati alla natura delle donne, prouocano i mestrui, & il parto. Il succhio instillato sana l'ulcere putride, & corrosiue, & il puzzore del naso. La goma dell'Hedera unta ammazza i pidocchi, et fa cascare i pesi. Il succhio delle radici beuto con aceto, giouà al morso di quei ragni, che si chiamano phalangi.

O no queste tre spetie d'Hedera, che per generalissime son qui assegnate da Dioscoride, note ueramente à ciascuno.
S Ma se pur solesse alcuno saperne p piu lunga historia le sue piu particolari spetie, legga in Theophràsto al. xviij. cap. del iij. libro, ouero il. xxxiiij. del. xvi. di Plinio: Percioche qui ne ritrouar à egli tutta l'historia, & quàte spetie particolari hablino queste tre generalissime, lequali non m'è parso commemorare in questo luogo, per non esser piu necessario l'uso loro particolare di quello, che si fà al generale. L'Hedera (siceuà Galeno al. vij. delle facultà de semplici) è posta di facultà contrarie: imperoche ella ha un certo, che di sustanza è costrettiua, laquale è ueramente terrea, & frigida. Ha anchora alquaito al gusto dell'acuto: ilche arguisce, che la sia calida. Et oltre à cio si conosce, & massime nella uerde, una certa sustanza acquea, & tepida, laquale nel seccarsi suanisce, & solo gli resta la qualità terrestre, frigida, & costrettiua, & quella che è calida, & acuta.

Della Chelidonia, ouero Hirondinarià maggiore. Cap.clxxi

A Chelidonia maggiore produce il fusto sottile, alto un gombito, & qualche uolta maggiore, con frondosi ramuscelli. Le frödi sà ella simili al ranoncùlo, ma piu tenere, di colore, che tende al ceruleo. Sono i suoi fiori simili alle uiole bianche, li quali escono secòdo l'ordine delle sue frondi. Ha il suo succhio giallo, acuto, mordace, amarette, & di graue odore. La radice nella parte disopra è solamete una, ma nel basso
D si diuide in piucapillari, di colore simile al zaffarano. Produce le silique simili à quelle del papauero cornuò, sottili, lunghe, di forma piramidale, nelle quali è il seme maggiore di quello del papauero. il succhio cotto à suoco de carboni in un àso di rame insieme cò mele, rischiara la uista. Spr emesi dalle frödi, da i fusti, et dalle radici il succhio nel principio della state, et seccasi all'omtra, et fassene poscia pastelli. La radice beuta cò uino biàco, et anesi, còferiscie à trabocco di fide: impiàstrata con uino guarisce l'ulcere serpiginose: masticata leua il dolore de denti. Credesi, che la si chiami Chelidonia, pche la nasce nel tempo, che uengono à noi le rondine, et seccasi, quando le si partono. Oltre à questo dissero alcuni, che se per sortes'acciecano i rondinini nel nido, le madri gli guariscono, mettendogli questa herba in su gli occhi.
A Chelidona chiamata da Dioscoride maggiore, si chiama uolgarmente Celidonia. Questa da alcuni, & massime Ar

translation:
206 LIBRO

On Ivy. Chapter 170.

Ivy has many differences among its varieties; the most general are three: one white, one black, and one called privately Helix. The white one produces a white flower. The black one, which they call Dionisia, is black or similar to saffron, and the one called Helix produces no fruit at all, only some small thin tendrils and short, red leaves shaped at the corners. All ivies are sharp and astringent: they are harmful to the nerves. The flowers of all of them, taken in a quantity of as much as can be pinched with three fingers, drunk twice a day with wine, cure dysentery, and all are usefully anointed with cerate on burns from fire. The leaves, when tender, cooked in vinegar, or else kneaded raw into bread, treat the spleen. The juice of the leaves and berries, put into the nose with iris ointment, honey, or saltpeter, relieves old pains of the head; for this purpose it is also spread on the head with vinegar and rose oil. It is distilled with oil into ears that run or are painful. The berries of the black ivy, when drunk, or likewise the juice of the leaves, make the body languid and disturb the mind: taken however in greater quantity. The rose oil is dripped into the opposite ear, in which five ivy berries taken from the cluster have been boiled in a pomegranate rind, for toothache. The clusters applied as plasters make the hair black. The leaves of all varieties cooked in wine treat all ulcers, however malignant, and burns from fire: cooked in the same manner they remove spots from the face. The clusters, ground and applied to the natural parts of women, provoke menstruation, and drunk in the weight of a dram after menstrual purgings, they render women sterile; the small stalks of the leaves infused in honey and applied to the natural parts of women, provoke menstruation and childbirth. The juice instilled heals putrid and corrosive ulcers and bad odor of the nose. The gum of the ivy applied kills lice and causes scales to fall off. The juice of the roots drunk with vinegar helps against the bite of those spiders called phalangi.

Now these three varieties of ivy, assigned here by Dioscorides as the most general, are known to everyone. But if anyone wishes to learn more of their longer history and their more particular varieties, let him read in Theophrastus at chapter 18 of book III, or in Pliny at chapter 34 of book XVI: for there he will find all the history and how many particular varieties these three most general ones have, which I did not see fit to commemorate in this place, as their particular use is no more necessary than what applies to the general. Ivy (as Galen says in book VII on the faculties of simples) is placed among things of contrary faculties: for it has something that in substance is astringent, which is truly earthy and cold. It also has somewhat of a sharp taste, which argues that it is warm. And beyond this one recognizes, especially in the green plant, a certain watery and tepid substance, which vanishes upon drying, and only the earthy, cold, and astringent quality remains, as well as that which is warm and sharp.

On Greater Celandine, or Greater Swallowwort. Chapter 171.

Greater Celandine produces a slender stalk, about a cubit tall, and sometimes taller, with leafy little branches. Its leaves resemble those of the ranunculus, but are more tender, of a color tending toward blue. Its flowers are similar to white violets, and they emerge in the order of the leaves. It has a yellow juice, sharp, biting, somewhat bitter, and of a strong odor. The root on top is single, but lower down it divides into several hair-like parts, of a color similar to saffron. It produces pods similar to those of the horned poppy, thin, long, pyramidal in shape, in which the seed is larger than that of the poppy. The juice cooked over a charcoal fire in a copper vessel together with honey, clears the vision. The juice is pressed from the leaves, stalks, and roots at the beginning of summer and dried in the shade, and then formed into pastilles. The root drunk with white wine and anise helps in cases of liver obstruction; applied as a plaster with wine it heals creeping ulcers; chewed it relieves toothache. It is believed that it is called Celandine because it is born at the time when the swallows come to us, and dries when they depart. Moreover, some have said that if the nestling swallows happen to go blind in the nest, their mothers heal them by placing this herb on their eyes.

Celandine, called by Dioscorides the greater, is commonly called Celidonia. This plant by some, and especially by alchemists, who do not properly understand that Chelidonia means Swallowwort, is called Gift of Heaven (donii coeli). In this belief, trusting themselves, they often preach that a certain essential spirit can be extracted from this plant, not only useful for advancing their false opinions, but also miraculously beneficial to the life of men. Celandine grows throughout Italy, and especially
