de Semplici, così dicendo. La Chelidonia è fortemente calida, & aftersiua, & il suo succhio per acuire la uista è molto com
modo, & massime in quelli occhi, nella cui pupilla si genera grossezza d'homori.

Della Chelidonia minore. Cap.clxxij.

LA Chelidonia minore, laquale alcuni hano chiamata grano saluatico, è picciola
herbetta. Le cui frondi escono col picciuolo di fatto dalla radice, simili à quelle del
l'hedera, quantunque piu ritonde, piu picciole, piu tenere, et alquato grassette. Ha
molte, et picciole radici, pendeti da una medesima base, aggomiciolate, simili al
grano, delle quali solamente tre, ouer quattro s'allungano. Nasce appresso all acque, et à i la
ghi. È acuta, et ulcera le parti supfitiali, come l'anemone: fa cadere l'unghie corrotte, et gua
risce la rogna. Tirasi il succhio, che si sprieme dalle radici su per il naso per purgare la testa. B
La dicottione delle radici gargarizzata con mele, purga i uitij del petto, & della testa.

Vella, che et si dimostra hoggi per la Chelidonia minore, nasce abbondantissima in ogni parte d'italia su per le riue
Q dei so si, & altri luoghi acquastrini, con frondi hederacee, ma piu picciole, & piu ritonde, & alquanto grassette.
Non produce alcun futto, et fa il fior giallo nel principio della primauera d'Aprile. Ha assai radici, simili ueramente à gra-
nella di formento, benche qualche uolta maggiori, bianche, & pendenti, tra lequali sempre ne sono alcune di lunghe capil-
lari. Dura questa pianta poco tempo: percioche sempre si perde, et si secca nella fine d'Aprile. Chiamarla alcuni per la so-
miglianza delle radici Scropholaria minore, & noi in Thoscana la chiamiamo Fauoscello: ne per altro si tiene, che la sia
chi imita Chelidonia, che per nascere ella nel uenire delle rondine, come parimente la maggiore. Ma se questa sia quella, di
cui intesero Dioscoride, & Galeno, non si puo dubitare: percioche ne nelle frondi, ne nelle radici sue si troua punto
d'acutezza, douen lo pero ella essere acutissima, et mordacissima al gusto assai piu della maggiore, essendo calida (come scri
ue Galeno) nel. iij. ordine. Ilche dimostra, che non sia questa la uera. Scrifsene Galeno al. viij. delle facultà de semplici, così
dicendo. La Chelidonia minore per essere piu acuta della maggiore, ulcera applicata la carne piu valorosamente, & fa ca-
dere l'unghie scabrose. Il suo succhio tirato su per il naso, purga come cosa acuta, la testa. Et però sipuo dire, che la sia
discccatiua, & calida nel quarto ordine. C

Dell'Othonna. Cap.clxxiij.

ONno alcuni, che dicono, che l'Othonna è succhio di chelidonia maggiore, altri
dell herba, che si chiama Glaucio, altri succhio di papauero cornuto, & altri di-
cono esser l'Othona una mistura fatta di succhio d'anagallo celesie, di ioseiamo,
et di papauero. Sono anchora altri, che si credono, che la sia il succhio d'una certa
herba Tragloditica, laqual si chiama Othona, et che la nasce in quella parte d'Arabia uerso
l'Egitto, con frondi simili alla ruchetta, squalide, & poche, ma pertugiate, come un criuel-
lo, & come se fussero mangiate da bruchi, et che il fiore si rassembri à quello del zaffarano, qua
tunque sia egli piu largo di frondi: il perchesi pensarono alcuni, che la fusse una spetie d'ane-
mone. Cauali di questa il succhio per le medicine de gli occhi, doue sia bisogno di mondi-
ficare: Imperoche la rode, & leua tutte quelle cose, che impediscono la chiarezza loro. Di-
cono oltre à questo, che da questa pianta distilla un certo liquore, del qualeben lauato, & D
ben netto da fassi, conformano pastelli utili à i predetti difetti. Dicono alcuni, che l'Othon-
na è una pietra, che nasce in Thebaide d'Egitto, bianca di colore, picciola, mordente, &
acuta, calida, & costrettiua.
E desi manifestamente, che le molte opinioni recitate da Dioscoride dell'Othonna dimostrano, ch'ella gli fusse icogni
V ta, non soggiognendo egli à quelle cosa alcuna del suo. Et imperò non è marauiglia, se anchora à i tempi nostri è in-
cognita à noi. Questa mettendo qualche uolta Pauolo Egineta con le sue medicine, dichiara in alcuni luoghi esser
fucchio di Chelidonia maggiore, standosene all'opinioni di coloro, che così scrissero, come riferisce Dioscoride.

Dell'Orecchia di Topo. Cap.clxxiiij.

LA Orecchia di Topo ha piu fusti tutti procedenti da una radice, alquanto rosset
ti, & concaui dal nascimento loro. Le frondi son lunghette, & stratte con il dosso
alto, et eleuato, nereggiano nel colore, procedeno per interuall à due à due, &
sono appuntate in cima. Produce dalle concauità de fusti alcuni sottili ramuscel-
description: Pietro Andrea Matthioli's landmark Italian translation of Dioscorides De Materia Medica. The first vernacular edition to make classical Greek botanical medicine accessible to European physicians.
translation:
SECOND BOOK. 207

especially near hedges along roads and on old walls. Some herbalists show as the greater celandine a certain plant that grows in the mountains, with nearly round leaves of a whitish color, which produces three or four stems, above which there is a dark violet flower with four small hollow horns inside. Some call this Aquilina. As for its virtues, I have not found them described by anyone. Galen mentioned Celandine in the seventh book on the Properties of Simple Medicines, speaking thus: Celandine is strongly heating and cleansing, and its juice is very useful for sharpening the sight, especially in those eyes whose pupil develops a thickness of humors.

On the lesser Celandine. Chapter 172.

The lesser Celandine, which some have called wild grain, is a small herb. Its leaves come out on a small stalk directly from the root, similar to those of ivy, but rounder, smaller, more tender, and somewhat fleshy. It has many small roots, hanging from the same base, coiled together, similar to grains of wheat, of which only three or four grow long. It grows near water and lakes. It is sharp and ulcerates superficial parts, like the anemone: it causes corrupted nails to fall off and cures mange. The juice pressed from the roots is drawn up through the nose to purge the head. The decoction of the roots gargled with honey purges the vices of the chest and head.

The plant shown today as the lesser Celandine grows most abundantly throughout Italy along riverbanks and other watery places, with ivy-like leaves but smaller, rounder, and somewhat fleshy. It produces no stem, and flowers yellow at the beginning of spring in April. It has many roots, truly resembling grains of wheat, though sometimes larger, white and hanging, among which there are always some that are long and hair-like. This plant lasts only a short time, always dying and drying up at the end of April. Some have called it, for the similarity of its roots, lesser Scrophularia, and we in Tuscany call it Fauoscello; and it is considered to imitate the Celandine only because it appears when the swallows arrive, as does the greater one. But whether this is the plant described by Dioscorides and Galen one may doubt: since neither in its leaves nor in its roots is there any sharpness at all, whereas it should be very sharp and biting in taste, much more so than the greater celandine, being hot (as Galen writes) in the third degree. This shows that it is not the true plant. Galen wrote of it in the eighth book on Simple Medicines, saying: The lesser Celandine, being more sharp than the greater, ulcerates flesh more powerfully when applied, and causes rough nails to fall off. Its juice drawn up through the nose purges the head like something sharp. And therefore one may say that it is desiccating and hot in the fourth degree.

On Othonna. Chapter 173.

Some say that Othonna is the juice of greater celandine, others say it is from the herb called Glaucium, others say it is the juice of horned poppy, and yet others say that Othona is a mixture made of the juice of scarlet pimpernel, henbane, and poppy. There are also others who believe it to be the juice of a certain Troglodytic herb called Othona, which grows in that part of Arabia toward Egypt, with leaves similar to rocket, rough and few, but perforated like a sieve, and as if eaten by caterpillars, and whose flower resembles that of saffron, though its leaves are broader: for which reason some thought it was a species of anemone. From this plant the juice is extracted for medicines of the eyes, where there is need of cleansing: because it erodes and removes all those things that impede the clarity of vision. They say furthermore that from this plant distills a certain liquid, which when well washed and cleaned of sediment is used to make pastilles useful for the aforesaid ailments. Some say that Othonna is a stone found in the Thebaid of Egypt, white in color, small, biting and sharp, hot and astringent.
It is evident that the many opinions recited by Dioscorides on Othonna show that it was unknown to him, since he adds nothing of his own about it. And therefore it is no wonder that in our times it is still unknown to us. Paul of Aegina, sometimes including it with his medicines, declares in some places that it is the juice of greater Celandine, following the opinions of those who wrote thus, as Dioscorides reports.

On Mouse-ear. Chapter 174.

Mouse-ear has several stems all proceeding from one root, somewhat reddish and hollow from their base. The leaves are rather long and narrow, with the back raised and elevated, darkish in color, proceeding at intervals in pairs, and pointed at the tip. From the hollows of the stems it produces small thin branch-

text:
208 LIBRO

A li,ne i quali nascono i suoi piccioli fiori celesti,come quelli dell'anagallo. La radice è grossa
un dito,tutta piena di capelli. Sana questa impiastrata le fistole lachrimali.Sono alcuni,che
chiamano l'Helsine Orecchia di Topo.

Ritrouansi alcuni uolumi di Dioscoride, che hano in questo luogo il capitolo dell'Alsine, che seguitanel quarto li
R bro dopo l'Helsine, per chiamarsi anchora ella Orecchia di Topo, dalche forse incitati alcuni scrittori la tolseno
dal quarto, oue era il proprio suo luogo, et la misero appresso à questa altra. Ma perche la istessa scrittura dimo-
stra, che la doueua seguire dopo all'Helsine per rassembrarliela molto Dioscoride, & dire, che la sarebbe stata una co-
sa medesima con l'Helsine, se la non fusse stata cosi picciola, mi pare di douer dirne nel suo proprio luogo nel quarto libro.
Ma parlado pure della presente, dico, che ueramente si uede fiorita il Maggio ne i prati, ne i campi, ne gli horti, lungo le
uie, & in ogni altro luogo. Ma non so però, che habbia ella alcuno uolgar nome in Italia.

Dell' Isatide, ouero Glasto domestico. Cap. chxv.

B L Glasto domestico, ilquale usano i tintori per tingere le lane, pduce le frondi
simili alla piantagine, quantunque piu grasse, & piu nere. Il suo fusto auanza l'al-
tezza di due gombiti. Le frondi impiaste risoluono tutte le poste me: saldano
le ferite fresche: ristagnano i flussi del sangue: guariscono il fuoco sacro, l'ulcere,
che mangiano, le putride, & quelle, che uan serpendo per il corpo.

Dell' Isatide, ouero Glasto saluatico. Cap. chxvi.

L Glasto saluatico è simile al domestico, come che produca egli le frondialquan
to maggiori, che s'accostano à quelle della Lattuga, & i fusti sottili, ramosi, al-
quanto rosseggianti, dalla cui sommità pendono molti follicoli, che rappresen-
tano una certa figura di lingua, ne i quali è dentro il seme. Produce il fiore rossi
gno, & sottile. Vale à tutte quelle cose, alle quali conferisce il domestico. Beuto, et impiastra-
to gioua à i difetti della melza.

C Chiamasi il Glasto, ouero Isatide uolgarmente in Thoscana Guado, & è adoperato da i tintori de i panni di lana,
c ouunque se n'eserciti l'arte: Imperoche questo consegua uiui tutti i colori, con i quali egis'acconuiene. Fassene un-
cetta nella Marca appresso à Nocera in una terra piu particolarmente, che in l'altre, chiamata Gualdo, nome uera-
mente datogli dal molto Guado, che ui si semina, & ui si ricoglie. Del saluatico fece memoria Plinio à. vij. cap. del. xx.
libro tra le lattughe saluatiche: peroche assai si grassa l'endeço, ilqual adoperano i dipintori per
i loro cilestri scuri, & per altri colori: Imperoche meschiato con orpimento fa bellissimo uerde. Scrisse del Guado Galeno
al. vi. delle facultà de semplici, in questo modo dicendo. L'Isatide domestica dissecca ualentissimamente senz'a mordacità, &
è insieme con l'amaritudine costrettiva, ma la saluatica è manifestamente acuta, il che si cognosce al gusto, & all'operare.
Et però è molto piu disseccatiua della domestica. La onde piu resiste alle putredini.

Del Telephio. Cap. chxxvij.

D L Telephio è simile alla portulaca, tato nelle frondi, quanto nel fusto. Produce
da tutti i nodi delle radici due eminenze, dalle quali escono hor sei, hor sette fusti
pieni di frondi, di colore celestino, grasse, uiscose, & carnose. Il fiore è hor celeste,
& hor bianco. Nasce ne i luoghi coltiuati, & massime tra le uiti. Le frondi impia-
strate per spatio di sei hore nel tempo della primauera, sanano le uitiligini: ma bisogna po-
scia fargli sopra un linimento di farina d'orzo. Ilche fa anchora ungendosene insieme con
aceto al sole, lauando però il luogo, come è secco il linimento.

Q Vantunque si tenga hoggi dalla maggior parte di coloro, che fanno la professione de i semplici, che sia il Telephio
quella pianta, chiamata da chi Rabaria, da chi Faua grassa, & da chi Faua inuersa; nondimeno per non ui si ritro-
uare al gusto alcuna qualità, per cui si possa ella giudicare secca, & astresiua, come afferma Galeno essere il Tele-
phio, & il produrre ella le frondi molto maggiori della Portulaca, ha fatto credere à molti, che non sia la Rabaria il Te-
lephio. Scrissene Galeno al. viij. delle facultà de i semplici, cosi dicendo. Il Telephio è secco, & astresiuo: ma non però tro-
po apparentemente caldo, & percio s'acconuiene all'ulcere putride, & alle uitiligini.

Fine del Secondo Libro.

208 BOOK

A nd those in which its small sky-blue flowers are born, like those of the pimpernel. The root is as thick as a finger, entirely covered with hairs. Applied as a poultice, it heals lacrimal fistulas. There are some who call the Helsine Mouse's Ear.

Some volumes of Dioscorides are found which, in this place, include the chapter on Alsine following the Helsine in the fourth book, calling it also Mouse's Ear, by which some writers were perhaps prompted to take it from the fourth book, where it properly belonged, and place it here alongside this one. But since the text itself shows that it should follow the Helsine, because Dioscorides compares it closely to the Helsine and says it would be the same thing as the Helsine if it were not so small, I think I ought to speak of it in its proper place in the fourth book. But speaking of the present plant, I say that it is truly seen in flower in May in meadows, fields, gardens, along roadsides, and in every other place. Yet I do not know that it has any common name in Italy.

On Isatis, or Domestic Woad. Chapter 125.

B Domestic Woad, which dyers use to dye wool, produces leaves similar to plantain, though somewhat fatter and darker. Its stalk rises to the height of two cubits. The leaves applied as a poultice dissolve all inflammations; they bind fresh wounds; they stanch flows of blood; they cure erysipelas, eating ulcers, putrid sores, and those which creep along the body.

On Isatis, or Wild Woad. Chapter 126.

Wild Woad is similar to the domestic, though it produces somewhat larger leaves resembling those of Lettuce, and slender, branching, somewhat reddish stalks, from the tops of which hang many little pods shaped somewhat like a tongue, within which lies the seed. It produces a reddish and slender flower. It serves all the same purposes as the domestic variety. Taken as a drink and applied as a poultice, it benefits ailments of the spleen.

C Woad, or Isatis, is called commonly in Tuscany Guado, and is used by dyers of woolen cloth wherever that craft is practiced: for it yields vivid colors to which it is suited. A market for it is held in the Marche region near Nocera, in a place called particularly, more than others, Gualdo — a name truly derived from the abundance of Guado sown and harvested there. Pliny mentioned the wild variety in the 7th chapter of his 20th book, among wild lettuces: for it fattens the blue color that painters use for their dark azures and other colors: mixed with orpiment it makes a very beautiful green. Galen wrote of Woad in his 6th book on the properties of simples, saying as follows: Domestic Isatis dries most powerfully without any sharpness, and is astringent together with bitterness; but the wild variety is manifestly acrid, as is perceived by taste and by its action. Therefore it is far more drying than the domestic, and thus better resists putrefaction.

On Telephium. Chapter 127.

D Telephium resembles purslane both in its leaves and in its stalk. From each node of the root it produces two swellings, from which grow six or seven stalks full of leaves, of a sky-blue color, fat, sticky, and fleshy. The flower is sometimes sky-blue, sometimes white. It grows in cultivated places, especially among vines. The leaves applied as a poultice for six hours in springtime heal skin blemishes called vitiligo; but afterward one must apply a liniment of barley flour. The same is achieved by rubbing them on with vinegar in the sun, washing the place once the liniment is dry.

Q Although the greater part of those who practice the study of simples today hold that the Telephium is the plant called by some Rabaria, by some Fat Bean, and by others Inverted Bean, nonetheless since no quality can be found in it by taste by which it might be judged dry and astringent, as Galen affirms the Telephium to be, and since it produces leaves much larger than those of Purslane, this has led many to believe that the Rabaria is not the Telephium. Galen wrote of it in his 8th book on the properties of simples, saying: Telephium is dry and astringent, yet not excessively warm in appearance, and therefore it is suited to putrid ulcers and to vitiligo.

End of the Second Book.

LIBRO TERZO DELLA MATERIA MEDICI-  A
NALE DI PEDACIO DIOSCORIDE ANAZARBEO TRADOTTO
in lingua volgare Italiana da Pietro Andrea
Matthiolo Sanese Medico.

Auiamo sin qui, carissimo Ario, narrato in due libri delle cose
odorisere, de gli unguenti, ogli, alberi, & frutti, & liquori lo-
ro: & oltre à cio de gli animali, delle biade, herbaggi d'horti,
& herbe, che sono acute. Ma hora in questo, che è il terzo del-
la nostra gia proposta opera, trattaremo delle radici, herbe, sue-
chi, & semi, tanto domestichi, & che s'hanno nell'uso cotidiano per il uitto, quanto di quelli, che solo all'uso della medici-
na si conuengono.

Dell'Agarico.          Cap. primo.

O Agarico si dice essere una radice, uguale al laserpitio, ma nelle parti sue su-
perficiali più solida, più rara, & per tutto son gosa. Ritrouasene di due spetie, ma
schio cioè, & femmina. Precede di bontà la femmina, che ha dentro di se le ue-
ne dritte. Il maschio è tutto inuolto in se stesso, ritondo, & serrato. Amenduni
nel primo gusto son dolci, ma amari come si spargono per la bocca. Nasce in quella regione
di Sarmatia, che si chiama Agaria. Dicono alcuni esser l'Agarico radice d'una pianta, & al
tri generarsi ne i tronchi de gli alberi fracidi, & putrefatti, nel modo che ui si generano i fon-
ghi. Nasce in Galatia d'Asia, & in Cilicia ne i cedri, ma fragile, et senza fermezza. Ha l'Aga-
rico uirtu costrettiua, & calida. E' buono à i dolori delle budella, à gli homori crudi, à i rotti,
& à coloro, che cascano dall'alto. Dassi nella febre con acqua melata, & doue non sia febre
con uino melato al peso di due oboli. Dassene utilmente una dramma à i segatosi, à gli stret
ti di petto, à trabocco di fiele, à mal di reni, alla disenteria, & à prouocar l'orina ritenuta: uale   C
anchora alla presocatione delle madrice, & à coloro, che sono scoloriti, & pallidi. Dassi à i
thifisici con uino passo, & alli difettosi di melza con aceto melato. Dassi cosi puro senza altro
liquore à chi uomita il cibo per debilità di stomacho, et à gli acidi rutti. Beuto con aqua al pe
so di tre oboli restringe gli sputi del sangue: tolto con aceto melato al medesimo peso conseri
sce alle sciatiche, al mal caduco, & à dolori di giuture: prouoca i mestrui, & uale alla uentosi-
tà della madrice: seua dato il tremore, & il freddo, che uiene nel principio delle febri. Beuto-
ne il peso d'una dramma, ouer di due cò acqua melata, purga il corpo: toltone una dramma
con uino annacquato conferisce à i ueleni. Soccorre grandemente al morso, & alle punture
de i serpenti beuto con uino al peso di tre oboli. In somma è conueneuole l'Agarico à tutti i
mali delle interiora dato secondo l'età, & le forze de gli huomini, à chi con acqua, à chi con
uino, à chi con aceto melato, & a' chi con acqua melata.

L'Agarico un fongo, che nasce in su gli alberi, & come dicemmo di sopra nel primo libro a°. lxxi. capitolo, ne na-  D
sce dell'eccellentissimo per le montagne di tutto il Trentino in sui Larici, dai quali con le proprie mani n'ho ri-
colto, & spiccato io infinite uolte bellissimi pezzi. Ma quantunque dica Plinio à gli. viij. capitoli del. xvi. libro,
che nasce l'Agarico in Francia in su tutti gli alberi, che producono le ghiande; non dimeno in sul Trentino, & in altri
luoghi d'Italia, non nasce però egli se non in su'l Larice. Dioscoride dice, che in Galatia d'Asia, & in Cilicia nasce egli in
su'l Cedro, nò facendo di quello del Larice, ne di quello delle piante glandiftre, che scrisse Plinio, mentione alcuna. Come-
morò Galeno l'Agarico chiamandolo radice al. yi. delle facultà de semplici, in questo modo scriuendone. La radice del-
l'Agarico, che nasce nel tronco, al primo gusto è dolce, ma nel processo amara, con alquanto d'acuto, & di leggiero co-
strettiuo. E' nella sua sustanza raro, & imperò è manifesto per tutte queste cose, che questo medicamento è com-
posto di sustanza aerea, & terrea, asottigliata però da calidità. E' ueramente nell'Agarico pochissima sustanza
acquea, & per questa ragione ha egli uirtu digestiua, incisiua, & aperitiua di tutte le uiscere. Et però guarisce
egli ualentemente coloro, à cui per oppilatione di fegato è traboccato il fiele. Scrisse dell'Agarico Mesue nel suo tratta-
to de i semplici solutiui, così dicendo, Solue l'Agarico la flemma grossa, & la cholera rossa, & la sua proprietà è di mori-

THIRD BOOK OF THE MEDICAL MATERIAL
OF PEDACIUS DIOSCORIDES OF ANAZARBUS, TRANSLATED
into the Italian vernacular by Pietro Andrea
Matthioli, Physician of Siena.

We have so far, dearest Ario, narrated in two books the things concerning odors, unguents, oils, trees, fruits, and their liquors; and beyond these, the animals, grains, garden herbs, and plants that are sharp. But now in this third book of our already proposed work, we will treat of roots, herbs, juices, and seeds, both those domestic ones used in daily sustenance, as well as those that serve only for medicinal purposes.

On Agaric.          Chapter One.

Agaric is said to be a root equal to laserpitium, but in its outer parts more solid, more porous, and altogether spongy. It is found in two kinds, namely male and female. The female surpasses in quality, having straight veins inside. The male is entirely wrapped within itself, round and compact. Both are sweet at first taste, but turn bitter as they spread through the mouth. It grows in that region of Sarmatia called Agaria. Some say that agaric is the root of a plant, while others say it is generated in the rotten and putrefied trunks of trees, in the same manner as mushrooms grow. It grows in Galatia of Asia and in Cilicia in cedar trees, but it is fragile and without firmness. Agaric has an astringent and warm virtue. It is good for pains of the bowels, for crude humors, for ruptures, and for those who have fallen from a height. In fever it is given with honeyed water, and where there is no fever, with honeyed wine at the weight of two obols. A drachm of it is usefully given to those who are jaundiced, to those suffering tightness of the chest, overflow of bile, kidney disease, dysentery, and to promote retained urine; it is also useful for suffocation of the womb, and for those who are discolored and pale. It is given to those with consumption in raisin wine, and to those with defective spleen in honeyed vinegar. Given pure without any other liquid to those who vomit food from weakness of the stomach, and for acid belching. Drunk with water at the weight of three obols it restrains the spitting of blood; taken with honeyed vinegar at the same weight it helps sciatica, epilepsy, and joint pains; it promotes menstruation, and is useful for flatulence of the womb; it relieves the trembling and cold that come at the onset of fevers. Taken at the weight of one or two drachms with honeyed water it purges the body; taken with diluted wine at one drachm it counteracts poisons. It greatly helps against the bites and stings of serpents, drunk with wine at the weight of three obols. In sum, agaric is suited to all ailments of the internal organs, given according to the age and strength of the person, with water for some, with wine for others, with honeyed vinegar for some, and with honeyed water for others.

Agaric is a fungus that grows upon trees, and as we said above in the first book at chapter seventy-one, there grows the finest quality throughout all the Trentino on larch trees, from which I myself have gathered and picked off an infinite number of beautiful pieces with my own hands. But although Pliny says in the eighth chapter of the sixteenth book that agaric grows in France on all trees that produce acorns, nevertheless in the Trentino and other parts of Italy it grows only on the larch. Dioscorides says that in Galatia of Asia and in Cilicia it grows on the cedar, making no mention of the larch or of the acorn-bearing trees that Pliny wrote about. Galen mentioned agaric, calling it a root in the sixth book of his work on the properties of simples, writing of it in this manner: The root of agaric, which grows in the trunk, is sweet at first taste, but in the course of time bitter, with a certain sharpness and a slight astringency. It is rare in its substance, and it is therefore manifest from all these things that this medicine is composed of airy and earthy substance, refined however by warmth. There is truly very little watery substance in agaric, and for this reason it has a digestive, incisive, and aperitive virtue on all the viscera. And therefore it powerfully cures those in whom, through obstruction of the liver, bile has overflowed. Mesue wrote of agaric in his treatise on simple purgatives, speaking thus: Agaric dissolves thick phlegm and red choler, and its property is to...

A denso, & graue, & per il contrario perde la uirtù sua nel pestarsi l'impuro, lasso, & leggiero. La dicottione risolue la uirtù tanto dell'uno, quanto dell'altro. Solue il Reubarbaro per il corpo la cholera, & la flemma, & la maggior sua proprietà è di mondificare il fegato, & lo stomacho, & di conferire à i loro dolori pungitìui. Chiarifica il Reubarbaro il sangue, conferisce à tutte l'oppilationi delle uiscere, & à tutte le malattie, che si causano da quelle, come sono hidropisie, trabocco di fiele, difetti di melza, & molte sorti di febri: ha proprietà per uigore della sustanza sua di conferire à gli sputi del sangue, & à i suoi flussi di qual si uoglia membro del corpo: gioua à coloro, che cascano dall'alto nei precipitij, & sana tutte le rotture intrinseche, & estrinseche, & massime dandosene una dramma con uino stittico insieme con mumia, & rubbi a de tintori. È il Reubarbaro medicina del singhozzo, & della disenteria, & propriamente l'arrostito beuto con acqua di piantagine, & uino stittico: conferisce alle febri periodice, à quelle delle oppilationi, & alle antiche. Conseruasi il buono tre, ò quattro anni, alche molto gioua il coprirlo di cera, il tenerlo nel mele, nel psillio, & nel miglio, peroche così si conseruia piu in lungo. Ritroua sene à i tempi nostri una certa spetie in Italia, già fatto uolgare à tutti i giardini, il qual ueramente molto si rassomiglia, & per quello, che ne dichino alcuni Medici, che l'hanno isperimentato così fresco, solue anchor egli benissimo la cholera.

B Della Gentiana. Cap.iij.

Redesi, che la Gētiana fusse ritrouata da Gentio Re della Illiria, dal quale su poscia chiamata Gentiana. Le frondi, lequali produce appresso alla radice, son simili à quelle del noce, ouero à quelle della piantagine, di colore rossigno: ma quelle, che sono da mezzo il fusto in su, et massime quelle della sommità, sono alquanto intagliate: produce il fusto concauo, liscio, grosso un dito, alto due gombiti, & compartito da piu nodi, nel quale sono le sue frondi con maggiori interualli: è il seme suo largo, & leggiero, simile à quello dello sphondilio: la radice è lunga simile à quella dell'aristolochia, grossa, & amara. Nasce nelle sommità de gli altissimi monti, in luoghi ombrosi, & acquastrini. Ha la radice sua uirtù di scaldare, et di ristringere. Beuta con ruta, pepe, & uino al peso di due drāme, gioua à i morsi de uelenosi animali. Vale una drāma del suo succhio à idolori laterali, & dallsene il medesimo peso à coloro, che caggiono dall'alto, alli rotti, & à gli spasimati. Beesi con utilità grande per i difetti del fegato, & per i uomiti del cibo causati per debolezza di stomacho. Messa la radice nella natura delle donne grauide, le fa partorire: & messa nelle ferite, come si fa col liscio, le consolida: & è uera medicina delle ulcere cauernose, & massimamente il suo succhio. Vale alle infiammagioni de gli occhi. Mettesi il succhio ne i collirii acuti in cambio di opio: la radice sana le uitiligini. Ricogliesene il succhio in questo modo. Pestasi la radice, & lasciaisi cinque giorni continusi in mollo nell'acqua, con la quale si cuoce poscia tanto, che restino quasi sole le radici, & come è fredda ogni cosa, si cola la dicottione, laquale poscia si ricuoce per fino, che s'ingrossi come mele, & così si serba in un uaso di terra.

C La Gentiana pianta uolgare, et nota à ciascuno. Nascene copia infinita per tutte le piu alte montagne del Trentino, doue in su i monti della ualle Anania spese uolte n'ho cauate io le radici della grossezza del braccio d'un homo. Et imperò diceua Plinio à .yij. capitoli del .xxy. libro. La Gentiana ritrouò Gentio re della Illiria, dellaquale quantunque sia la Illirica eccellentissima; ne nasce però copia grande ne i mōti, che sono sotto all'Alpi. Scrissene Galeno assai breuemente al .yi. delle facultà de semplici, così dicendo. La radice di questa herba è efficace molto doue sia dibisogno

D d'assottigliare, mondificare, astergere, et disopilare, et non è marauig lia, che la possa fare tutto questo essendo ella amarissima. È la Gentiana, secondo che commemora Auicenna, calda nel terzo, & secca nel secondo ordine, prouoca l'orina, & i mestrui, & è ella l'ultima medicina alle punture de gli scorpioni. L'acqua fatta dalle radici al bagno, che chiamano di Maria, sana mirabilmente, come piu uolte ho isperimentato io, le febri causate dalle oppilationi, ammazza i uermini nel corpo de i fanciulli, & purga tutte le macole della faccia, lauandosene spesso.

Dell'Aristolochia. Cap.iiij.

A Aristolochia, è così nominata, imperoche mirabilmente aiuta alle donne di parto. Ritrouasene tre spetie. Ritonda cioè, chiamata femina, le cui frondi si rassembrano all'hedera di buono odore, ma acuto, & son tenere, & ritonde. Produce questa da una radice molti germini, & lunghi sarmenti. Fa i fiori bianchi, simili à cappelletti, ne i quali quella parte, che ui si ritrouia rossa, spira di graue odore. La lunga è

A dense, and heavy, and on the contrary loses its virtue when pounded to an impure, slack, and light state. Decoction dissolves the virtue of both one and the other. Rhubarb purges from the body choler and phlegm, and its greatest property is to cleanse the liver and the stomach, and to relieve their sharp pains. It clarifies the blood, is beneficial for all obstructions of the viscera, and for all the ailments caused by them, such as dropsy, overflow of bile, defects of the spleen, and many kinds of fevers. By virtue of its substance it is beneficial for spitting of blood, and for fluxes from whatever member of the body; it is good for those who fall from heights into precipices, and it heals all ruptures both internal and external, and especially when given as a dram with astringent wine together with mummy and rubia of dyers. Rhubarb is a medicine for hiccups and dysentery, and particularly when roasted and drunk with plantain water and astringent wine: it is helpful for periodic fevers, for those of obstructions, and for old ones. The good root keeps for three or four years, for which purpose it is very useful to coat it with wax, to keep it in honey, in psyllium, and in millet, as it thus keeps much longer. In our times a certain species is found in Italy, now commonly grown in all gardens, which truly resembles it greatly, and according to what some physicians who have tested it say, when fresh it also purges choler very well.

B On Gentian. Chapter III.

It is believed that Gentian was discovered by Gentius, King of Illyria, by whom it was thereafter named Gentiana. The leaves which it produces near the root resemble those of the walnut, or those of plantain, of a reddish color; but those which grow from the middle of the stalk upward, and especially those at the top, are somewhat cut: it produces a hollow, smooth stalk, as thick as a finger, two cubits tall, divided by many nodes, on which its leaves grow at wider intervals. Its seed is broad and light, similar to that of sphondylium. The root is long, similar to that of aristolochia, thick, and bitter. It grows on the summits of the highest mountains, in shady and watery places. The root has the virtue of warming and astringent properties. Drunk with rue, pepper, and wine at a weight of two drams, it is good for bites of venomous animals. One dram of its juice is good for pains in the sides, and the same weight is given to those who fall from heights, to the ruptured, and to those with spasms. It is drunk with great benefit for liver defects and for vomiting of food caused by weakness of the stomach. Placed in the womb of pregnant women, it brings on delivery. Placed in wounds, as one does with lye, it consolidates them; and it is a true medicine for cavernous ulcers, and especially its juice. It is good for inflammation of the eyes. The juice is put in sharp eye-drops in place of opium; the root heals vitiligo. The juice is collected in the following way: the root is pounded and left to soak in water for five continuous days, with which it is then cooked until almost only the roots remain, and when everything is cold, the decoction is strained, which is then boiled again until it thickens like honey, and thus it is kept in an earthen vessel.

C Gentian is a common plant, known to everyone. An infinite abundance of it grows on all the highest mountains of Trentino, where on the mountains of the Anaunia valley I myself have often dug up roots as thick as a man's arm. And so Pliny said in chapter 7 of book 25: Gentian was discovered by Gentius, king of Illyria, of which, though the Illyrian is the finest, a great abundance nonetheless grows on the mountains below the Alps. Galen wrote about it quite briefly in book 6 of the Faculties of Simple Medicines, saying thus: The root of this herb is very effective where there is need to thin, cleanse, deterge, and unblock, and it is no wonder that it can do all this, being most bitter.

D Gentian, according to what Avicenna records, is hot in the third degree and dry in the second, provokes urine and menstruation, and is the last remedy against scorpion stings. Water made from the roots in the bath they call the Bath of Mary wonderfully heals, as I have experienced many times myself, fevers caused by obstructions, kills worms in the bodies of children, and often washing with it purges all blemishes of the face.

On Aristolochia. Chapter IV.

Aristolochia is so named because it marvelously assists women in childbirth. Three species of it are found. The round one, called the female, whose leaves resemble those of ivy, of good but sharp odor, and are tender and round. This produces from one root many shoots and long branches. A of lentils, but red and small. Only its long roots, like those of gentian, boxwood-colored, somewhat bitter in taste and sweet. The juice of these condenses in the manner of glycyrrhiza. It is effective against roughness of the windpipe, but one must hold it under the tongue to dissolve: it is good for inflammations of the stomach, chest, and liver; drunk with raisin wine it heals mange of the bladder and pains of the kidneys; dissolved in liquid it quenches thirst; applied it heals wounds; eaten it benefits the stomach. All these same virtues belong to a decoction of the fresh root, whose powder is usefully placed upon pterygium of the eyes.

In Tuscany it is commonly called Regolitia, but nearly all Apothecaries and Physicians who prefer Arabic terms to Greek call it Liquiritia. It is truly a plant little known to many, for although its roots abound in all apothecary shops, the living plants are seen in our times in only a few places in Italy. Yet it is not surprising that Pliny mentioned Regolitia among the thorny plants at the beginning of chapter nine of book twenty-two, saying thus: "Regolitia is without doubt one of those plants which are thorny, for it produces its leaves like a vine." And again in chapter fifteen of book twenty-one, enumerating nearly all thorny herbs, he said: "Thorny plants are of many kinds: entirely thorny are the Asparagus and the Scorpion; some are thorny in their leaves, such as the Thistle, Eryngo, Regolitia, and Nettle, for in all the leaves of these there is a thorny sharpness." From this one can understand that Pliny never saw the Regolitia, which, as Dioscorides said, produces its leaves not at all thorny, but similar to those of the lentisk, dense, thick, and gummy. The cause of this error may easily have been that Pliny had a corrupt Greek text of Dioscorides, where sometimes was written "schino" (meaning lentisk) instead of "echino" (meaning hedgehog), a change that had been made by few careful scribes, altering the "s" to "e." And this seems to me a better explanation than that of those who foolishly argued in defense of Pliny that the Regolitia had once been thorny, but that through careful cultivation its thorns had been lost — for if it was not thorny in the time of Dioscorides, it was even less likely to be thorny in the time of Pliny, who was born many years after him. Theophrastus calls Regolitia "Scythian" in chapter thirteen of book nine, stating that it grows near the Maeotian marsh. Galen mentions it in book six on the faculties of simples, describing it thus: "The juice of the roots of Regolitia is primarily useful and similarly sweet, and gently astringent, as are its roots. Beyond this it can relieve roughness not only of the windpipe but also of the bladder, and this it does by virtue of the moderation of its temperature, and therefore it is suited to our temperament. For it has been shown that sweet things have these properties, but since to this sweetness is joined a certain astringent faculty, its whole temperament, insofar as it has warmth and astringent faculty, is truly warm with a mild heat, approaching very closely to our own temperament. Furthermore, because that which is moderately sweet always has some degree of moisture, it is for good reason a medicine suited to thirst."

Of Greater Centaury. Chapter 6.

Greater Centaury produces leaves similar to those of the walnut, long, of the color of cabbage, toothed all around in the manner of a saw. Its stalk resembles that of the dock, stands two or three cubits high, and has many branches growing from the root, at whose tips are several heads, like those of poppies, which lengthen into roundness. The flower is sky-blue, and the seed is similar to that of safflower, wrapped in certain woolly tufts. It produces a large, heavy, firm root, three feet long, full of juice, reddish, and tasting somewhat astringent, with a certain sweetness and sharpness combined. It loves rich, open places, forests, and hills. It is found in great abundance in Lycia, in the Peloponnese, in Elis, Messenia, and in many other places near Pholoe, Lycia, and Smyrna. The root is useful for ruptures, cramps, pains in the side, and chronic cough; and for spitting of blood, given at the weight of two drams in water when there is fever, and in wine when there is none; it helps bodily pains and those of the womb taken in the same way. Scraped and applied in the form of a collyrium to the secret parts of women it provokes menstruation and childbirth; its juice does the same; it heals wounds, and therefore the root, fresh or somewhat dried and then pounded, consolidates them. Boiling the pounded root with meat cut in several pieces, it joins them together. In Lycia its juice is extracted and used in place of glycyrrhiza.

Regarding Greater Centaury (as was noted just above in the chapter on Rhapontic), it is nothing other than that notable root called commonly by those physicians and apothecaries who still follow the old ways, and know no more, Reupontico. Del Chameleone bianco. Cap. viij.

IL Chameleone biaco è chiamato da alcuni Ixia, per ritrouarsi in alcuni luoghi
appresso alle radici sue un certo uischio, ilquale usano le donne in cambio di ma

Del Chameleone nero. Cap. ix.

HArebbe il Chameleone nero le frondi simili al cardo, se non fussero di quelle al
quanto minori, piu sottili, & distinte di rosso colore. La gamba produce alta un
palmo, grossa un dito, di colore rossigno. I fiori fa ella nella ombrella spinosi,
hiacinthini, di diuerso colore. La radice ha grossa, nera, densa, & qualche uolta
corrosa, laqual rotta gialleggia, & nel mangiarla morde. Nasce nelle campagne in luoghi
secchi, montagnosi, & nelle maremme. La radice trita con un poco di uetriolo, oglio cedri
no, & grascia, ungendosene guarisce la rogna: la medesima aggiuntovi solpho, & bitume,
cotta nell'aceto, & messa in su l'imperigini le sana. La dicottione della radice lauandosene
D la bocca, leua il dolore dei denti, & ancho posta la radice sopra al dente, che duole, con altre
tanto pepe, & cera. Cotta nell'aceto conforta i denti, & gli rompe anchora, mettendouisi
calda dentro con un stile. Spegne applicata insieme con solpho le macole della pelle della
faccia, & le uitiligini. Mescolasi con le medicine, che corrodono: sana l'ulcere corrosiue, ne
re, & sordide. Chiamasi Chameleone dalla uarietà delle sue foglie, per mutare elle colore se
condo i terreni: Imperoche qui uerdi, li biancheggiati, & altroue cerulee, et rosse si ritrouano.

C Hiamasi il bianco Chameleone uolgarmente in Thoscana, come quasi per tutto il resto d'Italia, Carlina: imperoche
si crede il uolgo (come si dice) che dall'Angelo fusse ella dimostrata à Carlo Magno per uero rimedio della peste,
& però alcuni la tengono per cosa eccellentissima contra la peste, alla quale, per ualere ella contra à i uermini del
corpo, & parimente à i morsi delle uelenose serpi, non negarei io, che molto non potesse giouare. Errano di gran lunga
coloro, che si pensano, che'l Chameleone biaco sia quella spetie di Cardo simile à i Carciosi, che noi adoperiamo in Thoscana
per fare appredere il latte in uece di caglio. Delche da manifesto indicio il produrre egli sopra lunghi fusti il suo spinoso,
& ben ricciuto frutto. Al nero nasce similmente per tutta Italia, & copia grande se ne uede per i monti, & per i colli della
la valle

translation:
216 BOOK

A the body, and not the greater, as many of the Arabs confuse one with the other in their imaginings. Galen wrote of this, beyond his particular treatise, in book seven on the properties of simples, saying thus: The root of the lesser Centaury has no efficacy, but the tips of its stem, with the leaves that grow upon it, and likewise its flowers, are useful. It overcomes in those parts the bitter quality, which has within it a little of the astringent, by which temperament the lesser Centaury is a medicine highly desiccating without any sharpness. This herb, applied as a fresh poultice, heals all great wounds of the body, and ulcers that are difficult to consolidate. It is used dried with all conglutinating and desiccating medicines, and especially with those suited to healing cavernous, malignant, and difficult ulcers, and fistulas, and for softening old hardnesses. It is likewise mixed with those things that treat ailments, for whose fomentation it is suited in cases of rheumatism, in which those medicines are most effective that, by desiccating most powerfully with a certain astringent virtue, have no sharpness in themselves. Some use a decoction of this herb as a clyster in cases of sciatica, because it evacuates together with the bile also the gross humors, and inasmuch as its abundant action loosens even to the blood; nevertheless for this it gives considerably more benefit. The juice certainly, being of similar virtue, that is desiccating and cleansing, can equally accomplish all the aforesaid things. Applied to the eyes together with honey, it promotes menstruation, and causes miscarriage in pregnant women. There are some who give it to those who suffer in their nerves, so that it may loosen and desiccate without any harm the humors of which they are full, and similarly
B it is a good remedy applied externally for obstructions of the liver, and for hardnesses of the spleen; and it works no less when taken by mouth by those who can bear it.

Of the White Chameleon. Chapter 8.

The White Chameleon is called by some Ixia, because one finds in certain places near its roots a certain gum, which women use in place of mastic. Its leaves are similar to those of the silybum, or of the thistle, but rougher, more pointed, and more firm than those of the Black Chameleon. It produces no stem, but sends up spines in the middle, similar to the sea-urchin and the artichoke. Its flowers are red and woolly. Its seed is similar to that of carthamus. The root on pleasant hills grows thick, and on mountains thin, white in its depth, and somewhat aromatic, sweet in taste and heavy in smell. Drunk with austere wine and juice of boiled oregano, to the weight of one acetabulum, it kills the broad worms of the body. One dram of it is given most conveniently with wine to dropsical persons, because it desiccates them.
C Its decoction is useful for promoting retained urine. The root drunk with wine is very good against the venom of serpents. Mixed with polenta, or with water, and with oil, it kills dogs, pigs, and mice.

Of the Black Chameleon. Chapter 9.

The Black Chameleon would have leaves similar to those of the thistle, were they not somewhat smaller, thinner, and marked with red color. The stem grows a palm high, as thick as a finger, of reddish color. It produces flowers in a spiny umbel, hyacinth-colored, of varied hue. The root is thick, black, dense, and sometimes corroded, and when broken turns yellowish, and when eaten it bites. It grows in the countryside in dry, mountainous places, and in the coastal marshes. The root ground with a little vitriol, cedar oil, and grease, rubbed on, heals the scab; the same with the addition of sulfur and bitumen,
D cooked in vinegar and applied to pustules, heals them. The decoction of the root, used as a mouthwash, relieves toothache, and likewise the root placed on the aching tooth, with as much pepper and wax. Cooked in vinegar it strengthens the teeth, and can also loosen them, if a hot probe is inserted. Applied together with sulfur it removes blemishes from the skin of the face, and vitiligo. It is mixed with corrosive medicines: it heals corrosive, black, and foul ulcers. It is called Chameleon from the variety of its leaves, because they change color according to the terrain: for here they are found green, there whitish, and elsewhere blue and red.

C The White Chameleon is popularly called in Tuscany, as in almost all the rest of Italy, Carlina: because the common people believe (as is said) that it was shown by an Angel to Charlemagne as a true remedy against the plague, and therefore some hold it to be a most excellent thing against the plague, and since it is effective against the worms of the body, and likewise against the bites of venomous serpents, I would not deny that it could be very beneficial. Those are greatly mistaken who suppose that the White Chameleon is that species of thistle similar to the artichoke, which we use in Tuscany for curdling milk in place of rennet. Of which there is clear evidence in that it produces upon tall stems its spiny and well-curled fruit. The Black also grows similarly throughout all Italy, and a great abundance of it is seen on the mountains and on the hills of the valley

A & di fuori alcune bolle appuntate nel mezzo del dosso loro: nell'ali sono assai concaue, & però spesso la rugiada, o la pioggia ui rimane: onde ha preso nome di Dissaco. In cima della gamba tutti i ramuscelli hanno una testa, alquanto lunghetta, & spinosa à modo di riccio, laqual poscia nel seccarsi biancheggia. Ritrouansi dentro in queste teste alcuni uermicelli, quando si diuidono per lungo fino alla midolla. La radice cotta nel uino, & poscia pesta, sino che uenga à modo di cera, sana le fessure del sedere, & le fistole. Serbasi così acconcia in uaso di rame: Imperoche (secondo che si dice) sana i porri, & le pendenti formiche. Dicesi, che i uermini delle teste legati in cuoio, & appiccati al collo, ouero al braccio, sanano la febre quartana.

L Dissaco, ilqual chiamano Labro di Venere, è notissimo in tutta Italia, & massime in tutti quei luoghi doue si la
I uora di lana: imperoche con la ricciuta testa, che pro luce egli con ritorte spine nelle sommità de i fusti, si cardano i panni, & le berette per trarne fuore il pelo. Chiamasi uolgarmente in Thoscana Cardo, & in molti luoghi, & massime in su'l Bolognese si semina, & con molta cura si coltiua ne i campi, come che communemente ne nasca del saluatico per le campagne in su gli argini de i fossi, & de i campi, et per le publiche strade appresso alle siepi, con tutte quelle uere sembianze, che Dioscoride gli assegna, & come che dica Marcello fiorentino non hauer egli possato mai ritrouare nelle teste del Dissaco uermicello alcuno; nondimeno fermamente si ritrouanell'Autunno quando son ben mature, come l'esperienza chiaramente ne dimostra. Chiamasi il Dissaco uolgarmente da gli Spetiali Virga pastoris maggiore: Percioche la minore anchora ne dimostrano molto simile à questa; ma non però è nel fusto così strisciata, ne così spinosa, ne sono le sue frondi così grosse, ne le teste così grandi, ne così spinose; anzi che la quantità loro non è maggiore d'una ciregia, rassembrando un uerde, & ben ritondo fiocco. Ma è d'auertire, che queste sue spetie di Dissaco chiamate Verga di Pastore, non sono la Virga pastoris di Serapione, ne manco quella, che scriue Auicena: imperoche questa è il uero Poligonio, ouero Sanguinaria, che sotto le spetie di maschio, & di femmina nel. iiij. libro scrisse Dioscoride. Et però ho pensatio, che non da gli Arabi sia stato dato il nome di Verga di Pastore al Dissaco; ma da quelli Spetiali, che più si son confidati nelle lor Pandette, che in tutti gli altri buoni, & approuati autori; Percioche quiui Mattheo Siluatico autore di tal opera à cap. ctv. chiama il Dissaco Verga di pastore, confondendo scioccamente questo con il Poligonio; non accorgendosi, che la Verga di pastore de gli Arabi è la Corregiuola, ouero Centinodia uolgare, chiamata Sanguinaria, & Poligonia da Dioscoride, & non il Dissaco più differente da quello, che le lepri da gli orsi. Fece del Dissaco memoria Galeno al. vi. delle facoltà de Semplici con una sola riga di scrittura, così breuemente scriuendone. La radice del Dissaco dissecca nel

C secondo ordine, & ha alquanto dell'asterfuo.

Della Spina bianca. Cap. xij.

A Spina bianca, ouero regia nasce ne i monti, et luoghi seluosi, co srondi simili al bianco chameleone, ma più strette, più bianche, & alquanto horride, et spinose. Il fusto, ilquale ha alquanto maggiore di due gombiti, produce ella grosso un po lice, & qualcheuolta più, biancheggiante, & di dentro concauo: nelle cui sommità ha una testicciuola spinosa, simile al riccio marino, ma più picciola, & più lunga. Sono i suoi fiori purpurei, e i seme è simile à quello del carthamo, ma più tondo. Beesi la radice utilmente contra à gli sputi del sangue, & contra al uomito, & flussò dello stomacho: prouoca l'orina, & impiastrasi in su le posteme. Laurandosi la bocca con la dicottione di quella gioua al dolor de denti. Conferisce il seme beendosi à i fanciulli epilentici, & ai morsi delle ser-

D pi. Dicesi, che portato attaccato al collo disca ccia tutti gli serpenti.

C Hiamano uolgarmente gli Spetiali imitando gli Arabi, la Spina bianca Bedeguar, & non poca questione è tra lo ro, & parimente tra la più parte de i Medici, quale tra le molte spinose piante prodotte dalla natura, sia la Spina bianca. Delche non sapendosi eglino risolucre, pigliano chi il Cardo benedetto chiamato herba Tancci, ouero Turca, chi la Carlina, chi quel Cardo, che noi in Thoscana usiamo in uece di caglio per fare apprendere il latte, & chi altre spetie di Cardi saluatichi, così caminandosene senza alcuna uiuida luce nelle tenebre de gli errori. Intra i quali ritrouo io essere Leonardo Fuchsio Tedesco: percioche, come si legge all'ultimo capitolo del primo libro delle sue diuine Paradoxe, assai scioccamente quantunque gli paia dire miracoli si crede, che sia la Spina bianca quella spetie di Cardone saluatico, che sopra alle sue grandissime frondi di ainsinite macole bianche, ilqual chiamano alcuni Cardo di santa Maria, & altri herba del latte, non accorgendosi, che questa nasce ne i piani, & nelle capagne, come ne fa testimonio tutta Thoscana, oue infinitissima copia ne nasce, & no ne i monti, et nelle selue: & che più oltre produce le frondi il doppio maggiori, & non minori di quelle del Chameleone bianco. Et però è da sapere, che la Spina bianca nasce ne i monti, et massime ne i boschi, & nelle selue di quelli, come scriue benissimo Dioscoride. Ilche apertamente dimostrano le molte piante, che sene ritrouano in su i monti più alti della ualle Anania, conformi in ogni lor sembianza con gli scritti lasciatine da lui. & im-
però

218 BOOK

A And on their outer surface there are some pointed bumps in the middle of their back: their wings are quite hollow, and therefore dew or rain often remains in them; hence it has taken the name Dissaco [teasel]. At the top of the stem all the small branches have a head, somewhat elongated and spiny in the manner of a hedgehog, which then whitens as it dries. Inside these heads one finds certain small worms when they are split lengthwise down to the pith. The root, boiled in wine and then pounded until it becomes like wax, heals the fissures of the posterior and fistulas. It is kept thus prepared in a copper vessel: for (as is said) it heals warts and hanging warts. It is said that the worms from the heads, tied in leather and hung around the neck or arm, cure quartan fever.

L The Dissaco, which they call Labro di Venere [Venus's basin], is very well known throughout all Italy, and especially in all those places where
I wool is worked: for with its spiny head, which it produces at the tops of its stalks with curved thorns, cloths and berets are carded to draw out the nap. It is commonly called Cardo in Tuscany, and in many places, especially around Bologna, it is sown and carefully cultivated in the fields, though it commonly grows wild in the countryside along the banks of ditches and fields, and along public roads near hedgerows, with all the true characteristics that Dioscorides assigns to it; and even though Marcello the Florentine says he never managed to find any worm in the heads of the Dissaco, nonetheless they are certainly found in Autumn when the heads are well matured, as experience clearly shows. The Dissaco is commonly called by apothecaries Virga pastoris major [Shepherd's rod, large]: for they also show the smaller one as very similar to this; but its stem is not as ribbed, nor as spiny, nor are its leaves as large, nor the heads as big, nor as spiny; indeed the whole of them is no bigger than a cherry, resembling a green and nicely round tassel. But one must note that these its species of Dissaco called Shepherd's Rod are not the Virga pastoris of Serapion, nor the one written of by Avicenna: for this is the true Polygonum, or Sanguinaria, which Dioscorides wrote about under the species of male and female in the fourth book. And therefore I have concluded that the name Shepherd's Rod was not given to the Dissaco by the Arabs, but by those apothecaries who trusted their Pandects more than all other good and approved authors; for therein Mattheo Silvatico, author of that work, at chapter 105, calls the Dissaco Shepherd's Rod, foolishly confusing it with the Polygonum; not realizing that the Shepherd's Rod of the Arabs is the Knotgrass, or common Centinodia, called Sanguinaria and Polygonia by Dioscorides, and not the Dissaco, which differs from it as much as hares from bears. Galen mentioned the Dissaco in the sixth book on the Faculties of Simples with only a single line of writing, briefly noting: The root of the Dissaco desiccates in the

C second degree, and has something of an astringent quality.

On the White Thistle. Chapter 12.

The white thistle, or royal thistle, grows in mountains and wooded places, with leaves similar to those of the white chameleone but narrower, whiter, and somewhat rough and spiny. Its stalk, which reaches somewhat more than two cubits, it produces thick as a thumb, and sometimes more, whitish and hollow within: at its summit it has a small spiny head, similar to a sea urchin but smaller and longer. Its flowers are purple, and the seed is similar to that of safflower but rounder. The root drunk beneficially counteracts spitting of blood, vomiting, and flux of the stomach: it provokes urine, and applied as a plaster it helps swellings. Rinsing the mouth with its decoction helps toothache. The seed drunk benefits epileptic children, and helps against snake

D bites. It is said that worn hung around the neck it drives away all serpents.

C The apothecaries, following the Arabs, commonly call the White Thistle Bedeguar, and no small dispute exists among them, and likewise among most physicians, as to which among the many spiny plants produced by nature is the White Thistle. Being unable to resolve the matter, some take the blessed thistle called Herba Tancci or Turca, some the Carlina, some that thistle which we in Tuscany use instead of rennet to curdle milk, and others still other species of wild thistles, thus wandering without any clear light in the darkness of errors. Among these I find Leonardo Fuchsius the German: for, as one reads in the last chapter of the first book of his celebrated Paradoxes, quite foolishly, though he thinks he is saying something miraculous, he believes that the White Thistle is that species of wild Cardoon which on its very large leaves has countless white spots, which some call Cardo di Santa Maria and others Herba del latte [Milk thistle], not realizing that this grows in plains and in the countryside, as all Tuscany testifies, where it grows in infinite abundance, and not in the mountains and woods: and that furthermore it produces leaves twice as large, and certainly not smaller than those of the white chameleone. One must therefore know that the White Thistle grows in the mountains, and especially in the woods and forests of them, as Dioscorides very well writes. This is clearly demonstrated by the many plants found on the highest mountains of the Valle Anania, conforming in every respect to the descriptions left to us by him. And
therefore

text:
220 LIBRO
A Del Cardo. Cap. xiiij.

IL Cardo, ouero Scolimo ha le foglie simili à quelle del chameleone nero, ouero à quelle della spina bianca, ma piu nere, et piu grosse. Ha il fusto lungo, et frondoso, nella cui sommità ha il suo spinoso capo. La radice ha nera, & grossa, la qual applicata leua uia l'odore delle ditella, & similmente ogni altro odore graue del corpo: & il medesimo fa cotta nel uino, & beuta: prouoca similmente beuta l'orina copiosamente, ma puzzolente. L'herba teneretta, & nasciuta di nuouo, si mangia cotta come gli sparagi.

Vantunque qui habbia Dioscoride breuemente d'un sol Cardo trattato; nondimeno per quanto habbia io possuto
Q cauare da Theophrasto, Plinio, et altri buoni autori, assai sono le spetie de i Cardi. Ma parlando prima di quelli, che coltiuati dalla natura nascono saluatichi nelle campagne, & che noi uolgarmente in Thoscana chiamiamo Scardaci, sene ritrouano di piu, & diuerse spetie, quantunque Plinio à. xxiij. cap. del. xx. libro non metta de i saluatichi altro, che due spetie. Ne sono similmente de i domestichi, che per compiace re alla gola con gran coltura hoggi s'alleuano
B ne i giardini, uarie, & diuerse sorti, tra liquali primamente son quelli, che si chiamano Cardoni, liquali fatti con grande arte bianchi, & teneri, si danno hoggi per la maggior parte nella fine delle cene: imperoche con pepe, & sale per ultimo cibo si mangiano cosi crudi. Di questi intendeua Theophrasto al. iiij. cap. del. vi. libro dell'historia delle piante, quando così diceua. Quella spetie di Cardo, che si chiama Catto, nasce solamente in Sicilia, ne si ritrouaegli in Grecia. I fusti di questo, subito che escono dalla radice, si riuoltano uerso terra insieme con le lor larghe, et spinose frondi. Questi fusti, liquali chiamano propriamente Catti, mondati si mangiano, come che alquanto amareggino. A noi in Thoscana sono stati portati da Napoli, & quiui di Sicilia. Et però ben disse Theophrasto esser il Catto particolar pianta di quell'isola. Sono nelle spetie de Cardi domestichi anchora i Carciofi chiamati Archichiochi in Lombardia, de i quali nel medesimo luogo subito dopo il Catto scrisse Theophrasto, così dicendo. E' un'altra spetie di Cardo, laquale chiamano Pternice, simile al Catto, eccetto che piace questo il suo fusto dritto, ilquale è anchor egli usitato ne cibi. Cauasi già si suol mangiare prima del frutto il lanuginoso seme, ilquale è simile à quello degli altri Cardi, & mangiasi quello, che ui resta simile al ceruello della palma. Intendeudo Theophrasto di quelle Palme, che si chiamano in Sicilia, & à Napoli Cefaglioni, delle quali disopra nel primo libro al capitolo del Bdellio facemo mentione. Veggonsi oltre à ciò à i tempi nostri i Carciofi in Italia di diuerse sorti: imperoche di spinosi, serrati, & aperti, & di non spinosi, ritondi, lunghi, aperti, & chiusi sene ritrouano, nelle cui spetie ne sono di quelli, che quasi del tutto frassembrano alle pine de i pini. Ilche mi fa pensare, anzi piu presto credere, che quello, che chiama Theophrasto Cardus pinea per le molte corrispondenze, che ui si ueggono, non sia altro, che questa spetie di Carciofi, scriuendone egli al lungo in questo modo. Il Cardopino non nasce in molti luoghi: è pianta dalla radice molto frondosa, dal mezzo della quale esce nacofo tra le frondi il suo seminal frutto come un pomo. Spetie ueramente di Carciofo spinoso è quello, di cui noi in Thoscana adoperiamo il fiore, per fare apprendere il Latte: imperoche quel medesimo fanno i fiori dei Carciofi, liquali, secondo che ritrouò, nascono senza spine, se si pontail lor seme auanti che si semini. Ilche similmente dicono accadere quando nel seminarlo s'asconde nelle radici della lattuga, et questo puo ageuolmente hauer priuato delle spine quelli, che ne son senza. Fece del Cardo memoria Galeno al. viij. delle facultà de semplici, ne altro ne disse egli oltre quello, che ne scriue Dioscoride, se non che lo descrisse esser caldo nel fine del secondo, ò nel principio del terzo ordine, & secco nel secondo.

Del Poterio. Cap.xv.

IL Poterio, ilquale gl'Ionij chiamano neurada, è gran pianta, ha i rami lunghi, molli, sarmentosi, & arrendeuoli, simili alla tragacantha, & le srondi picciole, &
D rotonde. Vestesi il Poterio d'una sottile, & lanosa lanugine: & oltre à questo è per tutto spinoso. Produce i suoi fiori piccioli, & bianchi: & il seme di sapore al gusto acuto, & odorato, ma inutile. Nasce in luoghi acquosi. Sono le sue radici lunghe due, ouer tre gombiti, ferme, & neruose, lequali tagliare appresso terra distillano poscia un liquore simile alla gomma. Peste, & impiastrate consolidano i nerui tagliati. A commodarsi medesimamente la dicottione dell'herba quando si beè, à i difetti de i nerui.
N On si ritrouaalcuno à i tempi nostri, che ci sappi dimostrar e il Poterio in Italia. Il perchè da pensare, che non ui nasca, ne ui si ritrouì: percioche nascendoui, per esser molto chiaramente statone scritta l'historia da Dioscoride, ageuol cosa sarebbe il rintracciarlo.

Dell'Acanthio. Cap.xvi.

HA l'Acanthio le foglie simili alla spina bianca, spinose nell'estremità loro, coperte d'una lanugine simile alle tele de i ragni, della quale colta, & filata se ne tessono le

translation:
220 BOOK
A On the Thistle. Chapter 14.

The Thistle, or Scolymus, has leaves similar to those of the black chameleon plant, or those of the white thorn, but darker and larger. It has a long, leafy stem, at the top of which is its spiny head. The root is black and thick; when applied externally it removes the odor of the armpits, and likewise any other strong odor of the body; and it does the same when boiled in wine and drunk; it likewise promotes copious urination, though of an unpleasant smell. The young, freshly sprouted herb is eaten cooked, like asparagus.

Although Dioscorides has treated here only one Thistle briefly, nevertheless, as far as I have been able to gather from Theophrastus, Pliny, and other good authors, there are quite a few species of Thistles. Speaking first of those which, cultivated by nature, grow wild in the fields and which we in Tuscany commonly call Scardaci, there are several and diverse species to be found, although Pliny in chapter 23 of book 20 lists no more than two wild species. There are likewise various and diverse kinds among the domestic ones, which today are cultivated with great care in gardens to please the palate, among which the foremost are those called Cardoni, which today, made white and tender with great skill, are served for the most part at the end of suppers, since they are eaten raw with pepper and salt as a final course. These are what Theophrastus had in mind in chapter 4 of book 6 of his History of Plants, when he said: That species of Thistle called Catto grows only in Sicily and is not found in Greece. The stalks of this, as soon as they come out of the root, bend toward the ground together with their broad and spiny fronds. These stalks, which they properly call Catti, when peeled are eaten, though somewhat bitter. They have been brought to us in Tuscany from Naples, and there from Sicily. And so Theophrastus rightly said the Catto is a plant peculiar to that island. Among the species of domestic Thistles there are also the Artichokes, called Archichiochi in Lombardy, of which Theophrastus wrote immediately after the Catto in the same passage, saying: There is another species of Thistle, which they call Pternice, similar to the Catto, except that one likes its straight stalk, which is also used as food. The woolly seed, similar to that of other Thistles, is already eaten before the fruit, and what remains is eaten like the heart of a palm. Theophrastus here refers to those Palms called Cefaglioni in Sicily and Naples, of which we made mention above in the first book at the chapter on Bdellium. Beyond this, in our own times artichokes of various kinds are found in Italy: for there are spiny, serrated, and open ones, and non-spiny, round, long, open, and closed ones, among whose species there are some which closely resemble pine cones. This leads me to think, indeed to believe more firmly, that what Theophrastus calls Cardus pinea, given the many correspondences to be seen, is nothing other than this species of artichoke, writing about it at length in this way: The Cardopino does not grow in many places; it is a plant with a very leafy base, from the middle of which emerges, among the fronds, its seminal fruit like an apple. Truly a spiny variety of artichoke is the one whose flower we use in Tuscany to curdle milk, since the flowers of artichokes do the same, which, according to what I have found, grow without spines if one soaks their seed in advance before sowing. The same is said to happen when, in sowing them, one buries them in lettuce roots, and this can easily remove the spines from those that have them. Galen mentioned the Thistle in book 8 on the faculties of simples, and said nothing beyond what Dioscorides writes about it, except that he described it as hot at the end of the second degree, or the beginning of the third, and dry in the second.

On the Poterium. Chapter 15.

The Poterium, which the Ionians call neurada, is a large plant with long, soft, vine-like, and pliant branches, similar to the tragacanth, with small and round leaves. The Poterium clothes itself in a fine, woolly down, and beyond this is thorny all over. It produces small, white flowers, and a seed that is sharp and fragrant to the taste, but useless. It grows in wet places. Its roots are two or three cubits long, firm and sinewy; when cut close to the ground they then drip a liquid similar to gum. Pounded and applied as a plaster, they consolidate severed nerves. The decoction of the herb, when drunk, likewise serves to remedy ailments of the nerves.
No one in our time is to be found in Italy who can show us the Poterium. Which gives reason to think that it does not grow or occur there, since if it did grow there, its history having been so clearly written up by Dioscorides, it would be easy enough to track it down.

On the Acanthium. Chapter 16.

The Acanthium has leaves similar to the white thorn, spiny at their tips, covered with a down similar to spiders' webs, from which, once gathered and spun, there are woven

simo, che si chiama opisthotono.

Redo ueramente che l'Acantho, ilquale in questo luogo commemorò tra le spinose piante Dioscoride, non nasce,

Dell'Acantho. Cap.xvij.

Dell'Acantho saluatico. Cap.xviij.

NAsce l'Acantho saluatico simile al Cardo, spinoso, & piu breue di quello, che si se

Engono sicuramente tutti i piu ualenti Semplicisti de i tempi nostri, che l'Acantho esser no possa altro, che quella

THIRD BOOK. 221

clothing similar to those of silk. The root, or the leaves taken as a drink, are useful for that kind of spasm called opisthotonos.

C I truly believe that the Acanthus, which Dioscorides here commemorated among the thorny plants, does not grow nor is to be found in Italy, since there is no one who can show us the leaves of any thorny plant so woolly that cloth could be woven from their fleece, as Dioscorides wrote, and Pliny in chapter 12 of book 24. And therefore one may believe without deception that those who point to a certain species of mountain thistle, woolly all around its curly fruit, as the Acanthus, are greatly mistaken. For besides having no wool at all upon its leaves, what it has on the fruit is exceedingly fine, without any fiber, and entirely fragile and loosely structured.

On the Acanthus. Chapter 17.

The Acanthus, which the Romans call Pederota, grows in gardens and in humid, rocky places. Its leaves are longer and broader than those of lettuce, cut like those of rocket, dark-colored, smooth, and fat. It produces a stem two cubits long, as thick as a finger, clothed at intervals up to its top with small leaves, somewhat long, concave, and thorny, from which the white flower emerges. It produces a somewhat oblong seed of reddish color; the top of the stem has the shape of a thyrsus. Its roots are soft, slimy, moist, and reddish, and applied as a poultice to dislocated limbs and burns from fire they are very beneficial. Drunk, they provoke urination but constipate the bowels, and are greatly useful for consumptives, for those with hernias, and for those with spasms.

On the Wild Acanthus. Chapter 18.

The wild Acanthus grows similar to the thistle, thorny, and shorter than the one that is sown and cultivated in gardens. Its root is in every respect as efficacious as the one described above.

T All the most capable herbalists of our time are firmly convinced that the Acanthus can be nothing other than the plant we call Bear's Breech (Branca orsina). This I dare not deny, nor am I confident enough to affirm it; because, although I am compelled to believe it, beyond the opinion of such men, by seeing that Bear's Breech has leaves much broader and longer than lettuce, cut in the manner of rocket, dark-colored, fat, and smooth, and that its stem is likewise tall to the measure of two cubits, as thick as a finger, and clothed at intervals with certain small leaves from which the white flower grows, and from it an oblong and reddish seed; and furthermore that its root conforms well to that of the Acanthus — nevertheless, seeing that the small leaves on its stem lack spines, and that the plant seems hardly suited for weaving and adorning the borders of garden plots, as Pliny relates in chapter 22 of book 22, and seeing that in our own day it is held in no esteem although it was so highly prized and celebrated by the ancients, makes me somewhat suspect whether it is or is not truly Bear's Breech. Nor does the argument of those who say that the Acanthus leaves carved on ancient columns, and especially those made in imitation of Corinthian columns, are naturally those of Bear's Breech, carry weight against my reasoning; for one may easily reply that the resemblance between Bear's Breech and the Acanthus may exist without the two being the same plant. It therefore seems to me doubtful to affirm, and equally problematic to deny, that Bear's Breech is the Acanthus described here by Dioscorides. Yet since Bear's Breech does possess all the medicinal properties attributed to the Acanthus by Dioscorides and Galen, and since I reflect that when Dioscorides says it has small leaves on the stem that are thorny, this may be understood as meaning sharp in the manner of spines without actually being thorny — this compels me to say that those who hold and believe that the Acanthus and Bear's Breech are the same plant cannot be faulted. One also finds G (as Dioscorides says) a wild Acanthus similar to the thistle, with leaves much shorter than the domestic one, D and Pliny likewise said that the Acanthus was of two different species. Galen wrote of the Acanthus in book 6 of his work on the properties of simples, saying thus: Some call the Acanthus Melanphyllum, and others Pederota. Its leaves are moderately digestive in action, just as its root is desiccating, incising, and composed of fine parts.

On Anonis, or Ononis. Chapter 19.

Anonis, which some call Ononis, has loose branches longer than a span, ringed with many nodes and hollowed at the joints. Its small heads are rounded, and its leaves are small and thin, similar to those of the lentil, or of rue, or of meadow lotus, somewhat hairy and fragrant, with a not unpleasant smell. The herb is preserved in salt, before it produces its spines, as it is then very agreeable in food. Its small branches produce firm, strong, and sharp spines. Its root is white, warm, and desiccating. The bark of the root, drunk with wine, provokes urination and breaks up kidney stones; it erodes the edges of ulcers. When boiled —
