translation:
THIRD BOOK. 235

The best kind is that which has the smallest and fattest leaves. Melilot (as Galen testifies in the seventh book on the properties of simple medicines) combines its own qualities with a certain astringent quality; but it is digestive and maturative: because the warm substance found in it is more potent than the cold. However, from all this I cannot find from the Greeks whether in medicine they use the leaves, roots, stalks, flowers, or seeds of Melilot, as the Arabs well testify to me, and especially Serapion, citing the authority of Isaac. Melilot is an herb that produces round, green leaves, with thin branches and sparse foliage. It produces its seed in certain round, thin pods, in which there are scattered grains, round, smaller than mustard seeds, yellow in color: and what is used of Melilot are those pods with the seed enclosed within them.

On Maro. Chapter 44.

Maro is a common, well-known, and branching herb. It produces flowers similar to those of Oregano, but its leaves are whiter, and its flowers more fragrant. Its virtues are likewise similar to Sisymbrium: it is mildly astringent and mildly warm. For this reason it heals corrosive ulcers, and is used in warming ointments. It grows most abundantly in Magnesia and in Tralles in Lydia.

B Galen wrote about Maro in his book of antidotes, in the composition of Hedichronon (though he discussed it not at all in his own books on simple medicines), in this manner. There are some who do not put amaracus into Hedichronon, nor Maro, and others who put only one of these: because all perfumers do not recognize it, not being in the habit of seeking other herbs than those brought from Candia. But I have truly seen and recognized these two herbs in Asia, though not as abundantly elsewhere as in Cyzicus, where they are most abundant. I have also seen amaracus in Italy, and many other herbs, and amaracus is considerably less fragrant than Maro: for its fragrance is great. The amaracine ointment, which the perfumers of Cyzicus make, shows by its name that it contains a great deal more amaracus, and perhaps also among the ancients it was made with amaracus, even though in our time only Maro is put in it, in which I have truly found great bitterness when tasting it: and so I already asked one of those who make the amaracine ointment to make it for me with as much amaracus as was formerly put in Maro. He did as I asked, and this ointment had less fragrance, but was not much weaker in its effects in operation. All this was written by Galen. From which one may consider that Maro is quite similar to amaracus, but more bitter and more fragrant. And therefore, though it is not entirely to be condemned the opinion of those who hold that the species of marjoram which is most fragrant, whitest,

C and smallest in leaf, and most bitter, which some call gentle marjoram, and we in Tuscany call "minuta," is Maro, and the other, which is softer, with broader leaves, greener, and more acute in taste, and less bitter, is the true amaracus or sampsuchon: nevertheless it makes me think that Maro does not grow in Italy, from Galen's saying that he had seen amaracus there, making no mention of having seen Maro there, as he did of what he had seen most abundantly in Asia and Cyzicus. In this belief I am also confirmed by Pliny: since he shows Maro to be a stranger in Italy, having placed it among those aromatics brought to us from distant lands, writing thus in chapter 24 of book 12. Maro grows in Egypt, but is inferior to that of Lydia: for this produces large and varied leaves, and that short, small, and fragrant ones. But I truly believe that those who would substitute our more fragrant marjoram for Maro were not wrong, since Galen testifies that the ointment he had made with pure amaracus alone, though it was less fragrant, was not much weaker in its operation.

On Acinos. Chapter 45.

D Acinos produces thin, dry little branches: it is similar to basil, but its leaves are more hairy: it is fragrant, and garlands are made from it. Some sow it in gardens. Drunk, it stops the menses and the body's fluxes. Applied as a plaster, it heals the sacred fire and those swellings they call "pani."

Q Although Ruellius believes that Acinos is that species of Basil which is fragrant and produces very tiny leaves, which we customarily keep for decoration in summer in pots on the terraces and windowsills: nonetheless what Pliny says in chapter 15 of book 20, that Acinos never flowers, strongly contradicts this: for it is well known to us that ours flowers at the beginning of autumn. Furthermore, it does not at all agree with Ruellius's view that Pliny likewise says in chapter 27 of book 21: The Egyptians sow Acinos both for food and for garlands. It would be the same plant as Basil, if it did not have more hairy branches and leaves, and were not much more fragrant. But I agree with Manardo of Ferrara (if Acinos indeed grows in Italy, which seems to me quite doubtful) that it is nothing other than a certain little herb that grows in dry fields, along the banks of fields and roads, hairy and very fragrant, which some call wild basil.

translation:
236 BOOK

On Baccara. Chapter 46.

Baccara is a branching herb, used in garlands. Its leaves are rough, of a size midway between those of violets and of mullein; its stalk is angular, about a cubit tall, somewhat rough, from which small branches emerge. It produces fragrant flowers of a whitish purple color; its roots resemble those of black hellebore, with a scent close to cinnamon; it loves rough and humid places. The root boiled in water is beneficial for those suffering from spasms, bruises, those who have fallen from a height, those with tightness of the chest who breathe with difficulty, for old coughs, and for disorders of urination; it promotes the menstrual flow, and drunk with wine it is useful against the bite of serpents. The fresh root applied beneath draws out the birth. The decoction is suitable for women in labor to sit in; dried and powdered it is sprinkled on the body to produce a good fragrance. The leaves, having an astringent virtue, are usefully applied as a poultice for headache, and likewise for inflammations of the eyes and of the breasts arising from childbirth, for abscesses of the tear ducts when fresh, and for erysipelas. Besides all this, merely smelling it induces sleep.

The true and genuine Baccara (as was discussed at length in the first book) is not the Asarum, which has been used by apothecaries in place of Baccara without any scruple in former times, nor is it the domestic Scarleggia, as Brasavola almost believed, following Leoniceno in this. The proof of this — although the Scarleggia much resembles the Baccara — is that its roots do not correspond in appearance nor in the scent that Dioscorides attributed to those of the true Baccara, which he likened to the roots of Hellebore and said smelled close to Cinnamon. This is not at all seen or sensed in those of the Scarleggia, which has sparse, whitish, thin roots, and without scent. I therefore conclude that the Baccara does not grow nor is it brought from other lands into Italy. I do not find that Galen in his books on simples ever mentions the Baccara, although Paul of Aegina, writing of its virtues in his seventh book, says: Baccara is a fragrant herb similar to cinnamon, used in garlands, and sharp. The decoction of its roots opens obstructions, promotes menstruation, and causes urination; its leaves, being astringent, check fluxes.

On Rue. Chapter 47.

The mountain and wild rue is more potent than the cultivated kind and that of gardens, and therefore its use in food is harmful. The garden variety is more suitable for culinary use; it grows beneath fig trees. Both kinds burn, cause ulceration, and promote menstruation and urination; eaten or drunk they constipate the body. The seed drunk with wine in the measure of one acetabulum is an antidote against deadly poisons. The leaves taken beforehand on their own, or together with nuts and dried figs, dispel the power of poisons; they are likewise beneficial against serpents. Rue drunk or eaten destroys the procreative faculty; boiled with dry dill and drunk it relieves bodily pain. Given in the same way it is effective for pains of the chest and side, for impediments of breathing, for coughs, disorders of the lungs, sciatica, and other pains of the joints, and for shivering and the cold stage at the onset of fevers. The decoction of rue made in oil, and used as an enema, is likewise effective for inflammations of the bowel called colic, and also of the rectum and the natural parts of women; applied with honey in the space between the natural parts and the rectum, it revives those women who swoon away as if strangled by the fumes of the womb. Boiled in oil and drunk it kills intestinal worms. It is applied as a poultice for joint pains with honey, and for dropsical patients with figs; the decoction made in wine serves the same purpose, both drunk and used as a wash until the mere odor fades. Eaten in food preserved in brine, and likewise raw, it helps to clarify the sight; applied as a poultice with polenta it eases pains of the eyes, and those of the head when combined with rose oil and vinegar; pounded and inserted in the nose it stanches the flow of blood. Applied together with bay leaves it treats inflammations of the testicles, and incorporated with wax and myrtle it heals ruptures of hernias. It cures white vitiligo when rubbed with wine, pepper, and nitre. Applied as a poultice with the same ingredients it removes warts and those kinds of corns called thymi. It is most usefully combined with alum and honey and applied to spreading skin eruptions. The juice warmed in a pomegranate rind and dropped into the ears relieves pain in them; the eyes, when weak, are anointed with this juice mixed with fennel juice and honey; and anointed with vinegar, white lead, and rose oil it benefits the

THIRD BOOK. 237

...sacred uses, for ulcers that creep and spread, and for those of the head that persist. Eating rue tames the sharpness and smell of garlic and onions. Eating mountain rue in great quantity kills. When gathered to be put in brine at the moment it begins to flower, it causes swelling and reddening of the skin, inflames strongly, and causes itching; therefore before picking it one must anoint one's hands and face with oil. They say that sprinkling the juice of rue over chicks keeps away cats, martens, and stone martens. It is said that the rue which grows in Macedonia along the river Olcimo kills immediately upon being eaten; that place is mountainous and full of vipers. Its seed is drunk for disorders of the internal organs, and is usefully mixed into antidotes; the roasted seed is given to drink for seven consecutive days to those who cannot stop the flow of urine. The root of wild rue is called Mountain Moli. Wild rue is similar to domestic rue. It is drunk beneficially for epilepsy and for sciatica, promotes menstruation, and kills the fetus in the womb. Wild rue is sharper than domestic rue and more potent; therefore it is to be avoided in food, as it is certainly harmful.

A Rue is in Italy a very well known plant, both domestic and wild I say, not speaking however of that second species of wild rue that Dioscorides wrote about in the following chapter: for that (as we shall say here) is quite different from this one, which (as Dioscorides writes at the end of this chapter) is truly similar to the domestic kind, found abundantly in many places of Italy and in several other regions, growing on its own in the countryside, in the mountains and hills, entirely similar to domestic rue, as one can see on Mount San Valentino, and on that above Gargaro in the county of Gorizia, though much sharper to the taste and of more intense odor. Rue is sown, according to Pliny in the eighth chapter of the nineteenth book, after the autumnal equinox, when the Favonius wind begins to blow. It fears the winter, and dung and moisture are very harmful to it. It loves soil good for making bricks, and the driest and most sun-exposed places. It feeds on ashes and has such friendship with the fig tree that it grows much better under its shade than anywhere else. Weasels well know the virtue it has against poisons: for they always prepare themselves with rue when they must fight with serpents. In our times rue is used against evil spirits, because Aristotle recommended it in his Problems against fascinations. Galen mentioned rue in the seventh book of the Faculties of Simple Medicines, saying thus: Wild rue is among those things that heat in the fourth degree, and domestic rue in the third, and it is not only sharp to the taste but also bitter. For which reason it can digest and cut thick and viscous humors. By these same qualities it also promotes urination, and is composed of subtle parts, drives away wind; and therefore it dissolves flatulence and quenches the flames of Venus: it digests and dries out powerfully. Besides this, among the species of wild rue there is also what they have said is called Moli and Besano.

On Wild Rue. Chapter 48.

They likewise call Wild Rue that plant which in Cappadocia and Galatia in Asia is called Moli. It is a plant that from a single root produces many slender stalks, with fronds much longer and more tender than the other rue, of heavy odor. It produces a white flower with certain knobs at the top composed of three parts, slightly larger than those of domestic rue, inside which is the triangular seed, reddish in color and bitter to the taste, and this is the part used: it ripens in autumn. It is ground with wine, saffron, juice of fennel, and bile of a hen against impediments of the eyes. There are some who call it harmala. The Syrians call it besasa, and the Cappadocians moli, because it has some resemblance to moli in its black root and white flower. It grows on hillsides and in rich soils.

Many copies of Dioscorides, both Greek and Latin, are found to have at the beginning of this chapter more than half of the chapter on Hypericum, which Dioscorides wrote at the end of this book. This being recognized as due to the carelessness of scribes, as some old Greek manuscripts have since confirmed — which lack this addition — has made clear that this Rue is not any species of Hypericum, as some have believed who have not seen the corrected text. From which it is plainly evident that it is not only not a species of Hypericum, nor of Ascyron, nor of Androsemum; but it is also quite different from that species of wild rue mentioned by Dioscorides alongside the domestic one in the preceding chapter above. There is no one in our time who can show us this plant in Italy, since it is a plant peculiar to Cappadocia and Galatia. The Arabs call it, as one can see from Serapion and Avicenna, Harmel, because Dioscorides said, and likewise Galen, that some call it Harmola. But all these Apothecaries err, bringing no small danger to the human body, who, following the doctrine of that their Lumen Apotecariorum, substitute for this Rue, in place of Harmel, in fetid pills, aggregative pills, and other compositions, the seed of Hemlock, which is not only in its qualities entirely contrary to Harmel, but is a deadly and detestable poison. alla tosse,à i dolori di corpo,& distillatione d'orina. Gioua alla rogna della uisciga beuto
con uino,ouero con acqua melata:prouoca i mestrui. Fa sconciare le donne:& liquefatto
con mele risolue le uentosità,& le durezze della madrice. Impiastrasi alle sciatiche. Mettesi
ne i medicamenti delle lassitudini,& parimente ne i capitali:rompe i carboncelli.Impla- C
strato con uua passa gioua alle podagre:messo ne i denti pertugiati ne caua il dolore:

Del Panace d'Asclepio. Cap. li.

L Panace d'Asclepio produce il fusto sottile,alto da terra un gombito,nodoso,
con frondi simili al sinocchio,ma maggiori,piu pelose,& odorate. Fa nella som-

ungonsi parimente con oglio. Chiamano Panace alcuni anchora l'origano saluatico,&
altri cunila, della quale dicemmo tra gli origani.

Asce il Panace Chironio abondantemente nel monte Pelio. Sono le sue fron-

THIRD BOOK. 239

On Heracleum Panax. Chapter 50. A

The Panax that some call Heracleum is the plant from which opopanax is collected. It grows most abundantly in Boeotia, and in Pisophide in Arcadia, where it is cultivated with great care because of the trade and profit derived from its juice. It produces rough leaves that lie along the ground, similar to those of the fig, divided into five parts around the stem. It has a very tall stalk, like that of the Ferula, surrounded by white down, and smaller leaves; at its summit it produces a large umbel, like that of dill, and a flower that tends toward yellow. The seed is fragrant and sharp. It has many roots all dependent from a single origin, white, of strong odor, thick-skinned, and somewhat bitter to the taste. It also grows in Cyrene in Libya, and in Macedonia. The juice is collected by cutting the root as it first pushes out from the stalks. From this comes a white juice, which when dry turns saffron-colored on the outside. They collect it by placing the leaves in pits dug around the plant, and take it out when it is dry. They likewise collect it by cutting the stalk at the time the grain is harvested, then taking what drips from it. The best roots are those that are not wrinkled, but smooth, extended, white, and dry, not worm-eaten, sharp and aromatic in taste. The seed that is useful is that which is gathered from the middle stalk, for that which the branches produce is empty. The juice is praised as best when it is most bitter to the taste, white inside and reddish outside, yellow like saffron on the surface, smooth, dense, brittle, tender, heavy of odor, and easily dissolved in water: the black and soft kinds are condemned. It is adulterated with ammoniac or wax, but the fraud is detected by rubbing it in water with the fingers, since the genuine dissolves and turns the color of milk.
Panax warms, softens, and dries: it is therefore used for the cold and shivering that come at the onset of periodic fevers, for spasms, hernias, pains in the side, coughs, pains in the body, and retention of urine. It helps with bladder mange when drunk with wine or with mead; it promotes menstruation. It causes abortion in women; melted with honey it dissolves flatulence and hardness of the womb. It is applied as a plaster for sciatica. It is put into medicines for fatigue and also into capital remedies; it breaks up carbuncles. Applied as a plaster with raisins it helps with gout; placed in perforated teeth it draws out the pain; placed in the eyes it improves vision. Mixed with pitch it makes a most useful plaster against the bites of rabid animals. The root sharpened and placed in the female parts causes childbirth; it is good for old ulcers. Pounded and plastered on, or rubbed with honey, it covers bones with flesh. The seed drunk with wormwood promotes menstruation, and with birthwort is effective against all animals that leave venom when they bite. It is drunk with wine for strangulation of the womb.

On Asclepian Panax. Chapter 51.

The Panax of Asclepius produces a slender stalk, one cubit tall from the ground, knotted, with leaves similar to fennel but larger, more hairy, and more fragrant. At its summit it forms an umbel in which are its golden, sharp, and fragrant flowers; it has a small root. The flowers and seed, pounded and mixed with honey, are effective against malignant ulcers that eat away flesh, and against small tumors. They are drunk with wine against the bite of serpents, and likewise used as an ointment with oil. Some people also call wild marjoram a Panax, and others call it cunila, which we discussed among the marjorams.

On Chironian Panax. Chapter 52.

The Chironian Panax grows abundantly on Mount Pelion. Its leaves are similar to those of sweet marjoram, and its flowers are golden; the root is slender and superficial, sharp to the taste. The root is drunk against the venom of serpents, and the leaves are also usefully applied as a plaster for the same purpose.

N Heraclean Panax grows in Italy on its own in Apulia, and also along the Apennines and in the marshlands of Siena on Mount Argentario. It is also kept in several gardens by those who take pleasure in medicinal plants for public display. I do not know, however, of any place in Italy where it is used to extract the juice, which in common—

A mente si chiama nelle Spetiarie Opoponaco: Imperoche questo si porta à Vinetia per la uia d'Alessandria, del quale, co me che sene ritroui assai del falsificato: nondimeno dell'ottimo anchora, & del puro, & sincero se ne uede. Errò mani festamente Mesue commemorando l'Opoponaco, nel descriuere la sua origine, nel primo fronte del capitolo: imperoche in differentemente fece egli una mistura di tutti Panaci, de i quali i due ultimi, l'Asclepio cioè, e l'Chironio, non si ci mostra no, ne manco si ci portano in Italia. I cognomi de i quali (secondo che dicono) hanno hauto l'origine dai loro inuentori: Im peroche l'Asclepio ritronò Esculapio, il Chironio Chirone, & l'Heracleo Hercole, & imperò chiamato anchora Hercu leo, del quale è solamente in uso il liquore chiamato Opoponaco. Il seme, & la radice (quantunque ci fussero assai necessa rie) non ci si portano. Et però i diligenti chirurgici per ricoprire l'ossa, con gran diligenza cauano per far polucre di quei frammenti delle radici, quali eglino si seno, che si ritrouano nella gomma condensata. Scrissene Galeno al. viij. delle fa coltà de i Semplici in questo modo dicendo. L'Opoponaco si fa di quel Panace, che si chiama Heraclio, tagliandosi le sue ra dici, & parimente il fusto. E' l'Opoponaco ueramente attissimo à molte cose per esser egli calefattiuo, mollificatiuo, & di gestiuo: è caldo nel terzo ordine, & secco nel secondo. E' similmente la corteccia della radice calida, & secca: ma però meno del succhio, con ilche ha ella anchora dell'aftersiuo alquanto. Et però l'usiamo all'ossa discoperte, & all'ulcere ma ligne, & contumaci: imperoche queste tali cose generano sufficientemente la carne diseccando, & astringendo insieme, & non scaldando troppo forte. Ilche è tutto necessario per generare la carne, come hauiamo dimostrato ne i libri di curare i
B morbi. Il frutto è caldo anch'esso, & molto commodo per prouocare i mestrui. Solue l'Opoponaco (secondo che riferisce Mesue) la flemma grossa, & uiscosa dalle parti piu remote del corpo, & propriamente dalle giunture, & mondifica il uer uello, & i nerui, giouando molto alle loro frigide malattie.

Del Ligustico. Cap. liij.

IL Ligustico, il quale chiamano alcuni Panacea, & altri Panace, nasce abondan tissimo in Liguria, ondes'ha preso il nome, nel monte Apennino, che termina con le Alpi. Chiamanlo non fuor di proposito i paesani Panace, per esser egli ueramente nel fusto, nelle radici, & parimente nelle uirtu sue simile al panace heracleotico. Nasce in monti altissimi, asperi, & ombrosi, & massime appresso oue risor gono l'acque. Produce il fusto sottile simile all'anetho, nodoso, attorno al quale son frondi simili al meliloto, ma piu tenere, & piu molli, odorate, uerso la cima piu sottili, & molto piu
C diuise. Ha nella sommità del bastoneuna ombrella, nella quale è il seme nero, duro, lunghet to, come quel del finocchio, di sapore acuto, & aromatico. E' la sua radice bianca, simile à quella del panace heracleotico, & odorata. Hanno il seme, & le radici uirtu di scaldare, & di digerire: giouano à i dolori dell'interiora, & alla digestione, & parimente alle uentosità del stomacho, & à i morsi dei uelenosi animali: beute prouocano l'orina, & similmente i me strui. Ilche fa la radice applicata disotto. Mettonsil seme, & le radici ne gli oxipori, & nelle medicine digestiue: è aggradeuole alla bocca, & imperò l'usano quei di Liguria nelle ui uande in cambio di pepe. Sophisticasi con un seme, ilqual gli è molto simile, ma si conosce per esser amaro. Alcuni lo sophisticano mettendogli dentro seme di finocchio, & di seseli.
S Ognansi ueramente coloro, che si pensano, che'l uero Ligustico chiamato da Galeno Libistico, sia quella pianta te nuta in piu luoghi ne gli horti, d'acuto, & graue odore, che uolgarmente si chiama Leuistico: Imperoche questo non si ritroua nascere senon domestico ne gli horti. Produce il fusto altissimo, concauo, & grosso, et non sottile, co me dice Dioscoride del suo. Le frondi non sono in modo alcuno di mellodo, ma intagliate come quelle dell'Apio, quan tunque piu grosse, & assai maggiori. Il seme, come che si rassembri alquàto al finocchio: nondimeno nò è egli saldo ne aro matico, anzi frangibile, & squamoso. Il uero adunque Ligustico, quantunque à Genoua, et per tutta la Liguria, ondes'ha preso il nome, sia abondantissimo, & usato il seme uolgarmente ne i condimenti de i cibi: nondimeno non si porta publicamen te per il resto d'Italia, lo l'ho piu uolte ricolto ne i piu alti monti della ualle Anania, & del contado di Goritia, doue na
D sce il Ligustico abondantissimo: & in Vinetia si puo egli uedere nel ualghissimo giardino dell'Eccellentissimo messer Map heo di Maphei medico Vinetiano. Fecene breuemente memoria Galeno al. vij. delle facultà de semplici cosi dicendo. La radice, e'l seme del Libistico sono di quelle cose, che scaldano di modo, che prouocano i mestrui, & l'orina, & risoluono le uentosità.

Della Pastinaca saluatica. Cap. ltiij.

A la Pastinaca saluatica frondi di gingidio, ma piu larghe, & amarette: il fusto dritto, & ruuido, nella cui sommità è una ombrella simile à quella dell'anetho: i cui fiori son bianchi, nel mezo de i quali è un certo che di porporeggiante, & di colore di zaffarano. Produce la radice grossa un dito, lunga un palmo, et odo rata:

A it is called in the apothecaries' shops Opoponax: Because this is brought to Venice by way of Alexandria, of which, although much adulterated is to be found, nevertheless the finest, pure and genuine is also seen. Mesue was plainly wrong in recalling Opoponax in describing its origin, at the beginning of the chapter: for he indiscriminately made a mixture of all the Panaces, of which the last two, namely the Asclepian and the Chironian, are not shown to us here, nor are they brought into Italy. The surnames of these (as they say) took their origin from their inventors: For the Asclepian was found by Aesculapius, the Chironian by Chiron, and the Heraclean by Hercules, and therefore also called Herculean, of which only the liquor called Opoponax is in use. The seed and the root (though they would be quite necessary) are not brought here. And therefore diligent surgeons, in order to cover bones, carefully extract from those fragments of the roots, whatever they may be, that are found in the condensed gum, to make powder. Galen wrote of it in book eight of On the Faculties of Simples, saying thus: Opoponax is made from that Panax called Heraclian, by cutting its roots and likewise its stalk. Opoponax is truly most suitable for many things, for it is warming, softening, and digestive: it is hot in the third degree and dry in the second. The bark of the root is likewise warm and dry, but somewhat less so than the juice, with which it also has something of a cleansing quality. And therefore we use it on exposed bones and on malignant and stubborn ulcers: because such things sufficiently generate flesh by drying and binding together, and not heating too strongly. All of which is entirely necessary for generating flesh, as we have shown in the books on the cure of
B diseases. The fruit is also warm, and very useful for promoting the menses. Opoponax (according to Mesue) resolves thick and viscous phlegm from the more remote parts of the body, and especially from the joints, and cleanses the brain and the nerves, greatly benefiting their cold diseases.

Of Ligusticum. Chapter 53.

Ligusticum, which some call Panacea and others Panax, grows most abundantly in Liguria, from whence it takes its name, on the Apennine mountains, which border the Alps. The country people not unreasonably call it Panax, because it is truly similar in its stalk, roots, and likewise in its virtues to the Heraclean panax. It grows on very high mountains, rough and shady, and especially near where waters spring forth. It produces a slender stalk similar to dill, knotted, around which are leaves similar to melilot, but more tender and softer, fragrant, toward the top more slender and much more
C divided. At the top of the stalk it has an umbel, in which is the seed, black, hard, somewhat long, like that of fennel, of sharp and aromatic flavor. Its root is white, similar to that of Heraclean panax, and fragrant. The seed and roots have the virtue of warming and digesting: they help the pains of the internal organs and digestion, and likewise the flatulence of the stomach, and the bites of venomous animals: drunk, they promote urine and likewise the menses. The root applied below does the same. The seed and roots are put into oxymels and digestive medicines: it is agreeable to the mouth, and therefore those of Liguria use it in their food in place of pepper. It is adulterated with a seed very similar to it, but which is recognized by being bitter. Some adulterate it by putting in fennel seed and seseli.
S Let those be rebuked who think that the true Ligusticum called by Galen Libisticum is that plant kept in many gardens, of sharp and strong odor, which is commonly called Lovage: because this is found to grow only as a cultivated plant in gardens. It produces a very tall, hollow, and thick stalk, and not a slender one, as Dioscorides says of his. The leaves are not at all like melilot, but cut like those of Alexanders, though thicker and much larger. The seed, though it somewhat resembles fennel: nevertheless it is not firm nor aromatic, but rather fragile and scaly. The true Ligusticum, therefore, although in Genoa and throughout all Liguria, where it takes its name, it is most abundant, and the seed is commonly used in condiments for food: nevertheless it is not publicly sold in the rest of Italy. I have gathered it many times on the highest mountains of the valley of Anania and in the territory of Gorizia, where
D Ligusticum grows most abundantly: and in Venice it can be seen in the most excellent garden of the distinguished Messer Mapheo de' Maphei, Venetian physician. Galen made brief mention of it in book seven of On the Faculties of Simples, saying thus: The root and seed of Libisticum are among those things which warm in such a way as to promote the menses and urine, and resolve flatulence.

Of the Wild Parsnip. Chapter 54.

The wild parsnip has leaves like gingidium but wider and somewhat bitter: the stalk is straight and rough, at the top of which is an umbel similar to that of dill, whose flowers are white, in the middle of which there is something of a purplish and saffron color. It produces a root as thick as a finger, a hand's length long, and fragrant:

rata, laqual cotta è buona da mangiare. Il seme beuto, ouero applicato disotto prouoca i mestrui: gioua parimente beuto à chi non puo orinare, à gl'hidropici, & à i dolori del costastato: uale à i morsi, & alle punture de i uelenosi animali. Dicono, che coloro, che lo mangiano da prima non possono esser offesi dalle serpi: aita à far ingrauidare. Prouoca parimente la radice l'orina, & sauorisce à i uenerei appetiti: applicata disotto fa partorire. Le frondi trite con mele, et applicate mondisicano l'ulcere corrosiue. La domestica è migliore da mangiare, che la saluatica, et è utile alle medesime cose, quantunque nò sia ella così ualorofa.

Ono le Pastinache tanto domestiche, quanto saluatiche uolgarissime in Italia, delle quali si mangiano ne i cibi le
S radici saporatamente la quaresima. Ma pche forse in Francia le domestiche non si seminano: pensossi il Ruellio, che
fussero le Pastinache domestiche quelle, che noi chiamamo Carote, & che usiamo il uerno cotte per l'insalate. Del
che non posso se non marauigliarmi, pensandomi che'l Ruellio huomo ueramente dotto non considerasse, che nessuno authore di qual si uoglia fattione scritrroua, che le Pastinache domestiche hauessero la radice porporea, et sanguinosa, essendo una delle piu notabili parti, che era dibisogno di manifestare. Del qual errore danno manifesto indutole uere domestiche, che abondantissime si coltiuano per tutta Italia per la quaresima ne gli horti, bianchissime, & saporite. Oltre à ciò s'ingannano manifestamente tutti coloro, che prendono per il Dauco il seme della Pastinaca saluatica, di quella dico, che produce nel mezzo della sua ombrella quel picciol fiore di color di porpora. Percioche altra cosa è il Dauco, come poco qui disotto al proprio luogo diremo, doue tre spetie ne notò Dioscoride, & quantunque, per quello che se ne uegga scriuto, & da lui, & parimente da Galeno ne i libri de i semplici, & delle facoltà de gli alimenti, sieno quasi queste due piante d'una medesima qualità, & uirtu, per la qual ragione si potrebbero l'uno per l'altro adoperare; non timeno questa ragione non conclude però, che'l Dauco, & la Pastinaca saluatica sieno una cosa medesima. Scriuene Galeno al. vij. delle facultà de i semplici così dicendo. La Pastinaca domestica è meno ualorofa, come che piu potente in tutte le sue operationi sia la saluatica. Prouoca l'orina, & i mestrui non solamente l'herba; ma grandemente il seme, & la radice. Ha ueramente in se alquanto dell'aftersiuo. Et però n'impiastrano alcuni le frondi con mele in su l'ulcere corrosiue per mondificarle.

Del Seseli Massiliense. Cap. lv.

A il Seseli Massiliense le frondi simili, & piu grasse del finocchio: il fusto piu grosso, & l'ombrella simile all'anetho, nella quale è il seme quadrato, lungo, & al gusto subito acuto: la sua radice è lunga, & odorata. Scaldano le radici, e'l seme, & beonsi utilmente alle distillationi dell'orina, & à i difetti del rispirare. Giouano alle presocationi della madrice, & al mal caduco: prouocano i mestrui, e'l parto: uagliono à tutti i difetti dell'interiora: sanano la tosse uecchia. Il seme beuto con uino corrobora la digestione, & caccia uia i dolori di corpo: è utile à quelle febbri, che chiamano epiale. Beono lo i uiandanti contra al freddo con uino, & con pepe. Dassi alle capre, & à tutti gli altri bestiami, accioche ageuolmente partorlschino.

Del Seseli Ethiopico. Cap. lvi.

L Seseli Ethiopico cresce con frondi d'hedera, ma minori, & lunghettte, come quelle del periclimeno. E' pianta, che nereggia: produce i sarmenti lunghi due gombiti, da i quali escono i rami lunghi due spanne: la sommità si rassembra all'anetho. Il seme è denso, come quello del grano, nero, amaro, piu odorato, & piu acuto del Massiliense, & molto soaue.

Del Seseli del Peloponneso. Cap. lvij.

L Seseli, che nasce nel Peloponneso, produce le frondi di cicuta, ma piu sarghe, & piu grasse: il fusto piu grande del Massiliense, ferulaceo, & largo: nella cui cima è una larga ombrella, dalla quale pende il seme piu largo, odorato, & piu pieno. Ha le uirtu medesime. Nasce in luoghi aspri, humidi, & in su le colline: nasce anchora nelle Isole.

Del Tordilo, cioè Seseli Cretico. Cap. lviiij

L Tordilo, il qual chiamano alcuni Seseli Cretico, nasce nel monte Amano appresso à Cilicia. E' herba breue, ma ramosa: produce il seme doppio, tondo, si-

rata, which when cooked is good to eat. The seed, drunk or applied below, stimulates menstruation; it likewise benefits those who cannot urinate, those with dropsy, and those with pains in the side: it is useful against the bites and stings of venomous animals. They say that those who eat it first cannot be harmed by serpents; it also helps in becoming pregnant. The root likewise promotes urination and stimulates venereal appetites; applied below it induces childbirth. The leaves, pounded with honey and applied, cleanse corrosive ulcers. The cultivated variety is better for eating than the wild, and it is useful for the same purposes, even though it is not as potent.

Both the cultivated and wild parsnips are very common throughout Italy, and their roots are eaten with pleasure during Lent. But because perhaps in France the cultivated variety is not sown, Ruellius supposed that what we call Carrots were the cultivated parsnips, used in winter cooked for salads. I cannot but wonder at this, since Ruellius, a truly learned man, failed to consider that no author of any school records that the cultivated parsnip has a purple and blood-red root, which was one of the most notable features that needed to be noted. This error is plainly refuted by the true cultivated varieties, which are grown most abundantly throughout all of Italy during Lent in gardens, very white and tasty. Furthermore, all those who take the seed of the wild parsnip for Daucus are clearly mistaken — I mean that plant which produces in the middle of its umbel that small flower of purple color. For the Daucus is quite another thing, as we shall soon say in its proper place below, where Dioscorides noted three species; and although, from what is written by him as well as by Galen in the books on simples and on the properties of foods, these two plants seem to be of nearly the same quality and virtue, so that one might be used in place of the other, this reasoning does not prove that Daucus and the wild parsnip are one and the same thing. Galen writes about this in book seven of the Properties of Simples, saying: The cultivated parsnip is less potent, though in all its operations the wild is more powerful. It promotes urination and menstruation not only through the herb but greatly through the seed and the root. It has in itself something of an astringent quality. And therefore some apply the leaves pounded with honey on corrosive ulcers to cleanse them.

On Seseli of Massilia. Chapter 55.

The Seseli of Massilia has leaves similar to, and rather broader than, fennel; its stalk is thicker, and its umbel similar to dill, in which the seed is square, long, and immediately sharp to the taste; its root is long and fragrant. The roots and seed when warmed and drunk are useful for urinary problems and breathing difficulties. They help with uterine suffocations and epilepsy; they stimulate menstruation and childbirth; they benefit all internal complaints and cure chronic coughs. The seed drunk with wine strengthens digestion and drives away bodily pains; it is useful against those fevers called ephialtic. Travelers drink it with wine and pepper against the cold. It is given to goats and all other livestock so that they may give birth easily.

On Seseli of Ethiopia. Chapter 56.

The Seseli of Ethiopia grows with leaves like ivy, but smaller and somewhat elongated, like those of honeysuckle. It is a plant that appears dark; it produces stems two cubits long, from which branch out shoots two spans long; the top resembles dill. The seed is dense, like that of grain, black, bitter, more fragrant, and more pungent than that of Massilia, and very pleasant.

On Seseli of the Peloponnese. Chapter 57.

The Seseli that grows in the Peloponnese produces leaves like hemlock, but broader and thicker; its stalk is larger than that of Massilia, resembling fennel-giant, and wide; at its summit is a broad umbel, from which hangs a seed that is broader, fragrant, and fuller. It has the same virtues. It grows in rough, humid places and on hillsides; it also grows on islands.

On Tordilo, that is, Cretan Seseli. Chapter 58.

Tordilo, which some call Cretan Seseli, grows on Mount Amanus near Cilicia. It is a short but branching herb; it produces a double, round seed, si-

Hiamano gli Arabici il Seseli Sifileos, & uolgarmente gli spetiali Siler montino. Nasce il buono, & uero Seseli
C copiosissimo per tutti monti del Trentino. Ma quantunque in assai spetiarie si ne ritrovi di buono; nondimeno
molte altre n'ho uisto io di quello, che non corrisponde in conto alcuno di queste spetie scritte da Dio-
scoride: Imperoche non ui si sente altro, che amaritudine, & un certo odoraccio, come di cinici. L'Ethiopico, quello del
Peloponneso, & quello, che nasce in Cilicia chiamato Tordilo, per non si portare à i tmpi nostri in Italia, non è che i
sappi mostrare. Tanto la radice, quanto il seme del Seseli (diceua Galeno al. vij. delle facoltà de semplici, non facendo di-
stintione alcuna delle sue spetie) scaldano cosi forte, che possono valorosamente prouocar l'orina, & sono cosi di sottili
parti, che giouano al mal caduco, & à gl'impedimenti del rispirare. Credesi, che sia il seseli stato ritrouato dalle Cerne.
Peroche, come dice Aristotele al. v. cap. del. ix. libro della natura de gli animali, le Cerue subito dopo il parto mangia-
B no il Seseli, per tornare à ringrauidarsi.

Del Sisone. Cap Ix.

L Sisone è un picciol seme, che nasce in Soria, simile al'apio, lungo, nero, & al
gusto seruente. Beesi per i difetti della melza, per l'orina ritenuta, & per prouo-
care i mestrui. Vsanlo le genti di quei luoghi per condimento delle zucche lesse
inseme con aceto. Produce nelle sommità molte piccicle granella.
L Sisone, secondo che qui recita Dioscoride, è un seme, che nasce in Soria à noi del tutto incognito: perciò-
I che nissun a nota della pianta, che'l produce, se ne legge. Et però lo lasciaremo ir Soria, tenendolo tra quelle cose,
che non si conoscono in Italia.

Dell'Aniso. Cap Ix.

C O Aniso in somma scalda, & disecca: fa buon fiato, alleggerisce i dolori, prouoca
l'orina, risolue l'hidropisia, toglie la sete, è buono à i morsi, et alle punture de iue-
lenosi animali. Gioua alle uentosità: ristagna il flusso del corpo, & de i mestrui
bianchi delle donne: genera il latte nelle poppe, & fortifica al coito. Fattone pro-
fumo al naso alleggerisce i dolori di testa. Medica le percosse dell'crecchie prima trito con
oglio rosado, & poscia distillatoui. Il migliore è sèpre quello, che è fresco, pieno, nò sèmbolo
so, et che è odorifero. Lodasi il primo in bontà quel di Cadia, et dopo questo quel d'Egitto.
Aniso è uolgarissima pianta, & parimente molto uolgare è il suo seme: & imperò non accade à recitar ne qui al-
L' tra historia, quantunque per non preterire il nostro ordine, non sia da tacere questo, che ne scrisse Galeno al. vi.
delle facoltà de semplici, cosi dicendo. Il seme dell'Aniso è molto utile, acuto, & amaretto, di modo che s'ac-
costa alla natura di quelle cose, che brusciano. E' calido, & secco nel terzo ordine, & percio prouoca l'orina, dige-
risce, & risolue la uentosità del corpo.

Del Caro. Cap. lxi.

D L Caro è uolgarissimo seme. Scalda, prouoca l'orina: è stomachale, fa buona
bocca, aita alla digestione. Mettesi utilmente ne gli anidoti, & ne gli oxipori.
Corrisponde proportionalmente con l'aniso. Mangiasi la sua radice cotta, co-
me le pastinache.
Hiamasi il Caro uolgarmente nelle Spetiarie Carui: è seme notissimo per tutto. Nasce ne i prati, & nelle colline.
H E' il suo seme assai in uso appresso à i Tedeschi per metter nel pane, & in assai lor condimenti de cibi, come so-
no gli anesi à noi Thoscani. E' il Caro, per quanto testifica Galeno al. vij. dell. facoltà de semplici, quasi cali-
do, & secco nel terzo ordine, & mediocremente acuto: & però risolue le uentosità, & prouoca l'orina non solamen-
te il seme; ma anchora l'herba.

Dell'Anetho. Cap. lxij.

A dicottione delle frondi secche, & del seme dell'Anetho, beuta fa ritornare il
latte: risolue le uentosità, & leua i dolori del corpo: ristagna il corpo, et parimen-
te i uomiti: prouoca l'orina, alleggerisce il singhiozzo. Beuta cotidianamente
nuoce

242 LIBRO

A [Seseli is] similar to shields, aromatic, and somewhat sharp. Drunk, it provokes retained urine and menstruation.
The juice pressed from the stem and from the seeds when green, drunk with raisin wine for ten days at a weight of three obols, heals pains of the kidneys. The root mixed with honey in the form of an electuary facilitates expectoration in chest ailments.
The Arabs call Seseli "Sifileos," and apothecaries commonly call it Siler montino. The good and true Seseli grows most abundantly throughout the mountains of Trentino. But although one can find good specimens in many apothecaries, I have nonetheless seen much of it that does not correspond in any way to the species described by Dioscorides: for one tastes nothing in it but bitterness and a certain foul odor, like that of bedbugs. The Ethiopian variety, that of the Peloponnese, and that which grows in Cilicia called Tordilo, since they are not brought to our times in Italy, are not such that I can display them. Both the root and the seed of Seseli (said Galen in book vii of the Faculties of Simple Medicines, making no distinction among its species) heat so strongly that they can powerfully provoke urine, and are of such fine parts that they help with epilepsy and with impediments of breathing. It is believed that Seseli was discovered by hinds. For, as Aristotle says in chapter v of book ix of the Nature of Animals, hinds immediately after giving birth eat Seseli in order to become pregnant again.

Of Sisone. Chapter 9.

Sisone is a small seed that grows in Syria, similar to apium, long, black, and hot to the taste. It is drunk for ailments of the spleen, for retained urine, and to provoke menstruation. The people of those places use it as a seasoning for boiled squash together with vinegar. It produces many small grains at its tips.
Sisone, according to what Dioscorides recounts here, is a seed that grows in Syria and is entirely unknown to us: for no description of the plant that produces it is found in any text. We will therefore leave it in Syria, counting it among those things that are unknown in Italy.

Of Anise. Chapter 9.

Anise in sum heats and dries: it makes the breath fresh, relieves pains, provokes urine, resolves dropsy, quenches thirst, is good against bites and stings of venomous animals. It helps with flatulence: it checks the flux of the body and the white menstrual discharge of women: it generates milk in the breasts, and strengthens for coitus. Made into a fumigation at the nose it relieves headaches. It treats injuries to the ears when first crushed with rose oil and then distilled into them. The best is always that which is fresh, full, not wormy, and fragrant. First in quality is that of Cadia, and after it that of Egypt.
Anise is a very common plant, and its seed likewise very common: and therefore there is no need to recount further history here, although so as not to omit our proper order, one should not pass over in silence what Galen wrote of it in book vi of the Faculties of Simple Medicines, saying thus: The seed of Anise is very useful, sharp, and slightly bitter, in such a way that it approaches the nature of those things that burn. It is hot and dry in the third degree, and therefore provokes urine, digests, and resolves flatulence of the body.

Of Caraway. Chapter 61.

Caraway is a very common seed. It heats, provokes urine: it is stomachic, freshens the breath, aids digestion. It is usefully placed in antidotes and in oxymels. It corresponds proportionally with anise. Its root is eaten cooked, like parsnips.
Caraway is commonly called Carui in the apothecaries: it is a seed very well known everywhere. It grows in meadows and on hillsides. Its seed is much used among the Germans for putting in bread, and in many of their food seasonings, as anise is among us Tuscans. Caraway, as Galen testifies in book vii of the Faculties of Simple Medicines, is nearly hot and dry in the third degree, and moderately sharp: and therefore it resolves flatulence and provokes urine not only through the seed but also through the herb.

Of Dill. Chapter 62.

A decoction of the dried leaves and seed of Dill, drunk, brings back milk: it resolves flatulence and relieves pains of the body: it checks the bowels, and likewise vomiting: it provokes urine, relieves hiccups. Drunk daily it harms

TERZO. 243

nuoce al uedere, & difecca la sperma. E utile per sederui dentro le donne per i difetti della A
madrice. La cenere del seme dell'Anetho impiaftrata risolue le pofteme del sedere.

Anetho è ne gli horti uolgarissima pianta, tanto simile al finocchio, che spesse uolte, se'l gusto non ne fusse il giudice, ui s'inganarebbe l'occhio. Scalda tanto l'Anetho (diceus Galeno al. vi. delle facoltà de i semplici) che ueramente è da stimar caldo nell'ultimo del secondo grado, oueramente nel principio del terzo, & secco nella fine del primo, oueramente nel principio del secondo: & imperò meritamente cotto nell'oglio digerisce, leua i dolori, fa dormire, & matura i crudi homori. Fassi dell'Anetho oglio: la cui temperatura saria propinqua à quei medicamenti, che maturano, & generano la marcia, se la non fusse alquanto piu di quelli calida, & sottile, & percio digestiua. Bruciandosi l'Anetho diuenta calido, & secco nel terzo ordine: & imperò giuua egli all'ulcere, che son troppo humide, & molli, & massimamente à quelle, che sono ne i membri genitali, & che sono inuecchiate nel preputo, facendole benissimo saldare. Il uerde è piu humido, & manco calido, & però piu matura, & manco digerisce. Prouoca il sonno, la onde l'usarono gli antichi nelle ghirlande.

Del Cimino domestico. Cap. lxiij.

IL Cimino domestico è grato alla bocca: ma molto piu l'Ethiopico, ilqual chiamò Hippocrate regio. Tiene il secondo luogo di bontà l'Egittio, à cui son poscia dopo tutti gli altri. Nasce in Galatia d'Asia, in Cilicia, in Terentia, & in molte altre regioni. Scalda, strigne, et difecca. Cotto con oglio, et fattone crisieri, ouero impiaftrato di fuore con farina d'orzo, conferisce à i dolori, & alle uentosità di corpo. Dassi con aceto innacquato à i difetti del rispirare, & con uino contra à i morsi de uelenosi animali. Giouà impiaftrato con uua passa, ò farina di gioglio, ò saua franta, ouero cerato, alle posteme de i testicoli. Trito, & impiaftrato con aceto, & messo nel naso ui ristagna il sangue, & parimente applicato disotto i mestrui superflui. Beuto, ouero impiaftrato di fuore impallidisce tutto il corpo.

Del Cimino saluatico. Cap. lxiiij.

IL Cimino saluatico nasce ualoroso, & abondamente in Licia, Galatia d'Asia, & Carthagena di Spagna. E picciola pianta: produce il fusto lungo una spanna, sottile, su per ilquale son quattro, ouer cinque picciolse, & sottili frondi, dentate à modo di sega, & sfesse come quelle del gingidio. Ha oltra di questo in tima del fusto cinque, ouer sei bottoni teneri, & tondi, ne i quali è dentro il seme squamoso, piu acuto al gusto del domestico. Nasce nelle colline. Beesi il suo seme con acqua contra à i dolori, & uentosità di corpo, & con aceto al singozzo: beuto con uino giouà contra gli animali uelenosi, & parimente all'humidità dello stomacho. Masticato, et poscia applicato con mele, & uua passa, spegne i liuidi: & impiaftrato con le medesime cose giouà alle posteme de i testicoli. Enne pur di saluatico un'altra spetie simile al domestico, ilquale produce da ogni fiore un cornetto, nel quale è dentro un seme simile al melanthio, ilqual beuto è rimedio contra à i morsi delle uelenose serpi. Giouà oltre à cio à distillatione d'orina, alle pietre, & à coloro, che insieme con l'orina orinano il sangue appreso in pezzi: beendogli però sopra il seme dell'apio cotto.

L Cimino domestico è ueramente notissimo à ciascuno. Ma le due spetie del saluatico non si ritroua chi à i tempi D
I nostri ce le mostri in Italia, per non si ci portare di Licia, di Galatia, & di Spagna, doue nasce abondantissimo. Il domestico produce le frondi quasi simili al finocchio, & è un sol fusto, dal quale nascono diuersi ramuscelli. Fiorisce in ombrella, come il finocchio, nella quale si matura poscia copiosissimo il seme. Ha la radice bianca, quasi ritonda, nella superficie della terra. Ama luoghi putrescibili, & caldi, & imperò assai abondantemente fruttifica nelle nostre maremme di Siena, & parimente nel patrimonio di Roma. Vsasi il seme suo, secondo che testifica Galeno al. vij. delle facoltà de i semplici, come quello de gli anesi, de i carui, del ligustico, & del petroselino: Imperoche è egli calido, come ciascuno di quelli nel fare orinare, & risoluere le uentosità. E di quelle cose, che scaldano nel terzo grado.

Dell'Ammi. Cap. lxv.

CHiamano alcuni l'Ammi Cimino ethiopico, & alcuni si credono, che sia tra loro differenza. E seme uolgare, & noto, minuto, & molto minore del cimino: ha

translation:
THIRD BOOK. 243

It harms the sight and dries up the semen. It is useful for women to sit over it for disorders of the womb. The ash of Aneth seed, applied as a plaster, resolves abscesses of the seat.

Aneth is a very common garden plant, so similar to fennel that one would often mistake it by eye, were it not for the taste. Aneth is heating (as Galen says in Book VI of the Simples) to such a degree that it must be considered hot in the last degree of the second grade, or at the beginning of the third, and dry at the end of the first, or at the beginning of the second. Therefore, when properly cooked in oil, it aids digestion, relieves pain, promotes sleep, and ripens crude humors. An oil is made from Aneth whose temperature would be close to those medicines that ripen and generate matter, were it not somewhat hotter and thinner than those, and thus digestive. When burned, Aneth becomes hot and dry in the third degree, and thus it benefits ulcers that are too moist and soft, especially those in the genital members and those grown old in the foreskin, causing them to close up very well. The green plant is more moist and less hot, and therefore ripens more but digests less. It promotes sleep, which is why the ancients used it in garlands.

On Domestic Cumin. Chapter 63.

Domestic cumin is pleasant to the mouth, but much more so is the Ethiopian kind, which Hippocrates called royal. Egyptian cumin holds second place in quality, followed after it by all the others. It grows in Galatia of Asia, in Cilicia, in Terentia, and in many other regions. It warms, binds, and dries. Cooked in oil and made into clysters, or plastered externally with barley flour, it relieves pains and flatulence of the body. Given with diluted vinegar, it helps disorders of breathing, and with wine it counters the bites of venomous animals. Applied as a plaster with raisins, or with darnel flour, or with crushed beans, or with wax ointment, it benefits abscesses of the testicles. Ground and plastered with vinegar, and placed in the nose, it stops bleeding; and likewise applied below, it checks excessive menstruation. Drunk, or plastered externally, it causes the whole body to turn pale.

On Wild Cumin. Chapter 64.

Wild cumin grows vigorously and abundantly in Lycia, Galatia of Asia, and Cartagena in Spain. It is a small plant, producing a stem one span long, slender, along which grow four or five small, thin, saw-toothed leaves, similar to those of gingidium. Beyond this, at the top of the stem it has five or six small, tender, round buds, inside which is a scaly seed, sharper in taste than the domestic kind. It grows on hillsides. Its seed is drunk with water against pains and flatulence of the body, and with vinegar against hiccoughs; drunk with wine it benefits against venomous animals, and likewise against moisture of the stomach. Chewed and then applied with honey and raisins, it disperses bruises; and plastered with the same things it benefits abscesses of the testicles. There is also another variety of wild cumin similar to the domestic, which produces from each flower a small horn, inside which is a seed resembling nigella; this, when drunk, is a remedy against the bites of venomous serpents. It also helps with dripping of urine, with kidney stones, and for those who pass blood mixed with their urine when urinating, though one should drink it over cooked celery seed.

Domestic cumin is truly well known to everyone. But the two varieties of wild cumin are not to be found shown to us in Italy in our time, as they are not brought here from Lycia, Galatia, or Spain, where they grow most abundantly. The domestic kind produces leaves almost similar to fennel, and has a single stem from which various small branches arise. It flowers in an umbel, like fennel, in which the seed then ripens very copiously. It has a white root, almost round, at the surface of the earth. It loves putrid and warm places, and therefore bears fruit very abundantly in our marshlands of Siena, and likewise in the patrimony of Rome. Its seed is used, as Galen testifies in Book VII of the Simples, like that of anise, caraway, lovage, and parsley; for it is hot, like each of those, in promoting urination and resolving flatulence. It is among those things that heat in the third degree.

On Ammi. Chapter 65.

Some call Ammi Ethiopian cumin, and some believe there is a difference between them. It is a common, well-known seed, tiny and much smaller than cumin: it has

A firmità de gli occhi, & massime le muuolette, le cicatrici, & le caligini. Beuto al peso di due oboli nell'aceto inacquato, purgail corpo, & nel uino utile à i morsi delle serpi. Alche si beono anchora le frondi trite, e'l fusto, impiastr.anstinsu le ferite, & in su le punture de gli scorpioni. Ma contra al trafuggere di quei ragni, che si chiamano phalangi, giouano con uino, & aceto. Contrapongonsi parimente anchora à gli altri ueleni, eccetto quelli, che strangolano, ouero quelli, che nuocono alla ulsiga. il succhio giouà all'orina ritenuta, fa dormire, spegne il fuoco di uenere, rinfresca, purga lo stomacho, & aumenta il sangue.

Dell'Apio. Cap. lxix.

LA herba dell'Apio domestico de gli horti è conueneuole à tutte quelle cose, che si conuiene il coriandro. Impiastrasi con pane, & polenta all'infiammagioni de gli occhi: mitiga gli ardori dello stomacho: risolue le durezze delle poppe causate dal latte appreso. Mangiata cruda, & parimente cotta ne i cibi, fa orinare. La dì cottione delle frondi, & delle radici beuta, è contraria à i udeni, prouocando il uomito: ristagna il corpo. Il seme prouoca l'orina piu ualorosamente: giouà à i ueleni delle serpi, & à coloro, che hauessero beuta la spuma dell'argento: risolue le uentosità. Mettesi ne i medicamenti, che mitigano i dolori, nelle theriache, & ne i rimedij, che si fanno contra la tosse.

Dell'Eleoselino, cioè Apio palustre. Cap. lxx.

NAsce l'Apio palustre in luoghi humidi, piu grande del domestico, à cui è in ogni cosa parimente ualoroso.

Dell'Oreoselino, cioè Apio montano. Cap. lxxi.

LO Apio montano fa il fusto alto una spanna, che nasce da picciola radice: attorno alquale sono i ramuscelli, nelle cui sommità produce certi piccioli capi simili à quelli de papaueri, ma molto piu piccioli, ne i quali si riserra il seme lungo, acuto, sottile, & odorato, simile al camino: nasce nei monti, in luoghi sassosi. Il seme, & la radice beuti nel uino prouocano l'orina: prouoca i mestrui. Mettesi ne gli antidoti, ne i medicamenti, che fanno orinare, & in quelli, che ualorosamente scaldano. Ma è d'auuertire, che non ci ingannassemo, stimando che questo Apio fusse quello, che nasce tra sassi chiamato petroselino.

Del Petroselino. Cap. lxxij.

IL Petroselino nasce in Macedonia, in luoghi precipitosi. Produce il seme simile all'ammi, ma piu odorato, di sapore acuto, & aromatico. Prouoca l'orina, et i mestrui: giouà alle uentosità, & dolori colici, & parimente stomachali. Conferisce beuto à i dolori del costato, delle reni, & della ulsiga. Mettesi ne i medicamenti, che si compongono per prouocare l'orina.

D Dell'Hipposelino. Cap. lxxiiij.

CHiamano i Latini l'Hipposelino Olusatro, altri lo domandano Smirnio, quantunque sia egli propriamente altra pianta differente dallo Smirnio, come poco di sotto diremo. E' maggiore, & piu bianco dell'Apio de gli horti: produce il fusto alto, di dentro uacuo, tenero, segnato da alcune linee: le frondi piu larghe, & rossigne. La chioma fa egli simile al rosmarino, piena di fiori, & raccolta insieme, auanti che sfiorisce, à modo de corimbi: il seme nero lungo, saldo, acuto, & aromatico. Fa la radice sottile, bianca, odorata, & aggradeuolè alla bocca. Nasce in luoghi ombrosi, & appresso à i palu di. Mangiasi ne gli herbaggi, come l'apio, & parimente si mangia la sua radice cruda, & cotta: mangiansi anchora cotte per se sole le frondi, e'l fusto, & preparate col pesce, ouero condite crude con salamuoia. Il suo melato prouoca i mestrui: beuto anchora, & impiastrato scalda coloro, che tremano per il freddo: uale alle distillationi dell'orina. Questi medesimi effetti fa anchora la radice.

246 BOOK

A ailments of the eyes, and especially cataracts, scars, and dimness of vision. Drunk at a weight of two oboli in diluted vinegar, it purges the body; and in wine it is useful against serpent bites. The crushed leaves and the stalk are also applied as poultices on wounds and on scorpion stings. Against the bites of those spiders called phalangi, they are helpful with wine and vinegar. They are likewise applied against other poisons, except those that cause strangulation or harm the bladder. The juice is good for urinary retention, induces sleep, quenches the fire of lust, refreshes, purges the stomach, and increases the blood.

On Celery. Chapter 69.

The herb of garden celery is suitable for all the same uses as coriander. Applied as a poultice with bread and polenta, it treats inflammations of the eyes; it eases the burning of the stomach and resolves the hardness of the breasts caused by curdled milk. Eaten raw, and likewise cooked in food, it promotes urination. A decoction of the leaves and roots, when drunk, is harmful to the kidneys, provoking vomiting; it also constipates the body. The seed promotes urination more powerfully; it is good against serpent venoms and against those who have drunk silver foam; it resolves flatulence. It is used in medicines that ease pain, in theriacs, and in remedies made against coughing.

On Marsh Celery, that is, Water Parsley. Chapter 70.

Marsh celery grows in humid places, larger than the garden variety, and is equally valuable in all respects.

On Mountain Celery, that is, Mountain Parsley. Chapter 71.

Mountain celery grows a stalk a hand's-breadth tall, rising from a small root, around which are small branches, at whose tips it produces certain small heads similar to those of poppies, but much smaller, in which the seed is enclosed — long, sharp, slender, and fragrant, similar to cumin. It grows in the mountains, in rocky places. The seed and root, drunk in wine, promote urination and bring on menstruation. It is used in antidotes, in medicines that promote urination, and in those that warm powerfully. One must be careful, however, not to confuse this celery with the one that grows among rocks, called petroselinum (parsley).

On Parsley. Chapter 72.

Parsley grows in Macedonia, in steep places. It produces seed similar to ammi, but more fragrant, sharp in flavor, and aromatic. It promotes urination and menstruation; it is helpful against flatulence, colic pains, and stomach ailments. Drunk, it relieves pains of the sides, kidneys, and bladder. It is used in medicines compounded to promote urination.

D On Horse-parsley. Chapter 74.

The Latins call Horse-parsley Olusatro; others call it Smirnio, although it is in fact a different plant from Smirnio, as we shall explain shortly below. It is larger and whiter than garden celery; it produces a tall stalk, hollow within, tender, marked by several lines, and with leaves that are broader and reddish. Its head resembles rosemary, full of flowers, and gathered together before flowering into corymb-like clusters; the seed is black, long, firm, sharp, and aromatic. It has a root that is slender, white, fragrant, and pleasant to taste. It grows in shady places and near marshes. It is eaten among pot-herbs like celery, and its root is likewise eaten raw and cooked; the leaves and stalk are also eaten cooked on their own, prepared with fish, or pickled raw in brine. Its juice promotes menstruation; drunk and applied as a poultice, it warms those who tremble from cold; it is good for urinary distillations. The root produces the same effects.

Dell'Elaphobosco. Cap.lxxv. A

THIRD BOOK. 249

On Elaphoboscum. Chapter 75. A

Elaphoboscum has a knotty stem, similar to fennel or rosemary. It produces leaves two fingers wide but much longer, like those of the terebinth, folded and somewhat rough. Its stem has many branches, which produce tufts similar to dill, and likewise the seed. The flowers incline toward yellow, and the root is three fingers long and only one thick, white, sweet, and good to eat. When the stem is tender, it is eaten like other herbs. The seed of Elaphoboscum is drunk with wine against serpent bites, because it is said that deer, by grazing on it, free themselves from such bites.

Although some make efforts to identify Elaphoboscum in Italy, the leaves that those plants produce do not correspond, being much cut and smooth; one should rather trust the account of Dioscorides than that of Pliny, who in chapter 22 of book 22 described it with leaves of hipposelinum and with corymbs, saying thus: Elaphoboscum has a fennel-like stem, one finger thick, whose seed hangs from the corymbs; its leaves in shape resemble olusatrum, but are not bitter. Considering this, Manardo of Ferrara said that Pliny was evidently mistaken in this passage. Ruellius says that few today know Elaphoboscum, even though it grows everywhere, and that the true one is what is commonly called in apothecaries' shops Gratia dei, which has given its name to an ointment in which it is used. This does not quite correspond with my understanding, if he means by Gratia dei the plant mentioned above in the chapter on hyssop, which is used throughout Italy's apothecary shops to make their ointment; for this is a plant similar to hyssop, not to fennel — which is why I cannot but believe that in France the Gratia dei is a different plant from ours, which perhaps agrees equally well with Elaphoboscum. Galen wrote briefly about it in book 6 of On the Faculties of Simple Medicines, saying: Elaphoboscum has the virtue of warming, being composed of fine parts, and also of drying in the second degree.

On Fennel. Chapter 76.

Fennel eaten as a herb, or its seed drunk with barley water, generates abundant milk. The decoction of its leaves, when drunk, stimulates urine, relieves pains in the kidneys and ailments of the bladder. Drunk with wine it helps against serpent bites; it stimulates menstruation; drunk with fresh water in fevers it eases nausea and burning of the stomach. Its roots, ground up and mixed with honey and then made into a poultice, heal dog bites. The juice pressed from the stem and leaves, then dried in the sun, is usefully employed in medicines prepared for defects of the eyes that impede sight. The juice is likewise usefully pressed for all these purposes from the green seed, from the branches, and from the roots at the first sprouting of the leaves. From fennel in western Iberia there distills a resin-like liquor; and so when it flowers, the peasants cut the stems in the middle and bring them near the fire, so that the liquor may more easily sweat out through the force of heat, and this liquor is much more valuable than the juice for medicines of the eyes.

On Wild Fennel. Chapter 77.

Wild fennel is large; it produces a seed similar to cachry. It has a fragrant root, which when drunk helps with distillations of the urine; applied below, it stimulates menstruation. The root and seed taken as a drink check the body's looseness, help against the bites of venomous serpents, break stones, and purge an overflow of bile. The decoction of its leaves when drunk generates very abundant milk and purges women in labor. There is another variety, which has long, slender, and narrow leaves and a round seed similar to coriander, sharp and fragrant. This has the virtue of warming and corresponds in its properties to the other already described, though in every respect it is less potent.

Fennel, both cultivated and wild, is a very well-known plant in Italy. The cultivated kind is sown at the beginning of spring, in the month of February, in sunny and somewhat rocky places, being no less pleasing to the taste in the seasoning of foods than it is valuable in medicine. According to Pliny, serpents have been ennobled by it, shedding their old age by tasting it and restoring their already dimmed eyesight to sharpest acuity — from which men learned that it is highly valuable for the eyes. The second variety of wild fennel described by Dioscorides, which produces a seed similar to coriander, I find no one in our time who can show it to us in Italy. Of fennel, Galen said in book...

A vij. delle facultà de semplici scalda cosi valorosamente, che merita d'eser connumerato tra quelle cose, che scaldano nel ter
zo ordine, & disseccano nel primo, & però genera il Finocchio il latte. Ilche non farebbe egli se fusse piu disseccatiuo.
Per laqual ragione aita à trabocco di fiele, prouoca l'orina, & similmente i mestrui. Oltre à do è uno altro Finocchio,
che per eser molto grande lo chiamano Hippomarathro, la cui radice, & seme piu valorosamente disseccano, che'l dome
stico, & però pare, che per questa ragione ristagnino il corpo, quantunque la facultà loro costrettiua non si ueggia ma
nifesta. Di questo non solamente la radice, ma anchor il seme è simile al Cachrij, & però può rompere le pietre, tenare
il trabocco di fiele, & prouocare i mestrui, & l'orina; ma non però generare il latte, come quello già detto di sopra.
Enne una altra spetie pur di grande. Il cui seme è acuto, & tondo, come i coriandoli, simile nelle sue operationi all'al
tro, quantunque non cosi sia egli valoroso.

Del Dauco. Cap.lxxviij.

B IL Dauco chiamano alcuni daucio. Quello, che nasce in Creti, fa le frondi simi
li al finocchio, ma minori, & più sottili: produce il fustó alto una spanna, l'om
brella simile al coriandro, il fior bianco, & bianco parimente il seme, acuto, pe
loso, & soauissimo da mangiare: è lunga la sua radice un palmo, & grossa un di
to: nasce in luoghi sassosi, & aprichi. Enne un'altra spetie simile all'apio saluatico, ruuido,
aromatico, & al gusto seruente. Il migliore di tutti è quello di Creti. Assegnasene anchora
una terza spetie, che fa le frondi simili al coriandro, i fiori bianchi, & la testa, e'l seme d'ane
tho: è la sua ombrella simile à quella delle pastinache, e'l seme lungo come di cimino. Il se
me di tutti ha uirtù di scaldare: prouoca l'orina, i mestrui, e'l parto: toglie i dolori di corpo,
mitiga la tosse uecchia: gioua beuto nel uino à i morsi di quei ragni, che si chiamano pha
langi: risolue le posteme impiastratoui suso. Dell'altre spetie è solamente in uso il seme: ma
del Cretico anchora la radice, la quale per presentaneo, & ualoroso rimedio si bee contra à
i morsi de uelenosi animali.

C Vantunque contendino alcuni, che'l Dauco, & la Pastinaca saluatica sieno una pianta medesima, io lendo che cosi
habbino inteso Galeno, & Paolo Egineta; non dimeno à me pare, che manifestamente s'ingannino. Imperoche
quantunque benissimo dir si possa, che sia ueramente il Dauco spetie di Pastinaca saluatica; nondimeno non è però
egli quella istessa pastinaca, della quale poco di sopra faceua mentione Dioscoride: percioche se per il Dauco, & per la Pasti
naca saluatica hauesse inteso una pianta medesima, non gli sarebbe certamente stato necessario scriuerne per due diuersi ca
pitoli. Et come che paia ad alcuni, che Galeno non faccia differenza dal Dauco alla Pastinaca saluatica; nò dimeno chi ben
considera, che ne trattò egli per due diuersi capitoli nel. vi. prima, & poscia nel. viij. libro, potrà ageuolmente accorgersi,
che errano Marcello Fiorentino, e'l Ruellio. Il cui errore manifesta Galeno istesso: peroche oltre all'hauergli trattato
del Dauco, & della Pastinaca saluatica come diuerse piante, per diuersi capitoli, chiarisce egli però nel. vi. libro, che quiui
intende solamente del Dauco, & non della Pastinaca, qui 'lo cosi dice. Il Dauco saluatico, il qual chiamano alcuni Pastinaca,
è meno idoneo ne i cibi del domestico. Le cui parole manifestamente dimostrano, che non Galeno, ma altri si crederono, che
fussero queste due piante una cosa medesima. Delche fa ampia fede esso Galeno per hauer poscia nel. viij. libro scritto parti
colarmente della Pastinaca, come di cosa differente dal Dauco. Et però diro io insieme con Dioscoride, che i Dauchi sono di
tre spetie, delle quali quello è più frequente in Italia, che si rassembra alle pastinache, del quale nelle maremme di Siena, et
in piu altri luoghi di tutta Thoscana ne nasce per i sodi infinitissime piante. Il Cretico si porta di Candia, & quello della
terza spetie simile nelle frondi al coriandro, & nel seme al cimino, nasce in piu luoghi per Italia. Scrisssene Galeno al. vi. del
le facultà de semplici, cosi dicendo. Il Dauco saluatico, il qual chiamano alcuni Pastinaca, è maticone è i cibi conneuuole del
D domestico, come che in ogni altra sua operatione sia egli più ualoroso. È acuto, ha uirtù di scaldare, & di disseccare. La
sua radice oltre alle cose già dette, ha un certo che di uentosità, & di uenereo. Il seme del domestico ha anchor egli possanza
di fauorire à uenere, ma quello del saluatico manca di uentosità, & però prouoca egli i mestrui ritenuti. Ha uirtù ua
lorosamente calida, di modo che si tiene tra le prime medicine per prouocare i mestrui, & l'orina. Impiastrato di fuore fa
euaporare gli homori. L'herba ha quasi uirtù equiualente, non dimeno è ella assai men ualorosa del seme, per la mistura del
la humidità acquea, che ha in se, quantunque ne i suoi temperamenti anchor essa sia calida.

Del Delphinio. Cap. lxxix.

IL Delphinio produce i fusti da una sola radice, lunghi due palmi, & qualche
uolta maggiori, da i quali escono le frondi picciole, sottili, intagliate, & lunghe,
le quali nelle fattezze loro si rassembrano alla forma de delphini, da i quali ha
preso ella il nome. Il suo fiore è simile alle uiole bianche: ma è di porporeo colo

A vii. Among the faculties of simples, it heats so powerfully that it deserves to be counted among those things that heat in the third degree and dry in the first; and for this reason Fennel generates milk. This it would not do if it were more drying. For this reason it also helps with overflow of bile, promotes urine, and likewise the menses. Beyond this there is another Fennel, which on account of its great size is called Hippomarathro, whose root and seed dry more powerfully than the domestic kind, and it therefore seems that for this reason they restrain the body, even though their astringent faculty is not clearly evident. Of this plant not only the root but also the seed is similar to Cachrij, and it can therefore break stones, stop the overflow of bile, and promote the menses and urine; but it cannot generate milk, as the one mentioned above. There is yet another species, also large, whose seed is sharp and round, like coriander seeds, similar in its operations to the other, though not quite as powerful.

On Daucus. Chapter 78.

B Some call Daucus "daucio." The one that grows in Crete produces leaves similar to fennel, but smaller and more slender; it sends up a stem one span tall, an umbel similar to coriander, white flowers, and a seed likewise white, sharp, hairy, and very pleasant to eat; its root is a palm's length long and a finger's width thick; it grows in rocky, open places. There is another species similar to wild celery, rough, aromatic, and sharp to the taste. The best of all is the Cretan one. A third species is also identified, which produces leaves similar to coriander, white flowers, and a head and seed like dill; its umbel resembles that of parsnips, and its seed is long like cumin. The seed of all species has the power to heat: it promotes urine, the menses, and childbirth; it relieves bodily pains, eases an old cough; drunk in wine it is beneficial against the bites of those spiders called phalangi; applied as a poultice it resolves swellings. Of the other species only the seed is used; but of the Cretan one also the root, which, drunk as an immediate and powerful remedy, acts against the bites of venomous animals.

C Although some maintain that Daucus and wild Parsnip are one and the same plant — and I believe that is how Galen and Paul of Aegina understood it — it nevertheless seems to me that they are clearly mistaken. For even though one may rightly say that Daucus is truly a species of wild Parsnip, it is not the same parsnip of which Dioscorides was speaking just above; for if by Daucus and wild Parsnip he had meant the same plant, it would certainly not have been necessary for him to write about them in two different chapters. And although it may seem to some that Galen makes no distinction between Daucus and wild Parsnip, whoever looks carefully will see that he treated them in two different chapters, first in book six and then in book eight, and will easily perceive that Marcellus Florentinus and Ruellius are mistaken. Galen himself reveals their error: for beyond treating Daucus and wild Parsnip as different plants in different chapters, he clarifies in book six that there he speaks only of Daucus and not of Parsnip, where he says this: "Wild Daucus, which some call Parsnip, is less suitable in the foods of the domestic kind." These words clearly demonstrate that it was not Galen but others who believed these two plants to be the same thing. This is amply confirmed by Galen's having afterward written specifically about Parsnip in book eight, as something different from Daucus. I will therefore say, together with Dioscorides, that Daucus is of three species, of which the one most common in Italy resembles the parsnips, and of this an infinite number of plants grow in the marshlands of Siena and in many other places throughout all Tuscany. The Cretan one is brought from Candia, and the one of the third species, similar in its leaves to coriander and in its seed to cumin, grows in many places throughout Italy. Galen wrote of it in book six of the Faculties of Simples, saying thus: Wild Daucus, which some call Parsnip, is in food agreeable to the domestic body, though in every other operation it is more powerful. It is sharp, it has the power to heat and to dry. Its root, beyond the things already mentioned, has a certain tendency to produce wind and to provoke venereal desire. The seed of the domestic kind likewise has the power to promote venereal desire, but that of the wild kind lacks the tendency to produce wind and therefore it promotes the retained menses. It has strongly heating power, so much so that it is considered among the foremost medicines for promoting the menses and urine. Applied externally as a poultice it causes the humors to evaporate. The herb has nearly equivalent virtues, yet it is considerably less powerful than the seed, due to the mixture of watery moisture it contains, even though in its temperament it too is warm.
