A which is found in it, is quite agreeable to the taste when eating it. That which is ripe has in itself quite a bit of earthiness, since it is tart and drying. The flower has the same strength as the unripe fruit, and therefore both are useful in dysentery, in bodily flux, and in spitting of blood. The root, besides being constrictive, contains no small amount of subtle substance, by virtue of which it can break up kidney stones.

On Helsine. Chapter 41.

The Helsine, surnamed Cissampelos, has leaves similar to ivy, but smaller. Its stems are slender, with which it embraces whatever it touches. It grows in hedges, in vineyards, and among grain. The juice pressed from the leaves purges the body.

N There is truly no reason whatsoever to doubt that the Helsine named Cissampelos, that is, ivy-vine, is not a species of Bindweed or Convolvulus; but what exactly it is cannot be easily determined. Yet Dioscorides saying that it has leaves similar to ivy, but much smaller, with slender stems by which it clasps whatever it touches, and that it grows in hedges, vineyards, and among grain, seems to indicate that it is the plant which in the fields winds around grain, flax, and legumes, and in vineyards around stakes and vines, which we call Vilucchio, and in the Trentino region Minutola, although Leonardo Fuchs the German believes the Helsine to be that plant which winds around hedges and small trees, and which produces in summer those white little bells. Pliny calls this Convolvulus in chapter 15 of book 21, saying that nature learned to make lilies when it made the flowers of Convolvulus. Some call this flower (as Servius the Grammarian did, being mistaken) privet, but the error was demonstrated above in its proper chapter in the first book. Galen wrote briefly about Helsine in book 6 of the Faculties of Simple Medicines, saying: The Helsine called Cissampelos has the virtue of aiding digestion.

On Elatine. Chapter 42.

Elatine has leaves similar to Helsine, but smaller, hairy, and more rounded. Its small stems are slender, about a hand-span long, numbering five or six, full of leaves from the root upward, astringent to the taste. It grows among grain and in cultivated fields. It is useful for fluxes and for inflammations of the eyes, when the leaves are crushed and applied as a poultice with polenta. Drinking the decoction is beneficial in dysentery.

C Although Ruellius affirms that Elatine is found in France, and that the peasants call it wild turnip, eating it daily in salads; nonetheless in Italy I have not yet been able to find what it might be, knowing however for certain that our wild turnip cannot in any way be Elatine. Galen wrote very briefly about it in book 6 of the Faculties of Simple Medicines, saying: Elatine is slightly drying and slightly cooling.

On Eupatorium. Chapter 43.

Eupatorium is a tall plant, and produces a single stem, woody, blackish, straight, slender, hairy, about a cubit long, sometimes longer, along which the leaves are arranged at intervals, similar to those of cinquefoil, or more precisely of hemp, divided into five or more parts, blackish, and toothed around the edges. The seed grows from the middle of the stem upward, hairy, hanging toward the ground, and when dry, it clings to clothing. The leaves, when crushed and applied with lard, heal ulcers that are slow to consolidate. The seed, or the herb drunk with wine, benefits ailments of the liver, dysentery, and serpent bites. Some mistakenly call Eupatorium by the name Argemone, since this, as we have shown, is entirely different from Eupatorium.

D Some, indeed almost the greater part of pharmacists, offer for Eupatorium a certain plant that grows on the banks of streams and on the edges of ditches, up to three cubits tall, whose leaves, though larger, resemble those of hemp; they are whitish, hairy, and bitter to the taste. The stem is reddish, round, solid, and hairy, and where the branches emerge there are many hollow cavities. The flowers grow in an open umbrella shape at the tops of the stems, of a flesh color, and somewhat like those of our (though false) Italian oregano; when ripe they shed their down and float off into the air. The root, from which quite a few smaller ones branch off, is useless and of no value. And although they know that the true Eupatorium of the Greeks is that plant which we call Agrimony, as some also called it in the time of Dioscorides, nonetheless, unwilling to depart from their old habits, they are not easily persuaded to change for the purposes of preparations drawn from the Greeks. Yet I say this not to disparage their Eupatorium, which is the same one described by Avicenna, but only so that each plant may be given its proper place. A nel suo uolume de gli huomini illustri lo fa da Como, & non da Verona. Vsano questa quarta spetie assai i Chirurgii in deschi nelle beuande delle ferite intrinseche, delle rotture, & delle fistole, & in ogni altra cosa, oue si conuenghino le con solide. Ma è da sapere, che questo Sanniccolo non è quella pianta, che produce pur cinque foglie, & la radice bianca con grande arte intarsiata dalla natura, della quale dicemmo disopra al capitolo del Simphito; ma di gran lunga lontana. Scrisse del Cinque foglio Galeno al. viij. delle facultà de semplici, così dicendo. La radice del Cinque foglio dissecca grande mente, & non è punto acuta; & però è ella molto in uso, come sono tutte quelle altre cose, che essendo composte di parti sottili, disseccano senza mordere. E' adunque questa radice disseccatiua nel terzo ordine, ne ha alcuna caldità, che eui dentemente si possa conoscere.

Della Phenice. Cap. xlv.

L A Phenice ha frondi d'orzo, ma piu corte, & piu strette, la spiga simile al gio glio, i fusti lunghi sei dita, che escono d'intorno alla radice, con sei, ouer otto spi ghe: nasce nei campi, & nei tetti fatti di nuouo. Beuta in uino stitico ristagna i flussi del corpo, de i mestrui, & dell'orina. Dicono alcuni esser buona per rista-
B gnare i flussi del sangue, portandosi addosso inuolta in lana rossa.

Hitamasi la Phenice in Thoscana Gioglio saluatico, & nasce comunemente nelle ulle lungo alle strade, in sugli ar-
C gini dei campi, non punto differente dalla scrittura di Dioscoride. Plinio al. xxv. cap. del. xxij. libro disse, che dalli Latini si chiamaua la Phenice orzo dei topi, forse per mangiarsi loro quella, che nasce in su i tetti delle case. Copia ne nasce in Goritia in su'l cimiterio di San Francesco dinanzi alla porta grande della chiesa, & honne similmente vediu ta assai presso à Vinetia in su'l Lio.

Della Radice Idea. Cap. xlvi.

L A Radice Idea produce le frondi simili al rusco, appresso alle quali sono cer ti come piccioli capriuoli, da i quali esce il fiore. La radice è ualorosamente co strettiua, & conueneuole in ogni cosa, oue bisogni ristagnare: & imperò si bee utilmente per i flussi di corpo, & de i mestrui. Ristagna oltre à questo tutti
i flussi del sangue.

Vesta à tempi nostri non si porta in Italia, ne ritrouò io chi scriua, oue la nasca, quantunque il cognome suo dimo-
C Q stri esser ella pianta particolare del monte Ida di Creti, come fu poco qui disopra detto del rouo ideo. Dimostran ne le uirtù sue Galeno al. vi. delle facultà de semplici, così dicendo. La radice Idea è al gusto ualorosamente acer ba, & facen.tosene esperienza si ritrouua manifestamente operare, secondo che la dimostra al gusto: imperoche tanto beuta, quanto impiastrata, & applicata dissuore, ristagna la disenteria, i flussi del sangue, del corpo, de i mestrui, & d'ogni altro luogo della persona.

Della Radice Rhodia. Cap. xlvij.

L A Radice Rhodia nasce in Macedonia, simile al costo, ma piu leggiera, & piu disuguale. Pestandosi questa rispira odore di rose. Applicata trita in su'l fronte con oglio rosado gioua al dolore della testa.

A Ra lice Rhodia è conosciuta da pochi in Italia, quantunque ageuolmente ui possa ella nascere, & nel monte
L Apennino, & in quel di Santo Agnolo. Quella, che ho io piantata nell'horto in Goritia, mi fu mandata già di Stiria da Grazzo dall'Eccellentissimo medico Meser Pietro Saliceto, & accioche la possa uenire piu in cognitio-
D ne, ne dirò qui, per hauersele taciute Dioscoride, tutte le note. Dico adunque, che la Radice Rhodia produce da se piu fusti, tondi, alquanto concaui, alti da un palmo fino à un gombito, Talli quali escono le frondi lunghette, appuntate, grasse, come quelle della portulaca, & per intorno minutamente denti tt: produce nella sommità de i fusti una ombrella verde, quasi simile al lithibimalosma dopo al disforire diuèta rossigna. La radice è inequale, grossa come quella del costo, liscia, et lucida di fuore, & di dentro bianca quando è fresca; ma quando è secca, è leggiera, rossa di dentro, & squamosa di fuore. Questa masticata, ouero pesta, rispira naturalissimo odore di rose, da cui s'ha ella acquistato il nome di Rhodia. E oltre à questo tra tutte le radici uiuacissima: imperoche cauata, & riposta, se la non si tiene in luoghi molto secchi, & poscia dopo molti mesi ripiantata, subito germoglia. Nasce in monti altissi mi, sassosi, & precipitosi, doue à pena ha tàta terra intorno, che la ui si possa attaccare. Impiastrasi utilmente irrorataca n acqua rosa, ouero di lauanda, secondo la qualità del dolore in su'l fronte, & in su le tempie per il dolore del capo. Corrobora il ceruello con il suo giocondo odore, di modo che si puo ella usare in ogni mal di testa causato da qual si uoglia causa. Per esser ella composta di qualità temperata, come disce Galeno, & fa testimonio il suo sapore, con il quale imita le rose. Scrisse di questa Radice Galeno al. viij. delle facultà de semplici, così dicendo. La Radice Rhodia, quella cioè, che nasce in Macedonia, è composta di parti sottili. E digestiua, & calida nel fine del secondo grado, ò al piu nel principio del terzo.

A In his volume on illustrious men he names him from Como, not from Verona. German surgeons use this fourth variety frequently in drinks for internal wounds, fractures, and fistulas, and in every other case where consolidation is needed. But one should know that this Sanniccolo is not the plant that produces only five leaves and the white root so artfully inlaid by nature, of which we spoke above in the chapter on Comfrey; it is far from that. Galen wrote about Cinquefoil in book eight of his work on the faculties of simples, saying: The root of Cinquefoil desiccates greatly, and is not at all sharp; and therefore it is much in use, as are all those other things which, being composed of fine parts, desiccate without biting. This root is therefore desiccating in the third degree, and possesses no warmth that can be clearly perceived.

On the Phenice. Chapter XLV.

T he Phenice has leaves like barley, but shorter and narrower; the spike resembles darnel; the stalks are six fingers tall and grow up around the root, bearing six or eight spikes. It grows in fields and on newly made rooftops. Drunk in astringent wine, it restrains the fluxes of the body, the menses, and the urine. Some say it is also good for restraining
B fluxes of blood, when carried on the person wrapped in red wool.

The Phenice is called in Tuscany wild darnel, and grows commonly in the valleys along roadsides and on the
C banks of fields, differing not at all from Dioscorides' description. Pliny, in book twenty-five, chapter twenty-two, said that the Latins called the Phenice mouse-barley, perhaps because mice eat that which grows on rooftops. It grows abundantly in Gorizia in the cemetery of San Francesco in front of the great door of the church, and I have likewise seen plenty of it near Venice on the Lido.

On the Root Idea. Chapter XLVI.

T he Root Idea produces leaves similar to butcher's broom, and near them are certain small things like little tendrils from which the flower emerges. The root is powerfully astringent and suited to every case where staunching is needed; and so it is usefully drunk for fluxes of the body and the menses. It also restrains all fluxes of blood.

This plant is not brought to Italy in our time, nor could I find anyone who writes where it grows, although its name suggests
C Q it is a plant particular to Mount Ida in Crete, as was mentioned a little above regarding the Idaean bramble. Galen demonstrates its virtues in book six of his work on the faculties of simples, saying: The Root Idea is powerfully bitter to the taste, and experience shows it clearly to act as the taste suggests: for whether drunk or applied as a poultice externally, it restrains dysentery, fluxes of blood, of the body, of the menses, and of every other part of the person.

On the Rhodian Root. Chapter XLVII.

T he Rhodian Root grows in Macedonia, similar to costus but lighter and more uneven. When pounded, it gives off the scent of roses. Applied ground up on the forehead with rose oil, it helps with headache.

A The Rhodian Root is known to few in Italy, although it could easily grow there, and on the Apennine mountains and those of
L Sant'Angelo. The one I have planted in my garden in Gorizia was sent to me from Graz in Styria by the most excellent physician Messer Pietro Saliceto; and so that it may become better known, I will describe it here, since Dioscorides passed over its characteristics. I say, then, that the Rhodian Root produces several round stems, somewhat hollow, a palm to a cubit in height, from which grow fairly long, pointed, fleshy leaves, like those of purslane, with small teeth around the margins; it produces at the top of the stems a green umbel, somewhat like that of lithimimalosma, which after flowering turns reddish. The root is uneven, thick like that of costus, smooth and shiny on the outside, and white inside when fresh; but when dry it is light, reddish inside, and scaly outside. This root, chewed or pounded, gives off a most natural scent of roses, from which it has acquired the name Rhodian. Moreover, it is among the most long-lived of all roots: for once dug up and stored, if it is not kept in very dry places, and then replanted after many months, it immediately sprouts again. It grows on very high mountains, rocky and precipitous, where there is barely enough soil around for it to take hold. It is usefully applied as a poultice moistened with rosewater or lavender water, according to the nature of the pain, on the forehead and temples for headache. It strengthens the brain with its pleasant scent, so that it can be used for every kind of headache whatever the cause. For, as Galen attests, it is composed of temperate qualities, as its flavor, which imitates roses, confirms. Galen wrote of this Root in book eight of his work on the faculties of simples, saying: The Rhodian Root, that is, the one that grows in Macedonia, is composed of fine parts. It is digestive and warm at the end of the second degree, or at most at the beginning of the third.

dosi, pieni in se stessi, rosseggianti, & ruuidi, intorno à i quali sono le frondi simili

Beesi con uino per la disenteria, & per prouocare l'orina. Le frondi trite, et impiastrate con-

D'un' altra Coda di cauallo. Cap. xlix.

A altra Coda di cauallo è un fusto dritto, uguale, alto un gombito, & qualche B
uolta maggiore, uacuo, le cui chiome, le quali ha distinte per interualli, sono piu
breui, piu bianche, & piu tenere della soprascritta. Questa trita con aceto salda le
ferite, & ha le uirtu medesime della prima.

Hiamasi la Coda di cauallo per il piu Cauda equina, & ammendune queste spetie sono notissime in Italia: Impe-
C roche l'una chiamano per la piu parte Asperella, laquale adoperano le donne per far lucidi gli stagni, et l'altra si
chiama pur Coda di cauallo. Produce questa quasi nel nascimento suo un certo germollo grosso, & tenero, simile
à una ghianda, il quale chiamano i nostri Sanesi Paltrufali usati da loro nei cibi la quaresima, prima cotti lesse
nell'acqua, & poi infarinati, et fritti nella padella in cambio di pesce. Ma di tal sorte qualche uolta gli ristringono il cor-
po, che costipandosi incorreno ageuolmente nel male (come dicono) del madrone. Scrisse della Coda di cauallo Galeno al.
vi. delle facultà de i semplici, cosi dicendo. Ha la Coda di cauallo insieme con amarezza, uirtu costrettiua: & impe-
rò dissecca ella ualentemente senza mordacità alcuna. Salda le ferite grandi, quantunque ui fussero tagliati anchora
i nerui, & sana le rotture intestinali. L'herba beuta nel uino, ouer amente nell'acqua, è ualorsissimo rimedio à i uomiti, et
sputi del sangue, à i flussi delle donne, & massime rossi, alla disenteria, & altri flussi di corpo. Scrissero alcuni, che qual-
che uolta il succhio beuto ha saldato le ferite delle budella sottili, & parimente della uisciga. Gioua al flusso del sangue del C
naso, & alle passioni di corpo causate da flussi beendosi con uino austero, & con acqua, doue fuse la febre.

Della Grana. Cap. l.

A Grana, laquale adoperano i tintori, è una pianta ramusculosa, & picciola,
alla quale sono attaccate certe granella simili alle lenticchie, & queste si ricol go-
no, & si ripongono. L'eccellente nasce in Galatia, & in Armenia, & dopo que-
sta in bontà è quella, che si porta d'Asia, & di Cilicia. La manco buona di tutte
è la Spagnuola. Ha uirtu la Grana di ristagnare: mettesi utilmente trita con aceto in su le fe-
rite, & in su li nerui tagliati. Nasce in Cilicia in su le quercie, simile à picciole chiocciole, & la
colgono le donne di quel paese con la bocca, & chiamonla Grana.

Q Vantunque sia la Grana, con laquale si tingono à i tempi nostri in Italia infinitissimi panni di lana, & parimente
di seta, notissima molto à ciascuno; nondimeno non so io, che in alcun luogo d'Italia si ritroui l'alborsèello, che la
produce. Quella, che si tiene nelle Spetiarie, è tonda di granello, & uacua di dentro: & imperò non si rassembra D
punto alle lenticchie, come afferma Dioscoride. Il per che è da credere, che sia la Grana di piu spetie, & che sia questa ag-
giuolmente quella, che diceua Plinio nascere in Attica, & in Affrica, la cui midolla si conuerte presto in un picciolo uermi-
cello. E' la Grana tra le donne in uso per prohibire, che non si sconcino le grauide, nel cui timore la danno con buon suc-
cesso in poluere con la pari quantità d'Incenso maschio in uno uuono fresco à bere. Scrissene Galeno al. vij. delle facultà
de i semplici, cosi dicendo. La Grana di Tintori è nelle facultà sue costrettiua, et amara, & l'una, et l'altra di queste qua-
lità dissecca senza mordacità alcuna, & imperò è conueneuole molto alle ferite grandi, & massime de i nerui. Nelche al-
cuni la tritano con aceto puro, & altri con aceto melato.

Del Tragio. Cap. li.

sco, quantunque tutti sieno minori, & piu breui. Distilla da questo un liquore,

FOURTH BOOK. 313

On Horsetail. Chapter 48. A

Horsetail grows in watery places and along ditches. Its stems are hollow, knotted, full in themselves, reddish, and rough, around which grow leaves similar to rushes, dense and slender. It grows tall, surpassing the neighboring small trees, from which its dark tresses then hang, like a horse's tail: its root is woody and hard. The herb is astringent, and therefore its juice stanches nosebleeds. It is drunk with wine for dysentery and to stimulate urination. The leaves, ground and made into a poultice, consolidate fresh wounds. Some say that the leaves drunk with water consolidate wounds of the bowels and of the bladder, and likewise intestinal ruptures.

On Another Horsetail. Chapter 49.

The other Horsetail has a straight, uniform stem, a cubit tall or somewhat more, hollow, whose tresses, which it bears at distinct intervals, are shorter, whiter, and more tender than the one described above. This, ground with vinegar, closes wounds, and has the same virtues as the first.

Horsetail is most commonly called Cauda equina, and both these species are very well known in Italy: for one is called by most people Asperella, which women use to polish ponds, and the other is still called Horsetail. This produces, almost at its first sprouting, a certain thick and tender shoot, similar to an acorn, which our people of Siena call Paltrufali, used by them as food in Lent, first boiled in water and then floured and fried in a pan in place of fish. But eaten in this way they sometimes so constipate the body that those affected easily fall into what is called (as they say) the disease of the strawberry tree. Galen wrote of Horsetail in book six of the Faculties of Simple Medicines, saying thus: Horsetail has, together with bitterness, an astringent virtue, and therefore it dries powerfully without any sharpness. It closes large wounds, even if the nerves have been cut through, and heals intestinal ruptures. The herb drunk in wine, or indeed in water, is a most powerful remedy against vomiting and spitting of blood, against women's fluxes, especially the red ones, against dysentery, and other bodily fluxes. Some have written that at times the juice drunk has closed wounds of the delicate bowels, and likewise of the bladder. It benefits the flux of blood from the nose, and bodily ailments caused by fluxes, being drunk with dry wine and with water in which a fever has dissolved.

On Grain (Kermes). Chapter 50.

The Grain, which dyers use, is a small, branching plant, to which certain small grains similar to lentils are attached, and these are gathered and stored. The best comes from Galatia and Armenia, and next in quality is that which is brought from Asia and Cilicia. The least good of all is the Spanish. The Grain has the virtue of staunching: it is usefully applied, ground with vinegar, on wounds and on cut nerves. It grows in Cilicia on oak trees, resembling small snails, and the women of that country collect it with their mouths, and call it Grain.

Although the Grain with which in our time in Italy a very great quantity of woolen cloth is dyed, as well as silk, is very well known to everyone, I do not know that anywhere in Italy one finds the small tree that produces it. That which is kept in apothecaries' shops is round of grain and hollow within, and therefore does not at all resemble lentils, as Dioscorides asserts. For which reason one must believe that the Grain is of more than one species, and that this is indeed the one which Pliny said grew in Attica and in Africa, whose pith quickly turns into a small worm. The Grain is used among women to prevent miscarriages in pregnant women, for which purpose they give it with good success in powder, with an equal quantity of male Frankincense, in a fresh egg to drink. Galen wrote of it in book seven of the Faculties of Simple Medicines, saying thus: The Grain of the Dyers is in its faculties astringent and bitter, and both these qualities dry without any sharpness, and therefore it is very suitable for large wounds, especially of the nerves. For this purpose some grind it with pure vinegar, and others with honey-vinegar.

On Tragium. Chapter 51.

Tragium grows only in Crete, with leaves, fruit, and branches similar to the lentisk, though all are smaller and shorter. From it distills a liquid like milk, similar to gum. The seed, the leaves, and the liquid, applied externally...

A uano fuor della carne le spine, le saette, & ogni altra cosa appuntata. Beuti prouocano l'orina ritenuta, & i mestrui, & rompono la pietra della uisciga: togliesene per uolta la quantità d'una dramma. Dicesi, che le capre saluatiche ferite dalle saette si medicano con questa pianta: imperoche pascendosene gli escono le saette da dosso.

D'un altro Tragio. Cap. lij.

Vn'altro Tragio, il quale chiamano alcuni Tragoceros: le cui frondi sono simili alla scolopendria. La radice è bianca, & sottile, simile alla ramoraccia, la quale mangiata così cruda, come cotta, giova alla disenteria. Le frondi nell'autunno spirano odore di becco, dal che s'ha egli acquistato il nome di Tragio.

L Tragio, che scriue Dioscoride nascere in Candia, simile in ogni sua parte al lentisco, disse Plinio à xxj. cap. del.
I xiiij. libro esser simile al terebintho, & all'ultimo capitolo del. xxvij. lo fece in ogni sua parte simile al ginepro. Ilche dimostra non hauer lo egli conosciuto; ma hauerne scritto secondo l'opinioni di diuersi scrittori, da cui cau
B egli quello, che ne scrisse. Questo à i tempi nostri non si porta à noi: & però non ne so dare altra cognitione. Quello della seconda spetie è da giudicare più presto essere herba, che alboscello, mangandosi la radice così cruda, & cotta, & essendo simile alla ramoraccia. Ma non ritrovo chi mi sappi mostrare alcuna pianta, che produca le frondi simili alla scolopendria, che i Greci chiamano Aspleno, et Cetrach: gli Arabici, che habbi odore di becco; ne però so io affermare, che sia questo Tragio quella volgar pianta chiamata da chi Pimpinella, & da chi Sassifragia hircina, quantunque ui si senta l'odore del becco acutissimo, & vero: Imperoche le frondi non corrisspondono à quelle della scolopendria, ne è appresso ad alcuno il suo uso per la disenteria; ma ben per prouocare l'orina, & per aprire l'oppilations. Scrisse del Tragio Galeno al. viij. delle facoltà de semplici, così dicendo. Le frondi, il fusto, & la gomma del Tragio, hanno uirtù di digerire, & di tirare. Sono composte di parti sottili, & imperò calde nel principio del terzo ordine. La gomma tira fuore le spine, i bronconi, & ogni altra cosa appuntata, che fusse fitta nel corpo: rompe le pietre, et prouoca i mestrui, quando se ne bee il peso d'una dramma: ma nasce solamente in Creti simile al lentisco. L'altro assai minor di questo si uede in molti luoghi, cò frondi simili alla scolopedria, ilquale è non poco costrettiuo. Il perche si couiene assai nelli flussi. Nasce ne i monti, et luoghi precipitosi.

C Del Trago. Cap. liij.

IL Trago è una herba, la quale chiamano alcuni Scorpione, oueramente Tragano. Nasce abondantemente nelle maremme, crescendo all'altezza d'un palmo, & qualche uolta maggiore, ramuscolosa, bassa, alquanto lunga, & senza frondi: produce attorno à i rami assai piccioli acini, come granella di grano, appuntati in cima, rosseggianti, & molto al gusto costrettiui, de quali beendosene dieci nel uino, giouano à i flussi stomachali, & muliebri. Sono alcuni, che li pestano, & fannon trocisci, & conseruanli, & usanli quando fa loro di bisogno.

L Trago (diceua Plinio all'ultimo capitolo del. xxvij) è una herba, la quale chiamano alcuni Scorpione, alta mezzo piede, folta, & senza frondi. Produce alcuni piccioli racemi, pieni di granella appuntate in cima, simili al grano, & nasce nelle maremme. Et imperò ageuolmente puo essere ella quella spetie di piccioli giunchi, che à piedi del monte Argentaio nelle nostre maremme di Siena nasce folta, & cespugliosa, con alcuni racemi di granella rosse, & lunghette. Di questo non ritrovo io, che facesse Galeno mentione alcuna, forse per non esergli stato in consideratione.

D Del Giunco. Cap. liiij.

IL Giunco è di due spetie, uno, che si chiama liscio, & l'altro acuto, per esser egli bene appuntato in cima, & di questo sono parimente due spetie, uno cioè sterile, & l'altro, che produce il seme nero, & ritondo, & questo è più grosso di canna, & più carnoso. Enneuna terza spetie chiamato Oloscheno, più carnoso, & più aspro delli predetti, il quale produce il suo seme simile all'altro. Il seme d'ammenduni arrostito, & beuto con uino innacquato, ristagna il corpo, & i flussi rossi delle donne: prouoca l'orina, & fa dolore di testa. Le frondi tenere più propinque alla radice s'impiastrano utilmente à i morsi di quei ragni, che si chiamano phalangi. Il seme dell'Ethiopico è sonnifero: & imperò è da osseruare nel darlo un certo modo, accioche non facesse dormire oltre al douere.

translation:
314 BOOK

A They draw out from the flesh thorns, arrows, and every other pointed thing. Drunk, they promote retained urine and menstruation, and break up bladder stones: one takes a drachm's weight per dose. It is said that wild goats wounded by arrows heal themselves with this plant, for when they graze on it, the arrows fall out of their backs.

Of Another Tragium. Chapter 52.

Another Tragium, which some call Tragoceros: whose leaves are similar to those of scolopendria. The root is white and slender, resembling horse-radish, and eaten raw as well as cooked it benefits dysentery. In autumn the leaves give off the smell of a he-goat, from which the plant has acquired the name of Tragium.

The Tragium which Dioscorides writes grows in Crete, similar in every part to the mastic tree, Pliny in chapter 21 of book 14 said was similar to the terebinth, and in the last chapter of book 27 made it in every part similar to the juniper. This shows that he himself had not seen it, but had written about it based on the opinions of various writers from whom he gathered what he wrote. This plant is not brought to us in our time, and therefore I cannot offer any further knowledge of it. The second species is to be judged more readily an herb than a shrub, since the root is eaten both raw and cooked, and it resembles horse-radish. But I cannot find anyone who can show me any plant that produces leaves similar to scolopendria, which the Greeks call Asplenon and Ceterach, or one that, as the Arabians say, smells of a he-goat; nor can I affirm that this Tragium is the common plant called by some Pimpinella, and by others Saxifraga hircina, even though one does detect a very sharp and true goat-smell on it; for the leaves do not correspond to those of scolopendria, nor is it known to anyone to be used for dysentery, though it is good for promoting urine and opening obstructions. Galen wrote of Tragium in book 8 of his work on simples, saying thus: the leaves, the stem, and the gum of Tragium have the virtue of digesting and drawing. They are composed of subtle parts, and are therefore heating in the beginning of the third degree. The gum draws out thorns, splinters, and every other pointed thing embedded in the body; it breaks up stones and provokes menstruation when one drinks the weight of a drachm of it; but it grows only in Crete, similar to the mastic tree. The other, much smaller than this one, is seen in many places, with leaves similar to scolopendria, and it is not a little astringent, and so it is useful in fluxes. It grows on mountains and in steep places.

C Of Trago. Chapter 53.

The Trago is an herb which some call Scorpion, or alternatively Tragano. It grows abundantly in the coastal marshes, reaching the height of a palm's breadth, sometimes more, branchy, low, somewhat long, and without leaves; it produces around its branches many small berries, like grains of wheat, pointed at the tip, reddish, and very astringent to the taste, of which, drinking ten in wine, they benefit stomach fluxes and those of women. Some pound them and make lozenges, and preserve them and use them when needed.

The Trago (Pliny said in the last chapter of book 27) is an herb which some call Scorpion, half a foot tall, dense, and without leaves. It produces small clusters full of grains pointed at the tip, similar to wheat, and grows in the coastal marshes. And therefore it could readily be that species of small rushes which grows dense and bushy at the foot of Mount Argentario in our marshes of Siena, with some clusters of small red and somewhat elongated grains. Of this I find that Galen made no mention at all, perhaps because he had not taken it into consideration.

D Of the Rush. Chapter 54.

The Rush is of two species, one called smooth, and the other sharp, being well pointed at the tip, and of this there are likewise two sub-species, one sterile, and the other which produces black, round seeds, and this one is thicker than a cane and more fleshy. There is also a third species called Holoschoenus, more fleshy and more rough than the aforesaid, which produces its seed similarly to the others. The seed of both, roasted and drunk with diluted wine, restrains the body and the red fluxes of women; it promotes urine and causes headache. The tender leaves closest to the root are beneficially applied as a poultice to the bites of those spiders called phalanges. The seed of the Ethiopian variety is sleep-inducing, and therefore one must take care in administering it, so that it does not cause one to sleep beyond what is fitting.

Giunchi sono notissimi à ciascun, & ueggonsene in Italia appresso all'acque tutte le spetie, che in questo luogo
I ne scriue Dioscoride. Scrissene Galeno al. viij. delle facultà de semplici, così dicendo. De i Giunchi isfan è una spe-
tie, che si chiama Oxischenos, & un'altra chiamata Oligoschenos, il cui frutto fa dormire. Sono di quello, che si
chiama Oxischeno, due spetie, una sterite, laquale è di nifsun valore in medicina, & l'altra, che fa il seme utile parimente
per far dormire, quantunque non così efficacemente, come fa quello dell'Oligoscheno, ilquale fa anchora farneticare con
la mente. Fritto l'uno, & l'altro, & poscia beuti con uino, ristagnano il flusso del corpo, & parimente de i mestrui rossi.
Dal che si cognose chiaramente, che'l temperamento loro è d'una essenza terrena leggiermente frigida, & d'una acquea
leggiermente calda, di modo che possono diseccare le materie inferiori, & trasportare al capo sensituamente frigidi ua-
pori, dalli quali si causa il sonno.

Della Lichene. Cap. lv.

A Lichene familiarissima de i sassi, chiamano alcuni Brion. Attacasi questa al-
le pietre irrorate dall'acque, come fa il mosco. Ristagna impiastrata i flussi del
sangue: spegne l'infiammagioni, & sana l'impetigini. Applicata con mele, vale
al trabocco del fiele, & prohibisce i flussi, che scendono alla lingua, & alla bocca.

L A Lichene (secondo che tengono i più dotti Semplicisti) è quella, che chiamano gli Spetiali Epatica, et chiamaron-
la i Greci Lichen, per curare ella le uolatiche, lequali chiamano esslichene. Le frondi sue sono grosse, & lun-
ghette, attaccate alle pietre, oue risuda qualche rampollo d'acqua, disotto alle quali escono alcuni fusicelli, da i
quali nascono alcuni piccioli capitelli, stellati, & massime nel mese di Giugno. Plinio al. iiij. cap. del. xxvi. libro fece memo-
ria di due spetie, così dicendo. La Lichena herba nasce in luoghi sassosi con una fronde sola, larga appresso alla radice, &
ria produce un sol fusto picciolo, & sottile, dal quale pendono alcune lunghe frondi. Enne anchora un'altra spetie, laquale
s'attacca in su le pietre, come fa il mosco. Questa messa in su le ferite, & parimente in su le posteme, ui ristagna il flusso del
sangue, & fattone lettouario con mele, sana il trabocco di fiele: ma coloro, che si curano per questa uia, bisogna, che si laui-
no con acqua salata, si unghino con oglio di mandole, & s'astenghino da gli herbaggi. Fecene memoria Galeno al. vij. delle
facultà de i semplici, così dicendo. La Lichene, che nasce ne i sassi, è ueramente come un mosco: ma si può connumerare giu-
stamente tra le piante. E' stata così chiamata per curare ella le lichene. Ha uirtu aftersiua: ma poco refrigeratiua, & l'u-
na, & l'altra di queste diseccatiua. L'aftersiua, & diseccatiua ha ella dalle pietre, et l'infrigidatiua dall'acqua: imperoche
la nasce nelle pietre humide, che hanno fastidioso odore: & però essendo còposta di tali qualità, conferisce ella à quei slem-
moni, i quali chiamano aphlegmaton. Ma se la còferisce a i flussi del sangue, come scriue Dioscoride, io non lo so affermare.

Della Paronichia. Cap. lvi.

A Paronichia è picciola pianta, che nasce in su le pietre, simile al peplo, ma man-
co lunga, & ha le frondi maggiori. Questa pesta, & applicata è il rimedio delle
paronichie, & durezze delle dita.

N Asce la Paronichia per tutto, con frondi appresso alle radici ritonde, & maggiori di quelle del peplo: ma in cima
sono minori, & simili molto à quelle del peplo. Il fusto non è così lungo, ne così grosso, ne meno ui si ritroua il
latte, come si fa nel peplo. Copia infisita senevede nella gran selua, che si passanel uiaggio per andare da Lubia-
na à Goritia, su peri sassi, & tronchi de gli alberi secchi. Scrissene Galeno al. viij. delle facultà de semplici, così dicendo.
La Paronichia è così chiamata dall'effetto, che la fa nella medicina: imperoche la sana (come dice Dioscoride) le paroni-
chie delle dita, & parimente i faui. La uirtu sua è composta di sottili parti. Dissecca senza mordacità alcuna: imperoche
così bisogna, che sieno quelle cose, che sanano le paronichie.

Del Chrisocome. Cap. lvij.

L Chrisocome cresce all'altezza d'una spanna: la cui corimbacea chioma è si-
mile all'hissopo: ha la radice pelosa, sottile, simile à quella dell'helleboro nero, di
sapore al gusto non dispiaceuole, & assai simile al cipero, cioè con una certa dol-
cezza austero: nasce in luoghi opachi, & sassosi. E' la sua radice calida, & costret-

melata per prouocare le purgationi delle donne.

L Chrisocome non ritrouoio chi fino a questo tempo mi sappi dimostrare in Italia: & imperò lo lasciare-

cosa, & farne noi signori.

translation:
FOURTH BOOK. 315

Rushes are well known to everyone, and all the species that Dioscorides describes in this place can be found in Italy near water. Galen wrote about them in book eight of his work on the properties of simples, saying: Among the rushes there is one species called Oxischenos, and another called Oligoschenos, whose fruit induces sleep. Of the one called Oxischeno there are two varieties: one sterile, which is of no value in medicine, and another whose seed is likewise useful for inducing sleep, though not as effectively as that of the Oligoscheno, which also causes mental derangement. Both, when roasted and then drunk with wine, check the flow of the body and likewise of the menstrual blood. From this it is clearly understood that their temperament is of an earthy substance, slightly cold, and of a watery substance slightly warm, so that they can dry up the lower humors and carry cool vapors to the head, from which sleep is caused.

On Lichen. Chapter 55.

Lichen, most familiar among rocks, is called Brion by some. It attaches itself to stones moistened by water, as moss does. Applied as a poultice it checks flows of blood; it extinguishes inflammations and heals skin eruptions. Applied with honey, it is good for overflow of bile and prevents flows that descend to the tongue and mouth.

Lichen (according to the most learned herbalists) is what the apothecaries call Epatica, and the Greeks called it Lichen because it cures the skin patches they call esslichene. Its fronds are thick and somewhat elongated, attached to stones where some trickle of water seeps out; below these there emerge certain small stalks, bearing tiny star-shaped heads, especially in the month of June. Pliny in book four, chapter twenty-six, recorded two species, saying: The Lichena herb grows in rocky places with a single frond, broad near the root, and produces a single small, slender stem from which several long fronds hang. There is also another species which attaches itself to stones as moss does. Applied to wounds, and likewise to abscesses, it checks the flow of blood; and made into an electuary with honey it heals overflow of bile — but those who follow this treatment must wash with salt water, anoint themselves with almond oil, and abstain from greens. Galen recorded it in book seven of the properties of simples, saying: Lichen, which grows on rocks, is truly like a moss, but may rightly be counted among plants. It has been called thus because it cures lichen. It has a cleansing virtue, but little cooling one, and both varieties have a drying quality. The cleansing and drying it derives from the rocks, and the cooling from the water; for it grows on moist stones that have an unpleasant smell. Being thus composed of such qualities, it helps those phlegmy conditions they call aphlegmaton. But whether it helps flows of blood, as Dioscorides writes, I cannot affirm.

On Paronychia. Chapter 56.

Paronychia is a small plant that grows on stones, similar to peplo but shorter, and with larger fronds. Pounded and applied it is the remedy for whitlows and hardnesses of the fingers.

Paronychia grows everywhere, with fronds near the roots that are rounded and larger than those of peplo; at the tip they are smaller and closely resemble those of peplo. The stem is not as long nor as thick, nor does it contain the milky sap found in peplo. An immense abundance of it can be seen in the great forest along the road from Ljubljana to Gorizia, on rocks and dry tree trunks. Galen wrote about it in book eight of the properties of simples, saying: Paronychia is so called from the effect it produces in medicine, for it heals (as Dioscorides says) whitlows of the fingers, and likewise favus. Its virtue is composed of subtle parts. It dries without any biting quality, for that is what is needed in those things that heal whitlows.

On Chrisocome. Chapter 57.

Chrisocome grows to the height of a span; its corymb-shaped head resembles that of hyssop; it has a hairy, slender root, similar to that of black hellebore, with a taste not unpleasant to the palate, quite like cyperus — that is, austere with a certain sweetness. It grows in shady and rocky places. Its root is warm and astringent, beneficial for inflammations of the liver and lungs. It is taken boiled in honey-water to stimulate purgation in women.

As for Chrisocome, I have found no one up to this time who could identify it for me in Italy; and therefore we shall set it aside in that garden of nature which reserves for itself unknown simples, so as not to deprive itself of anything, and leave us as its masters.

text:
316 LIBRO

Del Chrisogono. Cap. lviij.

IL Chrisogono è solta pianta, le cui frondi son simili à quelle della quercia, & il fiore simile à quello del verbasco coronario. Produce la radice simile al rapo, & di dentro è rossissima, & di fuori nera. Questa trita, et impirastrata con aceto, con ferisice al morso del topo ragno.

I L Chrisogono se d'altronde non si portane i giardini d'Italia, restara anchor egli incognito à noi, come tutti gli altri, che ci asconde la natura nel suo secreto giardino.

Dello Helichriso. Cap. lix.

LO Helichriso, ilqual chiamano alcuni Chrisanthemo, & altri Amaranto, di cui coronano le statue delli Dei, ha il fusto dritto, bianco, uerdeggiante, & fermo: su per ilquale sono le frondi strette, simili all'abrotano, distinte tutte per intervalli. Produce la chioma ritonda, di colore d'oro, ridotta in ombrella, come di secchi corimbi pendenti: la radice è sottile. Nasce in luoghi aspri, & nelle riue, & letti de i fiumi. Gioua la sua chioma beuta con uino al morso delle serpi, alle sciatiche, alle distillationi del l'orina, & à i rotti: prouoca i mestrui. Beuta con uino melato risolue il sangue appreso nella uisciga, & parimente nel uentre: beuta medesimamente da digiuno in uino bianco innacquato al peso di tre oboli, prohibisce il catarro, che scende dal capo. Mettesi nelle uestimēta, accioche le conferui dalle tignuole.

N Asce l'Helichriso abondantemente in Thoscana ne i prati magri, per i terreni non coltiuati, per le colline, & similmente al magro in su la rena sassosa de i fiumi. Cresce all'altezza d'un gombito, con frondi d'abrotano, com partite per intervallli su per il fusto ben dritto, & saldo, nella cui sommità è una ombrella di color d'oro, simile nelle fattezze sue à quella del uolgare millesfoglio, & di quello eupatorio, che scriue Mesue. Il colore de i quali si conserua da poi che son secchi fiori, assai in lungo: & imperò il uerno nel mancare de i fiori, s'usano i secchi dell'Helichriso, come quelli dell'amaranto, ilqual chiamiamo fiore uelluto. Scrissene Plinio à xxv. cap. del. xxi. libro, così dicendo. L'Helichriso, ilqual chiamano alcuni Chrisanthemo, ha i fusti bianchi, & le frondi bianchiccie, simili à quelle dell'abrotano, la cui ombrella è piena di pendenti corimbi, che mai non si putrefanno. Quando uien percossa dalli raggi del sole, risplende come se fusse d'oro: la onde si costuma d'incoronarne gl'iddei. Ilche con grandissima diligenza osseruò Ptolemeo Re d'Egitto: nasce tra gli sterpi. Dell'Helichriso, quantunque sia glorioso, si inta non ritrouato, che ne suoi libri de i semplici facesse memoria alcuna Galeno, quantunque dopo lui non felo tacesse Pauolo Egineta.

Del Chrisanthemo. Cap. lx.

IL Chrisanthemo, ilquale chiamano alcuni Caltha, & altri Buphtalmo, è una herba tenera, & folta, che produce i suoi fusti lisci, & le frondi minutamente intagliate: sono i suoi fiori sopra modo splendenti, d'un colore, che nel giallo rosseggia, di forma simili alla rotondità dell'occhio, onde s'ha egli preso il nome di Buphtalmo: nasce attorno alle muraglie delle castella. Mangiansi i suoi fusti, come l'altre herbe de gli horti. I fiori triti, & incorporati con cera (secondo che si dice) risoluono quelle posteme, che si chiamano adipine: giouano al trabocco di fiele facendone presto andar uia il mal colore, se dopo al lungo uso del bagno si beono quando se n'esce fuore.

D Vantunque sieno alcuni, che si credino, che l'Buphtalmo, e l Chrisanthemo sieno una pianta medesima, per la perì corrispondenza, che si uede tra loro: non dimeno considerandosi alcune particolarità dell'uno, & dell'altro, pare, che ageuolmente si possa credere, che sieno piante l'una differente dall'altra. Ilche dimostra primamente Dioscoride, per hauerne fatto due particolari capitoli, uno prima nel terzo, & l'altro poscia qui nel. iiij. libro: percioche questo non harebbe fatto egli, se non hauesse veduta tra loro qualche differenza, la quale si conosce, per dire egli, che l Buphtalmo fa le frondi simili al finocchio, le quali sono capillari, & il Chrisanthemo minutamente intagliate. Oltre à cio disse, che i fusti del Chrisanthemo si mangiano ne cibi, come gli altri herbaggi de gli horti. Ilche si tacque prima del Buphtalmo, i cui fiori rassembrò egli à quelli della camomilla: ma non però gli rassembrò quelli del Chrisanthemo, il quale scrisse essere un herba tenera, & folta: ilche non recitò in quella del Buphtalmo. Oltre à cio parlando delle uirtù, & operationi loro, disse, che i fiori del Buphtalmo triti con cera, risoluonoi tumori, & le posteme parlandone uniuersalmente, & affermatuamente: & poscia diceva, che i fiori del Chrisanthemo incorporati con cera, (secondo che si dice) risoluono quelle posteme, che si chiamano adipine, & dai greci steatomatà, parlando particolarmente, & dubbiosamente.

translation:
316 BOOK

On Chrysogonum. Chapter 58.

Chrysogonum is a low plant whose leaves are similar to those of the oak, and whose flower resembles that of the coronary mullein. It produces a root similar to a turnip, which is very red inside and black outside. When ground and applied as a plaster with vinegar, it heals the bite of the wolf spider.

If Chrysogonum is not brought from elsewhere into the gardens of Italy, it will remain unknown to us, like all the other plants that nature hides in its secret garden.

On Helichrysum. Chapter 59.

Helichrysum, which some call Chrysanthemum and others Amaranth, with which the statues of the Gods are crowned, has a stem that is upright, white, turning green, and firm: along it grow narrow leaves similar to southernwood, spaced at intervals throughout. It produces a round head of golden color, drawn into an umbel like clusters of dry hanging corymbs; the root is slender. It grows in rough places, on riverbanks, and in riverbeds. Its head, drunk with wine, is beneficial against snake bites, sciatica, urinary distillations, and ruptures; it provokes menstruation. Drunk with honeyed wine, it resolves blood clotted in the bladder and likewise in the bowels; drunk likewise on an empty stomach in diluted white wine at the weight of three obols, it prevents catarrh descending from the head. It is placed among clothing to preserve it from moths.

Helichrysum grows abundantly in Tuscany in poor meadows, in uncultivated lands, on hillsides, and likewise in the sandy gravel of riverbeds. It grows to the height of a cubit, with southernwood-like leaves arranged at intervals along the very straight and firm stem, at the top of which is a golden-colored umbel, similar in appearance to common yarrow and to that eupatorium described by Mesue. The color of their dried flowers lasts quite a long time; and so in winter when fresh flowers are lacking, the dried ones of Helichrysum are used, like those of amaranth, which we call velvet flower. Pliny wrote about it in chapter 25 of book 21, saying thus: Helichrysum, which some call Chrysanthemum, has white stems and pale leaves similar to those of southernwood, whose umbel is full of hanging corymbs that never rot. When struck by the rays of the sun it shines as if made of gold; hence it is customary to crown the gods with it. This was observed with great diligence by Ptolemy, King of Egypt; it grows among scrub. Of Helichrysum, though it is so glorious, it is not found that Galen made any mention of it in his books on simples, though after him Paul of Aegina did not omit it.

On Chrysanthemum. Chapter 60.

Chrysanthemum, which some call Caltha and others Buphthalmum, is a tender and bushy plant that produces smooth stems and finely cut leaves; its flowers are exceedingly brilliant, of a color inclining to yellow, and in shape similar to the roundness of an eye, from which it has taken the name Buphthalmum; it grows around the walls of fortresses. Its stems are eaten like other garden herbs. The flowers, ground and mixed with wax (as they say), resolve those abscesses called adipine; they are good for an overflow of bile, quickly removing the discoloration if they are drunk after prolonged bathing when one exits the bath.

Although there are some who believe that Buphthalmum and Chrysanthemum are one and the same plant, because of the correspondence seen between them, nonetheless, considering certain particular features of each, it seems easy enough to believe that they are different plants. This is shown first by Dioscorides, who devoted two separate chapters to them, one earlier in the third book and another here in the fourth; for he would not have done this had he not seen some difference between them, which is apparent from his saying that Buphthalmum has leaves similar to fennel, which are hair-like, while those of Chrysanthemum are finely cut. Furthermore he said that the stems of Chrysanthemum are eaten in food like other garden vegetables, which he did not say of Buphthalmum; and he compared the flowers of Buphthalmum to those of chamomile, but did not compare those of Chrysanthemum to them, since he wrote that the latter is a tender and bushy plant, which he did not say of Buphthalmum. Furthermore, speaking of their virtues and properties, he said that the flowers of Buphthalmum ground with wax resolve tumors and abscesses, speaking generally and affirmatively; but then he said that the flowers of Chrysanthemum, mixed with wax (as they say), resolve those abscesses called adipine, and by the Greeks steatoma, speaking specifically and with some uncertainty.

translation:
FOURTH BOOK. 317

What makes me believe that some of the ancient Greeks imagined that Buphthalmon and Chrysanthemum were the same thing, is that they transferred to Buphthalmon everything that Dioscorides wrote in his third book, as one finds was also done with wild rue, St. John's wort, and likewise with asarum and baccara. For which reason I would say that the chapter on Chrysanthemum in Dioscorides should be read thus: THE CHRYSANTHEMUM is a tender and leafy herb, which produces smooth stems and finely cut leaves, whose flowers are of a color that shades toward yellow, exceedingly brilliant. Its stems are eaten like other garden greens. The flowers, ground with wax, are said to dissolve those swellings called steatomas, that is, fatty tumors. In this way, then, the Chrysanthemum is restored to its true history, which, upon careful consideration, differs greatly from that of Buphthalmon. I myself have seen the Chrysanthemum growing most abundantly in the territory of Montenero, a castle of our most magnificent city of Siena, entirely matching the reformed description noted here by us; our peasants eat it cooked, as one eats beets, spinach, and cabbage. However, I have never yet been able to see the true Buphthalmon anywhere in Italy. Leonardo Fuchs the German is deceived in his otherwise glorious herbal, believing that the Chrysanthemum is that species of Ranunculus which grows in meadows with parsley-like leaves and yellow flowers: for the true Chrysanthemum is quite different from this, and I find no mention of it in Galen's books that treat of plants.

Of Ageratum. Chapter 61.

Ageratum is a bushy plant, one span tall, simple, low-growing, very similar to oregano. It produces an umbel, in which the flowers resemble small golden buttons, smaller than those of helichrysum; and it bears the name Ageratum for no other reason than that it preserves the color of its flower for a long time. Its decoction is quite warming. The herb applied as a fumigation stimulates urine and softens hardness of the womb.

Ageratum grows commonly throughout Tuscany, with leaves and stems like oregano, although its umbel is full of tiny golden flowers. Galen wrote briefly of it in book seven on the faculties of simples, saying thus: Ageratum has the virtue of digesting and gently resolving inflammations.

Of Verbenaca. Chapter 62.

Verbenaca, or Peristereon, grows in watery places. It seems to have taken its name from being frequented willingly by doves, wherever it grows. It is a plant one span tall, sometimes taller, whose leaves, which come from the stem, are cut and whitish. This herb is often found with a single stem and a single root. It is believed that its leaves, combined with fresh pig fat or rose oil and applied as a poultice, relieve pains of the womb. Applied with vinegar, it extinguishes St. Anthony's fire and stops putrid and corrosive ulcers. It heals wounds and, with honey, cicatrizes old ulcers.

Of Sacred Herb. Chapter 63.

The sacred herb called Peristereon produces little branches about one cubit tall, sometimes somewhat taller, square-stemmed, on which the leaves are arranged at intervals similar to those of oak leaves, but smaller and narrower, though cut in the same manner, of a somewhat bluish color. The root is long and slender. The flowers are purple and fine. The leaves drunk with wine together with the root, and likewise applied as poultices, are good against snakebite; and drunk at the weight of one dram in a hemina of old wine with three obols of incense, for forty continuous days on an empty stomach, they help against overflow of bile; applied as poultices they soothe old swellings and inflammations, and cleanse foul ulcers. The decoction of the whole plant, used as a gargle, breaks up the crusts of the throat, and stops corrosive ulcers of the mouth. It is said that if its infusion is sprinkled in the places where banquets are held, the guests become merry. The third node of its stem, counting from the ground upward, with the leaves near it, is given for tertian fever, and the fourth node for quartan fever. It is called sacred herb because it is used greatly in the purification of places, and for being worn suspended about the person.

In Tuscany the Verbenaca is called Verminacola, and in other parts of Italy Berbena; of this plant, as is clearly seen from the above-written chapters, there are two species, between which there is no other difference than that one produces its stems upright with sparse leaves, and the other spreading toward the ground and more leafy; nor is there any further difference in leaves or flowers, as Fuchs imagined, who in his great herbal said that the upright Verbenaca bore flow-

LIBRO

A re giallo. Ilche non ritrouo io, che dicesse Dioscoride, ne Plinio, ilquale al. ix. capo del. xxv. libro ne scrisse, cosi dicendo. Sono di Verbena due spetie, una frondosa, laqual chiamano femmina, & l'altra con piu rade frondi, laqual chiamano maschio. I rami d'amendune sono assai, d'altezza d'un gombito, sottili, & riquadrati. Le frondi minori di quelle della quercia, piu strette, & maggiormente intagliate. Il fior glauco, cioè che nel celeste biancheggia. La radice lunga, & sottile. Nascono p tutto, nelle pianure, et ne i luoghi acquastrini. Sono alcuni, che nò le distinguono; ma ne fanno d'amendune una sola spetie, per hauere le medesime virtu l'una, che l'altra. Laqual dottrina dimostra, che si sognasse il Fuchsio, dicendo, che la retta produceua il fior giallo. Ma auanti da lui errò piu di grosso Othone Brunfelsio tedesco, ilquale nel suo herbario dipinse per Verbena femmina quella pianta, che uolgarmente chiamano alcuni Cardoncello, & altri Speliciosa, non accordandosi, che questa è l'Erigeron, ouero il Senetio scrittone nel processo di questo libro da Dioscoride. Galeno sapendo, che non era tra l'una, & l'altra differenza, ne scrisse breuemente sotto una sola spetie, cosi dicendo. Il Peristereon è stato cosi chiamato per conuersare, oue la nasce, le Peristere, cioè le colombe, la cui uirtu diseccatiua è cosi salorosa, che puo consolidare agenolmente le ferite.

Dell'Astragalo.          Cap. lxiiii.

B LO Astragalo è una pianta poco alta da terra, le cui frondi, & ramuscelli sono simili à quelli de i ceci: produce il fior porporeo, & picciolo, & la radice ritonda, grande, come quella del rafano, con altre radicette attorno, ferme, dure, nere, & intrigate in se stesse come corna, al gusto costrettiue. Nasce in luoghi uetosi, opachi, & doue lungo tempo giace la neue. Trouasene copia in Memphi d'Arcadia. La radice beuta nel uino ristagna il corpo: prouoca l orina. Poluerizzasi secca sopra l'ulcere uecchie: ristagna il sangue: ma è tanto dura, che malageuolmente si pesta.

Asce l'Astragalo copiosamente ne i monti della ualle Anania, con frondi simili à quelle de i ceci, coi fiore porporeo,
N & radice simile al rafano, dallaquale procedono piu radicette intrigate in se stesse. Ilperche parmi, che concordandosi con la scrittura di Dioscoride si possa agenolmente dire, che sia questa il uero Astragalo. Nasce parimente in sul contado di Goritia, & sono quiui in uso le sue radici per far orinare. scrissene Plinio diuersamente da Dioscoride al. viii. capo del. xxvi. libro, cosi dicendo. Ha l'Astragalo lunghe frondi, & molto intagliate, ritorte appresso ala radice. Produce tre, ouer quattro fusti, tutti pieni di frondi, il fiore di hiacintho, le radici capigliose, & intrigate in se stesse, rosse, & molto dure. Nasce in luoghi aprichi, sassosi, & neuosi, come è il monte Pheneo d'Arcadia. Scrissene Galeno al. vi. delle facultà
C dei simplici, cosi dicendo. L'astragalo è picciola pianta, le cui radici sono costrettiue, & però si consumano tra quelle cose, che ualorosaamente diseccano; imperoche consolida l'ulcere uecchie, & ristagna i flussi del corpo quanto si beono le sue radici cotte nel uino. Nascene assai nel monte Pheneo d'Arcadia.

Del Hiacintho.          Cap. lxv.

IL Hiacintho ha frondi di bulbo, & il fusto alto una spana, liscio, & piu sottile del dito piccolino, di uerde colore, la cui chioma si riuolge uerso terra, piena di porporei fiori. Produce la radice cipollina, laquale si crede, che applicata in sul pettinecchio à i fanciulli non ui lascia nascere i peli. Beuta ristagna il corpo: prouoca l'orina, et gioua al morso di quei ragni, che si chiamano phalagi. Il seme per hauere uirtu piu costrettiua, ristagna i flussi stomachali, & mondifica beuto con uino il trabocco del fiele.

Asce il Hiacintho uniuersalmente ne t campi per tutte le campagne tra le biade con frondi, et radica cipolline, fusto alto una spanna, sottile, liscio, & uerde di colore. Fiorisce alla fine di Marzo, & nel principie d'Aprile, quando fioriscono le uiole. Produce la chioma da mezzo il fusto in su, tutta piena di porporegg ianti fiori, che nel maturarsi s'inchinano à terra, et dur anni uso assai tepo, auanti che disfiorischino. in Thoscana non sapèdosi altro nome si chiamano Cipolle canine, ouero saluatiche, et ricolgongli i fanciulli nel spuntare fior della terra, per il lorobel colore. Ma qui da sapere, che questo non è il Hiacintho, che scriuono i poeti esser nato del sangue d'Aiace, oue si ritrovano anchora le lettere del suo nome scritte: percioche questo (secondo le fauole loro) produce un fiore rosso simile al giglio. Fece del Hiacintho mentione Galeno al. viii. delle facultà de i simplici, cosi dicendo. La radice dell'Hiacintho è cipollina, secca nel primo ordine, & frigida nella fine del secondo, ouero nel principio del terzo. Ilperche si crede, che impiastrata à i fanciulli proibibisce il nascere de i peli attorno alle membra uirili. Il suo frutto è leggiermente asterfsiuo, et costrettiuo et però si da egli à bere nel uino al trabocco del fiele. Disecca nel terzo ordine, et ritrouasi quasi tra la calidità, et la frigidità mediocre.

Del Papauero saluatico.          Cap. lxvi.

IL Papauero saluatico, ilquale si chiama Rhea, nasce la primauera nei campi, con fiore del tutto caduco, dalquale ha egli preso il nome appresso à i greci. Sono le sue frondi simili alla ruchetta, ouero all'origano, ouero alla cicorea, ouero al thimo: ma piu lunghe, intagliate, & ruuide. Il fusto è come un giunco, dritto, alto un

LIBRO

A re yellow. This I do not find stated by Dioscorides, nor by Pliny, who wrote about it in chapter nine of book twenty-five, saying thus: Verbena has two species, one leafy, which they call female, and another with fewer leaves, which they call male. The branches of both are numerous, an elbow's height tall, slender and square. The leaves smaller than those of the oak, narrower and more deeply cut. The flower grayish-blue, that is, tending toward sky-blue. The root long and slender. They grow everywhere, in plains and in marshy places. Some do not distinguish between them, but make both into a single species, since they have the same virtues one as the other. This doctrine shows that Fuchs was dreaming when he said that the upright one produced a yellow flower. But before him, Otto Brunfels the German erred even more grossly, who in his herbal depicted as female Verbena the plant that some commonly call Cardoncello and others Speliciosa, not agreeing that this is the Erigeron, or the Senecio described in the course of this book by Dioscorides. Galen, knowing that there was no difference between the one and the other, wrote briefly under a single species, saying thus: Peristereon has been so named from frequenting the places where it grows, the Peristere, that is doves, whose drying virtue is so powerful that it can readily consolidate wounds.

On Astragalus.          Chapter 64.

B The Astragalus is a plant of low height from the ground, whose leaves and small branches are similar to those of chickpeas. It produces a small purple flower, and the root is round and large, like that of the radish, with other small rootlets around it, firm, hard, dark, and tangled upon themselves like horns, astringent to the taste. It grows in shaded, wooded places where snow lies for a long time. It is found in abundance in Memphis of Arcadia. The root drunk in wine checks the bowels and stimulates urine. When dried and powdered it is applied to old ulcers; it stops bleeding, but is so hard that it is difficult to pound.

Astragalus grows abundantly in the mountains of the valley of Anania, with leaves similar to those of chickpeas, with a purple flower,
N and a root similar to the radish, from which proceed more small rootlets tangled upon themselves. It therefore seems to me that, agreeing with the writings of Dioscorides, one may readily say that this is the true Astragalus. It also grows in the region of Gorizia, where its roots are used to promote urination. Pliny wrote about it differently from Dioscorides in chapter eight of book twenty-six, saying thus: Astragalus has long leaves, deeply cut and twisted near the root. It produces three or four stems, all full of leaves, the flower of hyacinth, the roots hairy and tangled upon themselves, red and very hard. It grows in sunny, rocky and snowy places, such as Mount Pheneus in Arcadia. Galen wrote about it in book six of
C his work on simples, saying thus: Astragalus is a small plant whose roots are astringent, and therefore it is counted among those things that powerfully dry; for it consolidates old ulcers and checks the fluxes of the body when its roots are boiled and drunk in wine. It grows abundantly on Mount Pheneus in Arcadia.

On Hyacinth.          Chapter 65.

The Hyacinth has bulbous leaves and a stem one span tall, smooth and slimmer than the little finger, green in color, whose head bends toward the ground, full of purple flowers. It produces a bulb-like root, which it is believed, when applied to the pubic area of boys, prevents hair from growing. Drunk it checks the bowels and stimulates urine, and it helps against the bite of those spiders called phalangia. The seed, being more astringent, checks stomach fluxes, and when drunk in wine clears overflowing bile.

The Hyacinth grows universally in the fields throughout the countryside among the crops, with leaves and roots like an onion, the stem a span tall, slender, smooth and green in color. It flowers at the end of March and at the beginning of April, when the violets bloom. It produces its head from the middle of the stem upward, all full of brilliant purple flowers, which as they ripen bend toward the ground, and last for some time before the flowers drop. In Tuscany, not knowing any other name, they are called wild or dog onions, and children gather them when the flowers first push up from the ground, for their beauty. But it should be known that this is not the Hyacinth that the poets write was born from the blood of Ajax, where even the letters of his name may be found written upon it; for that plant (according to their fables) produces a red flower similar to the lily. Galen made mention of the Hyacinth in book eight of his work on simples, saying thus: The root of the Hyacinth is bulb-like, dry in the first degree and cold at the end of the second or beginning of the third. It is therefore believed, when applied as a plaster to boys, to prevent the growth of hair around the virile parts. Its fruit is mildly astringent and binding, and therefore it is given to drink in wine against overflowing of bile. It dries in the third degree, and is found to be almost midway between hot and cold.

On Wild Poppy.          Chapter 66.

The wild poppy, which is called Rhea, grows in the fields in spring, with a flower that is entirely fleeting, from which it takes its name among the Greeks. Its leaves are similar to those of rocket, or to oregano, or to chicory, or to thyme, but longer, cut and rough. The stem is like a rush, straight, tall as one

elbow, and rough. The flower resembles the wild anemone, red, and sometimes white, A
with a somewhat elongated head, but smaller than the anemone. The seed is reddish; the root is long,
whitish, thinner than the little finger, and bitter to the taste. A decoction of five
or six of its heads is made in three cups of wine, reduced to half, and drunk to induce
sleep. The seed drunk with honeyed water in the measure of one acetabulum softens the body
quite gently. It is put into confections and other sweet foods, and eaten for the same purpose. The
leaves plastered together with the heads extinguish inflammations, and by fumigating with them,
or spreading their decoction over the head, sleep is easily induced.

On the Domestic Poppy. Chapter 67.

Among the species of Poppies that are cultivated, the seed of that which grows in gardens
is put into bread for healthy people, and is also used mixed with honey in place
of sesame. This one is called Thilacite, whose head is long and full of white B
seed. The wild one has a flat and compressed head, and black seed, called Pithi-
te, though there are some who also call it Rhea, for extracting the liquid from it. The
third, the most wild of all and most powerful in medicines, is longer than the aforementioned, and has longer
heads. They all share the common nature of cooling; and therefore the decoction of
the leaves and heads made in water easily induces sleep when taken in quantity. The decoction is drunk
to cause sleep. The fresh heads, ground with polenta and made into a plaster, help against sacred fire,
and likewise against inflammations. They are pestled fresh and made into troches, and kept dried
for needs. The same heads are cooked in water until half is consumed, and then
honey is added, and they are cooked together until the mixture forms an electuary, which is
then a powerful remedy for relieving pains, for coughs, for catarrh descending to the throat,
and to the windpipe of the lung, and for stomach fluxes; but it becomes more efficacious by adding
acacia and the juice of hypocistis. The seed of the black poppy is given to drink ground with wine, for
fluxes of the body and menstruation. It is applied as a plaster with water against prolonged wakefulness on the temples
and on the forehead. OPIUM, which is made from it, cools more, thickens more, and dries more. Taken C
in the quantity of one grain of bitter vetch, it mitigates pains, ripens, causes sleep, helps with cough,
and with stomach fluxes; but taken in greater quantity it harms, because by making
those who drink it lethargic, it kills them. Mixed with rose oil and made into an
ointment, it mitigates pains of the head; it is distilled for pains in the ears, with almond oil,
myrrh, and saffron. Mixed with roasted egg yolk, it helps with inflammations
of the eyes, with vinegar for sacred fire, and with wounds, and with gout with woman's milk,
and saffron; placed as a suppository in the rectum, it provokes sleep. The best is that which is dense,
heavy, bitter to the taste, sleep-inducing when smelled, easily dissolved in water, smooth, white,
not rough, not granular, which when strained does not congeal like wax, which when placed in the
sun does not liquefy, which when lit does not produce a black flame, and which when extinguished retains the virtue of
its odor. Opium is adulterated by mixing in glaucium, gum, or the juice of the wild D
lettuce; but the fraud can be detected: for that which is counterfeited with glaucium, when placed in
water, tints it the color of saffron. The one counterfeited with lettuce juice has little odor,
and appears rough to the eye. That mixed with gum is shiny and breaks easily. Some
reduce themselves to such madness and ignorance that they adulterate it also by mixing in
suet. It is burned in a new earthenware vessel for medicines of the eyes, until it becomes softer
and redder in color. Diagoras (according to Erasistratus) condemned the use of Opium
in afflictions of the eyes and ears, forbidding it to be placed inside them, saying
that it weakened the sight and caused prolonged sleep. To which the physician Andreas added
that whoever anointed their eyes with it without adulterating it went blind. Mnesidemus praised it
only for smelling, saying it was thus suitable for inducing sleep, condemning it
then in every other use. But experience has shown this to be false, as is clearly
demonstrated by the effects of its virtues; therefore it will not be amiss to write about how

oglio, leuano uia l'eschara. Messe con oglio ne gli occhi del bestiame, chiarificano le nugole,
& l'albugini. Stimarono ingannandosi alcuni per la similitudine delle frondi, che'l glau-
cio si facesse di questo papauero.

Del Papauero spumeo. Cap. lxix.

L Papauero spumeo, ilquale chiamano alcuni Heracleo, produce il fusto alto
una spanna, le frondi picciolissime simili all'herba lanaria, & appresso à quelle
il suo frutto bianco: è la sua herba bianca, & tutta come una spiuma: ha la radi-
ce in sommo. Il seme se ricoglie la state, quando è interamente maturo, & che sec
cato casca. Questo preso con acqua melata al peso d'uno acetabolo, fa uomitare, & gioua pri
uatamente questa purgatione à coloro, che patiscono il mal caduco.

N Asce il Papauero cornuto abondantemente nelle nostre maremme di Siena in sul territorio di Grossetto, d'Orbe-
tello, et di porto Hercole, et mefime in piu luoghi del monte Argentaio, ma altroue in italiano non l'ho ueduto io, se
non seminato ne i giardini p publico spettacolo, come si suol fare d'altri rari, et non troppo uolgari semplici. Scrif-
sene Theophrasto al. xiij. capo del. ix. libro, cosi dicendo. Sono di Papaueri saluatichi piu spetie, delle quali quello, che si
chiama Corniculare, produce frondi simili a quelle del uerbasco nero, ma però manco neri: il fusto è alto un gombito, la ra
dice corta, et poco profonda in terra, & sono i suoi semi détro à certi cornetti ritorti. Ricogliesial tépo della mietitura, pur
ga il corpo: le frõ di leuano l'albugini de gli occhi delle pecore. Nasce appresso al mare in luoghi assiosi. Pensaronsi alcu-
ni, che il Glaucio, ilqual chi mano gli Arabi Memithe, si facesse del succhio del Papauero cornuto: ma come benissimo gli
auuertisce Dioscoride s'ingannano manifestamente. Quello, che chiamano Spumeo, non ho ueramente fin hora possuto ri-
trouare chi me lo dimostri in Italia, et però lo lascierò da parte con l'altre piante, che ne sono incognite. Del Cornuto scrif-
se Galeno al. vij. delle facultà de i semplici, cosi dicendo. Il Papauero cornuto è cosi chiamato per produrre egli il seme leg-
giermente ritorto, simile à quello del sien greco, di modo che par simile à un corno di bue. Chiamanlo alcuni Paralio, per na
scere egli abondantemente appresso al mare. Ha uirtu incisiua, & astrfsiua: et però la dicottione della sua radice bollita si-
no al calare della metà, gioua à i difetti del segato. Le frondi, & i fiori conferiscono all'ulcere sordide, & contumaci, ma nõ
s'usano se non fatta prima la mondificatione delle piaghe. So no le frondi cosi astrrsiue, che risoluono qualche uolta alquan-
to della carne purés; & imperò con la forza di tal uirtu, non solamente caua la marcia dell'ulcere, ma anchora l'eschara.

Dell'Hipecoo. Cap. lxx.

D O Hipecoo, ilquale altri chiamano Hipopheo, nasce nelle biade, & ne i campi,
con frondi simili alla ruta, & sottili rami. Ha la medesima uirtu del liquore del
papauero.

C Hi diligentemente cerca ne i campi tra le biade, & tra i legumi, facilmente ritrouara l'Hipecoo. Questo mi dimo-
straua Piero Spezzalancia spetiale, & mio dilettissimo compare per la Ruta saluatica, dicendomi, che cosi da altri
Spetiali gli era stato mostrato. Cresce all'altezza di una spanna, ò poco piu, con frondi assai simili alla ruta, fusto
tenero, & liscio, & fiori gialli, & minuti. Scrissene breuemente Galeno al. viij. delle facultà de i semplici, cosi dicendo.
L'Hipecoo ha uirtu d'infrigidare nel terzo ordine, di modo che poco è egli lontano dal papauero.

Dell'herba Apollinaria, ouero Hioseiamo. Cap. lxxi.

L Hioseíamo è una pianta, che produce i fusti grossi, & le frondi larghe, lunghet

simili à quelli de i melagrani, serrati d'alcuni scudetti, & pieni di seme, come di pa

description: Pietro Andrea Matthioli's landmark Italian translation of Dioscorides De Materia Medica. The first vernacular edition to make classical Greek botanical medicine accessible to European physicians.
translation:
FOURTH BOOK. 321

On the Horned Poppy. Chapter 68.

The Horned Poppy has white, hairy leaves similar to those of mullein, toothed around the edges like those of the wild poppy, from which its stalk is not so different. It produces a pale flower, and a small fruit, twisted like a horn, similar to the small horns of Greek hay, from which it takes its name; inside it are seeds similar to those of small poppies, and black. Its root lies near the surface of the dark, coarse soil. It grows in rough places and in coastal marshlands. A decoction of the root drunk in water, boiled down to half, is beneficial for sciatica, for disorders of the liver, and for those who pass thick, rough urine like cobwebs. The seed drunk at the weight of one acetabolo in honeyed water gently purges the body. The leaves, and likewise the flowers, applied as a poultice with oil, remove scabs. Placed with oil in the eyes of livestock, they clarify cloudiness and corneal opacities. Some people, deceiving themselves, thought that glaucium was made from this poppy, on account of the similarity of the leaves.

On the Foam Poppy. Chapter 69.

The Foam Poppy, which some call Heracleo, produces a stalk a span tall, with very small leaves similar to the woolly herb, and next to them its white fruit: the whole plant is white and entirely like foam; it has its root at the top. The seed is gathered in summer when fully ripe and when it falls off when dry. This, taken with honeyed water at the weight of one acetabolo, causes vomiting, and this purgation is privately beneficial for those who suffer from epilepsy.

N The Horned Poppy grows abundantly in our marshlands of Siena, in the territory of Grosseto, of Orbetello, and of Porto Ercole, and likewise in many places on Mount Argentario; but elsewhere in Italy I have not seen it, except sown in gardens for public display, as is done with other rare and not very common simples. Theophrastus wrote of it in chapter 13 of book 9, saying thus: Among wild poppies there are many species, of which the one called Cornicular produces leaves similar to those of black mullein, but somewhat less dark: the stalk is a cubit tall, the root short and not deep in the ground, and its seeds are inside certain twisted little horns. It is gathered at harvest time, purges the body; its leaves remove cloudiness from the eyes of sheep. It grows near the sea in sandy places. Some thought that Glaucium, which the Arabs call Memithe, was made from the juice of the Horned Poppy; but as Dioscorides very well points out, they are plainly mistaken. As for what they call Foam Poppy, I have truly not yet been able to find anyone to show it to me in Italy, and so I will set it aside along with other plants that remain unknown to us. Galen wrote of the Horned Poppy in book 7 of the Faculties of Simple Medicines, saying thus: The Horned Poppy is so called because it produces its seed slightly twisted, similar to that of fenugreek, so that it resembles a cow's horn. Some call it Paralio, because it grows abundantly near the sea. It has cutting and astringent properties; and therefore a decoction of its root boiled down to half is good for disorders of the liver. The leaves and flowers are good for foul and stubborn ulcers, but they should not be used until the wounds have first been cleansed. The leaves are so abrasive that they dissolve some of the fleshy matter; and so through the force of this property they not only draw out the discharge of an ulcer, but also remove the scab.

On Hipecoon. Chapter 70.

D Hipecoon, which others call Hipopheo, grows among grain crops and in fields, with leaves similar to rue and with slender branches. It has the same properties as the juice of the poppy.

C Whoever diligently searches the fields among grain crops and legumes will easily find Hipecoon. Piero Spezzalancia, an apothecary and my very dear companion, used to show this to me as wild rue, telling me that this is what other apothecaries had shown him. It grows to a height of a span, or a little more, with leaves quite similar to rue, a tender and smooth stem, and small yellow flowers. Galen wrote briefly of it in book 8 of the Faculties of Simple Medicines, saying thus: Hipecoon has a cooling virtue of the third degree, so that it is not far removed from the poppy.

On the herb Apollinaris, or Henbane. Chapter 71.

Henbane is a plant that produces thick stems and broad, somewhat long, cut, dark, and hairy leaves. The flowers come out in orderly fashion along the side of the stem, similar to those of the pomegranate, enclosed by certain little cups and full of seed, like the poppy. It comes in three varieties: one that produces black seed and flowers that are almost purple, the
