A the seed with wine; the lees of burnt wine, drunk in water, and vitriol drunk with vinegar. Useful also for these purposes are the root and seed of mustard, and likewise of nasturtium, when eaten. Galen wrote about Mushrooms in his seventh book on the properties of simples, saying thus: the mushroom is a cold and damp plant, and therefore it is associated with a poisonous and deadly quality, and certainly among them there are those that kill, and especially those that have naturally mixed within them a certain putrefying quality.

On Colchicum. Chapter 86.

The Colchicum, which some call Ephemeron and others the wild Bulb, produces at the end of autumn its whitish flower, similar to saffron, and after the flower the leaves similar to those of the bulb, but thicker. Its stalk is a palm's height, on which the red seed is produced; the outer bark of the root is blackish, but when peeled it is white, tender, sweet, and full of moisture. This bulbous root has a cleft in the middle, from which its flower rises. It grows most abundantly in Messenia and in Colchis. Eaten, the root kills by strangulation, as mushrooms do, and we have described it for no other reason than to warn people not to eat it without thinking, mistaking it for a bulb: for its agreeable taste remarkably entices the ignorant to eat it. The same remedies that are given for mushroom poisoning are useful here: cow's milk drunk is helpful for this, and if one has that, there is no need for other remedies.

On Ephemeron. Chapter 87.

The Ephemeron, which some call wild Iris, produces leaves like those of a lily, but more slender. The stalk is similar, the flower white and bitter, the seed tender; it has a single root, as thick as a finger, long, astringent, and fragrant. It grows in woods and shaded places. The root is useful for toothache when the mouth is rinsed with its decoction. The leaves cooked in wine dissolve tumors and abscesses that have not yet fully matured.

C There are the two species of Ephemeron placed together here by Dioscorides, namely the Colchicum Ephemeron and the Ephemeron called Wild Lily. The first is said to be so poisonous that when eaten it kills within a single day, and therefore Dioscorides said he wrote about it for no other reason than to warn people of its deadly nature: for many could easily be deceived, enticed by the sweetness of its taste. This teaching and warning has been little heeded by the Arabs and our other predecessors: and yet, though it was clearer than the sun, it has not prevented the continued falling into this error: for the Colchicum Ephemeron, a poisonous and deadly plant, is nothing other, when one examines all its characteristics, than the Hermodactyl used in apothecaries' shops, whose harmfulness to our bodies anyone can judge who understands what not only Dioscorides and Galen, but also Paul of Aegina, Nicander, and Pliny wrote about it as a kind of deadly poison; which, even if in our times it does not manifestly kill those who use it in medicines, this can easily be because it is not as poisonous in Italy as it is in Colchis, or because not enough of it is taken to be sufficient to kill a man: but there is no doubt that it can cause very great harm to our bodies. The true cause of this error was Serapion, who in a single chapter treated confusedly both the Ephemerons and the Hermodactyl under the heading of Hermodactyl, not noticing that to the Greek authors, from whom he drew everything, the Ephemerons and the Hermodactyl are quite different things. Of this Paul of Aegina gives clear evidence: for in his seventh book he treated both the Ephemerons and the Hermodactyl in separate chapters, saying thus: the root of the Hermodactyl alone, and likewise its decoction, has the virtue of purging, and is given privately for pains in the joints when the humors are in flux: but it greatly harms the stomach. And a little further on, about the Ephemerons, he said: the Ephemeron — not the one that is a poison, but the one called Wild Lily — is composed of mixed, repercussive, and wind-resolving qualities. This clearly demonstrates that the Hermodactyl is quite different from the Ephemerons, and that Serapion grossly erred here by lumping together in one bundle both the Ephemerons and the Hermodactyl, which the other Arabs and our predecessors then imitated, handing down to each other this continuous error. Therefore it must be considered that in no way can it be conceded that the Hermodactyls commonly used in apothecaries' shops should continue to be used, since not only do the above reasons show they are not the true ones, but it is clearly known that they are a deadly and detestable poison. Moreover, that last Ephemeron called Wild Iris grows abundantly in the meadows and woods of the high mountains of the valley of Ananis, and the inhabitants call it Crazy Lily: in which all the true characteristics that Dioscorides attributes to it can be seen, and therefore Leonardo Fuchs the German greatly erred in his great herbal, wishing to make people believe that the Ephemeron of the second species

si gli rassembra, eccetto che è alquanto piu tonda, piu grossa, & non ha quella fessura nel mezzo, onde esce il fiore, come

questa molto amara, & quella del Colchico è dolce, & grata al gusto. Questo uiamente non seppero i ueneran di Padri,
che di nuouo hanno comentato l'antidotario di Mesue: percioche, per quanto si legge nel comento fatto sopra alle pillule
d'Hermodattili, non fanno alcuna differenza tra gli Hermodattili ueri, e'l Colchico scritto nel. iiij. libro da Dioscoride. In
che, per quanto si puo considerare per le ragioni predette, assai importa per la uita de gli huomini. Scrisse de gli Ephemeri
Galeno al. vi. delle facultà de i semplici, cosi diceno. L'Ephemero, non dico quel mortifero, et uelenoso: ma quell'altro, che
chiamano anchora Iride saluatico, produce le frondi, e'l fusto simili al giglio, la radice lunghetta, & non ritonda, come il
Colchico, grossa un dito, costretta, & di buono, & soaue odore. Et però si conosce manifestamente e'sere il suo tempera
mento misto, & hauer facultà ripercussiua, et risolutiua per uapori. Tolto alla quantità d'un bic
chiere, cura la tosse uecchia. Gargarizzasi, & impiastrassi, per l'infiammagioni del gorgoz
zule. Distillato nell'orecchie con oglio rosado, ne caua il dolore.
Hiansi uolgarmente l'Helsine scritta qui da Dioscoride, Parietaria, per nascer ella in su le pareti delle muraglie,
C & Vetriola per esser in uso à spurare i bicchieri, & gli altri usi di uetro, & impero per eser notissima pianta,
non accade a trattarne per altra lunga historia. Fecene mentione Galeno al. vi. delle facultà de i semplici, cosi di
cendo. L'Helsine ha uirtu astrisiua, & costrettiua con una certa humidità frigidetta, & imperò sana tutti i flemmoni nel D
principio, & parimente nel crescimento loro, sino allo stato, & massime i caldi: ilche fa ella anchora nel cominciare de i
foroncoli, & altri tumori impiastratai suo uso. Gioua il succhio distillato nelle orecchie per i dolori apostemosi di quelle. Fan
none alcuni gargarismo nelle posteme del gorgozzule, & sono alcuni medici, che la danno a coloro, che sono del continuo
molestati dalla tosse uecchia. Vedesi manifestamente la uirtu sua astersiua ne i uasi di uetro.

Dell'Alsine. Cap. lxxxix.

A Alsine, laquale chiamano alcuni antillo, & altri miosota per rassembrarsi le
sue frondi alle orecchie de i topi, nasce nelle selue ombrose, & luoghi opachi, dal
che è stata chiamata Alsine. Sarebbe questa stata la medesima, che l'helsine, se la
nò fusse piu picciola, & non hauese le frondi piu lunghe, non pelose: pesta rispi
ra odore di cocomero. Ha uirtu di ristagnare, & d'infrigidire. Impiastrasi con polenta per
l'infiammagioni de gli occhi. Il suo succhio distillato nell'orecchie ne caua il dolore, et uale à
tutte quelle cose, che l'helsine.

FOURTH BOOK. 333

This is that plant which is commonly called Lily of the Valley, which produces that small white flower, almost in the shape of a pomegranate blossom, remarkably fragrant; for its leaves at first do not resemble those of the lily, nor do its stems, which are as slender as threads. The root, moreover, is hairlike, divided into many parts, and not as thick as a finger, as is that of the true Ephemeron. Beyond this, I do not find that the flower of the Ephemeron is fragrant, as is that of the Lily of the Valley, which is truly so fragrant and pleasing to the nose that there are few men who in the month of May do not carry it in their hand or keep it in their rooms — which is strong evidence that the Lily of the Valley, whose history we described above in the chapter on Hemerocalle in the fourth book, is quite different from this kind of Ephemeron. It also seems to me worth considering that the Hermodactyl, about which Paul and Actuarius wrote as being distinct from Colchicum and from Ephemeron, though not described by anyone, should perhaps resemble Colchicum in some way — which has always been used in apothecaries in its place — and that from this arose the error of taking Colchicum for Hermodactyl. I have often thought that the plant which grows abundantly in spring in nearly all meadows, thick with leaves broader than those of leeks, which without producing any flower yields a seed first white, then reddish as it matures, about the size of a cabbage seed, in certain small green shells like nuts that emerge from between the leaves without any stem, one next to another, is truly the Hermodactyl that Paul and Actuarius meant. For the root of this plant is covered by a thin membrane which in color is truly similar to that which surrounds the root of Colchicum, and the root itself also closely resembles it, except that it is somewhat more rounded, thicker, and lacks that cleft in the middle from which the flower emerges as in Colchicum; but in whiteness, in substance, and in appearance it much resembles it. It is true, however, that in taste this plant is very bitter, while Colchicum is sweet and pleasant to the palate. This, it seems, was not understood by those venerable Fathers who have recently commented on the Antidotary of Mesue; for, as one reads in the commentary on the pills of Hermodactyl, they make no distinction between the true Hermodactyls and the Colchicum written of in the fourth book of Dioscorides — which, as can be seen from the arguments given above, matters greatly for the lives of men. Galen wrote of the Ephemerons in the sixth book on the Faculties of Simple Medicines, as follows: "The Ephemeron — I do not mean the deadly and poisonous one — but that other which they also call wild Iris, produces leaves and a stem similar to the lily, with a somewhat long root, not round like that of Colchicum, a finger's breadth thick, and of a good and sweet odor. It is therefore clearly evident that its temperament is mixed, and that it has a repercussive and resolutive faculty for vapors. Taken in the quantity of a cup, it cures chronic coughs. It is used as a gargle and as a poultice for inflammations of the throat. Distilled into the ears with rose oil, it removes pain."

What is commonly called in the vernacular the Helsine written of here by Dioscorides is called Parietaria, because it grows on the walls of buildings, and Vetriola because it is used for scouring glass and other glass vessels. Since it is a very well-known plant, there is no need to treat it at length. Galen mentioned it in the sixth book on the Faculties of Simple Medicines, saying as follows: "The Helsine has an astringent and constrictive virtue with a certain cold moisture, and therefore heals all phlegmons in their beginning and likewise in their growth, even up to their peak, and especially hot ones — which it also does at the onset of boils and other tumors when applied as a poultice. The juice distilled into the ears is beneficial for apostematic pains in them. Some use it as a gargle for abscesses of the throat, and there are some physicians who give it to those who are continually troubled by chronic cough. Its detergent virtue is clearly seen in glass vessels."

On Alsine. Chapter 89.

Alsine, which some call Antillo and others Myosota, because its leaves resemble the ears of mice, grows in shady woods and dark places, from which it has been called Alsine. It would be the same as Helsine, were it not somewhat smaller and without longer, smooth leaves. When crushed it gives off the smell of cucumber. It has the virtue of stanching and cooling. Applied as a poultice with polenta, it treats inflammations of the eyes. Its juice distilled into the ears removes pain, and it is useful for all the same purposes as Helsine.

A        In Tuscany the Alsine is called Centone, of which several species are found, although Dioscorides mentions only one. Some Greek texts place this chapter at the end of the second book after Orecchia di topo [Mouse-ear]; but as was explained there at sufficient length, this present place is more properly its own. Galen wrote of it in book six of the Faculties of Simple Medicines, saying: The Alsine, or Mouse-ear, has truly the same faculties as Helsine, that is, cooling and moistening; for it is of a watery and cold essence. For which reason it refreshes without constricting, and is therefore suitable for hot swellings and moderate erysipelas.

                        On the Duckweed of the Marshes.              Chapter 90.

   Duckweed of the marshes is found in standing waters. It is a moss similar to lentils, whose virtue is to cool. Therefore it is conveniently applied as a poultice by itself, or with polenta, upon swellings, upon sacred fire [erysipelas], and upon gout. It also heals intestinal ruptures in children.
      Marsh Duckweed is commonly called Lenticularia. It is a thing well known to everyone. It grows for the most part in the ditches of water surrounding cities and towns. Galen wrote of this in book eight of the Faculties of Simple Medicines, saying: The Lenticula of the marshes is almost in the second degree of cold and moist.

                        On the Greater Houseleek.                     Chapter 91.

   The Greater Houseleek has been so named because its leaves are always green. It produces stalks a cubit high, sometimes more, as thick as a large finger, fleshy, green, and notched, like those of the sea spurge. The leaves are fleshy, thick, as long as a large finger, pointed at the top like tongues, the lower ones spreading along the ground, and the upper ones arranged together in the manner of an eye. It grows on mountains and in pots; it is also planted on rooftops. Its virtue is to cool and to constrict. The leaves are medicinal for sacred fire, for malignant and stubborn ulcers, and for creeping sores; they help with inflammations of the eyes, ruptures, and gout, applied both on their own and together with polenta. The juice used in infusion with polenta, or with rose oil, is usefully applied for headaches; drunk, it is good against the bite of spiders called phalangi, against dysentery, and other fluxes of the body; drunk in wine it expels long worms from the body. Applied below with wool it stops the flow of women. Anointed on, it helps defects of the eyes caused by blood.

                        On the Lesser Houseleek.                      Chapter 93.

   The Lesser Houseleek grows on rocks, on walls, in ruins, on the crowns of walls, and in tombs, where the sun does not strike. It produces many branches coming from a single root, slender, all covered with small, round, fleshy, pointed leaves. From the middle rises its stalk a span in height, at the top of which it forms an umbel, with small, pale-colored flowers. Its leaves have the same virtues as the one described above.

D                       On Another Houseleek.                         Chapter 94.

   The third Houseleek, which some call Wild Spider, others Telephion, and the Latins Illecebre, produces leaves that are fleshier and hairy, similar to those of purslane. It grows among rocks. Its virtue is warm, sharp, and ulcerating. Applied as a poultice with grease it resolves scrofulous swellings.

   These then are the species of Houseleeks mentioned here by Dioscorides, of which the greater and likewise the lesser are well known to everyone. The greater is called by the name Houseleek everywhere; but the lesser is called in some places Vermicularia, in others Herba grassa, and in others Granellosa, of which there are two kinds: one of which produces yellow flowers and smaller and more compact leaves, which I truly believe to be the male, and the other, which produces longer and sparser leaves, and white flowers, which can reasonably be believed to be the female. The one of the third species, of a contrary nature to these two, is found in some copies of Dioscorides described with more detail; but we have here followed the order of the Aldine correction, where many superfluities have been cut away. This one then, which produces leaves similar to wild purslane, I have not yet found anyone who can point it out to me in Italy; but the other two are found in great abundance everywhere. Galen made mention only of the first two species, saying thus: One and the other Houseleek, the greater...

Dell'Ortica. Cap.xcvi.

A Ortica è di due spetie, una delle quali produce le frondi piu saluatiche, piu
aspre, piu larghe, & piu nere, e'l seme come quello del lino, ma minore: l'altra
non è cosi aspra, & fa il seme minuto. Le frondi dell'una, & dell'altra impiastrate
con sale, giouano à i morsi de i cani: sanano le cancrene, i cancari, l'ulcere sordi-
de, contumaci, & malageuoli da consolidare, & parimente le membra smosse, i pani, i picciio D
li tumori, le posteme rotte, & quelle, che chiamano parotide: giouano applicate con cera à i
difetosi di melza: messe trite insieme co'l succhio nel naso, ui ristagnano il flusso del sangue:
peste insieme con mirtha, & applicate disotto, puocano i mestrui: toccandosi con esse freche
la madrice rilassata, la ritornano al suo luogo. Il seme beuto con uino passo, moue à lussuria:
apre la bocca della madrice: lambendosi con mele, gioua à i difetti di petto, à i dolori lte-
rali, & all'infiammagioni del polmone: purga il petto: mettesi con i medicamenti corrosi-
ui. Le frondi cotte con gongole mollificano il corpo, prouocano l'orina, risoluono le uen-
tositá: cotte con ptisana uagliono à i difetti del petto: beute con un poco di mirtha prouo-
cano i mestrui. Il succhio gargarizzato risolue l'infiammagioni dell'ugola.

E Cosi notissima pianta l'Ortica, che si cognosce da ciascuno sino nella notte scura: et imperò non accade à dire quale
ella si sia, quantunque non sia male il sapere quante siano le sue spetie, lequali se ben solamète esser due recite Dio
scorides; nondimeno tre sene ritrouano in Italia, le due cioè sopradette, & la terza con piccoline frondi, & bre-

FOURTH BOOK. 335

the greater and the lesser; it dries mildly and restrains moderately; but in both operations it is weak, because it contains more watery substance than any other. Yet truly its cooling virtue is not negligible, since it is ranked among those things that cool in the third degree. And so it is excellently suited against erysipelas and against hot swellings that arise from flows of matter.

On the Venus's Navel. Chapter 94.

The Venus's Navel has roundish leaves similar to a small cup, and so concave that they are not easily distinguished from one another; from the middle of each rises a short stem in which the seed is contained. Its root is round, like an olive. The juice, distilled or rubbed on with wine, reveals the genital parts that are covered with flesh, and it likewise benefits sacred fire, inflammations, scrofulous swellings, and bubo sores; it extinguishes the burning heat of the stomach. The leaves eaten together with the root break stones and promote urine; given with honey they benefit dropsical patients. Some use the herb for amorous purposes.

On another Venus's Navel. Chapter 95.

Another species of Venus's Navel, which some call Cymbalion, has leaves that are fat and broader, thick after the manner of small tongues, and near the roots they resemble the rim of an eye, as one sees in the greater houseleek. They are astringent in taste; they produce a thin little stalk on which the flowers are found, and the seed is similar to that of St. John's Wort; the root is larger. It is useful for all the same things as houseleek.

The first species of Venus's Navel grows most abundantly throughout all Tuscany on old walls, and the people commonly call its leaves "cupertouole," because they resemble the earthen covers made to cover pots; and it grows not only on walls but also on stones, wherever one wishes. The second species I recently saw in a small garden of simples belonging to Messer Giuliano da Marostica, an excellent physician, in Cividale d'Austria in Friuli. In Lombardy people use for Venus's Navel a certain herb called Cymbalaria, hanging like a mane from walls, with thin stems and ivy-like leaves, somewhat pointed at their tips in many places; they think that, since it is popularly called Cymbalaria, it must be the true Venus's Navel, because Dioscorides said that some call the second species Cymbalion. Galen mentions it in book seven of the Faculties of Simples, saying as follows: Venus's Navel is composed of mixed faculties, that is, of a mildly cold and humid quality, and of a certain not overtly astringent one, together with a slightly bitter one. And so it cools, repels, cleanses, and resolves. Thus it treats phlegmonous erysipelas and phlegmatic erysipelas; applied as a plaster with moisture it wonderfully relieves the burning of the stomach. It is believed that the leaves eaten can break stones and promote urine.

On the Nettle. Chapter 96.

The Nettle is of two species, one of which produces leaves that are wilder, rougher, broader, and darker, with seed like that of flax but smaller; the other is not so rough and has smaller seed. The leaves of both, plastered on with salt, benefit dog bites; they heal gangrenes, cancerous sores, foul and stubborn ulcers that are difficult to consolidate, and likewise dislocated limbs, buboes, small tumors, burst swellings, and those called parotids; applied with wax they benefit those suffering from a diseased spleen; placed ground together with juice in the nose, they stop the flow of blood; pounded together with myrrh and applied below, they bring on the menses; touching the relaxed womb with them fresh returns it to its place. The seed drunk with raisin wine stirs up lust; it opens the mouth of the womb; licked with honey it benefits defects of the chest, pain in the sides, and inflammations of the lungs; it purges the chest and is mixed with corrosive medicines. The leaves cooked with mussels soften the body, promote urine, and resolve flatulence; cooked with barley-water they benefit defects of the chest; drunk with a little myrrh they bring on the menses. The juice gargled resolves inflammations of the uvula.

The Nettle is so well known a plant that it is recognized by everyone even in the dark of night, and so there is no need to say what it looks like; though it is not without value to know how many species it has. A ui fusti, assai piu pungéti d' ammédune l' altre, chiamata d' alcuni Ortica saluatica. Seriffene Galeno al. vi. delle facoltà de semplici, così dicédo. Le fródi, & il seme dell' Ortica, di cui è l'uso, sono molto digestiue, di modo che sanano le posteme, & massime quelle, che nascono dopo all'orecchie. Hanno in se alcuna parte uentosa, con ilche muouono ageuolméte a lussarìa, composto, ne fa testimonio il cauar che fa egli dal petto de grossi, & de uscosi humori, & parimente il prurito, che causa nelle membra, che tocca. La parte sua uentosa, della quale s'è detto eser partecipe, gli nasce, mentre che si digerisce, & però non è l'Ortica uentosa attualmente, ma potentialménte. Solue al quanto il uentre, non però perche la sua solutione sana per eser aster siva, & tiillatoria. sana l'ulcere cancarose, et tutte quelle, che sia dibisogno diseccare senza mordacità alcuna: percioche per eser nelle parti sue sottile, et secca di temperaménto, non è però dalla così calida, che la possa mordere.

Della Galiopsi. Cap. xcvij.

B A Galiopsi è una pianta nel fusto, & nelle frondi del tutto simile all'ortica, ma sono le sue frondi piu liscie, & trite spirano di dispiaceuole odore: il fiore produce porporeo, & sottile. Nasce appresso alle siepi, nei cortili delle case, & per tutto lungo alle uie. Le frondi, il fusto, il seme, & parimente il succhio, risoluono le durezze, & i cancari: & guariscono le scrofole, i pani, & le posteme, che uengono dopo all'orecchie. A lche fare s'impiastrano tepide con aceto, due uolte il giorno, & somentafi con la sua dicottione. Mettonsi anchora con sale con giouamento in su l'ulcere putride, cancronate, & corrosiue.

N Asce la Galiopsi in ogni luogo, nei cortili, nelle uie, in su le piazze, et appresso alle case, et chiamasi in Italia Ortica fetida: imperoche molto puzza maneggiandola. Produce le frondi, e'l fusto simile all' ortica; ma non pungono, & il fiore porporeo, & sottile. È inuero notissima pianta: et imperò parmi, che di gran lunga erri in quel suo così grande herbario Leonardo Fuchsio Tedesco uolendo, che sia la Galiopsi quella, che uolgarmente si chiama Scrofolaria, Ferraria, Castrangola, & Millemorbia, per produrre ella il fiore simile a una celata, ouero elmetto. Del qual errore fa manifesta fede il produrre ella le frondi non troppo simili à quelle dell'ortica, ne spiaceuoli all'odorato. Oltre à questo una delle piu notabili parti, che sia in lei, è la sua molto nodosa radice, di cui è da pensare, che non si sarebbe taciuta l'historia Dioscoride, se hauesse inteso per la Galiopsi la comune Scrofolaria, la quale per la piu parte nasce appresso ai fossi delle acque, & in su le riue de i piccioli fiumicelli, & non per i cortili appresso alle siepi, & lungo alle uie. Il perche non è punto da credere, che sieno la Galiopsi, & la Scrosolaria una cosa medesima. Nascene un' altra spetie del tutto simile alla sopra detta, la quale in ogni sua fronde ha una macchia bianca come di latte, lunga, & appuntata, la quale chiamiamo noi in Thoscana Ortica lattea. Ache mi ha fatto piu uolte credere eser questa la uera Galiopsi, pensandomi, che piu agguolmente deriuasse il nome di Galiopfi da Gala, che uuol dire latte, che da Gales, che uuol dire elmo, piu presto nome latino, che greco. Imperoche Dioscoride non usa di comporre nomi parte di greco, & parte di latino, come si ua imaginando il Fuchsio, ne manco è questo in uso appresso ad altri greci. Oltre à ciò mi fa credere, che sia questa Ortica lattea la uera Galiopsi per ueder io, che Dioscoride subbito dopo lei mese il Capitolo del Gallio, herba così chiamata, per apprendere ella il latte, come fa il caglio. Percioche Dioscoride (come s'è detto) ha tenuto un ordine di mettere, & di congiungere insieme ordinatamente l'herbe, & l'altre piante per le similitudini loro, ò di figura, ò di uirtù, ò di nome, per fare una certa concatenatione d' ogni cosa: et imperò pare, che qui habbi messo il Gallio dopo la Galiopsi, per eser in ammendune il nome deriuato dal latte, & per non hauere altra sembianza, che si gli conuenisse per collocarle l'una dopo l'altra, & tanto piu, che non ritrouo, che Dioscoride, ne manco Plinio scriuessero, che'l fior suo fusse simile à gli elmi, da cui si sia poscia chiamata Galiopsi, come si sono imaginati alcuni de i moderni per hauer uedu ti i suoi fiori esergli assai rasembreuoli.

D Della Galiopsi non ritrouo io, che scriuesse cosa alcuna ne suoi libri de i Semplici Galeno, quantunque fusse poscia da Pauolo Egineta mesa tra gli suoi.

Del Gallio. Cap. xcviij.

L Gallio è stato così chiamato, per mettersi in uece di caglio per sar apprendere il latte. Produce questo il fusto dritto, & le frondi simili all'aparine, & il fiore nella sommità giallo, folto, sottile, copioso, & odorato. Il fiore s'impiasta in su le cotture del fuoco: et ristagna i sflussi del sangue. Mettesi il Gallio nei cerotti, che si fanno con oglio rosado, & si lasciano poi al sole, fino che diuentino bianchi, & usansi poscia per le lassitudini. La radice prouoca al coito. Nasce in luoghi paludosi.

N Asce il Gallio copiosissimo per tutto lungo alle uie, assai simile alla rubbia minore, la qual chiamano aparine; ma non però è nota à tutti la uirtù, che ha di fare apprendere il latte: imperoche s'usarebbe anchor eso in cambio di quell' altra herba, che noi chiamiamo presura, di cui è l'uso per fare il casio dolce per tutta la Thoscana.

A The stalks are considerably more stinging than either of the others, and are called by some Wild Nettle. Galen writes of it in book six of the Properties of Simple Medicines, saying this: The leaves and seeds of the Nettle, which are the parts in use, are highly digestive, such that they heal swellings, and especially those that arise behind the ears. They contain a certain windy quality, by means of which they gently move one to lust; a fact attested by the drawing out of gross and thick humors, and likewise the itching that it causes in the limbs it touches. This windy quality arises in it as it digests, and thus the Nettle is not actually windy in itself, but potentially so. It loosens the belly to some degree, not however through a solutive action, but rather because it is astringent and irritating. It heals cancerous ulcers, and all those that need to be dried without any mordant quality: for since it is subtle and dry in temperament in its parts, it is not so hot as to be able to bite.

Of Galeopsis. Chapter 97.

B Galeopsis is a plant whose stalk and leaves are in every way similar to the nettle, but its leaves are smoother, and when bruised they emit a disagreeable odor: the flower it produces is purple and slender. It grows beside hedges, in the yards of houses, and everywhere along roads. The leaves, the stalk, the seed, and likewise the juice dissolve hardnesses and cancers, and heal scrofula, lumps, and swellings that arise behind the ears. For these purposes they are applied warm with vinegar, twice a day, and fomentations are made with its decoction. They are also applied with salt with benefit upon putrid, gangrenous, and corrosive ulcers.

N Galeopsis grows everywhere, in yards, along roads, in public squares, and near houses, and is called in Italy Stinking Nettle, because it smells strongly when handled. It produces leaves and a stalk similar to the nettle, but they do not sting, and the flower is purple and slender. It is indeed a most well-known plant; and therefore it seems to me that Leonardo Fuchsius the German errs greatly in his celebrated herbal, in wishing the Galeopsis to be that plant which is commonly called Scrofolaria, Ferraria, Castrangola, and Millemorbia, on the grounds that it produces a flower similar to a helmet or casque. Of this error a clear demonstration is the fact that it produces leaves not very similar to those of the nettle, and not disagreeable to the smell. Furthermore, one of the most notable features of the plant is its very knotty root, which Dioscorides would surely not have omitted to mention, had he understood by Galeopsis the common Scrofolaria, which for the most part grows beside ditches and along the banks of small streams, and not in yards beside hedges and along roads. There is therefore no reason at all to believe that Galeopsis and Scrofolaria are one and the same thing. There is another species altogether similar to the above-mentioned, which on each of its leaves has a white spot like milk, long and pointed, which we in Tuscany call Milk Nettle. This has led me on more than one occasion to believe that this is the true Galeopsis, thinking that the name Galeopsis would more naturally derive from Gala, which means milk, than from Gales, which means helmet — a name that is more Latin than Greek. For Dioscorides does not use the practice of forming names partly from Greek and partly from Latin, as Fuchsius imagines, nor is this practice used among other Greek writers. Moreover, I am led to believe that this Milk Nettle is the true Galeopsis because I observe that Dioscorides placed immediately after it the Chapter of Gallio, a herb so called because it causes milk to curdle just as rennet does. For Dioscorides, as has been said, followed an orderly method of placing and connecting together herbs and other plants according to their similarities, whether of form, or virtue, or name, so as to create a certain chain of all things: and therefore it appears that he placed the Gallio after the Galeopsis because in both the name derives from milk, and because there was no other resemblance between them that would justify placing one after the other; and all the more so because I do not find that either Dioscorides or Pliny wrote that the flower of Galeopsis resembles a helmet, from which it would take its name, although some modern writers have imagined so, having seen its flowers to be fairly helmet-like.

D Regarding Galeopsis, I do not find that Galen wrote anything about it in his books on Simple Medicines, although it was later included by Paul of Aegina among his own.

Of Gallio. Chapter 98.

Gallio has been so called because it is used in place of rennet to curdle milk. It produces a straight stalk, with leaves similar to those of cleavers, and at the top a flower that is yellow, thick, slender, abundant, and fragrant. The flower is applied to burns from fire, and staunches fluxes of blood. Gallio is put into plasters made with rose oil, and left in the sun until they turn white, and these are used for fatigue. The root provokes desire. It grows in marshy places.

N Gallio grows in great abundance all along the roads, quite similar to the lesser madder, which they call aparine; but its virtue of curdling milk is not known to everyone: for otherwise it would also be used in place of that other herb which we call presura, which is used throughout Tuscany to make fresh cheese.

dere egli il latte, oue si mette dentro. E' simile all'aparine, & ha uirtu diseccatiua, & alquanto acuta. il suo fiore uale à i
flussi del sangue, & alle cotture del fuoco. Ha buono odore, & il suo colore è giallo.

Del Senetio, ouero Erigero. Cap. xcix.

IL Senetio, ouero Erigero fa il suo fusto alto un gombito, rossigno, con frondi
continuate, & intagliate come quelle della ruchetta, ma assai minori: produce i
fiori gialli, i quali sfioriscono presto, & sene uolano in piuma: ne per altro è egli
stato chiamato Erigero, senon perche la primauera i suoi fiori diuetano canuti,
come fanno i capelli: non è la sua radice d'alcun ualore: nasce per il piu nelle macie, & at-
torno alle castella. Le frondi, & parimente i fiori hanno uirtu d'infrigidire: & però im-
piastrate le frõdi cõ un poco di uino, ouero per se sole, sanano l'infiammagioni de i testicoli,
& del sedere, & oltre à cio mescolate con manna d'incenso medicano non tanto comune-
mente à tutte le serite, ma à quelle dei nerui particolarmente. Fa il medesimo la piuma dei B
fiori impiastrata per se sola con aceto: ma beuti quando sono freschi, strangolano. Cotto tut
to il fusto, & beuto con un passo, sana i dolori cholerici dello stomacho.

Chiamasi uolgarmente il Senetio, ouero Erigero Cardoncello, ouero Spellicciosa, & è pianta assai nota à ciascuno,
C i cui fusti, come scriue Dioscoride, sono rossigni, le frondi lunghe, & intagliate, come quelle della ruchetta, come
che minori: produce i fiori gialli, i quali diuentando poscia canuti, et pelosi, sene uolano uia all'aria. Nasce per tut-
to, & sino sopra le muraglie uecchie. Questo non cognoscendo Othone Brunfelsio Tedesco lo messe nel suo herbario per
una spetie di Verbena. Scrisene Galeno al. vi. delle facultà dei semplici, così breuemente dicendo. L'Erigero ha facultà
mista, & parimente refrigeratiua, con alquanto di digestiua.

Del Thalietro. Cap. c.

HA il Thalietro frondi di coriandro, ma alquanto piu grasse: il fusto come di ru
ta, nel quale sono le frondi, lequali trite, & impiastrate saldano l'ulcere anti-
che. Nasce per il piu nelle campagne.

L Thalietro dice il Ruellio esser un herba chiamata da gli herbolatti Argentina: imperoche molto risplendono
I le sue frondi coriandrine, & che la si ritroua per tutto: ma piu spesso nelle campagne, & nelle macie. Ilche non
fo io negare, ne meno affermare, per non hauer fin hora ritrouato chi mi sappi dimostrare il uero Thalietro, di
cui scriuendo Galeno al. vi. delle facultà de i semplici, così diceua. Il Thalietro ha frondi di coriandro, & il fusto produce
grosso come di ruta. Ha uirtu di diseccare senz'amordere, & però sana egli ualorosamente l'ulcere uecchie.

Del Mosco marino. Cap. ci.

IL Mosco marino nasce ne gli scogli, & ne i nicchi de i pesci appresso al mare, sot-
tile, capigliioso, senza alcun fusto. Ha uirtu ualorosa di costrignere, & risoluere le
posteme, & parimente le podagre, oue sia bisogno di ristagnare.

Comune opinione di ciascun Semplicista de i tẽpi nostri, che sia il Mosco marino qui recitato da Dioscoride, quel-
E' la, che uolgarmente si chiama Corallina, laquale sogliono spesse uolte per i uermini de fanciulli uendere i Ciurma- D
dori di banca: alche ueramente, come ho piu uolte ueduto io l'isperienza è ella ualorosissima, dalla quale opinio-
ne non mi posso ueramente partire, sapendo io, che coloro, che uanno pescando i coralli, da cui s'ha ella ricauato il nome,
la ritrouano attaccata à gli scogli, à i nicchi, & anchora attorno à i coralli, nel modo che s'attacca il mosco alle scorze, &
à i rami de gli alberis: ma lodano per la migliore quella, che ritrouano attaccata à i coralli, sotto la cui spetie ne uendono in-
finiti sacchi dell'altra. Questa proprietà, che ha ella d'ammazzare i uermini, non fu cognosciuta da gli antichi: per cio-
che non ritrouò alcuno, che la descriua. Scrisene Galeno al. vi. delle facultà de semplici, così dicendo. il Mosco marino è
composto di terrea, & acque a sustanza, l'una, & l'altra fredda. Il perche è egli al gusto costrettiuo, & impiastrato in fi-
le malattie calde, le rinfresca, & le guarisce.

Del Phuco marino. Cap. cij.

IL Phuco marino è di piu spetie, uno cioè largo, l'altro lunghetto, & rosseggiante, & il terzo, che nasce in Candia, è bianco, floridissimo, & incorrotto. Hanno

FOURTH BOOK. 337

About this Galen wrote in book six on the properties of simples, saying thus: Cleavers (Galium) has taken that name because it causes milk to curdle when placed inside it. It is similar to Aparine, and has a drying virtue, somewhat sharp. Its flower is good for flows of blood, and for burns from fire. It has a pleasant smell, and its color is yellow.

On Senecio, or Groundsel. Chapter 99.

Senecio, or Groundsel, produces a stem about a cubit tall, reddish, with continuous leaves cut like those of rocket, but much smaller: it produces yellow flowers, which shed their petals quickly and fly away as fluff: it is called Erigero for no other reason than that in spring its flowers turn white like hair, as hair does with age. Its root is of no value; it grows mostly in waste places and around fortifications. The leaves, and likewise the flowers, have a cooling virtue: and so, applying the leaves with a little wine, or by themselves, they heal inflammations of the testicles and of the seat, and beyond this, mixed with frankincense resin, they commonly treat not only all wounds, but those of the nerves in particular. The fluff of the flowers applied by itself with vinegar does the same: but drunk fresh, it causes choking. Cooked entire with the stem, and drunk with raisin wine, it heals choleric pains of the stomach.

Senecio, or Groundsel, is commonly called Cardoncello or Spellicciosa, and it is a plant well known to everyone, whose stems, as Dioscorides writes, are reddish, the leaves long and cut like those of rocket, though smaller: it produces yellow flowers, which then turning white and downy, fly away into the air. It grows everywhere, even on old walls. Not recognizing this, the German Otto Brunfels placed it in his herbal as a species of Verbena. Galen wrote of it in book six on the properties of simples, saying briefly: Groundsel has a mixed virtue, and likewise cooling, with some digestive quality.

On Thalictrum. Chapter 100.

Thalictrum has leaves like coriander, but somewhat thicker: the stem like rue, on which are leaves which, crushed and applied as a poultice, heal old ulcers. It grows mostly in open fields.

Ruellius says that Thalictrum is a herb which herb-gatherers call Argentina, because its coriander-like leaves shine greatly, and that it is found everywhere, but more often in fields and waste places. I neither deny nor affirm this, having not yet found anyone who can show me the true Thalictrum; of which Galen, writing in book six on the properties of simples, said: Thalictrum has leaves of coriander, and its stem grows thick like rue. It has a drying virtue without biting, and so it heals old ulcers with great effect.

On Sea Moss. Chapter 101.

Sea Moss grows on rocks and in the shells of fish near the sea, thin, hair-like, without any stem. It has a powerful virtue to restrain and resolve abscesses, and likewise gouty conditions, where it is necessary to staunch them.

The common opinion of every herbalist of our time is that what Dioscorides records as sea moss is what is commonly called Corallina, which vendors at market stalls often sell for children's worms: in which use, as I have many times seen by experience, it is extremely effective, from which opinion I cannot truly depart, knowing that those who go fishing for corals, from which it takes its name, find it attached to rocks, shells, and also around corals, in the same way that moss attaches to the bark and branches of trees: but they praise as best that which is found attached to corals, under the guise of which they sell countless bags of the other kind. This property it has of killing worms was not known to the ancients, since no one is found to have described it. Galen wrote of it in book six on the properties of simples, saying: Sea moss is composed of earthy and watery substance, both cold. Wherefore it is astringent to the taste, and applied as a poultice to hot conditions, it cools and heals them.

On Sea Wrack. Chapter 102.

Sea Wrack (Phuco) is of several kinds: one broad, another rather long and reddish, and the third, which grows in Crete, is white, very florid, and incorruptible. All have a cooling virtue, not only for gout, but also for inflam-

A magioni. Ilche fa egli efficacemente, quando ui s'impiastra suso: ma bisogna usarli freschi, auanti che si secchino. Nicandro diede il rosso per i morsi delle serpi. Credonsi alcuni, che questo fusse quel Phuco, che adoperano le donne per colorirsi la faccia, non sapendo, che quello, che usano, è una radice di questo nome medesimo.

Crisi del Phuco marino Plinio al.xxiiij.cap.del.xiij.libro, cosi dicendo. Nascono nel mare sterpi, & alberi ma
S nel nostro sono minori, che nel Rosso: peroche questo, et l'Oceano orientale sono pieni di selue. Non ha in altra lin
gua nome proprio quello, che i greci chiamano Phicos: peroche Alga è piu presto uocabolo d'herba; ma questo è
sterpo. Il perche essendomi tal pianta incognita altro non mene accade à dire senon, che senon è Alga, ne sia almeno una
spetie. Theodoro nella interpretatione di Theophrasto nò chiama il Phuco marino altrimenti, che Alga. Il che se ben bli
nioin questo luogo disse non si conuenire tal nome, in altri luoghi (come disse anchora Marcello Fiorentino) lo chiamò pe
rò Alga. Ma non per questo affermarei io, che fusse egli questa Alga, che si mette à Vinetia tra i uetri, accioche non si
rompino; ma ben direi, che sia il phuco chiamato anchor egli Alga, per non hauere altro nome latino. Fecene mentione
Galeno all'ottauo delle facultà de i semplici, così dicendo. Il Phuco cosi humido cauato dal mare disecca, & infrigidisce nel
secondo ordine, & ha alquanto dell'acerbo.

Del Potamogeto. Cap.ciij.

L Potamogeto produce le frondi simili alla bietola, ma pelose, & alquanto so-
pra l'acqua eminenti. Infrigidisce, & ristagna: è utile al prurito, & all'ulcere
uecchie, & corrosiue. E gli stato messo il nome di Potamogeto, per nascer egli
nelle paludi, & altri luoghi acquosi.

E desi il Potamogeto nuotare con le frondi simili alla bietola ne i laghi, & nelle paludi in molti luoghi. Hollo piu
V uolte ueduto io spetialmente in alcuni laghi della ualle Anania, & ricoltolo con le proprie mani. Il Potamoге-
to (diceua Galeno al.viij. delle facultà de semplici) ristregne, & infrigidisce come il poligonios; ma la sua essenza
è piu grossa, che quella del Poligonio.

Dello Stratiote. Cap. ciiij.

C O Stratiote, il qual nasce nell'acque, nuota sopra à quelle, & uiue senza radice,
donde ha egli preso il nome. E questo un'herba simile al sempreuiuo, se l'non ha
uesse però le frondi maggiori. Rinfrescano queste, & beute ristagnano il san-
gue, che uiene dalle reni: prohibiscono l'infiammagione nelle ferite, che minac-
ciano postema. Impiastransi con aceto al fuoco sacro, & parimente à i tumori.

N On è marauglia se in Italia non nasce lo Stratiote acquatico. Imperoche (come riferisce Plinio al.xviij.cap.del.
xxiiij.libro) nasce solamente in Egitto nell'inondationi, che fail Nilo, simile al sempreuiuo, ma cò frondi maggiori.

Del Stratiote Millefoglio. Cap. cv.

L O Stratiote millefoglio è picciola pianta, alta un palmo, & qualche uolta mag-
giore, le cui frondi sono rassembreuoli alle penne de gli uccellini, breui molto,
& nel nascimento intagliate. Rassembransi le frondi al cimino saluatico, et mas-
sime nella ruuidezza, & breuità loro, sono però piu breui: ma l'ombrella è piu
D densa, & piu piena. Produce nella sommità del fusto sottili sistuchi, de i quali si forma l'om
brella come d'anetho, di cui sono i fiori piccioli, & bianchi: nasce ne i campi aspri, & lungo
le uie. E' in grande uso all'ulcere uecchie, & alle nuoue, al slusso del sangue, & alle fistole.

L Millefoglio Stratiote ritiene anchora in Italia al tempo nostro il nome di Millefoglio: imperoche si uede il com
I mune Millefoglio nascere nei campi non coltiuati, ne i prati, & lungo alle uie, con fusti maggiori d'un palmo, si
per i quali sono le frondi simili quasi alle penne de piccoli uccelli, & simili molto à quelle del cimino saluatico,
con ombrella di fiori bianchissimi, quantunque alcune uolte nel bianco rosseggino d'incarnagione, & produce da una sola
radice hora quattro, hora cinque, & hor piu fusti. Ilche dimostra, che'l Millefoglio, che è in comune uso, sia questo Stra-
tiote, & non il Miriophillo poco qui di sopra scritto da Dioscoride, come si credè il Brasauola: imperoche'l Miriophilo è
un gambo tenero, & solo, che nasce ne i paludi, con copiose, & iscese frondi, simili à quelle del finocchio. Ilche conclude,
che'l Millefoglio comune, & usuale sia lo Stratiote terrestre qui descritto da Dioscoride. Fece d'ammenduni gli Stra-
tioti memoria Galeno al.viij. delle facultà dei semplici, così dicendo. Lo Stratiote acquatico è ueramente frigido, & hu-
mido: ma il terrestre ha alquanto del costrettiuo. Il perche puo egli saldare le ferite, & esser utile all'ulcere. Sono alcu-
ni, che'l usano ne i slussi del sangue, & nelle fistole.

A greater uses. This it does effectively when plastered on fresh: but one must use it fresh, before it dries. Nicander prescribed the red variety for serpent bites. Some believe this was that Phucus which women use to color their faces, not knowing that what they use is a root of the same name.

On marine Phucus Pliny in chapter 24 of book 13 writes thus: In the sea there grow shrubs and trees,
S which in our sea are smaller than in the Red Sea: for that sea and the eastern Ocean are full of forests. In no other language does the plant that the Greeks call Phicos have a proper name: for Alga is more of a word for herbs; but this is a shrub. Since this plant is unknown to me, I can say nothing other than that if it is not an Alga, it may at least be a species thereof. Theodorus in his interpretation of Theophrastus calls the marine Phucus nothing other than Alga. Though Blinius in this passage said that name was not appropriate, in other places (as Marcello Fiorentino also said) he called it Alga. But I would not for this reason affirm that it is this Alga which is placed in Venice between glass vessels to prevent them from breaking; but I would say that the Phucus is also called Alga, for lack of another Latin name. Galen mentions it in the eighth book of the Faculties of Simples, saying thus: The Phucus, so moist when drawn from the sea, dries and cools in the second degree, and has some astringency.

On Potamogeton. Chapter 103.

Potamogeton produces leaves similar to beet, but hairy and somewhat raised above the water. It cools and stops bleeding: it is useful for itching and for old and corrosive ulcers. It has been given the name Potamogeton because it grows in marshes and other watery places.

Potamogeton is said to float with its beet-like leaves in lakes and marshes in many places. I have seen it many times myself, especially in certain lakes in the valley of Anania, and collected it with my own hands. Potamogeton (said Galen in book 8 of the Faculties of Simples) constricts and cools like Polygonum; but its substance is coarser than that of Polygonum.

On Stratiotes. Chapter 104.

Stratiotes, which is born in water, floats upon it and lives without roots, from which it takes its name. It is an herb similar to houseleek, except that it has larger leaves. These leaves, when drunk as a beverage, cool and stop bleeding from the kidneys: they prevent inflammation in wounds that threaten to suppurate. They are applied as a plaster with vinegar for erysipelas, and likewise for tumors.

It is no wonder that the aquatic Stratiotes does not grow in Italy. For (as Pliny reports in chapter 18 of book 24) it grows only in Egypt during the flooding of the Nile, resembling houseleek but with larger leaves.

On Stratiotes Milfoil. Chapter 105.

The milfoil Stratiotes is a small plant, a hand-span tall or sometimes taller, whose leaves resemble the feathers of small birds, being short and cut at their origin. The leaves resemble wild cumin, especially in their roughness and shortness, but are even shorter: the umbel however is denser and fuller. It produces at the top of the stem fine flower-stalks, from which the umbel is formed as with dill, with small white flowers: it grows in rough fields and along roadsides. It is in great use for old and fresh ulcers, for the flux of blood, and for fistulas.

Milfoil Stratiotes still retains in Italy today the name of Milfoil: for the common Milfoil is seen growing in uncultivated fields, in meadows and along roads, with stems taller than a hand-span, along which are leaves almost like the feathers of small birds, very similar to those of wild cumin, with an umbel of very white flowers, which sometimes blush with an incarnate tinge, and it produces from a single root four, five or more stems. This shows that the Milfoil in common use is this Stratiotes, and not the Myriophyllum described a little earlier by Dioscorides, as Brasavola believed: for Myriophyllum has a single tender stem growing in marshes, with abundant spreading leaves similar to those of fennel. This concludes that the common and everyday Milfoil is the terrestrial Stratiotes described here by Dioscorides. Galen made mention of both Stratiotes in book 8 of the Faculties of Simples, saying thus: The aquatic Stratiotes is truly cold and moist: but the terrestrial has some astringency. For this reason it can heal wounds and be useful for ulcers. There are some who use it for fluxes of blood and for fistulas.

text:
QVARTO. 339

Del Verbasco. Cap. cvi.

A
L Verbasco è in somma di due spetie, bianco cioè, & nero, nelche s'intende il
maschio, & la femmina. Le frondi della femmina son simili à quelle del cauolo,
bianche, molto piu pelose, & piu larghe: il fusto bianco, pelosetto, alto un gom-
bito, & qualche uolta piu: i fiori bianchi, ouero gialli pallidi: il seme nero, & la
radice lunga, acerba al gusto, grossa un dito: nasce nelle campagne. Quello, che si chiama
maschio, produce le frondi lunghette, strette, & bianche, & il fusto sottile. Il nero ueramente
sarebbe simile al bianco, se non hauesse le sue frondi piu nere, & piu larghe. Quello, che chia-
mano saluatico, cresce con frondi simili à quelle della saluia, fusti alti, & legnosi, & intorno
à quelli sono i rami simili à quelli del marrobio, & il suo fiore è giallo, della splendenza del-
l'oro. Enne due altre spetie di pelosi, & bassi, che producono le frondi ritonde: et oltre à que-
ste un'altra terza spetie chiamato d'alcuni Lichnite, & da altri Thrialli, che produce al piu
tre, ouer quattro frondi, ouer poche piu, ruuide, grosse, & grasse, lequali sono à proposito
per brusciare nelle lucerne. La radice delli due primi è costrettiua: il perche si da ella con ui-
no alla quantità d'una tessera ne i slussi del corpo: la cui decottione gioua à i rotti, à gli spasi-
mati, à i tracassati, & alla tosse antica, & lauandosene la bocca mitiga il dolore de i denti. Il
Verbasco, che produce il fior aureo tinge i capelli, & messo in qual si uoglia luogo, tiga à se
le tignole. La dicottione delle frondi fatta nell'acqua, conferisce à i tumori, & infiammagioni
de gli occhi. Accouiensi con uino, & con mele all'ulcere estiomenate, & con aceto alle feri-
te: medicano à i morsi de gli scorpioni. Le frondi del saluatico s'impiastrano anchora in su
le cotture del fuoco. Dicono, che serbandosi i sichi secchi nelle frondi della femmina, non
si putresanno.

C
Hiamasi uolgarmente il Verbasco Tasso barbasso, di cui le prime due spetie del domestico, & quella del saluati-
co, che fa frondi di saluia, et i fiori aurei, con un poco di rosso nel mezzo, sono note à ciascuno. Ma le tre altre spe-
tie non ho possute ueder io in Italia, & quantunque dica il Ruellio esser alcuni dotti, che dicono esser queste due
spetie di Verbasco quelle due poco diuerse piante, che escono nella primauera con frondi crespe molto, & quasi simili al
dissaco, & fiori nell'una gialli, & nell'altra bianchicci, ritondi, & per intorno intagliati, chiamati da alcuni fiori di pri-
mauera, & da altri herba Paralisis: non dimeno non me lo posso io per alcun modo persuadere. Percioche primamente
non si rassembrano le frondi di queste due piante, lequali in una sono ritondette, & nell'altra lunghe, in alcun modo al
Verbasco, ne sono in modo alcuno pelose, come le fece Dioscoride, anzi per il contrario liscie, & ben crespe. Oltre à cio
non ritrouo, che facesse del fiore memoria alcuna Dioscoride, ne altro de gli antichi, che ne scriua le spetie de i Verbashi.
Ilche non era da tacere nell'herba Paralisis: percioche era da esser celebrato il suo aureo fiore, per esser ueramente il
primo, che ne annuntij la primauera. Il perche parmi, che manco si debbi approuare quello, che nel suo grande herba-
rio ne dipinge il Fuchsio: percioche credendo egli piu presto al Ruellio, che à quello, che ricerchi la chiarezza del-
la cosa, dipinse per i due predetti Verbashi queste due spetie di piante, chiamate herbe da paralisia, lequali usano
indifferentemente alcuni moderni per i dolori delle giunture. Le cui radici (secondo che dicono) si cuocono, & beese-
ne posta la loro dicottione utilmente per l'oppilationi delle reni, & della uisciga. Dassi il succhio dell'herba à bere,
& parimente s'impiastra di suore nelle rotture, & dislogagioni dell'ossa. Vsano le donne di bagnarsi spesso la faccia
con il succhio de i fiori: imperoche ui si distendere la pelle, & ne leua uia ogni macchia. Ma ritornando à i ueri Ver-
baschi, dico, che per quanto m'ha dimostrato l'esperienza, sono uniuersalmente tutti molto costrettiui, & disseccatiui: &
imperò uale il fumo de i bottoni de suoi fiori secchi, insieme con terbenthina, & fiore di chamamilla riceuuto per una
banca forata, al sedere, alle rilassationi del budello, & per i premiti nella disenterìa, che chiamano i Greci tenasmo-
ni, & noi male della pondora. L'herba fresca pesta con due pietre uiue, & messa nelle inchiouature de i caualli,
subito gli guarisce. Il succhio delle radici della femmina, quando non ha produtto anchora il fusto, dato alla quantità
di due dramme con altretanta maluagia calda, ò altro uino aromatico nel principio del parossimo, cura (secondo che
riferisce Arnaldo) la febre quartana; ma bisogna farlo tre, ouer quattro uolte. Il fiore fregato in su quella spetie di
porri, che sono ruuidi, gli manda uia. Scrisse del Verbasco Galeno al. uiij. delle facultà de i Semplici, così dicendo.
È nelle spetie del Verbasco il bianco, e'l nero. Il bianco adunque è il maschio, le cui frondi sono piu strette, & quelle della
femmina sono piu larghe, & maggiori. Enne oltre à questo un'altro saluatico, i cui fiori sono aurei, & rossi, & enne
anchora senza le predette, un'altro, ilqual chiamano propriamente Plomide, & Triallide. La radice de i primi due è
al gusto acerba: gioua à i slussi. Vsasi la sua dicottione per lauarsi la bocca nel dolore de i denti. Le frondi hanno uirtu
digestiua, & massime di quello, che produce i fiori, aurei con peli rossi. Hanno le frondi di tutte le spetie uirtu disce-
catiua, & astresiua.

FOURTH BOOK. 339

On Mullein. Chapter 106.

A
Mullein is in sum of two kinds, white and black, by which we mean the male and the female. The leaves of the female are similar to those of cabbage, white, much more hairy and broader: the stem white, somewhat hairy, a cubit tall and sometimes more: the flowers white or pale yellow: the seed black, and the root long, bitter to the taste, as thick as a finger: it grows in the countryside. That which is called the male produces rather long, narrow and white leaves, and a slender stem. The black would indeed be similar to the white, if it did not have somewhat darker and broader leaves. That which is called wild grows with leaves similar to those of sage, tall and woody stems, and around them branches similar to those of horehound, and its flower is golden yellow, with the brilliance of gold. There are two other kinds, low and hairy, which produce rounded leaves: and besides these, yet a third kind called by some Lichnite and by others Thriallus, which produces at most three or four leaves, or a few more, rough, thick and fat, which are suitable for burning in lamps. The root of the first two is astringent: for which reason it is given with wine in the quantity of a tessera for fluxes of the body: its decoction is beneficial to those with ruptures, to the spasmodic, to those badly shaken, and for chronic coughs, and rinsing the mouth with it eases toothache. The Mullein that produces golden flowers dyes the hair, and placed anywhere draws moths to itself. The decoction of the leaves made in water benefits tumors and inflammations of the eyes. It is combined with wine and honey for spreading ulcers, and with vinegar for wounds: they cure the bites of scorpions. The leaves of the wild kind are also applied as a poultice to burns. They say that dry figs kept in the leaves of the female will not putrefy.

C
Mullein is commonly called Tasso barbasso, of which the first two kinds of the domestic, and that of the wild which makes leaves like sage and golden flowers with a little red in the middle, are known to everyone. But the other three kinds I have not been able to see in Italy, and although Ruellius says that some learned men hold these two kinds of Mullein to be two slightly different plants that appear in spring with very crinkled leaves somewhat like those of teasel, and flowers in one yellow and in the other whitish, rounded and notched around the edge, called by some primrose flowers and by others herb of paralysis: nonetheless I cannot in any way persuade myself of this. For first, the leaves of these two plants, which in one are rather rounded and in the other long, in no way resemble Mullein, nor are they hairy in any way, as Dioscorides described it, but on the contrary smooth and well crinkled. Beyond this, I do not find that Dioscorides made any mention of the flower, nor any other ancient writer on the kinds of Mullein. Which would not have been passed over in silence regarding the herb of paralysis: since its golden flower deserved to be celebrated, being truly the first to announce spring. Wherefore it seems to me that one should even less approve of what Fuchs depicts in his great herbal: for believing Ruellius sooner than one who seeks clarity in the matter, he painted for the two aforesaid Mulleins these two kinds of plants, called herbs of paralysis, which some moderns use indiscriminately for pains of the joints. Whose roots (according to what they say) are cooked, and their decoction is usefully given for obstructions of the kidneys and the bladder. The juice of the herb is given to drink, and likewise applied as a poultice upon ruptures and dislocations of bones. Women are accustomed to bathe their faces often with the juice of the flowers: since it stretches the skin and removes every blemish. But returning to the true Mulleins, I say that, as far as experience has shown me, they are all universally very astringent and desiccative: and therefore the smoke of the buttons of its dried flowers, taken together with turpentine and chamomile flower received through a perforated board, sitting over it, is beneficial for relaxations of the bowel, and for the straining in dysentery, which the Greeks call tenesmus and we call the evil of bearing down. The fresh herb beaten between two grinding stones and placed in nail wounds of horses, heals them immediately. The juice of the roots of the female, when it has not yet produced the stem, given in the quantity of two drams with an equal amount of warm Malvasia or other aromatic wine at the beginning of the paroxysm, cures (according to Arnaldo) the quartan fever; but it must be done three or four times. The flower rubbed on that kind of leek that is rough drives them away. Galen wrote of Mullein in book eight of the Faculties of Simples, saying thus: Among the kinds of Mullein is the white and the black. The white then is the male, whose leaves are narrower, and those of the female are broader and larger. Beyond this there is another wild one, whose flowers are golden and red, and there is also, besides the above, yet another which is properly called Plomis and Triallus. The root of the first two is bitter to the taste: it is beneficial for fluxes. Its decoction is used for rinsing the mouth in toothache. The leaves have a digestive virtue, especially those of the one that produces golden flowers with red hairs. The leaves of all kinds have a desiccative and astringent virtue.

text:
340 LIBRO

Della Ethiopide. Cap.cviij.

A Ethiopide produce le sue frondi simili à quelle del uerbasco, molto pelose, & grosse, ridotte in terra al tondo sopra alla radice: il suo fusto è quadrangolare, ruuido, simile à quello dell'apiastro, ouero dell'arctio, nel quale sono molte cauità d'ali: il seme è alla grossezza di quello dell'eruo, & doppio in un solo in uoglio. Ha dal medesimo cesto molte radici, lunghe, piene, & al gusto uiscose, le quali seccan dosi diuentano nere, & indurisconsi come corna. Nascene assai copia in Ida monte di Troia, & in Messenia. Gioua à gli sputi della marcia, alle sciatiche, à i dolori del costato, & al l'asprezza della canna del polmone, quando si bee la dicottione della radice. Il che fa ella an chora composta in lettouario con mele.

L' Ethiopide non nasce in Italia, ne meno so io, che la si ci porti d'Ethiopia, ne d'Ida monte di Troia, ne manco di Messenia, oue dissero Dioscoride, & Plinio, che la nasceua.

B Dell'Arctio. Cap.cviij.

O Arctio, il quale chiamano piu presto alcuni Arturo, è simile nelle sue frondi al uerbasco, eccetto che sono piu pelose, & piu ritonde. Il fusto è lungo, & tenero, e'l seme picciolo, simile al comino: la radice è bianca, tenera, & dolce. Questa cotta con il suo seme con uino mitiga il dolore de i denti, tenendosi la dicottione in bocca, con la quale si fomentano utilmente le cotture del fuoco, & le bugancie. Beesi la ra dice nel uino per le sciatiche, & per prouocare l'orina ritenuta.

Redestil Ruellio, che sia l'Arctio quella uolgar pianta, che nasce lungo alle uie, laquale chiamano uolgarmente
C gli Spetiali Lappa minore: ma secondo il mio giuditio non mi pare l'opinion sua troppo efficace: imperoche chi legge nel processo di questo libro il capitolo del Xanthio descritto da Dioscoride, ritrouarà manifestamente esser quello istesso la Lappa minore usitale, laquale nasce abondantissima ne i laghi asciutti, & disseccati dell'acque. Ma ue ramente qual pianta si possa dimostrare per l'Arctio hoggi in Italia, non saprei io gia per hora affirmare. Scrisse dell'Ar ctio Galeno al.vi. delle facultà dei semplici, cosi dicendo. L'Arctio, ilquale è simile al tasso uerbasco, che ha la radice te nera, bianca, & dolce, il fusto lunghetto, & tenero, & il seme simile al cimino, è composto di sottili parti, & imperò è egli disseccatiuo, & asteriuo, quantunque poco. Il perche la radice, e'l suo seme cotto nel uino, medicano qualche uolta al dolore de i denti. Oltre à cio conferisce alle cotture del fuoco, & alle bugancie, non solamente il bagnare della loro dicottio ne; ma anchor a l'applicarui suoi suoi fusti quando son teneri.

Della Personata, ouero Lappa. Cap.cix.

A Personata produce le frondi maggiori di quelle delle zucche, piu hirsute, piu nere, & piu grasse, & il fusto biancheggiante, quantunque si ritroui anchora qual cheuolta senza fusto: è la sua radice nera di fuore, & bianca di dentro. Questa beuta al peso d'una dramma con le pine, gioua à coloro, che sputano il sangue, & la marcia. Pesta, et impiastrata, mitiga i dolori de i ligamenti delle giunture. Impiastransi le frondi utilmente in sul'ulcere antiche.

Crisse della Personata Plinio al.ix. cap. del.xxv. libro, cosi dicendo. Alcuni chiamano l'Arctio Personata, delle cui
S frondi nissuna altra è maggiore: produce le Lappole grandi. Il che manifestamente dimostra esser la Personata quella pianta di grandissime frondi uestita, che noi chiamiamo Lappola maggiore, della quale si ritroua una spetie, che produce anchor à le frondi maggiori, che nasce in su gli argini de fossi senza fusto. Senza fiore, & senza seme, le cui frondi seruono spesso in cambio di capelli à gli affanati lauoratori, quando la state si mettono, ò tribbiano sotto l'ardente canicola. Il Brasauola uuole, che la Lappa sia l'Aparine di Dioscoride. Il che lascio al giuditio di coloro, che ben sanno, che l'Aps rine non è altro (come dicemmo di sopra nel.iij. libro al suo proprio capitolo) che quella pianta molto simile alla rubbia minore, laqual uolgarmente si chiama Speronella, & nasce per il piu tra le lenticchie. Scrisse dell'Arctio Galeno al.vi. delle facultà de i semplici, cosi dicendo. L'altro Arctio, ilqual chiamano Prosopitide, le cui frondi sono similissime à quel le delle zucche, se non che le sono, & piu dure, & parimente maggiori, digerisce insiememente, & dissecca, costregne an chora alquanto. Il perche possono le sue frondi medicare l'ulcere uecchie.

Del Petasite. Cap.cx.

IL Petasite è un gamboncello maggior d'un gombito, grosso un pollice, del quale nasce una fronde molto grande, dell'ampiezza d'un capello, attaccata à mo do d'un

translation:
340 BOOK

On Ethiopis. Chapter 108.

Ethiopis produces its leaves similar to those of mullein, very hairy and thick, lying flat on the ground above the root. Its stem is quadrangular, rough, similar to that of wild parsley or of burdock, with many hollow spaces along it. The seed is the size of a bitter vetch seed, and doubled in a single wrapping. From the same base it has many roots, long, plump, and mucilaginous to the taste, which when dried turn black and harden like horn. It grows in abundance on Mount Ida in Troy and in Messenia. It is beneficial for spitting of pus, for sciatica, for pains in the side, and for hoarseness of the windpipe, when the decoction of the root is drunk. This it also does when prepared as an electuary with honey.

L: Ethiopis does not grow in Italy, nor do I know of it being brought here from Ethiopia, nor from Mount Ida in Troy, nor from Messenia, where Dioscorides and Pliny said it grew.

B On Arctium. Chapter 108.

Arctium, which some call more readily Arturo, resembles mullein in its leaves, except that they are hairier and more rounded. The stem is long and tender, and the seed is small, similar to cumin. The root is white, tender, and sweet. This, cooked with its seed in wine, relieves toothache when the decoction is held in the mouth, and it also usefully foments burns from fire and swellings. The root is drunk in wine for sciatica and to promote retained urine.

Ruellius holds that Arctium is that common plant which grows along roadsides, called by apothecaries Lesser Burdock. But in my judgment his opinion does not seem very convincing, because whoever reads further in this book the chapter on Xanthium as described by Dioscorides will find that it is clearly that same Lesser Burdock, which grows most abundantly in dry, drained lakes. But truly what plant might be shown to be Arctium in Italy today, I cannot at present affirm. Galen wrote about Arctium in book VI of the Properties of Simple Medicines, saying thus: Arctium, which resembles mullein, having a tender, white and sweet root, a somewhat long and tender stem, and seed similar to cumin, is composed of subtle parts, and is therefore drying and astringent, though only slightly. For this reason the root and its seed cooked in wine sometimes relieve toothache. Beyond this, it is good for burns from fire and for swellings, not only by bathing with its decoction, but also by applying its stems when they are tender.

On Personata, or Lappa. Chapter 109.

Personata produces leaves larger than those of gourds, hairier, darker, and fatter, and the stem is whitish, though it is sometimes found without a stem. Its root is black on the outside and white within. Drunk in the weight of one dram with pine nuts, it benefits those who spit blood and pus. Crushed and applied as a poultice, it eases pains in the ligaments of the joints. Its leaves are usefully applied as poultices on old ulcers.

Pliny wrote about Personata in book 25, chapter 9, saying thus: Some call Arctium Personata, whose leaves none surpass in size; it produces large burs. This clearly shows that Personata is that plant dressed with very large leaves, which we call Greater Burdock, of which there is found a kind that also produces even larger leaves, growing on the banks of ditches without a stem, without flower and without seed, whose leaves often serve in place of hats for weary laborers when they put them on in summer or thresh under the blazing dog-star. Brasavola holds that Lappa is the Aparine of Dioscorides. This I leave to the judgment of those who know well that Aparine is nothing other (as we said above in book III in its own chapter) than that plant very similar to small madder, commonly called Speronella, which grows mostly among lentils. Galen wrote about Arctium in book VI of the Properties of Simple Medicines, saying thus: The other Arctium, which they call Prosopitis, whose leaves are very similar to those of gourds, except that they are harder and likewise larger, digests together and dries, and is also somewhat astringent. For this reason its leaves can heal old ulcers.

On Petasites. Chapter 110.

Petasites has a stalk larger than a cubit, as thick as a thumb, from which grows a very large leaf, of the width of a hat, attached in the manner of a...
